title: ‘Whose job is it to empty the dishwasher?’ Experts on the conversations every couple needs to have | Homes | The Guardian
description: Burnout or breakup are constant dangers when one partner carries too much of the mental load of looking after the home and family. Here’s how to spread the burden more evenly
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: Burnout or breakup are constant dangers when one partner carries too much of the mental load of looking after the home and family. Here’s how to spread the burden more evenly
Content: Composite: Guardian design; Anastasiia Krivenok;Wavebreakmedia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design; Anastasiia Krivenok;Wavebreakmedia/Getty ImagesThe expertsHomes‘Whose job is it to empty the dishwasher?’ Experts on the conversations every couple needs to haveBurnout or breakup are constant dangers when one partner carries too much of the mental load of looking after the home and family. Here’s how to spread the burden more evenlySarah PhillipsMon 28 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany households have an imbalance in domestic duties, and women often struggle from carrying the weight of the organisational side of life. Here, mental load experts share the secrets to having a more equitable home – and the rewards that can be gained from it.Get your head around the mental loadThere are three categories of household labour, according toKate Mangino, who lives in Washington DC and is the author of Equal Partners: Improving Gender Equality at Home. These are “physical, like unloading the dishwasher or doing laundry; cognitive, which is the thinking, scheduling and anticipation of needs; and theemotional work”. The mental load is the weight of carrying all these elements at the same time, which can often get too much, says Mangino. “I hear from people who carry the bulk in their household that they feel trapped or like they are suffocating. They’re not getting enough sleep. They’re not taking care of their bodies. It’s even gone so far as depression. I’ve talked to couples who are considering separation or divorce, so it can get quite severe.”Leah Ruppanner, a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne and the author of Drained: Reduce Your Mental Load to Do Less and Be More, says that mental load burnout is a precursor to physical burnout. If you are organising everything, explains Ruppanner, you can’t enjoy life because you are constantly thinking about what is happening next. The first step is accepting how it is affecting you: handily, Ruppanner has created a website –lightenlab.com– where you can measure your mental load and get advice on how to manage it.Both partners can experience a mental load, as Mangino points out: “There is a lot of pressure around employment and being a provider that we don’t always acknowledge,” for whoever that falls to. Mangino is also keen to stress that it isn’t always a negative thing: “There is a certain amount of mental load that is actually healthy and makes you feel good.” Interacting with your family, she says, is what builds relationships.View image in fullscreenBoth partners can experience mental load, say experts.Photograph: Maskot/Getty Images (posed by models)Fight for more equal policiesWe need to campaign for policies that equalise the distribution of caregiving, saysAna Catalano Weeks, a political scientist at the University of Bath. “In the UK, statutory paternity leave for fathers is two weeks of very low-paid leave, so right from the get-go, the assumption set by the state is that mums are going to be the ones staying home and are mostly responsible for children. We need policies that incentivise men to take leave, because that is the way to get them noticing that the socks are too small or the milk is running out. Otherwise, it is too easy to slip into the assumptions for heterosexual partners that are just so dominant in society.”Mangino points out that in the US, one member of a couple often feels pressure to be in full-time employment to access health insurance for the family, which can lead to an imbalance. But she adds: “We can’t sit around and wait for policies to save us – that’s going to take too long. We need to advocate for policy change and then work on household change today.”If you have a breakdown over blueberries, it is time to make a changeEve Rodskyis an LA-based author, lawyer and founder of theFair Play Policy Institute, which trains facilitators to help couples run more equitable households. Rodsky had a revelation about domestic inequality when she was on maternity leave with her second child and her husband texted her saying, “I’m surprised you didn’t get blueberries,” which caused her to pull over in her car to cry. “It was a really difficult time, then on top of it I felt psychologically abandoned by my husband, who seemed to think I was the fulfiller of his smoothie needs.” In all her preparations for having children, Rodsky says that no one suggested “having a conversation about the division of domestic labour, and so I want to be the person to say that now for every woman until the day I die”.View image in fullscreen‘Time spent in service of the home is as worthy as time spent in service of work.’Photograph: Johnce/Getty Images (posed by models)These experiences inspired Rodsky to write 2019’s Fair Play, which she says is about “understanding that in all patriarchies, women’s time is viewed as sand, it is infinite, and men’s time is viewed as diamonds, it is protected … the ‘non-valuable work’ goes to the people with infinite time. Fair Play aims to correct that.” She says that the benefits for her have been massive. “My husband is a different human. I have a partner, not a helper, and that is the only reason why we’ve stayed married.”Admit that you can’t do it allBrian Pageis a financial therapist and Fair Play facilitator from Atlanta, Georgia, who quit his job to support his family. “My wife has a big job – I had a big job – and it was too much with three children. So I made the decision to step back, in part because she was, at the time, more ambitious than me.”What are some of the common missteps that couples he works with make? “The most challenging dynamic is when one partner is ultimately the default parent and the default home manager, and the other partner doesn’t recognise that or see how much work that takes. Then, on top of that, when the default parent or the default home manager needs help, the other person feels like they are being nagged.”Accept that your home is an organisationRodsky defines an organisation as “people working together towards a common goal. If someone does not believe that the home is an organisation, I can’t help them.” Fair Play will work for any home, says Rodsky, and it has been used by housemates, in communes and by polyamorous couples. But be careful not to fall into the trap of having a boss-and-helper situation, warns Mangino, as that rarely helps.Reject the myth that time is more precious for someone who earns more“A lot of us hold the belief that if somebody is paid more, either because they have a better paid job or they work more hours, their time is worth more,” says Helen Mason, a women’s leadership coach and Fair Play facilitator in Milton Keynes. “We all have 24 hours in a day, so there often needs to be a shift in belief for both of the members of the couple that time spent in service of the home and the family is as worthy as time spent in service of work.”Mason continues: “Men are better now than possibly the previous generations were, but if you’re a woman – and I’m talking very much about heterosexual couples – so much of the thinking, the cognitive load, still sits with you.”“Broadly speaking, heteronormative couples struggle more than same-sex couples,” says Mangino. “However, even in queer couples, you do see an imbalance, where one focuses on work and one focuses on home.”“There are inequities between couples without children, but because there is less to do, one person can do more and still get that rest and rehabilitation time,” says Mangino. Ageing parents and other caring responsibilities can add to the mental load. “It is especially taxing when you are managing elder care and that person is living with you.”Gamify household choresAt the heart of the Fair Play system is a pack of cards, which is available to buy (or adigital versioncan be accessed for free online). A 2024study by the University of Southern Californiafound that using the system had the potential to reduce burnout and improve relationship quality.View image in fullscreen‘One of the biggest myths around sharing the domestic and mental load is that it needs to be 50-50.’Photograph: LeoPatrizi/Getty Images (posed by models)Mason explains how it works: “There are 100 cards that represent all the domestic tasks that have to be done around a home. It is not all chores; it also includes things like self-care, adult friendships and “unicorn space”, which is your creative outlet. The first thing to do as a couple is to reduce those 100 cards as much as you can, deciding what is important to you as a family. One of the cards, for example, is potty training. Around 40 cards are only appropriate for households with children, so if you don’t have kids you can ignore them. Then the idea is to divide cards and responsibilities, so it is clear who is in charge. Cards can be redealt at any point.“One of the biggest myths around sharing the domestic and mental load is that it needs to be 50-50. That is not the goal. The goal is fair,” says Mason, because, as we all know, some jobs are bigger than others. “If either partner is feeling resentment in some way, the balance probably isn’t right, and something needs addressing within the dealing of the cards.”Draw on your strengths to divide out tasks. “Our skillsets and our personalities are excellent determinants of what it is that is most appropriate to tackle in the home,” says Page, “and it’s not always lined up perfectly with gender expectations.”Establish boundaries and don’t breach themThis can be easier said than done, says Rodsky, because of ingrained “toxic time messages” that suggest our time isn’t as important as someone else’s. Women will say they won’t pick up their phone today, and then the school calls and they do; the call is to say the child forgot their lunchbox and the woman will stop everything to take it in. “We boundary breach because women have been taught that we’re better multitaskers than men, which is fundamentally completely erroneous,” says Rodsky.As in the common misconception: “In the time it would take me to tell my husband to pick up the phone from the school, I could just do it myself.”View image in fullscreenWhat’s important to you as a family?Photograph: SolStock/Getty Images (posed by models)In actual fact, no one is good at multitasking, says Ruppanner. “Our brains are terrible at multitasking. What we are good at is switching between tasks, which makes us feel like we’re multitasking, but that is just task switching. And every time we switch between tasks, what we’re doing is a cognitive turn.” This “fragments your thinking and it makes you tired”.Find a calm moment to discuss potential changes“Set aside time to talk when you’re both calm,” says Mason. “If this topic rises to the surface in a heated moment, and somebody attacks and somebody else defends, it descends quickly into an argument and nothing gets resolved.”Mangino recommends a technique devised by theGottman Institute, where you take it in turns to talk for 10 minutes. “The other person is not allowed to respond, just listen. And you talk about all the things that are on your mind. Often, both partners are surprised at how much the other person is thinking about. If it is dramatically imbalanced, that will come to light.”What can actually work best, says Ruppanner, is to start any such conversations by focusing on your goals and dreams, rather than merely who does what.Agree on a minimum standard of careFor each household, this standard will be different, but you need to decide on what is non-negotiable to you for each task. Rodsky gives the example of serving the kids’ dinner, which of the people she surveyed came out as having two priorities: “Relatively healthy and timing. So the minimum standard of care is that they have something healthy on the plate and do not try to feed the kids at eight o’clock. It’s not rocket science – that’s the system.”Furthermore, what “done” looks like to one person can look entirely different to another, says Page. If you are in charge of the dishes, says Mason, “does that mean it is all washed up? Is it fine to leave it on the draining board, or does it all need to be put away? What goes in the dishwasher? Whose job is it to empty it?”Have a weekly check-in“Let’s say you have a meeting every Sunday,” says Page. “It might only take you 15 or 20 minutes, but you just go through the week and decide who is responsible for A, B and C.” Maybe you have a big work presentation and need to focus on that, or have to travel somewhere – this is the time to flag that up, not when you are in the midst of it and feeling stressed and overwhelmed.View image in fullscreenInclude children in the household tasks.Photograph: Andie Mills/Getty Images/Tetra images RF (posed by models)Get tech helpIt has never been easier to synchronise diaries, set alarms, or use apps to help manage domestic life. Mason says that she and her husband sit down with their electronic calendars. “If there is anything that affects the other person, we send invites to each other, so it is blocked in each other’s diaries.” Mason also suggests apps likeNipto, which you can use to split household chores and give points to jobs depending on how arduous they are. Embracing this kind of tech can particularly help members of the household who struggle with organisational tasks.Ensure all household members are involvedMason puts jobs on Post-it notes on the wall, which also includes her six-year-old son, who puts his clothes away, feeds the dogs in the morning, and sets the table. She says: “We hope that making the domestic and mental load visible means he grows up knowing that a home runs on shared effort.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Michael Palin in the Philippines review – who else could cause such a weird moment with the president? | Television | The Guardian
description: From ‘recycled chicken’ being sold on a stall to Bongbong fanboying over the Fish-Slapping Dance, Palin’s travel shows always explore fascinating things that others don’t. It is a reminder that his work is increasingly precious
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: From ‘recycled chicken’ being sold on a stall to Bongbong fanboying over the Fish-Slapping Dance, Palin’s travel shows always explore fascinating things that others don’t. It is a reminder that his work is increasingly precious
Content: Assured and joyful … Michael Palin at a street market in Manila.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/ITN Productions/Neil Ferguson/Jaimie GramstonView image in fullscreenAssured and joyful … Michael Palin at a street market in Manila.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/ITN Productions/Neil Ferguson/Jaimie GramstonTV reviewTelevisionReviewMichael Palin in the Philippines review – who else could cause such a weird moment with the president?From ‘recycled chicken’ being sold on a stall to Bongbong fanboying over the Fish-Slapping Dance, Palin’s travel shows always explore fascinating things that others don’t. It is a reminder that his work is increasingly preciousJack SealeMon 28 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a moment in episode one ofMichael Palinin the Philippines where our host surveys a group of children swimming gaily in the harbour of Pangasa, a tiny island in what western atlases traditionally refer to as the South China Sea. “Oh, if only I were young again,” he muses. “Eighty-one would do!”Palin is now 83 and into his fifth decade of travel presenting, which is longer than he spent as an active member of Monty Python. Naturally, he is not a dynamic or imposing presence on screen. His insights are applied with a soft, broad brush and jokes like the one about pining for the lost vigour of his early 80s are his metier now: simple, classic, corny, even.This is despite late-period Palin, in the documentaries he has made since signing up with Channel 5 in 2018, visiting places scarred by conflict. Having previously journeyed toNorth Korea, Iraq, Nigeria and Venezuela, he’s taking it relatively easy in the Philippines, although all is not well there, either.There is an old meme about hack foreign correspondents who conclude that every country they visit is “a land of contrasts” – Palin would never stoop to such inelegance, but the contrasts in thePhilippinesare an inescapable theme. He sees destitution next to stately luxury, political fury expressed by warm and friendly people, and paradisiacal destinations ruined by excessive tourism when there are still untouched havens a short boat hop away.View image in fullscreenParadisiacal … Palin by his beach hut at El Nido.Photograph: Neil Ferguson & Jaimie Gramston/5 Broadcasting Limited/ITN ProductionsHe starts in Manila, where citizens are celebrating 40 years since the removal of the loathed autocrat Ferdinand Marcos, while also protesting against corruption and inequality in a country whose elected leader is now … Ferdinand Marcos’s son, Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. A chat with an anti-Marcos campaigner is pleasant without throwing up much analysis, beyond head-shaking bemusement at the electorate’s apparent act of self-harm.But in his voiceover, Palin regularly makes reference to hard work being done by his crew behind the scenes, to gain access that other films – ones with less respected presenters, perhaps – might not be able to score. Soon he is stepping into the lavish Marcos residence, Malacañang Palace, where – after flexing the old comic muscles by observing that Ferdinand Sr’s notorious spendthrift wife Imelda “certainly knew how to buy a carpet” – he meets Bongbong himself.Palin confesses that Marcos has refused in advance to answer difficult questions, so none are asked. Our man doesn’t mention what he’s just witnessed on the streets of Manila, where deprivation is so acute that there is a stall selling large plastic bags of “recycled chicken” – scraps from the bins outside fried chicken chain restaurants, scavenged and reheated.However, the facade Bongbong presents is fascinating, since it doesn’t tally with rumours spread on national television by his estranged sister that he is a drug addict (which he denies). Instead, he is more like the sort of mid-ranking executive Palin might have to tolerate at a corporate do in the home counties: smooth and charming, despite his self-deprecating patter almost certainly being insincere. He is also, having been educated in England in the 1970s, a Python superfan, possibly because it gave him a sense of humour to borrow in lieu of possessing his own. Palin politely fields every comedian’s least favourite question – the one about where they get all their crazy ideas from – as Bongbong fanboys over the Fish-Slapping Dance.After that, Palin hits the archipelagos, watching as tourist boats clog up the waters at El Nido, an area popular with influencers; he escapes and spends the night instead at a restorative micro-resort that pointedly doesn’t have hot water or electricity in its bare bamboo huts, enabling guests to focus serenely on a stunning bay surrounded by the region’s signature jagged limestone islets.Michael Palin on the loss of his wife of 57 years: ‘I’d love Helen to still be here, telling me off’Read moreYet tension and strife are never far away – and these days they’re encroaching from abroad. The hour concludes with a military flight to what Palin’s local guide firmly labels the West Philippine Sea, a part of the ocean to the west that the Philippines claims. China disagrees and so, as the children on Pangasa play, the horizon teems with Chinese craft; when Palin boards a boat and sails into disputed waters, a Chinese coastguard vessel warns them to turn back. Legally, they’re not obliged to, but the safe option is to comply.With the first of three episodes down, Palin is on the way to providing another assured primer on a part of the world that has more going on than many westerners may know about, mainly because so much has gone wrong there. But it feels as if nothing can be too bad if Michael Palin is there – his enduring ability to find joy in all things human is more precious than ever.Michael Palin in the Philippines airs on Channel 5Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMichael PalinPhilippinesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Reality pays a visit to the Labour party conference, but it’s the ‘Hope Again’ that kills you | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Most MPs are clinging to this year’s Beckettian slogan, but the chancellor brought his own brand of despair
Author: John Crace
Headline: Most MPs are clinging to this year’s Beckettian slogan, but the chancellor brought his own brand of despair
Content: The chancellor, John Healey, struggled to bring the advertised optimism to Labour’s conference hall.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe chancellor, John Healey, struggled to bring the advertised optimism to Labour’s conference hall.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe politics sketchLabour conference 2026Reality pays a visit to the Labour party conference, but it’s the ‘Hope Again’ that kills youJohn CraceMost MPs are clinging to this year’s Beckettian slogan, but the chancellor brought his own brand of despairMon 28 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.32 EDTShareIt could be just me, but I’m beginning to find that all this “hope” stuff is getting me down. Everywhere you go at theLabourparty conference, you are being urged to “Hope Again”. It’s on the screens in the main hall and on banners in the exhibition area. It’s on T-shirts, balloons and coffee mugs. It’s all just a bit much. Overkill. You now bump into Labour MPs who are visibly collapsing under the strain of having to walk around with an optimistic perma-grin. And the conference is only into its second day. Come Wednesday they will all be on intravenous Valium.What does “Hope Again” even mean? Is it an instruction? Have we all been hoping in a highly unsatisfactory way so far? Are we being sent back to hope school to learn how to be more upbeat? In which case, I rather think these remedial classes in hoping will be wasted on me. I’ve always been a bit miserable. It feels a bit like someone going round and telling you “Smile. It may never happen.” Or to “Keep calm and carry on.” There are also distinct echoes of Samuel Beckett: Fail again. Fail better. Only in Liverpool it’s: Hope again. Hope better.You also can’t help feeling that all this talk of hope is wasted onJohn Healey. He is a man with a naturally low-energy vibe. Someone in touch with the darker, more depressing side of his own personality. A man after my own heart.As someone with the touch of Harry Potter’s Dementors, ready to suck the joy out of any occasion, he knows that anything that can go wrong almost certainly will go wrong. Anything good is merely a transitory, illusory state. Take Healey to the football and he will show you a bad time. His home team of Rotherham might go 2-0 up in the 88th minute and John will assure you they’ve peaked too soon – they are nailed on to lose 3-2. I speak from experience. I’ve done it myself. John, meet John.Luckily for me, no one is expecting me to be a ray of sunshine. That’s way above my pay grade. Unfortunately for Healey, optimism was precisely what he was required to deliver in his first speech as chancellor to a nearly full Labour conference hall. To be the fiscal embodiment of “Hope Again”. To give us all a reason to live just a little longer.View image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Andy Burnham, raises John Healey’s fist aloft after the chancellor’s conference speech.Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOnly he just couldn’t do it. He was never going to be able to do it. When John sees a “Hope Again” banner, what he reads is “Despair Again”. Come the end of his half hour on stage, he had managed to convert most of the audience to his way of thinking. At lunchtime, the queues for the assisted dying helpline tailed back into the city centre.Not that Healey didn’t give it his best shot. He dropped the word hope into almost every sentence – or his minders had dropped it in for him – and every time, the lights seemed to get a bit dimmer. It was a battle of hope against hope. People had come willing him to succeed. To pull off one of the most astonishing personality transplants of the year.Within minutes, though, a pall of depression hung over the hall. We were all just waiting for it to end. Hardly anyone could be bothered to even clap. The only standing ovation came for the reintroduction of the £15m Union Learning Fund. To give this some perspective, £15m is just a bit more than what the London townhouse of the Tory shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, is worth. Not that it’s a bad idea. It’s just not going to reboot the economy.And it’s hard to blame Healey. Maybe another more dynamic and charismatic chancellor could have shifted the mood in the hall with feelgood vibes. But as well as being a bit miserable, Healey is also a realist. He knows things are tough and likely to get tougher. No amount of energy price caps and £2 bus fares are going to make a major dent in a cost of living which is only heading in one direction. Nor is it his fault. He is not responsible for austerity, Brexit, the war in Iran and the cost of borrowing. But he is the current fall guy. The chancellor tasked with fixing the unfixable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo what we got instead was a touch of nostalgia. A deep dive into the stories Labour has written about its achievements. Times when hope was very much alive. Just not now, no matter how often Healey prefixed his sentences with the H-word. Inevitably, though, the truth came out. How he wished he was chancellor back in the late 90s when the economy was on track and there was money to spare. Instead, we were where we were. You can tell people that the UK is the fastest-growing economy in the G7, but it counts for little if everyone still feels broke and broken.There was talk of growth. Of reindustrialisation. But mostly of the need for fiscal discipline. Which is code for saying that the budget in four weeks’ time is unlikely to be a bundle of fun for anyone. Look forward to some tax rises and welfare cuts. There was also a commitment to spend £6m on shipyards to build the UK’s nuclear submarines. Money that had already been promised. Always the best money for a government to spend. Old money repurposed as new.Come the end, no one could have been in any doubt about the scale of the challenge ahead. Despite trying to be someone else, Healey had not been able to be anything but himself. And why not? It’s not as if there are any easy answers. Nor do the Tories and Reform have any solutions. They are just chancers pedalling pipe dreams. But most of the Liverpool audience hadn’t come for this. They had been told to come for hope and they wanted half an hour off to enjoy themselves. Instead they had been confronted with cold reality.Explore more on these topicsLabour conference 2026The politics sketchLabourJohn HealeycommentShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: Anxiety had me hiding from the world – then two magic questions set me free | Mental health | The Guardian
description: I used to be terrified of socialising, certain I would embarrass myself the moment I opened my mouth. And as for dates …
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I used to be terrified of socialising, certain I would embarrass myself the moment I opened my mouth. And as for dates …
Content: ‘If I bump into an old school friend in Tesco, I know what to do’ … Farryn Stock in Regents Park, London, June 2026. Photographs: courtesy of Farryn StockView image in fullscreen‘If I bump into an old school friend in Tesco, I know what to do’ … Farryn Stock in Regents Park, London, June 2026. Photographs: courtesy of Farryn StockThe one change that workedMental healthThe one change that worked: Anxiety had me hiding from the world – then two magic questions set me freeI used to be terrified of socialising, certain I would embarrass myself the moment I opened my mouth. And as for dates …Farryn StockMon 28 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs with a lot of teenagers, social confidence was not my strong suit. Throughout my time at school in the early 2010s, I hated the prospect of new social situations and would often lie awake at night overthinking the day to come.What I now know to be social anxiety I dismissed as just nerves at that young age. Although I knew something wasn’t quite right, for most of my early teens I managed to disguise my discomfort. Sharing a friendship group with my twin sister meant I could hide behind my sibling.As we got older, the disparity started to grow and her flourishing social confidence magnified my lack of it. By my late teens, I often found myself building up social situations to an unbearable point. The false narrative I’d created of embarrassing myself socially had begun to completely overshadow my desire to be around other people. So I hid away a lot.My mumfound me a therapist. She was phenomenal and talked me through a lot of emotions that I didn’t really understand. When the end of my therapy sessions neared and we had spoken as much as we could, all that was left to do was for me to go out into the world and put into practice everything we had discussed.View image in fullscreenFarryn atop Roys Peak, overlooking Lake Wānaka in New Zealand, June 2025.When I began to spiral over this, as I usually did, and voiced my concern, she asked me: “What’s the worst thing that could happen?” I replied: “Well, I could be embarrassed, I wouldn’t know what to say, I’d make an idiot of myself.” These were all the usual thoughts that plagued me. But then she said: “And then what?”Not for the first time, she had made me second-guess the anxiety voice in my brain. I stopped and thought about it for a second and said: “Well, then I’d just go home and go to bed.” She replied: “Exactly, and then you’d wake up tomorrow and start the day again, and that would be over.”In that moment, even my spiralling brain couldn’t catastrophise the situation any further. I realised those two simple questions brought me back down to reality when my mind tried to race ahead and find problems that, more than likely, weren’t going to happen.Those questions have saved me from my anxiety time and time again. They saved me on my first day of university, when we had to introduce ourselves one by one. Standing up in a room full of strangers and sharing a “fun fact” about myself would have been a nightmare for me previously. But asking myself: “And then what?” made me realise that even if this were the most embarrassing day of my life, I could still just go home at the end and never go back. Funnily enough, it wasn’t the most embarrassing day of my life. I graduated three years later with a first-class degree and never thought twice about that moment till now.Dates used to be awful. The anxiety they instilled in me often led to me cancelling last minute or getting blackout drunk just to get through them. Shortly after finishing therapy, I went on a date with those two questions swirling around in my brain. That was one of the first dates where I didn’t feel physically sick at the prospect of going – all simply because I reminded myself that even my worst-case scenario meant I could just go home after, put on some pyjamas and watch a film.Since then, asking myself: “What’s the worst that could happen?” and: “And then what?” has got me through a plethora of anxiety-inducing moments, including job interviewsand moving across the world, from the UK to Australia, with my boyfriend. Now, if I find my social anxiety spiking just because I bumped into an old school friend in Tesco, I know what to do. These questions bring me back to reality and calm me down.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
