title: ‘We wanted it to be a battlecry’: how Republica made 90s anthem Ready to Go | Music | The Guardian
description: ‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’
Content: ‘Do you fancy being dangerous?’ … Saffron Sprackling at T in the Park in 1997.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Do you fancy being dangerous?’ … Saffron Sprackling at T in the Park in 1997.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyHow we madeMusic‘We wanted it to be a battlecry’: how Republica made 90s anthem Ready to Go‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’Interviews by Chris LordMon 28 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaffron Sprackling, vocalsWe always had a vision of mixing acid house with indie rock, and we managed to rent a space and build our own studio in London’s Shoreditch area, long before it got trendy. I had a little vocal booth called Hattie Jacques, in honour of the Carry On films but also because it’s Cockney rhyming slang [for shakes]. We spent all our money rewiring it, and that’s where we wrote, recorded and produced Ready to Go – 100 mixes later!We were perfectionists and wanted to do it all ourselves. Every sonic element had to be special up to the point where we ended up arguing. Like at a rave when you stand and dance by the speakers, everything was done with the listener in mind.It was a collaborative effort, but Johnny Male and I wrote most of the song’s lyrics and the melody. We had a really good camaraderie, finishing each other’s sentences, him on an acoustic guitar and me scribbling things down. Tim Dorney and Andy Todd worked more on the technology and synth sounds. We pooled our skills, resources and dreams.The song is all about daily life and things that happened to us. We didn’t write anything too existential – I don’t really like singing about myself – but I’ve always believed in language and the power of the pen. I think it was Johnny who came up with the line, “Ready to go.” It had an anthemic feel and we wanted it to be a bit of a battlecry: “It’s a crack, I’m back!” That line was inspired by the Irish slang, craic. Writing lyrics and big choruses over electronic beats was one of the most difficult things because of the BPM, but I’ve always had a sort of punky voice that suits it.It was as much about the delivery as it was the words. My personality was becoming feistier and I think the song came from that, but also it’s about being positive, making good out of bad, and coming together as one. That’s what the vibe is like in the acid-house scene.It was an exciting time. Zeke Manyika, who was the drummer in Orange Juice, lived across the way and I used to shimmy across the roof and go down a ladder where he and his wife would make me sandwiches. Every Tuesday night we would go to Matt Johnson’s house [from the The] to play table football with Paul Webb from Talk Talk. Me being a lot younger, I was like, “Oh my God, these are my idols!” They treated me with respect and it really gave me a sense of confidence. And I got quite good at table football.One day, a girl at my hairdressers said to me: “Saff, do you fancy being dangerous?” I went “All right then,” and they dyed my hair blood red like a London bus. Jarvis Cocker always said: “If you’ve got a hook and a great hairdo, you’ll be a pop star.” Visually, it really helped us, and people seemed to like it.At the time it was hard to get gigs as a girl: it was important to be in one of the few female-led bands. There are some fantastic female artists today, but I still wish we had more women in bands. Last year Olivia Rodrigo invited me backstage because she had been singing Ready to Go on her world tour – such a lovely lady and so talented. She said that Republica were one of her favourite bands and that growing up she had a poster of me because she’s of Asian heritage, too. I gave her a big hug.When Sunderland beat Chelsea in the Premier League in May 2026, the whole stadium was singing Ready to Go and it brought a tear to my eye. I was asked to sing on the pitch at the 2022 Fifa World Cup – I turned around and Lionel Messi was standing there.Johnny Male, guitarWe had some good songs but we hadn’t had a hit yet. I remember the day Saff came in the studio with red hair. I said: “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link.Ready to Go’s music came first. Toddy found these great chords which became the chorus. They were simple but effective, so we thought we’d better write a verse.View image in fullscreen‘You could see by the crowds that the monster was unleashed’ … Republica with Johnny Male, right.Photograph: Stephen Sweet/ShutterstockWe sampled all the guitars into an Akai S1000 out of necessity, as in those days we were using an Atari ST computer which only had MIDI. The vocals were recorded on an 8-track digital recorder. Computer music was still in its infancy, we were learning as we went along. Any money we earned from gigs was spent on studio equipment and outboard gear.Lyrically, we were trying to talk about the things surrounding us at the time. Going out and staying up late, witnessing the world in the middle of the night, then reporting back. We tried to create something that incorporated all the things we loved about the house scene in a song with an alternative edge.Touring America, we started to get picked up on MTV and we noticed it in the hotels at night. It was on heavy rotation and you could see by the crowds that the monster was unleashed. It was fantastic, but we still wanted to be on Top of the Pops. Then we came back and it all happened in the UK and Europe. There was a lot of goodwill behind us and we often said that with a title like Ready to Go you could probably sell anything.I’m always slightly disappointed that on one of the last vocal takes, the line was: “Went home, stayed in bed all day / In your T-shirt”, which I thought was really good, but because I wasn’t concentrating as I should have been, the other line – “Your T-shirt’s dish dirt” – got in.The funny thing about playing the song live is that it always feels like it’s building towards the next bit, even when it drops down. Especially when an audience is responding to it. It’s a trick I wish I could do every time I write a song, but there’s a kind of magic alchemy that somehow appears then vanishes again.Republica’s 30 Years of Ready to Go UK tourbegins on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicHow we madePop and rockDance musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than ever | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: After public backlash, the Trump administration changed its tactics from ‘siege’ to ‘soft feet’. Now, ICE is everywhere
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: After public backlash, the Trump administration changed its tactics from ‘siege’ to ‘soft feet’. Now, ICE is everywhere
Content: People being arrested in a raid on a nightclub in Memphis, Tennessee, on 30 August.Photograph: Vecindarios 901View image in fullscreenPeople being arrested in a raid on a nightclub in Memphis, Tennessee, on 30 August.Photograph: Vecindarios 901ICE 2.0: inside Trump's new immigration dragnetICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than everAfter public backlash, the Trump administration changed its tactics from ‘siege’ to ‘soft feet’. Now, ICE is everywhereMaanvi Singh,Will Craft,Andrew WitherspoonandJulius Constantine MotalMon 28 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTShareVecindarios 901Those who lived through it describe the ICE raids as a “siege” or an “occupation”.At the height of the raids last year, agents in armored military vehicles rolled through residential neighborhoods. Masked agents patrolled public parks and stationed themselves outside elementary schools; squadrons of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents snatched pedestrians off the streets.Then,officers killedtwo US citizens during an ICE “blitz” on Minneapolis. After a public backlash, the Trump administration said it would try a new approach.“I learned that maybe we could use a little bit of a softer touch,” Donald Trump said in February. He chose a new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, who promised to cut the flash and fanfare. “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day,” he saidat his Senate confirmation hearingin March.Six months on, that’s what his agency has delivered.LoadingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The GuardianNow ICE is anywhere and everywhere, embedded in all corners of everyday life.A Cuban man in Miami who stepped outside his house to take out the trashwas detainedmoments after he had dropped the garbage bag into the bin. An Ecuadorian father wasarrestedin Danbury, Connecticut, just after seeing his six-year-old son on to the school bus. People have been arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home.Y, a Venezuelan native, was stopped at the Phoenix Sky Harbor airport by immigration officers whom he said wouldn’t tell him why he was being arrested, or accept proof of a judicial order expressly prohibiting deportation to his home country. Four days later, he was on an airplane departing to Venezuela. Just before takeoff, he was deboarded – ICE officers admitted they may have made a mistake.Though agents appear to be moving with more stealth than they were before, ICE arrests are still, often, violent. Glimpses of that violence are – despite Mullin’s initial intentions – still making national headlines.Last week, an ICE agentshotWilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Austin, Texas. The Venezuelan asylum seeker, who had received a deportation order after missing a letter to appear in immigration court, was discharged from a local hospital with a bulletstill lodgednear his spine and then taken to ICE detention. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan mandied in a fiery crashwhile fleeing federal immigration agents.Still, for every arrest that breaks through into public view, countless others happen quickly, before anyone can notice. “The detentions are happening in a flash – we’re talking, like, 90 seconds from the time ICE shows up to that person being driven away,” Willis said. “And often they are moving very quietly, with very soft feet.”The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the US government agency thatoversees ICE, declined to comment on how its tactics had changed. “DHS will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations, strategy or tactics,” said Chandler Rebel, a spokesperson for the agency. But Rebel confirmed the agency’s focus on airports, noting the DHS was “working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport”.Bolstered by $75bn infundingfrom Congress, the Department of Homeland Security – the US government agency that oversees ICE – has more than doubled its workforce this year to more than 22,000 officers and staff. It has also vastly expanded its capacity by working with local police, sheriffs, highway patrol and even fish and wildlife agents. As of 15 September, ICE had signed more than 2,500287(g) agreements.ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before.LoadingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The GuardianAn expanded dragnet fueled by police partnerships“The administration is able to essentially hide a multiplied ICE force not only in unmarked cars, and not only behind masks, but also within local law enforcement through the 287(g) program,” said Willis. “I call it the invisibilizing of immigration enforcement.”Operations that now originate with local police are taking place across the country.At the El Corralón bar in Memphis on 29 August, an operation that began as a police raid targeting illegal gambling and drugs turned into one of the largest sweeps of undocumented immigrants in Tennessee – 120 people were detained. Immigration agents worked with state law enforcement to execute search warrants at the bar related to drugs and gambling, and targeting the bar’s owner. But then, at 1am that night, more than a dozen agents walked into the bar, shut off the music, instructed everyone to gather on the dancefloor and asked them one by one if they had legal status,according to witnesses.A spokesperson for the DHS said partnerships with law enforcement agencies were key to the agency’s immigration enforcement. “We have had tremendous success when local law enforcement works together with us,” said Rebel.Lawyers across the US said they worried that local law enforcement officials are not adequately aware of the nuances of immigration policy. “People are getting detained if they don’t have their green card on them. They’re getting stopped even if they have legal status,” said Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, an immigration attorney based in Austin.Last month, her client Brian José Morales García, 25, was deported to Mexico despite repeatedly telling officers that he was a US citizen, born in Denver.Morales García was on his way to work as an air-conditioning installation tech, riding with his boss, when officers from the Gillespie county sheriff’s department and the Texas department of public safety (DPS) pulled them over. Both law enforcement agencies were working with ICE. Morales García told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him. Days later, he was deported to Mexico.Eventually, the federal government reached an agreement with Morales García’s lawyers to let him back into the country, after Lincoln-Goldfinch submitted documents proving his citizenship.“We’re seeing a lot of racial profiling,” she said. Local law enforcement appear to be especiallyactive in Hispanic neighborhoods, she said, or in areas where Latino construction workers gather.“They might have their sights set on a big job site, in some neighborhood under construction, and just slowly patrol that site and just take people in day after day until nobody’s going to work there any more,” she said.‘New pathways to deportation’The Trump administration has alsorelentlessly reshapedimmigration policies and bent the country’s vast bureaucracy to advance its mass-deportation agenda and boost arrest numbers.“In order to sustain those numbers, they have to create more categories of people who can be subject to detention,” said Willis. “They do this by creating new pathways to deportation.”In recent months, the supreme courtcleared the wayfor the administration to end temporary humanitarian protections for 350,000 Haitians and Syrians in the US and made it easier to end protections for a total of about 1.3 million immigrants from a number of countries designated for temporary protected status (TPS). Currently, about170,000Salvadorians living in the US are anxiously waiting for the administration to announce whether it will renew or axe the same protections for them.View image in fullscreenBrandon Peterson (center) of Greater Grace Temple and Viles Dorsainvil (right) of the Haitian Support Center, both of Springfield, Ohio, at the US supreme court in Washington DC on 17 March.Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/AFP/Getty ImagesAt the same time, the administration unrolled a new tactic of scheduling“mega-master” hearings– mass hearings in immigration courts, scheduled at the last minute so that many people do not know to, or are unable to, attend their mandatory court appointments. The no-shows are then ordered removed from the country in absentia, making them immediately subject to arrest and deportation.After attorneys began reporting such hearings in May, judgesissued53,808 removal orders in absentia in June – a 55% increase. More than 13,000 of those removal orders followed mass hearings with a hundred or more people, according to researchers Joseph Gunther and Brandon Marrow, who created the sitebklg.orgto track and analyze procedural immigration data.In the coming weeks, the Trump administration is also expected torevokethe business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners. It has implemented a rule allowing officials to block people from becoming lawful permanent residents if they or certain relatives use public benefits such as Medicaid, food stamps or even student financial aid.It is also increasingly pursuing“third-country” deportationagreements, so it can arrest and remove immigrants who were previously immune to removal because a judge had deemed that they would face torture or persecution if they were returned to their home countries. Now, more than23,000 peopleover the last year have been expelled to countries where they have never been and where they have no ties. Some of these deportations are to countries with civil unrest, political instability, armed conflict and known human rights abuses.View image in fullscreenLiberia’s national police officers stand guard for a plane carrying immigrants deported from the US, in Harbel on 20 August.Photograph: Matthew Jacobs/AFP/Getty ImagesThere are constantly shifting rules about who can or cannot be detained or deported, and for how long. And there are constantly shifting norms on who will be detained or deported.On one day, a client might go to an ICE check-in and leave without incident, Willis said. The next day, a different client with the same immigration status might be detained. “It makes it very hard to counsel people,” Willis said. “It’s very hard to prepare people for what they can expect.”Pressured to self-deportNot everyone who is arrested is immediately deportable – many people have pending immigration cases, or legal status. Indeed, there is a wide gulf between the number of people ICE is detaining each month, and the number of people who are deported.Many of the people who are arrested languish in detention for months. Others – even those who may have a good chance of gaining asylum or another legal status – choose to accept voluntary deportation rather than wait months or years for their immigration case to process.View image in fullscreenSheriff’s deputies in Laramie county, Wyoming, briefly detain a man from Venezuela after a traffic stop on 12 May.Photograph: Todd Heisler/The New York Times/Redux/eyevineFederal circuit courts are currently split on whether immigrants who came to the US without lawful admission, including many asylum seekers, can be detained indefinitely without access to bond hearings. In some states, including Texas, the prospect of spending years inside a detention center can wear on immigrants.“Almost every single detained parent that I talk to has been pressured into signing a voluntary deportation,” said Lincoln-Goldfinch. “Because they are told that if they sign, they get to go home and they can choose what happens to their kids.”The Guardian is not using full names in some instances to protect sources’ privacy and safetyQ&AMethodologyShowThe data for this story is based on the rolling seven-day average arrest figures from theDeportation Data Project, an effort led by a team of academics and lawyers at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles tracking immigration enforcement using government data. The Guardian followed the Deportation Data Project's methodology for simplifying the apprehension methods listed by ICE in the group's data. Immigration enforcement in communities are labeled as "at large arrests", and include apprehension methods labeled "non-custodial arrest", "located", "probation and parole" and "worksite enforcement". Transfers from jail or prison are "custodial arrests", from apprehension methods labeled "CAP local incarceration", "CAP federal incarceration", "CAP state incarceration" and "custodial arrest". Local police under 287(g) program arrests are from the apprehension method labeled "287(g) program". The Guardian measured the date of the new approach from 24 March 2026, the day that Markwayne Mullin was confirmed as secretary of the DHS.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.

title: Burnham promises to roll back privatisation with government-backed grid plan | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Creation of GB Grid will be major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public control
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Creation of GB Grid will be major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public control
Content: GB Grid will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid.Photograph: CW Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenGB Grid will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid.Photograph: CW Images/AlamyAndy BurnhamBurnham promises to roll back privatisation with government-backed grid planExclusive: Creation of GB Grid will be major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public controlKiran Stacey,Jessica ElgotandPippa CrerarMon 28 Sep 2026 17.33 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will take his first major step to putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when, at theLabour conference, he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.The prime minister will use his first speech as party leader to announce the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great BritishEnergyto compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid.In a speech focusing heavily on undoing what the prime minister calls “40 years of neoliberalism”, he will promise greater public control of energy, water and housing.He is also set to lay out more details on how he will pay for his pledge to create a national care service, with senior ministers refusing to rule out scrapping the pensions triple lock after the next election to free funding.Government sources have suggested Burnham would signal his willingness to review the policy, but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether.Burnham will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We have a cost crisis. We all know it. The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British bill payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe.“We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.”He will add: “Within 10 years, I want our energy costs to be in line with other nations in Europe. That means we must reform a broken energy market so it serves the public interest.”Burnham’s first conference speech as leader and prime minister caps a remarkable turnaround in his political fortunes since this time last year, when he was criticised by many in the party for talking openly about his desire to replace Keir Starmer.Having ousted Starmer from office, Burnham has spent much of his first few weeks promising a radical shift in tone and policy.He will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We can’t carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.”Though the conference has been upbeat, Burnham will tellLabourdelegates he wanted to strike a serious tone with his speech and address some of the most intractable issues in British politics, such as social care, energy costs and youth inactivity.In the speech, the prime minister will say that he will resist “the usual tub-thumping conference speech … the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed”.He will say “everyone wants less drift and more direction” and that he will “answer that call” today. His offer – expected to contain a number of new policies – will be “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”.“I accept people will not agree with every part of it, but I believe it can turn Britain around,” he will say.The creation of GB Grid is his first significant step to challenging the power of private companies to run Britain’s infrastructure.The organisation will be given access to a pot of £4bn that has already been allocated to the government-backed Great British Energy – although it is not expected to use all of that money.With businesses complaining about how long it takes to get a grid connection for new buildings and projects, GB Grid will use the funding to build more connections, as well as to maximise and speed up the rollout of renewables across the UK. It will be the first publicly owned player in electricity networks since privatisation.Officials said the government would also expand the rights of businesses to build their own connections, allowing them to tap GB Grid’s funding to help pay for it – a move which they said helped speed up connections in Ireland by 11 months.1:02Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh on her plans for electricity grid | Politics WeeklySpeaking to the Guardian’sPolitics Weekly podcaston Monday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “One of my frustrations with the last government is that they didn’t recognise the need to invest in the system, and so we’re having to do that at record pace over the course of the next decade.”On social care, the prime minister will promise “an honest conversation” with the public, saying: “Hope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.”Hispromise to “rip the plaster off”when it comes to funding for the national care service has sparked speculation he could use the next Labour manifesto to scrap the pension triple lock and use the savings for social care instead.The triple lock – which guarantees the state pension will rise by the highest of inflation, earnings and 2.5% every year – is forecast to cost £15.5bn by 2030, but so far no major party has remained committed to scrapping it.Speaking to ITV’s Robert Peston on Monday, the chancellor, John Healey, repeatedly refused to commit to funding the triple lock beyond the next election.“I’m not telling you what the next manifesto will or won’t contain – I can’t do that,” he said. “I’m not going to tell you what the budget in a month’s time is going to take.”The prime minister is also set to talk about youth unemployment ahead of a planned report by former minister Alan Milburn on why the number of unemployed young people is rising.While the government has already announced additional support for young people to get into work, ministers have said relatively little about whether they will reduce benefits for those who remain out of work in the long term.Answering calls on LBC Radio on Monday, Burnham said he would use his speech to outline “how I think we should go forward in the next decade”.“It will require some significant changes, but I’m doing it with the best of intentions,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamEnergy industryEnergy billsLabour conferenceLabour conference 2026Household billsLabourShareReuse this content

title: Five UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford released on bail | UK news | The Guardian
description: Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state
Content: The men were pictured on Sunday being apprehended near the RAF base in Gloucestershire.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenThe men were pictured on Sunday being apprehended near the RAF base in Gloucestershire.Photograph: BBCUK newsFive UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford released on bailPolice say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign stateVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentMon 28 Sep 2026 18.02 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 07.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as police investigate why they were so close to the airbase in three vans with suspicious material in the back.The five suspects were revealed to be British men, all in their 20s and from London. They had been arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside early on Sunday morning on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.An Iranian link is still under investigation, as is whether any of the five were paid to gather in the village of Whelford, two miles from RAF Fairford.On Monday, Donald Trump expressed surprise that the suspects had been bailed. The US president said: “I would not have released them.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a meeting of the government’s crisis committee Cobra over the events and Iran’s possible role.An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release it emerged that no explosive material had been found.The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.“We have, as you would expect, ensured that our protective security advice and posture remain commensurate to the threat. But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”8:29Who is behind suspected bomb plot at RAF base? - The LatestIran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.Taylor said: “Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity, often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain. It can be harder to spot, and to that end I would ask the public to remain vigilant and report anything suspicious to police.”Trump claimed on Sunday that the men “were looking to do big damage” at the base, used by the US air force, which was taken as revealing a serious terror plot.Taylor said: “I can confirm that following extensive interviews and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry.”Police said the five men were all from London, one aged 23, three aged 24, and one aged 25. They were arrested after a farmer driving home from a party spotted them. She said she believed they were wearing balaclavas and they ran away when her headlights illuminated them. She then called the police.Trump also suggested the plot was known to the US authorities. But British sources suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown.View image in fullscreenAn armoured vehicle on patrol at RAF Fairford on Monday.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesThe base had been at its highest state of alert, called delta, for several days beforehand because of a general threat, with extra security measures.The farmer said she was surprised it had been left to her to disrupt the activities of the men.In a round of broadcast interviews, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said the woman had only a “partial picture” of the events.About 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated early on Sunday morning to a leisure centre, with a 400-metre cordon placed around the white vans as bomb-disposal robots examined them.At the Labour party conference, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the evacuated residents should shortly be able to return home.Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air baseIran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had made threats against RAF Fairford in July.Iran’s embassy in London denied any involvement in the events in Whelford. It said: “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: High screen time can hurt children’s learning and language skills, study suggests  | Technology | The Guardian
description: Effect of elevated screen exposure could be as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, report says
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Effect of elevated screen exposure could be as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, report says
Content: Children who spend more time on screens were found to have higher ‘socioemotional’ and mental health problems, researchers found.Photograph: Imago/AlamyView image in fullscreenChildren who spend more time on screens were found to have higher ‘socioemotional’ and mental health problems, researchers found.Photograph: Imago/AlamyTechnologyHigh screen time can hurt children’s learning and language skills, study suggestsEffect of elevated screen exposure could be as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, report saysDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 28 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe effect of high screen time on children is as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, if not greater, a global study has found.Researchers examined data on more than 2.8 million children across 64 countries and concluded that elevated screen exposure could affect children in areas including academic achievement and emotional problems. It is one of the largest ever studies on the subject.The impacts are “similar in magnitude to or larger” than other factors linked to child development and mental health outcomes including family wealth, the behaviour of parents and whether or not children were born prematurely.Higher screen use for gaming, social media and streaming can lead to lower academic achievement and language development issues, the study suggests.Some experts said the report had limitations, arguing that the findings in “no way” support the belief that screens are the main cause of adolescent distress.Researchers found in the review, published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, that children who spend more time on screens have higher “socioemotional” and mental health problems. Academics conducted a so-called umbrella review, which summarises results from previous large reviews on the topic.Time limits, curfews or a full ban: how UK may restrict social media for under-16sRead moreResearchers found that longer durations of digital and social media use were linked to “less favourable outcomes across multiple (although not all) measured domains of children’s developmental health”. The analysis covered a variety of devices, from smartphones to televisions, and a range of activities including scrolling social media, gaming and FaceTime calls.“Together, the findings suggest that screen use may represent one potentially modifiable factor associated with children’s wellbeing across multiple domains,” the report said.It found that greater screen exposure was associated with overall lower grades at school. When academics examined specific subjects, screen time did not appear to be linked to maths, reading or science attainment, but the researchers said these were “among the least studied”, so the finding may be due to a lack of evidence.The researchers, led by academics at the University of Calgary in Canada, did find that higher screen time was also linked to poorer language development.When they looked at mental health, they found that higher screen use was linked to emotional and “peer problems”; “internalising behaviour”, which includes symptoms of depression and anxiety; and externalising behaviour, including aggression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms.“Our review revealed that higher so-called doses of screen exposure are associated with lower overall academic achievement and poorer language development, as well as higher internalising and externalising behaviour, emotional problems and peer problems,” the authors wrote.“Notably, these effect sizes are similar in magnitude to or larger than those reported for other well-established predictors of children’s outcomes, such as socioeconomic status, parenting behaviour and preterm birth.”Tatiana Íñiguez Berrozpe, a senior lecturer in sociology at the University of Zaragoza in Spain, said the report showed an association between screen time and poor mental health and academic performance, but it was small.“This is not an insignificant finding, but it in no way supports the mantra that screens are the main cause of adolescent emotional distress,” she said. “Screen use alone does not explain why a teenager is emotionally distressed or performs less well academically.”Esther van Sluijs, a professor of behavioural epidemiology at Loughborough University, said the study was “high-quality” but could not differentiate between different types of screen use.“It cannot draw robust conclusions about specific types of screen use, like social media use or gaming, as there was not enough data to study this. We should therefore be cautious in interpreting these results in the context of young people’s current screen use habits,” she said.Additional reporting by Press AssociationExplore more on these topicsTechnologyChildren's healthChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: AI godfathers warn of runaway ‘intelligence explosion’ | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: OpenAI chief scientist also among authors of report on prospect of ‘most consequential technological development in history’
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: OpenAI chief scientist also among authors of report on prospect of ‘most consequential technological development in history’
Content: Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton is among more than 20 authors of the report.Photograph: Johnny Guatto/University of Toronto/ReutersView image in fullscreenNobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton is among more than 20 authors of the report.Photograph: Johnny Guatto/University of Toronto/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)AI godfathers warn of runaway ‘intelligence explosion’OpenAI chief scientist also among authors of report on prospect of ‘most consequential technological development in history’Dan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 28 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI andAnthropichave warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history.A report co-authored by theNobel laureate Geoffrey Hintonand theCanadian computer scientist Yoshua Bengio, considered godfathers of modern AI for their work in the field,urges politicians to act nowbefore there is runaway progress in the technology.The authors say they are concerned about an “intelligence explosion”, which they describe as a “dramatic AI-driven acceleration of AI progress, compressing advances that would otherwise take years into months or less”.The paper, titled “What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion?”, is authored by more than 20 people including Hinton and Bengio. Other authors of the paper include Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, and Jakub Pachocki, the chief scientist at OpenAI.Their concerns focus on the possibility of AIs being able to improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as “recursive self-improvement”. In the paper it is broadly referred to as automated AI research and development. Once AI systems reach expert-level capabilities at AI R&D, a single developer could run a workforce equivalent to “millions” of top human researchers, the paper says.The authors say the automating of AI R&D is the most likely source of an intelligence explosion, because AIs are already contributing to improving their own technology and the resulting improved systems can be rapidly deployed once built.“An intelligence explosion could be the most consequential technological development in human history, compressing years of progress into months or less, threatening human control over AI systems, and severely eroding checks on power within and between states, companies, and branches of government,” the paper says.Urging governments to take action quickly, the authors say: “Once an intelligence explosion begins, the window for action may close.”They recommended a trio of policy priorities: requiring transparent progress reports on AI-related R&D, including embedding independent auditors in companies; finding ways to constrain breakneck AI development; and preparing to adapt to an intelligence explosion.Anthropic and OpenAI have both agreed to having independent evaluators assess their models after warning that AI development wasreaching a critical pitch in terms of safety.Anthropic says AI now produces 80% of its own code, whileOpenAIuses autonomous AI agents in areas such as the training of new models.“Preliminary evidence suggests that a software-driven intelligence explosion is possible,” the paper says, adding this would lead to the “extremely rapid development of highly capable or superhuman AI systems”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile this could produce medical breakthroughs and technological leaps, it would bring a trio of risks: powerful systems could enable biological and cyber threats that develop faster than the measures needed to counter them; as humans become less involved in AI R&D they could lose the opportunity to control systems; states could use an intelligence explosion to convert a modest lead in areas such as cyberspace into a decisive one.The report acknowledges these impacts are “uncertain”. For instance, a technological breakthrough could take time to implement given the need to set up supply chains for any special materials involved or to comply with regulations. AI systems could also accelerate the speed at which risks are mitigated, say the authors.If such a breakthrough happened, the authors say, AI systems could rapidly eclipse human experts in most fields and “radically accelerate” technological progress. Preparing for this “should be an urgent priority, including at the highest levels of government leadership”.They say governments should consider policies that address the potential for an intelligence explosion, including: requiring transparent progress reports on AI-related R&D, including embedding independent auditors in companies; limiting how fast an AI can improve in a certain time period; working with datacentres to enable pausing certain AI R&D projects; making sure automated AI R&D systems are fully isolated and cannot escape human control; creating “emergency response plans” for the various scenarios that could emerge from an intelligence explosion.Despite some glitches shown by systems, such as disobeying instructions, R&D projects that would take humans months to carry out could be fully automated by AI by 2028. “Productivity gains from AI R&D automation have not yet reached the threshold needed to trigger an intelligence explosion, but gains from newer systems are likely approaching that threshold,” they said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicComputingResearch and developmentScience policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Golders Green stabbings no longer being treated as suspected terrorism | UK news | The Guardian
description: Police say attack on two Jewish men in north London in April now being treated as alleged hate crime
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Police say attack on two Jewish men in north London in April now being treated as alleged hate crime
Content: Forensic officers at the scene after two men were seriously injured in a stabbing in Golders Green in April.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenForensic officers at the scene after two men were seriously injured in a stabbing in Golders Green in April.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAUK newsGolders Green stabbings no longer being treated as suspected terrorismPolice say attack on two Jewish men in north London in April now being treated as alleged hate crimeVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentMon 28 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe stabbings of two Jewish men in Golders Green, north London, in April are being treated as an alleged hate crime and not as a terrorist attack, police have said.Essa Suleiman, 45, was arrested by the Metropolitan police on suspicion of attempted murder shortly after the stabbings on 29 April.At the time, police said they were treating the attacks, in an area with a large Jewish population, as suspected terrorist offences.Suleiman has also been charged with attempted murder over the unconnected stabbing of another man earlier that same day.On Friday, Suleiman appeared in court for a pre-trial hearing where he denied all charges and the prosecution said the case was no longer being treated as a suspected terrorism case.In an email message sent to communities across London on Monday, the Met said: “At the hearing, the Crown Prosecution Service advised the court that it will not be pursuing a terrorist connection as part of the criminal proceedings.” It said it would treat it instead as a suspected hate crime.“We understand this announcement may cause concern, particularly within the Jewish community, given the impact this incident had locally and against the backdrop of recent incidents affecting Jewish communities across London. We would like to reassure residents that the seriousness with which this matter is being treated has not changed.”Cmdr Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing for London, said: “I fully recognise the impact this incident has had on the three victims as well as the public, particularly the Jewish community.“I’m also aware this news comes shortly after the arrests of two men in Manchester for a suspected plot to target the Jewish community during the High Holy Days period. Counter-terrorism policing continues to work closely with the Met police to provide as much visibility and security as we can to Jewish communities across London.”The victims of the Golders Green attacks were Shloime Rand, 34, and Moshe Shine, 76. The victim of the other stabbing earlier the same day in south London was Ishmail Hussein.The case continues and the full trial is scheduled for March 2027.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City chief maintains club’s innocence as rivals push for verdict to be published | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The Manchester City chief executive, Ferran Soriano, told European clubs that the club will fight the verdict
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Manchester City chief executive, Ferran Soriano, told European clubs that the club will fight the verdict
Content: Manchester City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano (right) has joined the club’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak (left), in vowing that they will continue to fight the Premier League charges.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano (right) has joined the club’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak (left), in vowing that they will continue to fight the Premier League charges.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityManchester City chief maintains club’s innocence as rivals push for verdict to be publishedFerran Soriano tells European clubs City will fight verdictPremier League clubs complain of ‘void’ over timelineMatt Hughesin CopenhagenMon 28 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA number of Premier League clubs are pushing for theManchester Cityverdict to be published as soon as possible, with the club digging in for a long battle to clear their name.City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, told a meeting of the European Football Clubs board on Monday that they will fight to prove their innocence afterbeing found guiltyby an independent commission of the vast majority of the Premier League’s 115 charges of breaching financial rules.Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility | Barney RonayRead moreSoriano’s willingness to address the guilty verdict against City, which first emerged on Friday but has yet to be confirmed publicly by the club or thePremier League, was a surprise to other members of the EFC board, which includes two domestic rivals in Jean-Claude Blanc, the head of Ineos Sport and chief of international football relations at Manchester United, and the Everton owner, Dan Friedkin.Soriano is understood to have addressed the board at the start of the meeting by requesting permission to make a brief statement. The Spaniard said that he wanted to make it clear that he disagreed with the ruling of the commission, and that he and Citywere confident of eventually winningtheir battle. He also added that whileit had been eight yearssince the allegations of financial misconduct were first made against City, it could take considerably more time for a definitive conclusion to the saga.The ongoing delay is a growing source of frustration to other clubs, who remain in the dark over the details of the case and the likely timeframe of any resolution. While club executives received a broad outline of the independent commission’s findings against City last Thursday there has been no update since, and the verdict has yet to be published. One club source said on Monday: “All we have is a void, and it would be better for everyone if it was filled as soon as possible.”Soriano declined to comment when approached by reporters after the EFC board meeting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Premier League has not commented or provided any indication of when the judgment will be published.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Merseyside blaze that killed mother and three children caused by lithium-ion battery | Merseyside | The Guardian
description: Local fire and rescue service says tragic incident early on Tuesday highlights risks the batteries can pose
Author: Charlie Moloney
Headline: Local fire and rescue service says tragic incident early on Tuesday highlights risks the batteries can pose
Content: Tributes near the scene in Bootle, Sefton, where Elisha Brabin, 36 and  her three children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, were killed in a house fire.Photograph: Eleanor Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenTributes near the scene in Bootle, Sefton, where Elisha Brabin, 36 and  her three children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, were killed in a house fire.Photograph: Eleanor Barlow/PAMerseysideMerseyside blaze that killed mother and three children caused by lithium-ion batteryLocal fire and rescue service says last week’s tragic incident highlights risks the batteries can poseCharlie MoloneyMon 28 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA fire thatleft a mother and her three children deadwas caused by a lithium-ion battery, firefighters in Merseyside have said.An electrical event caused the battery, of a type commonly used in vapes, ebikes and e-scooters, to go into “thermal runaway”,Merseysidefire and rescue service said.Crews arrived at the blaze, which ripped through the house in Bootle, at about 3.45am on Tuesday 22 September.Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. North West ambulance’s hazardous area response team later confirmed that all four had died.They were named by police as Elisha Brabin, 36, Leo Brabin, 16, Ellis Brabin, eight, and seven-year-old Prudence Brabin.At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house.The fire service’s head of prevention, Kevin Johnson, said: “This is a devastating incident and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of the mother and children who lost their lives and those who were injured.“This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire.”The service did not confirm what the lithium-ion battery at the home was being used for.Johnson said: “We’re urging people to follow the manufacturer’s instructions, only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk.“It’s also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge or is smoking, please stop using immediately.”In a tribute issued on Wednesday, relatives of the victims said: “Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, aunty, niece and cousin. She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us.“Our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure and brought so much joy, happiness and love to our family. They filled our lives with laughter and precious memories that we will cherish for ever.“The tragic loss of Elisha and our three precious children has left us heartbroken. They have all been taken from us far too soon. The loss we are experiencing is unimaginable, and the impact on our family will be felt for ever.”Explore more on these topicsMerseysideFirefightersEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Wynn-Jones, husband of Delia Smith, dies aged 85 | UK news | The Guardian
description: Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on Monday
Author: Charlie Moloney
Headline: Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on Monday
Content: Delia Smith and Michael Wynn-Jones celebrate Norwich City’s Championship victory in 2019.Photograph: Stephen Pond/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDelia Smith and Michael Wynn-Jones celebrate Norwich City’s Championship victory in 2019.Photograph: Stephen Pond/Getty ImagesUK newsMichael Wynn-Jones, husband of Delia Smith, dies aged 85Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on MondayCharlie MoloneyMon 28 Sep 2026 15.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Wynn-Jones, the journalist and husband of the TV chefDelia Smith, has died at the age of 85.Wynn-Jones was honorary life president ofNorwich Cityfootball club, which said everyone at the club was “deeply saddened” by his death.The club said in statement: “Michael died peacefully at home on Monday morning, aged 85. He will be greatly missed. His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth hospice in Ipswich.“Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom [Smith, the couple’s nephew], and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones. At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.”Wynn-Jones lived with Smith near Stowmarket in Suffolk and they had been married for more than 50 years.The couple oversaw several promotions to the Premier League for the Canaries, putting the club on a solid financial footing. Smith had a more prominent, public role at Norwich City but Wynn-Jones was reportedly regarded as a trusted adviser and influential figure in the boardroom.Darren Huckerby, a former player for the club, posted a tribute saying Wynn-Jones “stayed out of the limelight but all at Norwich City FC owe him so much”.Wynn-Jones worked as a journalist for titles including the Daily Mirror and the Spectator and founded his own publishing company.He began attending Norwich City games in April 1955 at the age of 13. He wrote fondly of the club’s unlikely run to the FA Cup semi-final in 1959.Norwich City Fans Social Club said in a statement: “All of us at NCFSC are devastated to hear the news about Michael Wynn-Jones passing. Michael is a true NCFC legend and what he did for the club cannot be underestimated. We are thinking of Delia, Tom and all of Michael’s family at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Michael.”Delia Smith previously told BBC Radio 4’s Desert Island Discs that she and Wynn-Jones bonded over their passion for food and football.Shesaid in 2021she rarely cooked at home, leaving Wynn-Jones to hover over the stove while she went “to the end of the garden”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsDelia SmithNorwich CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Gisèle Pelicot’s daughter launches awareness campaign for potential victims of drugging and sexual assault  | Gisèle Pelicot | The Guardian
description: Campaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attack
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Campaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attack
Content: Gisèle Pelicot and another woman in the campaign led by her daughter, Caroline Darian. The caption on Pelicot’s picture reads: ‘For years, I was ... by my husband.’Composite: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisView image in fullscreenGisèle Pelicot and another woman in the campaign led by her daughter, Caroline Darian. The caption on Pelicot’s picture reads: ‘For years, I was ... by my husband.’Composite: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisGisèle PelicotGisèle Pelicot’s daughter launches awareness campaign for potential victims of drugging and sexual assaultCampaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attackKim Willsherin ParisMon 28 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGisèle Pelicot is the figurehead of a new campaign run by her daughter to encourage people who suspect they have been drugged and sexually assaulted to come forward, even if they have little to no memory of the attack.Caroline Darian, 47, who believesshe was also drugged and assaultedby her father, Dominique Pelicot – her mother’s ex-husband – launched a primetime public information push on Monday across France’s television network, on social media, in the press and on posters.Her 73-year-old mother became an international symbol of courage and resistance when she insisted shame must change sides during the trial of her former husband and dozens of men who raped her while she was unconscious.Video clips featuring Gisèle Pelicot state that in 75% of cases of sexual abuse while drugged, the perpetrator is a relative or friend. She urges those who believe they may be victims to contact theCentre of Excellence on Substance-Facilitated Assaults(CRAFS).View image in fullscreenAnother poster in the campaign reads: ‘On my birthday, I was … by my stepfather.’Photograph: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisThe centre is attached to the Paris university hospital service (AP-HP) and staffed by experts who can suggest to those who believe they may have been a victim of drugging and abuse what evidence there might be and how it can be obtained.Caroline Darian, daughter of Gisèle Pelicot, speaks: ‘How can you rebuild when your father is the worst sexual predator in decades?’Read moreDarian, the founder of the associationMendorspas(Don’t Put Me to Sleep), said: “When you launch a campaign of this scale, having my mother’s backing sends a really powerful message. It’s also a message of hope for victims, showing that it is possible to get back on your feet.”The trial of Dominique Pelicot two years ago shocked the world. For almost a decade he had drugged his wife, raped her and invited strangers into their home in the village of Mazan, 20 miles from Avignon, to rape her while she was in a state of near coma.Pelicot’s horrific ordeal might have gone unremarked had she not decided to waive her anonymity and insist the case be held in public. Dominique Pelicot and 50 other men were convicted.The trial sparked the reporting ofother casesof what UK police call drug-facilitated sexual abuse, or DFSA. Earlier this month, a man in his 60spleaded guiltyto drugging and raping his wife over two decades and inviting strangers to abuse her, in the latest in a string of similar crimes.After the publication of her bookA Hymn to Life: Shame Has to Change Sidesearlier this year, Pelicot said: “Shame sticks to you, it sticks to your skin. And that shame is a double sentence, it’s a suffering you inflict on yourself.”View image in fullscreenThis poster’s caption reads: ‘Last night, I was … by my brother.’Photograph: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisDarian told Le Parisien: “It’s not because someone doesn’t remember that there aren’t traces or tests possible. Our aim is that these women can take back their own stories, so they no longer feel ashamed or afraid of not being heard by the police, not believed by the legal system and not supported by their family or those close to them.”She added: “Launching a campaign on this scale is quite unprecedented for an issue that was not recognised at all as a public health concern as recently as five years ago. When I started campaigning, nobody had heard of it [chemical submission] apart from a small circle of doctors. The Mazan trial was a major turning point with a global reach.“We’re getting somewhere but the fight is far from over. The message we want to send is that if you have a doubt, you need to look into it. Just because you cannot remember something, doesn’t mean there are no traces of it.”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsGisèle PelicotFranceEuropeRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland
Content: A resident of Garvaghy Road, Portadown: there has been growing nationalist self-confidence about a border poll on a united Ireland.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersView image in fullscreenA resident of Garvaghy Road, Portadown: there has been growing nationalist self-confidence about a border poll on a united Ireland.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersNorthern IrelandAnalysisAbsence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significantDaniel BoffeyChief reporterRow comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern IrelandMon 28 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.39 EDTShareThree decades ago, it took the deaths of three Roman Catholic children – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s CountyArmaghchaplain said at the time.It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then.Northern Irelandis very different place today.Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday.Faced withthousands of membersof the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain.View image in fullscreenA march of members of the Orange Order is blocked by police near Drumcree church, Portadown, Northern Ireland, on Monday.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersEvery half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful.The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and historysometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us.The divisions and tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland, papered over by the 1998 Good Friday agreement – when all sides were exhausted by the hate and misery of the three decades of Troubles – have been all too evident of late.This particular dispute can be reasonably argued either way. The independent Parades Commission has ruled that the march down the Garvaghy Road is permissible. The marchers are simply taking advantage of their rights, it may be said. But is it really necessary to take this road after 28 years of the march being banned? Who is served by the provocation?The detail of the argument is perhaps less important than the fact that it is happening, and what that says about Northern Ireland today, and what it may mean for the future.View image in fullscreenMichelle O’Neill, the Northern Ireland first minister (left), and the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, (centre) in the Garvaghy Road area on Sunday.Photograph: Peter Morrison/PAOn the nationalist side, there has been growing and bristling self-confidence about the prospects of a border poll on a united Ireland. This was only inflated by Donald Trump’srecent suggestionthat a unified Ireland should happen sooner rather than later. “The days of unionist supremacy and domination are gone,” said the first minister, Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, on Monday after appearing herself in Drumcree. “We will not be going backwards.”The numbers gathering from the nationalist community, some of whom were bussed in from Belfast and Derry, appeared to surprise the Police Service of Northern Ireland. It was a moment of unity within an often fractured nationalist community.Those in attendance included Colin Duffy and his brother Paul, who were both acquitted of terror charges in 2015, along with the SDLP party leader Claire Hanna, a vehement critic of those who reach for violence as an answer.Meanwhile, for the unionists, the changed relationship with the rest of the UK brought about by the Brexit deal and changing demographics has arguably engendered a distinct lack of confidence about the future.View image in fullscreenDUP MLA Jonathan Buckley (left), the party leader, Gavin Robinson, (centre) and DUP MLA Diane Dodds at Parliament Buildings, Stormont, on Monday.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAGavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP), the largest unionist party, claimed on Monday that “standards have been shattered” by the presence of the first minister with the protesters in Drumcree.When O’Neill and Mary Lou McDonald, the leader ofSinn Féinin the Republic of Ireland, arrived at the protest, it was to chants of “bring it down” and “fuck Stormont”, in reference to power-sharing arrangements in Northern Ireland, structured to make unionists and nationalists work together.“How we can go forward when there is such a level of disdain for the simple fundamental democratic principles of society?” asked Robinson of the attempt by the first minister to block a lawful march.It is likely that the prospect of elections for the Northern Ireland assembly next year, and the need to rally the faithful to their respective cause, is not helping to calm the rhetoric.In Stormont, the speaker, Edwin Poots, a former leader of the DUP, condemned the first minister for her “gross discourtesy” and “contempt” in not coming to answer an urgent question about the crisis.In this context, there is concern that even if Sinn Féin’s leaders, with the crowds’ chants ringing in their ears, do not walk out of the Northern Ireland executive, that the DUP could well do so.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Orange Order near Drumcree church on Monday.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersAfter a prolonged period in which agreement on a budget for Northern Ireland’s collapsing public services has not been found with Westminster, such further fracturing risks a whole new level of instability.The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, spoke to Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, on Monday. The possibility of mediation was discussed, Mac Cionnaith said. Speaking in the Republic, Micheál Martin, the taoiseach, called for cool heads. “No one wants to go back to the past divisions, to past trauma that we experienced at Garvaghy Road, Drumcree, in the past,” he said. “I would say to Sinn Féin and to everybody else: time to dial back now and time to engage in dialogue, and to work this out in a sensible, community-based way.”Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandDemocratic Unionist party (DUP)Sinn FéinNorthern Irish politicsArmaghnewsShareReuse this content
