title: ‘12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog’: what happens when you’re pregnant and can’t stand your pet? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rare
Author: Adrienne Matei
Headline: There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rare
Content: ‘A family’s capacity to meet an animal’s needs may change substantially.’Illustration: Timo Kuilder/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘A family’s capacity to meet an animal’s needs may change substantially.’Illustration: Timo Kuilder/The GuardianWell actually‘12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog’: what happens when you’re pregnant and can’t stand your pet?There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rareAdrienne MateiMon 28 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout three weeks into her first pregnancy, Sylvia Luu began to loathe the smell of her border collie mix, Ranger.Luu could hardly be in the same room as Ranger without becoming nauseous. His drool repulsed her, and she found the smell of his fur so disgusting she wore a nose plug all day.“Before pregnancy, I used tosmell my dog’s pawsa lot,” says Luu. “But during pregnancy, I would throw up if I ever tried that.”At the time, Luu, 35, and Ranger had enjoyed 12 happy years together. Ranger slept in Luu’s bed. She walked him in all weather, and let him lick her face.Luu’s doctor said that her nausea was normal and simply advised her to drink more water to avoid dehydration from vomiting, but that didn’t alleviate Luu’s distress. “I was so heartbroken that I couldn’t love my dog as much as I wanted to,” says Luu, whose husband took over pet care duties. She wondered about rehoming Ranger, and was relieved when, upon delivering her firstborn, her aversion vanished.By the time of her second pregnancy, Luu was diagnosed withhyperemesis gravidarum. The condition is caused byhormonal shifts, much like the more familiar morning sickness. For 1%-3% of pregnant people, these shifts result in extreme nausea and disgust sensitivity that can be triggered by any number of things – in this case, pet odour.Although the diagnosis was helpful, the changes were a difficult and destabilising addition to an already labile time. Luu now wishes that she had received some emotional support from her medical team, practical tips for coping with her diagnosis or validation of the unsettling shift in her feelings toward Ranger.Sit, stay and be a good boy: 21 rules for dogs and their humansRead moreBut there is almost no research into the specific phenomenon of pet aversion during and post-pregnancy.“This topic is at an intersection of women’s health being underfunded and human-animal bond work being trivialised,” says Dr Katherine Compitus, director of veterinary social work at New York University’s Silver School of Social Work, who has helped clients experiencing pet aversion.Yet there are signs that prenatal pet aversion isn’t particularly rare.View image in fullscreenSylvia Luu with Ranger.Photograph: Sylvia LuuA survey of 1,077 women who had been pregnant within the past three years found that 15% of pet-owning respondents experienced aversion to their dog during pregnancy, according to 2025researchfrom the UK pet insurer ManyPets.On Reddit, pregnant posters complain about feeling annoyed or repelled by their pets’ noises, smells and behaviours. “I’m a huge animal lover but this pregnancy I hate all of them,” wroteone user. “12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog,” anotheradmitted.Perinatal depression, anxiety and OCD may contribute to intense, confusing feelings, and a pet may become an outlet for difficult emotions too risky to direct at a partner or child, Compitus says. She recommends that anyone whose feelings about their pets are becoming distressing or out of proportion speak with a therapist, particularly those who use exposure therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy, as these practices can be particularlyusefulfor working through repulsion, rage and disgust.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’For others, pet aversion may ramp up once the baby is home.Katherine Davidson, a dog trainer based in Montreal, noticed herself becoming irritated with the shedding of her three dogs when she became pregnant. “It had never bothered me before,” she says.But when her daughter was born, the aggravation spiked – something she attributes to practical hygiene concerns and new-mom burnout. “I started feeling resentful” of the dogs, she says, “and that surprised me, because prior, my dogs were my entire life … they were my babies.”“My postpartum loathing of [pet cat] Lucky made me wonder whether I might be a late-onset psychopath,” mused an anonymous writer in a controversial 2024essayin the Cut.The postpartum period can be a vulnerable time for the human-animal bond, says Dr Shelby McDonald, an human-animal interaction researcher and director of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville’s Center for Veterinary Social Work.New families with pets face challenges including the safety of their baby around a rambunctious dog, and irritation due to barking, shedding and the click-clack of canine nails. “A family’s capacity to meet an animal’s needs may change substantially,” whether physically, emotionally, practically or financially, she says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Research with new parents has documented reductions in time and attention devoted to pets … and, for some people, changes in feelings of closeness to their animals,” says McDonald, who is currently collaborating on a study with the University of Edinburgh involving in-depth interviews with mothers in the UK about their experiences with companion animals during pregnancy and postpartum.Many mothers describe their relationships to their animals improving with time, according to McDonald’s early research.“A parent can remain deeply attached to an animal while temporarily having much less capacity to care for or interact with them in the way they did before the baby arrived,” she says.While not yet complete, McDonald’s work also indicates that a minority of mothers relinquish their pets during the postpartum period, seemingly out of concern for the animal’s welfare and quality of life; clear population-level data is not yet available.View image in fullscreenKatherine Davidson with Harlow.Photograph: Vanessa CyrThere can be “tremendous shame” associated with relinquishing or rehoming an animal, notes McDonald. Yet it’s important for new parents to notice when normal frustration and caregiver fatigue cross into the territory of abuse or neglect, which McDonald describes as an animal being denied adequate food and water, opportunities for exercise and elimination, a reasonably clean and safe environment, veterinary care or social interaction.“Recognizing that an animal’s welfare and wellbeing is being compromised and making a thoughtful plan for their care can itself be an act of responsible caregiving,” she says. “The priority should be the wellbeing and safety of both the person and the animal, rather than preserving a particular living arrangement at all costs.”Compitus suggests getting ahead of this issue by getting help from a friend, relative or petsitter. A reputable shelter or rescue may be able to provide guidance; some may even have safety-net programs designed to offer temporary reprieve to overwhelmed pet owners.Davidson considered rehoming her pets postpartum, but her dilemma was as existential as it was practical. She’d always been a “big animal person”, she says, and the change was confronting.Paws for thought: how to tell if your dog is happyRead more“You’re just like: ‘Oh, my God, I just need someone to understand, and to tell me these feelings are normal,” says Davidson. Shame and guilt may also contribute to silence around the topic, says Compitus. “If a mother is feeling this aversion toward her pets, it might call into question their identity as a mother: ‘What kind of mother will I be if I can’t even take care of my pet?’”For Davidson, who ended up keeping her dogs, the negativity she felt toward her pets passed in a matter of months as the household adjusted to a new routine.Now, when she works with dog-training clients who have growing families, Davidson tells them it’s not unusual to feel frustration or a lack of love for their animals postpartum, and that it often goes away. She shares strategies that worked for her, such as creating pet-free spaces in her home, using a robot vacuum for shedding, and getting help with duties like dog-walking, vet and grooming appointments, and cleaning.Today, Davidson has three children under six, and has added a six-month-old puppy to her menagerie. “It’s nice having my animals with me, and seeing them grow up with my children,” she says.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyPregnancyPetsHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What you need to know about Your First Home scheme for first-time buyers | First-time buyers | The Guardian
description: Government announcement sparks a rally in FTSE-listed housebuilders, but there are still a lot of unknowns
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Government announcement sparks a rally in FTSE-listed housebuilders, but there are still a lot of unknowns
Content: The Your First Home scheme will be available to first-time buyers in England.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenThe Your First Home scheme will be available to first-time buyers in England.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAFirst-time buyersExplainerWhat you need to know about Your First Home scheme for first-time buyersGovernment announcement sparks a rally in FTSE-listed housebuilders, but there are still a lot of unknownsLabour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a tryRupert JonesMon 28 Sep 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government will unveil a fresh scheme to help people on to the housing ladder next month but a debate is already raging over whether it is first-time buyers or housebuilders who will be the biggest winners.At the weekend, Andy Burnhamannouncedplans for Your First Home, which aims to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have the luxury of being able to call on the “bank of mum and dad”.Only a few details have emerged, but the news was enough to send theshare prices of many UK housebuilders surgingon Monday. Persimmon closed 14.7% higher, while Barratt Redrow added 11.7%, Taylor Wimpey 11.5%, Crest Nicholson 11% and Vistry 10.7%.What do we know so far?While it has a different name, it is not unfair to say that Your First Home appears to be an updated version of the Conservatives’ flagship help-to-buy scheme, which ran for a decade.Like that initiative, YFH applies to England only and is just for prospective first-time buyers looking to buy a new-build flat or house.While there were separate help-to-buy programmes for Scotland and Wales, it is not clear yet whether the devolved governments will do their own versions of YFH.Those taking part in the new scheme will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price. Meanwhile, the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%. That means the buyer will only need to take out a standard mortgage for 77.5% of the property’s value.Because the equity loan part will initially be interest-free, the government says participants “could save hundreds of pounds per month” compared with the standard 95% mortgage popular with many first-time buyers.The 2.5% deposit cap eliminates one of the biggest challenges facing would-be homeowners, who can find it hard to save up after covering their costs for rent, household bills and in some cases childcare.What’s the catch?There’s a lot we do not know yet about how it will work, who will be eligible and who will not.The government has said there will be measures to ensure support “is targeted at those who need it” and to avoid YFH being exploited by those who can already afford a home.A household income cap will be introduced to exclude those on bigger salaries from taking part. There will also reportedly be a deposit cap to restrict how much an applicant could put down upfront and local property price caps limiting how much people can spend on their first home, depending on where they live.There is no information yet about these caps, which will be the make-or-break factors for many people.It is also not known how the government-backed equity loan will work, where the money will come from and, crucially, how long it will be interest-free for and what happens after that. When a buyer does have to start paying interest, will it be fixed or will it go up? Can they pay off this loan early, and what happens if they want to move house or get into financial difficulty?What is known is that this loan will have to be repaid, perhaps when the home is sold or the mortgage is paid off.In addition, it is not known what the timescales are for when YFH will go live. The government says further details will be announced in the budget on 28 October, with the scheme open for registration by the end of 2026.How does the maths work in practice?The average asking price for a typical first-time buyer home is £225,199, according to the property website Rightmove. A 5% deposit on a property of that value would be £11,260. But under the new scheme, the buyer would only need to put down £5,630 (2.5%).They would be able to get a government equity loan of £45,040 (20% of the purchase price) and would need to take out a mortgage for the remaining £174,529.Nicholas Mendes, of the broker John Charcol, says: “Because the equity loan covers 20%, the mortgage itself sits at 77.5% loan-to-value, which gives buyers access to lower rates than they would typically see on a 95% mortgage.”How does this compare with help to buy?There were various versions of help to buy over the years, and itended in March 2023. The final version had a lot of similarities to what we know so far about YFH: it offered an equity loan, was for newly built properties, and also had price caps on what you could buy.With help to buy, the equity loan on offer was between 5% and 20% of the purchase price. However, that rose to up to 40% in London, so the new scheme appears less generous for those in the capital.On the flipside, with help to buy, buyers needed to stump up a deposit of at least 5%, twice that of the new scheme.Help to buy had regional property price caps – in London it could be used to buy a home costing up to £600,000 – but did not have a maximum household income.With the old scheme, the equity loan was interest-free for the first five years. After that, what you paid went up each year by the consumer prices index inflation measure plus 2%. The ongoing row over soaring student loan debts means the government will be under a lot of pressure to be very clear about how the equity loan will work in terms of interest.Ministers will also be acutely aware that help to buy was very controversial: while it was credited with helping 328,000 first-time buyers on to the housing ladder and a recent government review found itdelivered “very high value for money”, it was accused of pushing up property prices and boosting housebuilders’ profits.Developers will be expected to make a “contribution” to the new scheme when signing up, to help cover costs.Explore more on these topicsFirst-time buyersPropertyHouse pricesHelp-to-buy schemeHousing marketEconomic policyexplainersShareReuse this content

title: The hunk shortage: where are England’s handsomest men hiding? | Men | The Guardian
description: When the Mr England contest put out a call for entrants, only seven people signed up. Now, with 13 days to go until the final, the organisers are getting desperate
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When the Mr England contest put out a call for entrants, only seven people signed up. Now, with 13 days to go until the final, the organisers are getting desperate
Content: It’s a tough job …Photograph: Posed by models; Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreenIt’s a tough job …Photograph: Posed by models; Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFPass notesMenThe hunk shortage: where are England’s handsomest men hiding?When the Mr England contest put out a call for entrants, only seven people signed up. Now, with 13 days to go until the final, the organisers are getting desperateMon 28 Sep 2026 10.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAge:At least two years old.Appearance:A hunkless vista, as far as the eye can see.Hunks of what?Hunks of the male persuasion – masculine, well-built, handsome fellows.And there’s a shortage of those? A bigger-than-usual shortage?A dire shortage.Where did all the hunks go?Nobody knows.So how do we know there’s a shortage?Because the organisers of theMr England contestare having difficulty attracting sufficient hunks to participate in this year’s competition.Despite the launch of the biennial search over the summer, only seven men have entered the contest.Seven?Seven so far. Oddly enough, a very similar thing happened two years ago, when men were “a bit shy and slow in coming forward”, according to the organisers.So what we’re actuallytalking about is anation­wide disinclination on the part of men to submit themselves to a competition based on physical appearance.Exactly – a hunk shortage.I must admit, I’m not terribly surprised.But the Miss England contest, which is run by the same organisers, attracts thousands of entrants each year.Yeah, still not that surprised.The hunk drought remains a mystery: what happened to England’s strong, chiselled, 17- to 22-year-old men? And why are they so reluctant to take part in a beauty pageant?What did they do about the lack of interest two years ago?They sent the reigning Miss England, a lifeguard calledMilla Magee, to her local beach in Newquay, Cornwall, in search of recruits. Another 100 men joined up as a result of the publicity.And this year?TheMiss England semi-finalistsare being asked to nominate their friends and boyfriends.When is the contesthappening?The winner will be crowned on 11 October in Melton Mowbray, Leicestershire.They’ve left things a bit late, haven’t they?Don’t blame the organisers. How could they possibly have foreseen a second hunk shortage?Perhaps the cost of signing up is putting men off.It’s free to enter! Just download the Miss England app, upload some headshots …Don’t you mean the Mr England app?No, it’s all on the same app – the one with the tiara logo. Once you’re on there, you’ll figure it out.Could that be part of the problem? ThattheMr Englandcontestis treated as a mere adjunct to the women’s event?Let’s not jump to conclusions about the causes of the hunk shortage until all the evidence is in.Do say:“The Mr England competition opens doors for its participants, and offers an opportunity to represent England at an international level.”Don’t say:“Where do I sign? You had me at Melton Mowbray.”Explore more on these topicsMenPass notesModelsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham has a battle plan, with social care the flagship. Risks lie ahead, but Labour now travels in hope | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Here in Liverpool, the PM’s ambition for the party – and the country – is evident. There should be no complacency, but also no fear, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Here in Liverpool, the PM’s ambition for the party – and the country – is evident. There should be no complacency, but also no fear, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: People at the Labour Party annual conference in Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople at the Labour Party annual conference in Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOpinionLabour conference 2026Burnham has a battle plan, with social care the flagship. Risks lie ahead, but Labour now travels in hopePolly ToynbeeHere in Liverpool, the PM’s ambition for the party – and the country – is evident. There should be no complacency, but also no fearMon 28 Sep 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTShareHis ambition is big enough to see from space as he promises the “biggest change to Britain in 40 years”. Andy Burnham pledges what no prime minister until now has dared to, breaking the long spell of Thatcherism. Her sham monopoly markets in public services have crashed. The chancellor, John Healey, promises a“new age of industrialisation”, breaking with her era of industrial desertification. The social care system she blew into disconnected privatised fragments will become a national care service. Something new is waiting to be born.Things happen fast. Only a year ago, the Labour party was on its knees in despair, thunderstruck to find Nigel Farage ruling the roost so soon after its landslide win, with Reform UK12 percentage points aheadof Labour’s dismal 22%. Farage was themost popular leader, with a 30% favourability rating, compared with Keir Starmer’s-71%. When Burnham came to Liverpool last year he had no seat, no prospect of a challenge and a numbskull national executive committee bent on barring him, his charisma wasted.Now here he is in the middle of a mini-bounce, the only leader with a positive score, while Farage has sliddown the scaleto -30%.Polls showthat Labour could win the next election, with the left bloc outscoring the right, though without an overall majority. Relish every second of this period. Burnham has three precious years, rightly not risked in a needless election, and time enough to start his 40-year revolution.With the wind in his sails, he has the wit, agility, experience and ruthlessness of leadership, alongside his skill of being able to talk of dilemmas ahead without plunging everyone into gloom. “Have faith in the country” seems to be his useful attitude, casting doubters as anti-patriotic wreckers. Odysseus-like, he needs wax in his ears to block the sound of his enemies bellowing on Elon Musk’s X that he will never prove himself a real man, a true leader, until he inflicts severe pain – preferably on the weakest. He says he won’t make “crude cuts”. The way to bring down welfare bills is by helping the young out of benefits.Those who thought Healey would be the undertaker chancellor, countering Pollyanna Burnham with graveyard gloom, heard optimism in his speech on Monday instead. “It’s tough,”he had previously toldthe BBC economics editor, Faisal Islam, but “we’ve got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain”. Amid the cacophony of doom from the right, Islam, a fairer adjudicator, says there has been “a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits”. Burnham’s “hopeful optimism ‘vibes’ strategy” appears to have had “some impact”, Islam adds. That is the psychology of economics that eluded Starmer and Rachel Reeves: a good mood lifts markets too. Consumer confidence in the UK hit atwo-year highin August.Look what happened when the financial markets opened after Burnhamannounced“Your first home”, a better version of the help-to-buy scheme. FTSE-listedhousebuilders’ shares soared, with investors keen to get spades in the ground again with this incentive. Unlike George Osborne’sscheme, this is only for those with no “bank of mum and dad”, enabling them tobuy newbuildswith only a 2.5% deposit. Kitchen and tile manufacturers’ shares surged, too, after the news.The flow of “Hope again” announcements has been so prolific that it’s easy to lose track, so here are some: most bus fares in England will be capped;VAT on electricity bills in Great Britain will be cut;pub business rates in England have been reduced; there is apolicy to end rough sleeping in Englandand policies to support Neets; there are plans for the devolution of powers from Westminster, for “buying British”, for building council homes, for renewing high streets, for bringing arts andvocational skills back to the English school curriculum, for taking over empty homes, for more public control of public services and for repairing EU trade. And here’s a surprise from the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood: a safe and legalroute outfor Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. Hot air? Small beer? So far, cynicism bounces off Burnham.But yes, money must be raised to hit a defence spending target of3% of GDP, and to pay upfront to get Neets into work. The cost of living tops public concern, here and right across Europe, but that’s in the hands of Donald Trump’s calamitous war on Iran.The art of politics is to lead the national conversation, and to distract from current troubles to focus on the future. There’s a risk, with such a plethora of plans, that direction and purpose become diluted. Wisely, Burnham has singled out one above all others – a flagship policy that authentically marks who he is, what he stands for and what he cares about.Social care will be the beacon shining for every family sooner or later in this ageing population. As Burnham spoke movingly of his father’s death, there was a national nodding of the head in recognition. His father had the best care, he said, but hundreds of thousands encounter the worst, if they get any at all. The key to unlocking national wallets and purses for this expensive task is reminding everyone of their pride in the NHS and contempt for the US alternative. Social care in England is “as unfair as American healthcare,”said Burnham, where the “most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out, not just by the condition that they have, but wiped out financially”. That chimes.The pitch is rolled now to change the unaffordable triple lock on pensions in order to pay for the new social care service. It will need the wealth of older people to contribute, without taking money from the struggling younger generation whose incomes are lower than their parents’ were at the same age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat will be the heart of the next manifesto – when Burnham knows, from bitter experience of the 2010 election, how that policy gets turned into a “death tax”. The knives were out again on hearing the plan. But this time, he thinks they mistake the public mood. That’s brave but essential.All this Labour celebration, sheer relief and surprised delight at every new announcement comes with a stern warning. In this volatile era, what changed so fast in a year can swing back again. Harder tests are to come, warns the University of Manchester professor of political science Rob Ford, with the budget, the spending review and unknown global perils on the horizon. Labour’s lead is still thin. Farage may be down after his scandal-ridden summer, but he has roared back before.Analysis by Survationfor Hope not Hate reminds us that in many Labour seats Reform UK is close behind, often by a tiny margin. With Marine Le Pen’s support surging in France this week, complacency is the danger.Everything at this conference suggests that Burnham has the full measure of what heavy lifting it will take to persuade more voters of his way. He feels the national pulse, as he hopes to make social care stand for everything elseLabourmeans to do. Labour can rejoice in this moment, but never stop looking over its shoulder.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabour conference 2026OpinionAndy BurnhamLabourSocial careHousingJohn HealeyEconomic policycommentShareReuse this content

title: Gen Z has very strong opinions about age-gap relationships – and it could be right | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Older men and younger women were once an unremarkable screen pairing. But watching them with a new generation is a real education, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Older men and younger women were once an unremarkable screen pairing. But watching them with a new generation is a real education, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘The average gen Zer thinks an age gap of a single school year is a red flag of exploitation.’Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The average gen Zer thinks an age gap of a single school year is a red flag of exploitation.’Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyOpinionMoviesGen Z has very strong opinions about age-gap relationships – and it could be rightZoe WilliamsOlder men and younger women were once an unremarkable screen pairing. But watching them with a new generation is a real educationMon 28 Sep 2026 09.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTShareIlooked up the cast before I saw the new film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, thinking: “Who could be as good as Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet?” because of course I did. One,they were peerlessand two, this is the condition of middle age, constantly looking at the world thinking: “This could be considerably improved by the presence of Emma Thompson.”The notable casting update was Col Brandon, whose passion for Marianne would now be known as an “age gap” relationship. In the last film,Alan Rickman(born 1946) was in love with Winslet (born 1975), who cycles through a fair amount of: “Yuck, no thanks,” before having an epiphany.Sorry if that spoiled the end. I don’t really seeJane Austenas a suspense-monger.Winslet could easily have been Rickman’s daughter and, biologically speaking, just about his granddaughter. In the 90s, though, the age gap was a distant second consideration to the fact that Brandon was grumpy and boring, although his gruff exterior masked a serious mind and a heart of gold. I have my own thoughts on this romantic trope as a long‑term cohabitation prospect, but we can do those another day. Besides, look at that age gap. The term might not be all that long.To the modern audience, however, the age gap simply wouldn’t “sit right”, as one gossip zine put it. I’m not wild about this terminology: “sit right”, “uncomfortable”. The subtext is: “You are in breach of absolutely fundamental and self-evident values, which I am too gracious and polite to mention, yet not to do so is bringing me discomfort.”Nevertheless, those valuesareself-evident and fundamental. The average gen Zer thinks an age gap of a single school year is a red flag of exploitation. So the film-makers got Herbert Nordrum, who is only 13 years older than Esmé Creed-Miles, but – per my point about school years – this is still way too many.Some age gap must be present, however, to stay true to the text, with its 19-year difference. So they cover him in a bushy beard and make him unaccountably Norwegian, thereby creating enough visual ambiguity and sensory confusion that he could be any age. Now, there’s an indeterminate gulf between them, which could be due to their respective ages or the stark differences in their personalities (in other words, it could be senseorsensibility), but none of that amounts to a hill of beans once their true feelings have been unearthed.Rats, sorry, just spoiled the ending again.Sense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcomRead moreObviously, that wasn’t the only age gap to grace a 90s screen, but it was sufficiently unusual for it to be part of the plot. More often, in those days, you were supposed to simply not notice that a woman with newly minted A-levels had fallen in love with a guy who was surely nearly ready for his free bus pass. If all that sounds very UK-centric, that’s only because I’m feverishly trying not to use words such as “Jack”, “Nicholson”, “Richard” and “Gere”.Often, when you watch a classic film with youngsters today and they’re doing wild vomit-mimes and yelling: “No, seriously, what is wrong with you people?” it’s not immediately obvious what they’re objecting to. It could be that what you thought of as a sudden and dramatic romantic clinch assumes consent that has not been expressed, or it could be that the woman is visibly 15 years younger than the man, or it could be something else entirely, like: “She is quite cool and he is a jerk.” I’m thinking, specifically, of Hannah and Her Sisters, which I erroneously put on once, trying to introduce the younger generation to jazz. I think it’s safe to say that I learned more from that experience than they did.In fact, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles are different from Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, but equally good. And gen Z’s perception of what is acceptable on screen and how it might feed into wider society is different from mine, but possibly better. Maybe it’s time I make my peace with the condition of modernity.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
