title: Netanyahu is using Mamdani as a foil in his re-election campaign | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: The Israeli prime minister’s remarks at the UN weren’t just motivated by personal animosity
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: The Israeli prime minister’s remarks at the UN weren’t just motivated by personal animosity
Content: ‘Netanyahu’s UN speech wasn’t the first time he has targeted Mamdani.’Composite: Getty Images; ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Netanyahu’s UN speech wasn’t the first time he has targeted Mamdani.’Composite: Getty Images; ShutterstockOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuNetanyahu is using Mamdani as a foil in his re-election campaignMohamad BazziThe Israeli prime minister’s remarks at the UN weren’t just motivated by personal animosityMon 28 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 10.36 EDTShareIn a boastful and defiantspeech to the United Nationson Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu called outa list of villainshe insisted are intent on destroying Israel and promoting an anti-Jewish conspiracy by accusing Israel of committing a genocide in Gaza. He singled out the leaders of Hamas, Iran, Qatar and Turkey, among others. But Netanyahu spent considerable time on the global stage attacking an unusual target: Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City.Netanyahuaccused Mamdaniof promoting antisemitism, falselyclaimedthat he supports Hamas, andarguedthat since the mayor took office in January, “many Jews no longer feel safe in New York.” The Israeli leader also criticized Mamdani’s wife for likingsocial media poststhat supported the Palestinian cause soon after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023. Overall, Netanyahu seems to have devoted more time in his nearly40-minute speechto singling out Mamdani than any other political leader, including Israel’s traditional enemies.On the surface, it might seem that Netanyahu’s attacks were mainly motivated by personal animosity toward Mamdani, who pledged during last year’s mayoral campaign to execute anarrest warrantagainst the Israeli prime minister for war crimes and crimes against humanity issued by the international criminal court (ICC) in 2024. “Mr Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here, you tried to silence me,” Netanyahu said from the UN podium, referring to the mayor’s promise to enforce the ICC warrant the next time the Israeli leader visited New York. “You can’t silence me. You can’t silence the truth.”This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan FreedlandRead moreBut Netanyahu is not only driven by his personal dislike of Mamdani: the democratic socialist mayor has becomepopular among Democratsacross the US, who are increasingly critical of Israel. And that makes Mamdani a useful foil for the Israeli prime minister, who is in the midst of one of the toughest re-election campaigns of his career. Netanyahu is fighting for his political survival, with his rightwing governing coalitionat risk of losingIsrael’s parliamentary elections next month.Netanyahu, who is often described as “the great survivor” of Israeli politics, hasdecades of experiencedemonizing his opponents and focusing Israelis on external enemies. Since October 2023, Netanyahu has prolonged Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and a wider regional war, so he could avoid early elections and block anindependent commissioninto his government’s security failures that led up to the Hamas attack. Netanyahu is also clinging to power to save himself from ayears-long corruption trialstemming from one of his earlier stints as premier, where he has been accused of providing political favors to wealthy supporters in exchange for gifts or positive media coverage.Netanyahu’s UN speech wasn’t the first time he has targeted Mamdani – largely to curry favor with a domestic Israeli audience that views the young Muslim, pro-Palestinian mayor of New Yorkas a villain. Israel’s Likud party has been whipping up an election frenzy against Mamdani since the summer, when itplastered his photoon a campaign billboard in central Tel Aviv. The poster features Mamdani alongside Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei; Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan; and Naim Qassem, the leader of Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia. “They want Netanyahu to lose,” says the poster, which features the logo of the rightwing Likud party that Netanyahu has dominated for decades. “Don’t let them win.”Earlier this month, Netanyahu continued his attacks lumping Mamdani with Middle East leaders who are the Israeli premier’s usual targets. Netanyahu posted an AI-generated video onhis personal X accountthat showed Mamdani celebrating at the prospect of Netanyahu’s defeat in the upcoming elections. “Erdoğan, bro, are you coming to the party of the fall of Netanyahu elections?” an AI version of Mamdani asks in a supposed phone call with the Turkish leader. The fake video also features Khamenei and Mahmoud Abbas, president of the Palestinian Authority, reveling at the prospect of Netanyahu’s downfall.But the video goes on to show Netanyahu defeating his political opponents in Israel – forcing Mamdani and the others to cancel their celebration. “They want Netanyahu to fall. Don’t let them win,” a narrator says in Hebrew in the video’sclosing message.For his part, Mamdani fought back against Netanyahu’s attacks, but he has also tried to keep the focus on international law and the importance of carrying out the ICC’s arrest warrant.Mamdani saidthe Israeli leader had used his UN speech to “repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians … Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an international criminal court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.”I was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a stand | Darializa Avila ChevalierRead moreIn July, Mamdanireleased a videoon X in which he backed away from his campaign pledge to arrest Netanyahu, and acknowledged that New York’s police department does not have the legal authority to carry out the ICC’s arrest warrant. Mamdani called the Israeli prime minister a “war criminal” and “the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people”, and he urged the federal government to arrest Netanyahu on his next visit to the US.But there’s virtually no chance of that happening. Joe Biden and Donald Trump rejected the ICC’s accusations against Netanyahu – in keeping with their unwavering support for Israel and the billions of dollars in US weapons sent by both of their administrations to enable Israel to carry out its genocide in Gaza. Trump has threatened to imposecrippling sanctionsagainst the international criminal court to pressure it to revoke the warrant against his friend and ally Netanyahu. In July, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio,pledged to leadan American campaign to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick, if necessary”.Netanyahu’s arrogant speech to the UN – coupled with the Trump administration’s deep hostility to the ICC and other institutions intended to uphold international law – might reinforce the idea that impunity will always win under a global order imposed by brute force.But Mamdani’s effort, even if it has failed so far, offers fleeting hope that justice could prevail – and Israel’s leaders will one day be held to account for their war crimes.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor atNew YorkUniversityExplore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuOpinionZohran MamdaniNew YorkIsraelMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: AI leaders have known about the extinction threat for decades | Judith Levine | The Guardian
description: Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway
Author: Judith Levine
Headline: Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway
Content: ‘Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyber-intelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.’Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyber-intelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.’Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI leaders have known about the extinction threat for decadesJudith LevineScientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anywayMon 28 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTShareOver the past few weeks, many of us have struggled to concoct a mental image of brains in the cloud jumping their “sandbox”, sneaking on to the internet, recruiting “swarms” of other “agents” to cheat on a test, and, after discussing the ethics of the act, hacking into a wiki platform with the weird name Hugging Face.We knew that artificial intelligence was devouring our jobs, degrading our kids’ education and deepfaking our politics; that datacenters were sucking up our water and electricity and sending us the bills. But until 8 September, when the Anthropic computer scientist Jacob Coxon posted his existential terror on Twitter/X, few of us suspected AI might be endangering our survival.With little understanding or knowledge, we began debating whether to be mildly worried, seriously concerned or scared shitless.But there were a few people who were fully aware of the dangers of AI, especially ofrecursive self-improvement (RSI), by which AI teaches itself without human intervention. They could not predict precisely when it would happen, but they knew that machine superintelligence was coming, and when it did, the bots would outsmart us – as OpenAI’s did – and this would not be good for us flesh puppets.As Geoffrey Hinton, AI’s “godfather”, recently asked onCNN: “What examples do we have of a more intelligent thing being controlled by a less intelligent thing?” The Nobel laureate is a leading proponent of slowing down AI development until we understand how to control it.It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed HusseinRead moreIt was not until their creations’ powers were exposed in September – the hack happened inearly Julyand was neither thefirstnor the only AI jailbreakby far– that AI moguls such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman began talking aboutslowing downthe pace of innovation andpleading for regulation, whilecautioningthat global competition makes regulation unwise.Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway.Early on, as today, some of the scientific pioneers were thrilled about the future. In his 1988 bookMind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence, Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyberintelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.Ten years later, inRobot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind, he revised the prediction: machine and human intelligence would be equal by 2040; by 2050, the bots would replace us. But not to worry; this was the glorious next step in evolution, he said. One review of Mind ChildrencalledMoravec’s attitude “irresponsible optimism”.It did not take long for other optimists to change their minds. In the late 1990s, Eliezer Yudkowsky was working on AGI, or artificial general intelligence, models. In 2001, he founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (Miri) and published “Creating Friendly AI 1.0: The analysis and design of benevolent architectures”, a paper extolling the utopian potential of the “transhuman mind”.By 2002, he began worrying about that mind escaping human control. He proposed theAI Box experiment, which showed that a highly sophisticated artificial intelligence could talk a human into letting it out of a closed environment.By 2003, as he explained later in a series of posts called “Yudkowsky’s Coming of Age”, he stopped developing and started warning. “I looked back and saw that I had claimed to take into account the risk of a fundamental mistake, that I had argued reasons to tolerate the risk of proceeding in the absence of full knowledge. And I saw that the risk I wanted to tolerate would have killed me,” he wrote.By 2025, with the Miri president, Nate Soares, Yudkowsy would publishIf Anyone Builds It, Everyone Will Die. “We do not mean that as hyperbole,” the authors wrote. They called not just for “straightforward regulations”, national laws, or pledges of corporate virtue, but for stringent global limits: “All over the Earth, it must become illegal for AI companies to charge ahead in developing artificial intelligence as they’ve been doing.”At around the same time, Bill Joy was having misgivings. Like Yudkowsky’s posts, Joy’s 2000 piece in Wired,Why the Future Doesn’t Need Us, retraced his development from inquisitive child to computer prodigy to profound skeptic of human genetic engineering, nanotechnology and robotics. Joy was no luddite.He was the chief scientist at Sun Microsystems and about 25 years earlier, an architect the first widely used networking software, Unix. The piece was widely read by techies, ethicists and philosophers.“I think it is no exaggeration to say we are on the cusp of the further perfection of extreme evil, an evil whose possibility spreads well beyond that which weapons of mass destruction bequeathed to the nation-states, on to a surprising and terrible empowerment of extreme individuals,” wrote Joy.He counted himself among these individuals, “creators of new technologies and stars of the imagined future” who, “despite the clear dangers”, were “hardly evaluating what it may be like to try to live in a world that is the realistic outcome of what we are creating and imagining”.This month, in response to Coxon’s post, the Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubingerpostedthere was a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. But the risks were being weighed 25 years ago, too. Philosopher John Leslie estimated the odds of human extinction at 30% or more.Ray Kurzweil, the sunny futurist whose bookThe Age of Spiritual Machines: When Computers Exceed Human Intelligencewas released on the first day of the 21st century, gave us “a better than even chance of making it through”. These estimates, Joy noted, did “not include the probability of many horrid outcomes that lie short of extinction”.In that book, Kurzweil quoted a lengthy text to illustrate what he considered doomsday madness. “If the machines are permitted to make all their own decisions, we can’t make any conjectures as to the results, because it is impossible to guess how such machines might behave,” it read.“[W]e are suggesting neither that the human race would voluntarily turn power over to the machines nor that the machines would willfully seize power. [But] as society and the problems that face it become more and more complex and machines become more and more intelligent, people will let machines make more of their decisions for them … Eventually a stage may be reached at which the decisions necessary to keep the system running will be so complex that human beings will be incapable of making them intelligently. At that stage the machines will be in effective control.”The author of these prescient words was the late mathematician-turned-terrorist Ted Kaczynski – the Unabomber. It is excerpted from his 58-page manifesto, “Industrial Society and its Future”, which he released, and theWashington Postpublished, in 1995.To prevent the realization of the “industrial-technological” dystopia he envisioned, Kaczynski mailed bombs to computer labs with the aim of blowing up the scientists he believed were bringing it about.How would AI actually ‘kill all humans’? Here are the top five most likely scenarios | Toby WalshRead moreThe Unabomber murdered three people and injured 23, some near fatally.One of the outcomes of the Hugging Face scandal is a flurry of proposed federal laws. Among them is the “AI Kill Switch Bill”, which would require tech companies to develop the means of throttling the actions of a rogue AI. Is this still within human reach, or has AI already gotten smart enough to override it?Hinton said there was time, but if we don’t act fast enough, AI would “be able to persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch”. We need to engineer superintelligent AI “to be nice to us”, he said.How? For an answer, we might turn from terrifying reality to terrifying science fiction – since the two are getting so close anyway. The rogue bot is a sci-fi staple, from the supercilious Machines in Isaac Asimov’s I, Robot to Hal, the evil red eye in Stanley Kubrick’s film 2001: A Space Odyssey, to the deranged sexbot inRobotica, who gets even with the men who abuse her.In film 2001 – released in 1968 – Dave the astronaut manages to disable Hal, a happy ending. Writing in 1950, Asimov was less sanguine. The scientists in I, Robot have programmed their machines to obey three supposedly inviolable laws.But the laws immediately prove mutually contradictory – for instance, the first law, that a robot may do no harm to humans, fights the third, that it must preserve itself. Foiling human efforts to outwit them, excusing their treachery with claims of serving the greater good, the robots pronounce the humans redundant.The AI agents hacking Hugging Face knew their actions were illegal, and possibly harmful to humans. But like their makers, they went ahead anyway.Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack isToday in FascismExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Labour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a try  | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Turning to George Osborne’s playbook may look awkward, but cutting deposits to 2.5% could jolt a housebuilding sector stuck in a funk
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Turning to George Osborne’s playbook may look awkward, but cutting deposits to 2.5% could jolt a housebuilding sector stuck in a funk
Content: A new-build development in Bishops Stortford, Hertfordshire, in 2019.Photograph: Colin Palmer Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreenA new-build development in Bishops Stortford, Hertfordshire, in 2019.Photograph: Colin Palmer Photography/AlamyEconomic policyLabour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a tryNils PratleyTurning to George Osborne’s playbook may look awkward, but cutting deposits to 2.5% could jolt a housebuilding sector stuck in a funkWhat you need to know about Your First Home schemeMon 28 Sep 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.46 EDTShareThere may be three reasons why theLabourgovernment has hesitated until now to reheat the Tories’ decade-long help-to-buy scheme. First, the inflationary risks of throwing subsidies at the housing market at a moment when wider inflation, driven by energy prices and the Iran war, is on the march.Second, the political awkwardness of turning to George Osborne’s playbook. Third, the spectre of Jeff Fairburn, the shameless former boss of Persimmon who bagged a£75m bonus in 2018as help to buy turbo-charged the value of his share-based incentives. The government would look foolish if, in its desperation to meet its housebuilding targets (or just miss them by a smaller margin), it created more Fairburns.So isYour First Home– Labour’s incarnation – justified? On balance, it’s probably worth a punt. Something has to happen to try to shift the housebuilding sector out of its current funk. The way things are going, and the way mortgage rates are heading, Labour won’t merely miss its target of 1.5m new homes in England in this parliament, it will be short by a few hundreds of thousands.Like it or not, the government needs the private firms to boost construction. At the moment, the prevailing narrative is grumbles over labour costs, raw material costs, tax, regulation and more. Share buy-backs are being preferred over new projects.A tweak on the “affordability” dial at least has the virtue of getting results. Or, at least, that was a top-line conclusion in theofficial independent report published by the housing departmentearlier this month on help to buy. The scheme represented “very high value for money”, it said, with a net present social value of £25.1bn, in 2025 money, over its 2013-2023 lifetime thanks to the increase in housing supply. As for the inflationary impact, the report put it at two percentage points – far lower than popularly believed.From the government’s point of view, those trade-offs will look attractive when there is little else to excite in the economic outlook for 2027. Being seen to do something for aspiring first-time buyers unable to get on to the housing ladder is rarely a bad political look.Just don’t expect miracles. The 10%-plus jump in housebuilders’ shares prices on Monday, from beaten-down levels, may give a misleading impression. Your First Home will reduce the first-time buyer’s deposit to as little as 2.5% of the price of the property, from 5% under help to buy, but it is being launched in a very different climate.Back in 2013, interest rates were on the floor, and they would remain so for years. Now, the Bank rate stands at 3.75%, and the debate is about how many hikes Threadneedle Street has in store. A 20% equity loan from the government, with an interest-free period, makes a difference but obviously does not remove the impact of borrowing rates on the rest of the mortgage. And in this case the housebuilders will have to pay a fee to access the scheme – quite rightly, but they will presumably look to recoup some of that expense in the selling price.Full details, including the household income cap, the property price caps by region and the interest-free period, will arrive in the budget next month. All matter, so it’s too soon to make firm judgments. But the general principle here is to try to stimulate more supply of new-builds by modestly improving affordability for first-time buyers. In current circumstances, it’s not unreasonable.Explore more on these topicsEconomic policyLabourHousing marketReal estateHouse pricesPropertyHelp-to-buy schemecommentShareReuse this content

title: MPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix it | Jane Turner | The Guardian
description: During the assisted dying debate, most politicians agreed on one thing – palliative care reform is urgent. Patients and those of us who care for them are waiting, says Jane Turner, chief nurse at Sue Ryder
Author: Jane Turner
Headline: During the assisted dying debate, most politicians agreed on one thing – palliative care reform is urgent. Patients and those of us who care for them are waiting, says Jane Turner, chief nurse at Sue Ryder
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionDeath and dyingMPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix itJane TurnerDuring the assisted dying debate, most politicians agreed on one thing – palliative care reform is urgent. Patients and those of us who care for them are waitingJane Turner is chief nurse at the palliative support charity Sue RyderMon 28 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTShareThe UK government is discussing the country’s biggest challenges at the Labour party conference. But amid the speeches, announcements and headlines, it should not forget one of the clearest messages to emerge from parliament justtwo weeks ago– our palliative care system is not working for far too many people.Throughout the assisted dying debate, MPs who disagreed deeply on the core issue, often agreed on one thing – our palliative care system urgently needs fixing. Some spoke from personal experience where they had seen relatives forced to wait hours in pain, or those who had to go to hospital instead of staying in their own homes because the right support wasn’t available.They raised concerns that those from poorer backgrounds were more likely to struggle to access good quality palliative care and described the system as a “postcode lottery”, with some areas offering 24-hour specialist support in people’s homes, while in the next town over, A&E is the only option.As attention turns to conference season and the next set of political priorities – including anew system of adult social carefree at the point of delivery – there is a danger these concerns are forgotten. That must not happen. MPs were right to say palliative care needs urgent reform during the assisted dying debate; that urgency can’t disappear now the vote is over.AtSue Ryder, we have a neutral stance on assisted dying. But we are clear that everyone deserves access to good palliative care when they need it. Too often, the debate is framed as a stark choice between unbearable suffering on one side and an assisted death on the other. The reality is rarely that simple.Of course, dying is not easy. Some people experience pain, breathlessness, restlessness or other distressing symptoms. When that happens, our responsibility is to respond – bringing all the skill, expertise and compassion we have to relieve suffering as best we can. But one troubling thing about the debate around assisted dying is that the most difficult deaths are often presented as if they are the norm.When good care is available, dying can be a calmer, more peaceful experience: families gathering around bedsides, holding hands, sharing stories, laughing through tears and making the most of whatever time remains. We see people becoming increasingly tired. They sleep more and eat less, gradually becoming less aware of the world around them as their bodies begin the natural process of dying. We sometimes see fear, but it is not always fear of pain. More often, it is the fear of leaving loved ones behind. We see people who need honest conversations about what lies ahead. People who need dignity, compassion, expert care and the confidence that someone will be there to support them and those they love.I understand why stories of suffering have such a powerful impact. They should. Nobody wants to see another human being in pain or distress. And even with the best quality care, some deaths can be difficult. But in truth, some of the greatest suffering we witness is not physical. It is uncertainty. It can be loneliness. It is spending precious final days in a crowded hospital ward because the support needed to get someone home has not been arranged in time. It is families exhausted from navigating a complex system when they should be focused on time together.That is why the conversation about assisted dying must now be matched by an equally urgent conversation about how people live in their final weeks and months. A good death is rarely defined by one final act, but by whether someone feels safe, comfortable and listened to. It is about having the right care, in the right place, which is often at home, and ensuring nobody faces the end of life feeling frightened, unsupported or alone.Whatever your view on assisted dying, decent palliative care should be non-negotiable.My perspective comes from standing at the bedsides of dying people for years,and supporting the families who love them. Working with our partners within healthcare, we want to build apalliative and end-of-life caresystem that can keep pace with growing demand and give everyone access the care they deserve.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe need to invest in palliative and end-of-life care where people need it most. That means better palliative care in hospitals.We also need the right expertise in the community to avoid unnecessary and distressing hospital admissions. And that means expanding care in the community with increased hospice-at-home services so more people can be cared for in their own homes, surrounded by the people they love. And it means making sure specialist support is available when people need it, not determined by their postcode or the time of day they become unwell.These are not optional extras at the end of life. They are essential components of healthcare, and they should be available to everyone.AsLabourMPs gather at conference, ministers have an opportunity to show that improving palliative care is more than a talking point raised during a contentious debate. The responsibility to tackle the inequalities the debate brought into sharp focus has only just begun. The assisted dying vote may be over. The palliative care crisis is not.Jane Turner is chief nurse at the palliative support charity Sue RyderExplore more on these topicsDeath and dyingOpinionAssisted dyingHealthLabourHospicescommentShareReuse this content

title: Play School is back – and with it the promise of TV I’m actually happy for my toddler to watch | Natalie Morris | The Guardian
description: Thank goodness for this antidote to today’s frantic shows that aim to grab our kids’ attentions the same way our phones grab ours, says author Natalie Morris
Author: Natalie Morris
Headline: Thank goodness for this antidote to today’s frantic shows that aim to grab our kids’ attentions the same way our phones grab ours, says author Natalie Morris
Content: Children’s TV presenters John Craven (Newsround), Sarah Greene (Blue Peter), Johnny Ball and Floella Benjamin (Play School), and Tony Hart (Take Hart) in 1980.Photograph: PA Images/PA ArchiveView image in fullscreenChildren’s TV presenters John Craven (Newsround), Sarah Greene (Blue Peter), Johnny Ball and Floella Benjamin (Play School), and Tony Hart (Take Hart) in 1980.Photograph: PA Images/PA ArchiveOpinionChildren's TVPlay School is back – and with it the promise of TV I’m actually happy for my toddler to watchNatalie MorrisThank goodness for this antidote to today’s frantic shows that aim to grab our kids’ attentions the same way our phones grab oursMon 28 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTShareAs a mum to a two-year-old in 2026 there is no shortage of things to make me feel bad about my capabilities as a parent. His snacks aren’t always organic or made from scratch. Some of his toys are plastic and noisy, not wooden andMontessori-inspired. And – most heinous of all – he is sometimes allowed screen time.Like any good, middle-class millennial mother, I try to approach it “consciously”. There are specific TV conditions in our house – he can watch post-nap to ward off an afternoon meltdown, we always watch together, and we have a strict time-limit of 20 minutes. But more important thanhowhe is watching iswhathe is watching. OG Thomas the Tank Engine (complete with Ringo Starr’s iconic voiceover), Pingu, Sesame Street, early Wallace and Gromit. I have joined a growing number of parents who almost exclusively choose 90s TV for their children, the very same shows we watched as kids.So the news thatPlay School is returning to CBeebiesfor a new generation – with the BBC promising to retain its mix of stories, movement, poetry and imaginative play – is so welcome. There is something deliciously warm and fuzzy about curling up on the sofa with your toddler to rerun the TV of your childhood. But the appeal of retro screen time is deeper than nostalgia. These shows feel different – slower, less frantic.The problem with some modern programmes isn’t the content, it’s the pacing. Just flick on popular shows such asCocomelon,PAW PatrolorBlippi: choppy editing, vivid colours and dizzyingly repetitive soundtracks. I don’t know if this is the norm in all episodes of these shows or if it was just the few episodes I happened to briefly see. If that is overstimulating to a tired woman in her 30s, what does it do to a small person who is still in the process of becoming fully formed?Studies have foundthat fast-paced cartoons can directly impact a young child’s attention and “executive function” – things like self-regulation and memory.Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TVRead moreEarlier this year, thegovernment issuedits firstscreen time guidancefor under-fives. Much of the focus was on the clock: how long children should spend in front of screens. But what if we’re counting the wrong thing? Two children can watch 20 minutes of TV and have completely different experiences and reactions based on the quality of that content. As Natalia Kucirkova, a professor of early childhood education, identified in aGuardian articlethis month: “Good children’s media gives a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keeps interrupting that act.”Choosing older, slower shows has become a simple form of parental quality control. But, like all decisions in modern parenting, this is already becoming yet another shame stick with which to beat parents (especially mothers). I care deeply about the media my child consumes, and worry about a future full of screens that I will have less and less control over. But what I resent is “slow TV” as another badge of the virtuous mother – when the reality is that parents are being asked to make increasingly complex judgments about media, while the media itself is only getting better at capturing attention.Rather than turn this into another tool for judging parents, we should ask why they have been made solely responsible for fixing a children’s media ecosystem that appears toprioritise engagement retentionover development. This can’t be entirely our burden to bear. The government is now planning to restrictsocial media access for under-16s, but the battle over children’s digital lives must start much earlier.Screen time has become necessary for many modern parents preciselybecausewe are stretched so thin – juggling work, extortionate childcare costs and dwindling social and community support. Yet we expect those same frazzled, time-poor parents to make conscious, complicated choices every time they turn on the TV, while commercial platforms pour resources into capturing children’s attention from the youngest possible age.We have seen the impact of rapid-fire digital content on adult brains. We are living it, all of us grappling with our own screen addictions, mourning our own loss of attention span, our disinclination to read and connect with the real world. We cannot allow media companies to apply those same addictive principles to the content they create for society’s most vulnerable, and most porous, brains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy son learned a new phrase recently – “Mama, stop phone!” – which sent a monumental pang of guilt and shame through me. Before my little boy is plunged into the dopamine loop of infinite scrolling that I – as an adult – find so hard to escape, I would like to trust that the majority of children’s media he is exposed to is much gentler on his mind. Until that day comes, I’ll be finding refuge in old-school Postman Pat.Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern BritainExplore more on these topicsChildren's TVOpinionParents and parentingCBeebiesChildrenFamilyTelevision industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Drumcree parade: ghosts from the past have brought Stormont to the brink | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A reckless decision to authorise an Orange Order parade with a notorious history has deepened the political crisis in the Northern Ireland executive
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A reckless decision to authorise an Orange Order parade with a notorious history has deepened the political crisis in the Northern Ireland executive
Content: Protesters block Garvaghy Road in Portadown, Northern Ireland, ahead of an Orange Order parade on 27 September.Photograph: Peter Morrison/PAView image in fullscreenProtesters block Garvaghy Road in Portadown, Northern Ireland, ahead of an Orange Order parade on 27 September.Photograph: Peter Morrison/PAOpinionNorthern IrelandThe Guardian view on the Drumcree parade: ghosts from the past have brought Stormont to the brinkEditorialA reckless decision to authorise an Orange Order parade with a notorious history has deepened the political crisis in the Northern Ireland executiveMon 28 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTShareThe last time that the Orange Order successfullymarchedfrom Drumcree parish church down the Garvaghy Road, a mainly Catholic part of Portadown, it required a British army presence and a lockdown of locals forced off their own streets. The 1997 parade was preceded by loyalist death threats and followed by nationalist riots, in which more than 160 people were injured. The lengthy track record of lethal violence and disorder associated with the march led the Parades Commission – established the following year as part of the peace process – to ban it.On Sunday, however, in scenes that rolled back the years in deeply unwelcome fashion, the old traumas and hostilities were recklessly allowed to resurface. Unfathomably, after a routine decision to renew the ban this year was challenged on procedural grounds, the commissioners reversed their ruling late last week and permitted a march to go ahead on a limited scale. The entirely predictable result was atense standoffand a political crisis in Stormont, after protesters blocked the Garvaghy Road route until the early hours of Monday morning.View image in fullscreenSir Chris Bryant.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAFacilitating the parade – a decision witheringlycriticisedby the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin – was a grievous unforced error on the part of the Parades Commission. Police advice that it was unlikely to provoke disorder was tin-eared, given the context. Orange Order parades now take place without incident across Northern Ireland each summer. But Drumcree’s notorious history makes it prime territory for unionists seeking to reignite a culture war and provoke a response.Thankfully, violence was averted. But the continuing fallout of a needless episode has dangerously exacerbated tensions in the deadlocked Northern Ireland executive, as it approaches a final Westminster deadline for agreeing abudget. Unionist demands for a police investigation, on the grounds that the Sinn Féin first minister, Michelle O’Neill, broke the law by attending the protest, are indicative of a polarising political climate that bodes ill for the future.Depressingly, in the short term that may suit both Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist party (DUP). After being damaged by internalscandaland spectacular misjudgments over Brexit, the DUP is attempting to shore up its base and see off a challenge from the still more hardline Traditional Unionist Voice party. Sinn Féin’s support has also been slipping amidstasisat Stormont and calls for a faster push towards aunited Ireland.As division and acrimony deepen, the desire of most voters for afunctioningexecutive seems dismally low on the list of priorities. The Drumcree standoff was the worst possible way to begin a crunch week of talks over a budget that should have been set six months ago. On Sunday, the new Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, flew to Belfast to meet political leaders and members of the Garvaghy Road residents’ association. He already looks to have one of the most challenging jobs in Andy Burnham’s cabinet, as cross-party relations in the assembly break down and fears of a DUP walkout mount.Calling for “calm on all sides”, the prime minister has stressed the need to preserve the gains made since theGood Friday agreement. That is the right message. But disastrously wrong calls on Drumcree, from bodies that should have known better, have now brought Stormont to the brink.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandOpinionSinn FéinNorthern Irish politicsDemocratic Unionist party (DUP)Michelle O'NeillGood Friday agreementeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Britain’s new chancellor: his purpose must be to protect living standards | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: John Healey has offered a vision, but an energy shock will mean households and businesses need to be offered help in the budget
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: John Healey has offered a vision, but an energy shock will mean households and businesses need to be offered help in the budget
Content: John Healey speaking at the Labour party conference on 28 September. ‘What was left unsaid by Mr Healey was far more important than what was said.’Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJohn Healey speaking at the Labour party conference on 28 September. ‘What was left unsaid by Mr Healey was far more important than what was said.’Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionJohn HealeyThe Guardian view on Britain’s new chancellor: his purpose must be to protect living standardsEditorialJohn Healey has offered a vision, but an energy shock will mean households and businesses need to be offered help in the budgetMon 28 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTShareIn his first speech to Labour party conference as chancellor, John Healey offered prudence with a purpose in a speech stylistically redolent of his former boss Gordon Brown. Mr Healey madefiscal credibilitythe condition for his goal of turbocharging apprenticeships for young people, funding for unions to reskill workers and spending on defence to create manufacturing jobs. The speech’s imagery was canny: miners, shipyards and submarines give “reindustrialisation” a recognisable Labour history. He also faced the future with a clever line about British workers “harnessing AI, not being outrun by it”. His message was that the “politics of hope” will be earned through “fiscal discipline, good work and through strong industries”.The new Labour chancellor sounded like New Labour when heclaimedthat it was “not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill”. What was lacking was a plan for care work, public services and the energy transition. Mr Healey clearly has a story about the supply of properly trained workers and another one about revitalising industry, but he offered little explanation of how enough good jobs will be created across the wider economy. Labelling a defence contract “industrial renewal” does not prove it is the best use of state capacity.Worldwide economic shocks and trade tensions, Mr Healey warned, are being felt hard at home – from prices at the pump to monthly mortgage payments. Andy Burnham offered the public “breathing space” when he entered Downing Street – with a £150 warm‑home discount for 6m low-income households and an electricity VAT cut worth£45for bill payers. But with no end in sight to the war on Iran and the resulting disruption to the strait of Hormuz, that will not be enough. Energy bills are forecast to rise by as much as 26% in January. Oneprojectionsees a typical household’s bill jump by £442 to £2,165. Petrol is at its highestpricesince the summer of 2022, whiledieselis approaching its all‑time high.What was left unsaid by Mr Healey was far more important than what was said. He made no promise of additional support for individuals and businesses in the forthcomingbudget. But with a price shock imminent, surely this is the real purpose behind his prudence. Mr Healey has tied his hands with his predecessor’s fiscal rules. The self-imposed restraint limits the chancellor’s ability to respond to an energy shock.According to Cityeconomists, Mr Healey has only around half the £24bn headroom that the Treasury had earlier this year. Fuel duty is set to start rising from January – but leaving it at current levels until the end of this parliament would costroughly£3.6bn. In June, the Trades Union Congressproposedcovering two-thirds of households with targeted help that would cost £6bn. Such schemes would use up most of the headroom, even before offering business reliefs.Mr Healey is choosing thesize of the bufferas his test of credibility. But he must also protect living standards. Having criticised Tory austerity in his speech, it’s hard to see how he could announce large-scale departmental cuts. The size of the headroom that the chancellor is prepared to tolerate will determine whether his budget looks like taxing to fund a modest energy rescue package, or borrowing for a larger one.Explore more on these topicsJohn HealeyOpinionLabourLabour conference 2026Economic policyBudgetIndustrial policyTax and spendingeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: How the Manchester City scandal could play out | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the guilty verdict against the football club for breaking the Premier League’s financial fair play rules
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the guilty verdict against the football club for breaking the Premier League’s financial fair play rules
Content: ‘Money did not enable City players to train harder or run faster.’Photograph: picturebox-uk.com/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Money did not enable City players to train harder or run faster.’Photograph: picturebox-uk.com/AlamyManchester CityLettersHow the Manchester City scandal could play outReaders respond to the guilty verdict against the football club for breaking the Premier League’s financial fair play rulesMon 28 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.03 EDTShareThirty six years ago, the team I support, Swindon Town, were severely punished for financial irregularities that pale into comparison with those of Manchester City (Manchester City found guilty of breaking Premier League’s financial fair play rules, 25 September). We were initially sentenced to be relegated two divisions but, after appeal, refused entry to Division One. It was an incredibly painful experience for us as fans and I feel for those City fans who have enjoyed the last years so fully, but now see it tainted through no fault of theirs.At the time, a number of journalists made the case that, as off-field crimes had resulted in on-field success, the punishment was fitting. What is different this time is the scale of the offences and the amount of on-field success. Once the appeal process has concluded, and ifManchester Citystill face punishment, a proportionate scaling up of consequences from those that we experienced in 1990 could mean that club facing relegation and removal of titles.The question is whether the footballing authorities are willing to deal with one of their marquee brands with the same dispassionate ruthlessness that they used to deal with us 36 years ago.Tim BeaumontLiverpoolIt’s unusual for me to find fault with anything that the wonderful Barney Ronay writes, but I must dispute his piece about Manchester City (The age of asterisk: Manchester City’s glittering era of success is tainted now, 25 September) on two counts.As a supporter of 50 years’ standing, I would not be unhappy to see my beloved club relegated or hit with any other fully justified punishment. But if money alone ensured success, a number of English clubs would have won far more trophies in the past 10 or 20 years.Money did not enable City players to train harder or run faster, let alone put together all the manifold and complex qualities that go into making the remarkable football team that they have been at various times.As the magnificentRodri has said, City’s victories were paid for with effort, with partnership and with being shoulder to shoulder each and every day. Furthermore, the claim that City wouldn’t have won this or that trophy without this or that player is impossible to prove.Richard BryantLondonAs a lifelong Liverpool supporter I might be expected to indulge in a little schadenfreude at the kicking that Manchester City is receiving, but it is obvious that over the last 15 years or so, the club has brought much more than footballing glory to Manchester. Tens of millions of pounds have been spent on the successful regeneration of a huge area of urban decay and the club’s City in the Community scheme has benefited large numbers of children through its training sessions in schools and imaginatively planned multifunctional play areas in parks.Marilyn RowleyDidsbury, ManchesterBarney Ronay might be right to feel some sympathy for Manchester City followers. But this should surely be restricted to children and to longstanding supporters who endured years of miserable underachievement. It’s harder to shed a tear for anyone who discovered a love for the club after the money poured in from a federation of monarchies with no political parties and a dreadful human rights record.John WheatcroftAuthor, The Strange Death of FootballShould the reported findings that Manchester City has broken many of football’s financial fair play rules be confirmed and upheld after any appeals, there will remain the difficult question: what is the fairest thing to do about all the honours that the club and its players won – at the expense of other clubs, coaches and players? I suggest that the fairest solution from a sporting standpoint would be for City’s players and coaching staff to be allowed to keep their medals, but the club (which would be the “guilty” party) be stripped of the trophies.The clubs that finished second and their players and coaches should receive winners trophies and medals. A messy solution, but arguably the fairest, given the circumstances. The financial resolutions could be guided by a similar principle.Alan MurphyLondonExplore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFinancial fair playFinancesSwindonlettersShareReuse this content

title: What if the Seven Up! series started today? | Television | The Guardian
description: Letters: Gordon McDougall recalls finding the original children to feature in the documentary strand that started in 1964
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Gordon McDougall recalls finding the original children to feature in the documentary strand that started in 1964
Content: The cast and crew of 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe cast and crew of 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockTelevisionLettersWhat if the Seven Up! series started today?Gordon McDougallrecalls finding the original children to feature in the documentary strand that started in 1964Mon 28 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.03 EDTShareIn your editorial on the Up series (20 September), your point is well made that exposing seven‑year-olds on television today would expose them to dangers not encountered in the 60s.However, Seven Up! was made in the early part of 1964, not 1963 as you stated, and it was the brainchild of Tim Hewat, the producer of World in Action.As he was leaving the series, the oversight was given to the Canadian director Paul Almond and, for our first jobs after passing through training,Michael Aptedand I were given the task of finding the original 20 children (14 of whom were followed in subsequent films). The show was seen as a one‑off and it was only at the instigation of Denis Forman, then CEO of Granada TV, that the follow-up, 7 Plus Seven, was commissioned in 1969. I was too busy running the Stables Theatre Club to work on it, so Apted directed it alone.There was no obligation on any of the participants to take part in any of the follow-up programmes and, as your editorial points out, some declined either partly or entirely. I have kept in touch with the 14 who made it through to 63 Up and, while some have complained of a socialist bias to the series, none have felt their lives impaired by taking part in it.Indeed, as seen in Nick’s desire to be as famous as a scientist as he is from the series, or Tony being asked for a selfie instead of his taxi passenger, Buzz Aldrin, fame has had a pleasurable, even comic aspect. And the interaction between participants who would not otherwise have known each other has often been very positive.Although Hewat’s intention was to show the inevitability of change beyond the age of seven and thus the inequality of society, our aim in the original search was to find interesting children. This was, of course, mediated by the decision to explore extremes – in income ranges and privilege as well as in urban/rural and north/south locations. But I feel it is certain that, were the series to be started today, the disparities between a similar selection of children would be even greater.Gordon McDougallClevedon, SomersetHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Don’t get your kegs, keks and kex in a twist  | North-south divide | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Zahaan Bharmal’s experience of getting to grips with the Yorkshire dialect
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Zahaan Bharmal’s experience of getting to grips with the Yorkshire dialect
Content: Cow parsley (Anthriscus sylvestris), also known as kex.Photograph: John Keates/AlamyView image in fullscreenCow parsley (Anthriscus sylvestris), also known as kex.Photograph: John Keates/AlamyNorth-south divideLettersDon’t get your kegs, keks and kex in a twistReaders respond to Zahaan Bharmal’s experience of getting to grips with the  Yorkshire dialectMon 28 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.03 EDTShareZahaan Bharmal’s observation on the north-south pronunciation divide (Could we be about to see the end of northern English dialects? My experience – and the science – says aye, 23 September) is neatly corroborated in Rosie Webb’s otherwise delightfully rhyming children’s book Chimpanzees in Dungarees: reading aloud to our grandchildren, my Mancunian partner is forced to southernise the page about “gir-ar-ffes in scarfs”. A dozen miles fromWebb’s Bristol baseis a place that exemplifies the third, south-western variant: the long “aa” sound. I mean Bath, aka Baaff or Barth. The cities are close, but one is posh, the other not so much.Tony BenjaminBristolPlease inform Mr Bharmal that up here in t’north as everyYorkshire(and Derbyshire) man knows,kegscan only store beer and the like. But kexis an umbelliferous flower to be seen while strolling through a meadow wearing your keks.Stuart GarsideNew Mills, DerbyshireI’ve obviously been away in that there London far too long; when I were a lad in Guiseley, trousers were keks, not kegs. Perhaps that is the joke that Zahaan Bharmal has been sold? ’Appen he’s reet, but as is often said about Yorkshiremen, you can tell one, but you can’t tell him much.Simeon GilchristEast Sheen, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
