title: Do the British Museum’s links with Palantir and BP bring it into disrepute? | British Museum | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Chris Garrard responds to an article about George Osborne assuming that Palantir founder Peter Thiel’s visit to view the Bayeux tapestry would remain secret
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Chris Garrard responds to an article about George Osborne assuming that Palantir founder Peter Thiel’s visit to view the Bayeux tapestry would remain secret
Content: The British Museum: ‘Osborne’s austerity policies led to job losses and the closure of many cultural organisations.’Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe British Museum: ‘Osborne’s austerity policies led to job losses and the closure of many cultural organisations.’Photograph: Andy Rain/EPABritish MuseumLettersDo the British Museum’s links with Palantir and BP bring it into disrepute?Dr Chris Garrardresponds to an article about George Osborne assuming that Palantir founder Peter Thiel’s visit to view the Bayeux tapestry would remain secretMon 28 Sep 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTShareAs the chair of the British Museum, George Osborne is aholder of public office with a dutyto be transparent. His comment that “it wasn’t like we expected anyone to know” about the billionaire Peter Thiel’s private view of the Bayeux tapestry suggests his loyalties lie more with the founder of Palantir and friend of Jeffrey Epstein over the openness that a national museum should demonstrate (George Osborne ‘thought Peter Thiel’s Bayeux tapestry visit would be secret’, 19 September).Osborne then made the claim that the museum would shut down without unethical corporate sponsors such as BP. In fact, just a few weeks ago London’s Science Museumended its decades-long partnershipwith BP, joiningTate, theNational Portrait Galleryand others. Last year, 91% of members of the Museums Association also ratifieda new code of ethics, which says that museums should “Transition away from sponsorship from organisations involved with environmental harm (including fossil fuels), [and] human rights abuses”.What is categorically true is that Osborne’s austerity policies led to job losses and the closure of many cultural organisations, while he subsidised oil and gas producers including BP, whose emissions fuelled the wild fires and droughts we now face. By giving the perception of personally aligning the museum with Palantir,Igor Tulchinskyand BP, Osborne is unnecessarily bringing it into disrepute.Dr Chris GarrardCo-director,Culture UnstainedExplore more on these topicsBritish MuseumGeorge OsborneBayeux tapestryPalantirPeter ThielBPMuseumslettersShareReuse this content

title: Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City have come out fighting against the guilty verdict but the Premier League faces questions of its own
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Manchester City have come out fighting against the guilty verdict but the Premier League faces questions of its own
Content: Vincent Kompany and his Manchester City teammates lift the Premier League trophy in 2018.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVincent Kompany and his Manchester City teammates lift the Premier League trophy in 2018.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesManchester CityScale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibilityBarney RonayManchester City have come out fighting against the guilty verdict but the Premier League faces questions of its ownMon 28 Sep 2026 15.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTShareNothing is over, nothing is done. Or at least not judging by the bravura, balls-out confidence of Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, who remains convinced the past three days of whiplash are simply the drumroll before the big reveal, prelude to some clinching piece of evidence that will swish away the initial finding of guilt on the Premier League’s 100-plus charges.This appears to be the official City position right now. Rope‑a‑dope litigation. Scooby‑Doo justice. A verdict that is simply exposition, buildup to that moment where we finally get to rip off the zombie mask and reveal the cranky old amusement park owner underneath, with his bulging ring‑binder full of irrefutable evidence of City’s innocence.Mancini refers to ‘double’ Manchester City contract and says it ‘isn’t my problem’Read moreThis is certainly one way of going about things. Lord Pannick KC, Mystery Machine Chambers. Come for the legal expertise. Stay for the unfathomable brinkmanship.That great escape may still present itself in more nuanced ways, most obviously in the question of what the actual punishment is here. But even in the current in-between days this feels like the end of an era. The greatest decade in the history of nation-state football projects is over. They’re selling Pep wigs in Woolworths. And we have failed, barring that promised deus ex machina, to paint it sky blue.So what next? It is understandable there should be a great deal of confusion. This has never happened before. It is without precedent. The common assumption is that events will unfold like this: sanctions first, perhaps as early as midweek. Then an appeal. Then whatever comes next. But someone is suing someone. And it won’t be cheap or quick.For now, the scale of City’s punishment is the only story in town. A verdict means nothing without the hammer of actual consequences. The triumphalism of those who seem personally invested in seeing City fail could still turn out to be premature.There are many suggestions of how this may play out. Among the more lenient is a combination of a major fine, a one-season points deduction and a transfer ban. In other words, punishment that looks like punishment but isn’t really. Everyone feels vaguely vindicated. We carry on.View image in fullscreenThe Manchester City chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, issued a statement on Saturday that has only added to the sense of confusion.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAThere is the suggestion of political pressure applied by City’s owners, as reported most recently by Bloomberg, with the idea floated that the United Arab Emirates government wishes to see its investment protected as a quid pro quo for its trading partnership with the UK. This is not actually a conspiracy theory. It’s how the world works. Politics is real. Football is not.At the other end of the scale is a suggestion thePremier Leaguewill press for major sanctions as a means of heading off a disastrous round of internecine litigation, club-on-club action that would risk torpedoing the thing we’ve all been watching for the past 15 years. Yes: truth, fair play, stolen glory. But won’t someone think of the brand?Here is one small suggestion. If the verdict does hold up, the punishment handed down should include a lengthy ban on City having any kind of sponsorship. This would at least speak to the core of the charges, the allegation that state-owned companies were used to funnel in direct investment. It would force City to grow their revenue by more standard means. It may even have a beneficial effect.Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?Read moreNot that anyone is talking about compromise yet. One of the most notable aspects is how utterly entrenched aspects of City’s fanbase seem to be on this. Facts are malleable, principles relative. Everything must be bent to your interests.There is a very important distinction here. It is entirely legitimate to question the existing rules. Maybe outside investment should be allowed. Spending your own money on your own property, pumping funds into the system, adding not taking: this seems not just reasonable but commendable. How can it be a crime?This is to wilfully misunderstand the equation. If everyone else is obeying the rules, if the entire culture is based around competitiveness, then this becomes not just deceit and deliberate cheating, but a trashing of the basic idea of sport.And, in the end, this affects people’s lives in tangible ways. Not just hopes and dreams, but employment, wellbeing, the goals you work for all your life. How many families have been uprooted, incomes affected, moments of happiness scrubbed byoutcomes that might have gone the other way?This is the state of cognitive dissonance described in al-Mubarak’s statement, which is also the only official comment by any party so far. It is not surprising there should be zero acknowledgement of any culpability, or even legitimacy to the charges. Hang on to a rising balloon and you face a difficult decision. Let go before it’s too late or just keep getting higher. Al-Mubarak is in a difficult position here, frontman for a propaganda project that has spectacularly crashed. Faced with this he has trebled and quadrupled down, and in the most tribalist way.View image in fullscreenManchester City fans at the Etihad Stadium in 2012, when they had just won their first Premier League title.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/Getty Images“This club matters to me,” al-Mubarak begins, a club executive who is, as things stand, guilty of destroying that club’s future prospects. There is dark talk of “media reporting”, with its implication of lies and fake news, as though this is all just another structural obstacle in the way of the true victims here, inherited dictatorial billionaires.“Here’s what I said to my family,” al-Mubarak goes on, weirdly dragging his own relatives into the picture, before offering once again the most intriguing element, the suggestion there is some key detail here, some game-changing element City are desperate to get out, but which has so far been prevented from entering a properly constituted legal tribunal. “There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident.” This is not a standard line after being found almost unanimously guilty.So what is he getting at? Part of the problem is the rush to demonise only one side, to see simply bad guys and good guys. In reality, it seems likely the written judgment will heavily criticise the Premier League’s governance.Rightly so. These charges have been doggedly pursued, but what about, well, everything else? How did an organisation that maintains its serial champions have been cheating for a decade and a half allow this entity into its competition in the first place? How did it fail so completely to regulate it?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow about, to choose one example, Roman Abramovich, the Kremlin-connected oligarch on whom the British government overnight imposed sanctions as an unfit person, whose own irregularities are well documented? The Premier League has always basically been a TV rights agency masquerading as a regulator. As long as the show rolls on, well, the show rolls on.This is the only real conclusion to be drawn from any of this. Some kind of governance is being effected here. But this remains a leaking, lurching pirate ship of an organisation. In any sane version of the current timeline there would be pressure for a complete reconsideration of how and why the Premier League exists.One thing was obvious years before the current state of emergency: countries should not own football clubs. Sovereign wealth funds should not own football clubs. There is an irreconcilable conflict of objectives here. All is fair in foreign policy. Countries will spy, steal and misdirect to gain influence. It is pretty much a patriotic duty to do these things.But you really don’t need to invite that level of supra-judicial chicanery into your delicate cultural treasure of a sport. What did anyone think was going to happen here? What would the people of the Netherlands think if the UK government bought AZ Alkmaar and began pumping in funds via sponsorship deals with National Rail and the Highways Agency, all the while promising to play fair? This is what the Premier League has permitted. You don’t really get to act surprised when it goes a bit wonky.View image in fullscreenThe sun sets over the Etihad Stadium.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAIt is also important to remember that English football hovers like a locust cloud over every other league. The reeling-in of talent and expertise is hugely destabilising. How are you supposed to feel in Germany or Belgium about the fact City and Chelsea have between them spent more than £3bn on transfer fees, all of which is now tainted, apparently put into circulation by something other than a legitimate sporting project?There is a fair case for Uefa to seek recompense, even to withdraw its patronage until this bandit league gets its own house in order. This won’t happen, because of eyeballs and income flows. But this is down to the balance of power, not any sensible idea of procedure or morality.What next, then? It is hard to see how a combined 89 charges of failure to provide accurate information or to cooperate with an investigation can be overturned on appeal. But it is also far from impossible. City’s bullishness is presumably based on information from their legal team. The next stage after appeal would be the high court, where different rules on evidence and the law may apply. Perhaps the long game is to get to that stage. It may even work, as it did at the court of arbitration for sport with the Uefa case. Or maybe they’re just planning to spin it out until everyone goes broke, dies or gets into esports.But in the end, why would you do this? What do you actually want from football? Is proving to the last decimal point that this is all technically admissible really a desirable outcome? The level of sustained, destructive aggression is telling in itself. As are the potential macro-implications.Ever feel you’ve been cheated? Consequences could be profound after Manchester City guilty verdict | Jonathan WilsonRead moreMost obviously, this case speaks more widely to the way money and power flow in and out of Britain. One version of the endgame is that City’s owners could be forced by the football regulator to sell up. Manchester City are a vast going concern. Imagine the wider shockwaves if this were to happen.View image in fullscreenPep Guardiola with the Manchester City chairman, Khaldoon al-Mubarak.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PATo take one example, a significant amount of the UK property market’s enduring rock‑solid value is built on the idea of inviolable property rights, safety in ownership. Where better to park your funds than a place where the rule of law seems to work for and not against you? London alone is said to have more than £4bn worth of value bound up in dark money. Imagine the ripple effects if a decision on a set of sporting regulations ends with a sovereign state being ordered to forfeit property. Never mind the abrupt lurch into negative equity. It’s enough to make you feel a little pride once more in the power of the wig and the rulebook.More directly, this remains an existential threat to the league. Not least in the depth of ill-feeling. City’s owners clearly have a deep hostility towards their fellow Premier League members, who are being portrayed as partial and culturally biased. Why would you want to remain part of this organisation? Why would you make any effort to protect it?Nothing is over, nothing is done. All that seems certain is that this would probably be a good time to hoist the death’s‑head flag and get that old Super League ship rolling again. There might just be a few more takers this time.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFinancescommentShareReuse this content

title: Gianni Infantino ready to accept demands for larger payouts from $6bn reserves | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The Fifa president has said ‘the ambition is welcome’ in a letter sent to all six confederation presidents, while also mounting a fresh defence of his failed FFE scheme
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Fifa president has said ‘the ambition is welcome’ in a letter sent to all six confederation presidents, while also mounting a fresh defence of his failed FFE scheme
Content: Gianni Infantino has pledged to ‘support the greatest level of additional funding’.Photograph: Andrea Amato/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino has pledged to ‘support the greatest level of additional funding’.Photograph: Andrea Amato/NurPhoto/ShutterstockFifaGianni Infantino ready to accept demands for larger payouts from $6bn reservesFifa president says: ‘The ambition is welcome’Infantino mounts fresh defence of failed FFE schemeMatt HughesMon 28 Sep 2026 18.14 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Fifa president,Gianni Infantino, is poised to bow to demands from Uefa and Concacaf to distribute more money from its $6bn cash reserves to member associations.In a letter sent on Monday to all six confederation presidents and copied to members of theFifacouncil, Infantino indicated his willingness to “support the greatest level of additional funding”, without committing to the $10m-per-member that has been proposed.Europe’s top-flight clubs to get share of £185m from Club World CupRead moreInfantino was responding to ajoint letter sent by the Uefa and Concacaf presidents, Aleksander Ceferin and Victor Montagliani, earlier this month, who called for an additional payout for all of Fifa’s 211 members of at least $10m during the 2027-2030 commercial cycle, a demand which was subsequently endorsed in a separate letter from the Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa.Infantino said the presidents’ proposals will be considered by the Fifa council during its next meeting on 15 October, after the secretary general, Mattias Grafström, has consolidated the suggestions. Under the proposed terms ofInfantino’s abandoned Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, the member associations would have received an additional $20m during the next four-year cycle, plus a further payment of $20m had they signed up before a 53-day deadline that would have expired last week.“I will not prejudge the amount,” Infantino wrote in the letter. “I will support the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered through Fifa’s proper governance process, applied fairly and supported by transparent and auditable arrangements. The ambition is welcome. The financial evidence, governance and implementation must now support it.“A single figure can begin the discussion, but it cannot complete a global policy. I have therefore instructed the Secretary General to consolidate all submissions into one integrated assessment for consideration by the Fifa council on 15 October 2026.”Infantino also used the letterto mount another defence of his role in FFE, which he claimed was an attempt to increase Fifa’s investment in football. “The recent commercial proposal, now withdrawn, was intended to enable Fifa to invest more in football – not to replace support that could responsibly be provided from existing resources,” he wrote.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I welcome the constructive intent reflected in each of your letters. We may differ on the best route forward, but I have no doubt that each of us wants what is best for Fifa, its member associations and football.”Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoUefaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thomas Tuchel resists change against Czechia despite England defensive errors | England | The Guardian
description: The head coach, who has injury concerns over Nico O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa, said: ‘We defended well [against Spain] but we had big individual mistakes’
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: The head coach, who has injury concerns over Nico O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa, said: ‘We defended well [against Spain] but we had big individual mistakes’
Content: Errors from Marc Guéhi (above) and Nico O’Reilly led to two Spain goals in defeat at Wembley on Saturday.Photograph: Frankie OKeeffe/PPAUK/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenErrors from Marc Guéhi (above) and Nico O’Reilly led to two Spain goals in defeat at Wembley on Saturday.Photograph: Frankie OKeeffe/PPAUK/ShutterstockEnglandThomas Tuchel resists change against Czechia despite England defensive errors‘We defended well [v Spain] but had individual mistakes’Nico O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa are injury doubts for matchJacob Steinbergin PragueMon 28 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel will resist making drastic changes to his defence despite England going six games without a clean sheet before facing Czechia in theNations Leagueon Tuesday.Although Tuchel acknowledged that his side were a “danger to ourselves” when theylost 3-2 against Spainlast Saturday, the head coach stood by Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly after their errors against the world champions.Defensive flux gives Tuchel headache but Alexander-Arnold could be remedy | Jacob SteinbergRead moreThe message was one of continuity asEnglandarrived in Prague for their second game in Nations League Group A3. Tuchel has injury concerns over O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa but is likely to keep the changes to a minimum at the back. James Trafford will continue in goal and Tuchel believes the defeat against Spain was down to individual mistakes rather than structural issues with England’s defending.“I didn’t see a pattern,” the German said. “It was individual mistakes. I didn’t see a pattern in defending. I think we defended very well in a block when we were organised, but we had just big individual mistakes. But I could not see any defensive pattern that would concern me.“From a purely defensive approach I felt that we defended much more disciplined, cohesive and organised than in some matches in the World Cup. That was a step in the right direction. We constantly pushed out from our middle block, we tried to go into the opponent’s half and pushed out of the deep block. We didn’t suffer too for long periods of time in defending. We never lost our structure.“I will not change now because someone made an individual mistake, and they’ve been good for us through all the other matches.”Two of Spain’s goals came from Guéhi and O’Reilly losing the ball in dangerous positions. “We need to improve these things but when we had the ball we were the biggest danger to ourselves around the box because we just had too many individual mistakes,” Tuchel said. “Purely in defending, I have no concerns.”Lewis Hall is in line to replace O’Reilly at left-back againstCzechiaand Trevoh Chalobah will hope to get the nod over Jarrad Branthwaite as Guéhi’s partner in the middle if Konsa is out. England want to reach next year’s finals and losing to Spain means they cannot experiment too much against Czechia, who were beaten by Croatia in their opening game.The big question is whether Trent Alexander-Arnold replaces Jarell Quansah at right-back and wins his first cap since June 2025. Alexander-Arnold, who did not go to the World Cup, was an unused substitute against Spain.“He had a very good training week and an excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us,” Tuchel said. “Today was a good training session. Everything is fine. He’s ready to go.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTuchel has explained that starting Trafford in England’s first two Nations League games is to see whether the Leeds goalkeeper can compete at this level. Jordan Pickford, who has been the No 1 since 2018, will return for the trip to Croatia on Saturday and the home game against Czechia next Tuesday.“We use the Nations League to see where we are with the other goalkeepers,” Tuchel said. “There was no reason from performances to open up this position for competition.“I think it’s necessary with every other player that we are aware of ‘what if’. If a player that starts a season well, like Traff at Leeds, [he] has the chance to prove it and to play in our style. We just need to see it at some point. We use this competition to actually give him the chance to push on.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelCzechiaNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel captain stokes feud by saying ‘our country is 10 times better than Ireland’ | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Manor Solomon has reacted angrily to the Republic of Ireland team’s behaviour before their Nations League match in protest at Israel’s military action in Gaza
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Manor Solomon has reacted angrily to the Republic of Ireland team’s behaviour before their Nations League match in protest at Israel’s military action in Gaza
Content: Republic of Ireland players bow their heads and wear black armbands during the Israel anthem.Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/ReutersView image in fullscreenRepublic of Ireland players bow their heads and wear black armbands during the Israel anthem.Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/ReutersNations LeagueIsrael captain stokes feud by saying ‘our country is 10 times better than Ireland’Manor Solomon angry at Ireland’s stance over Gaza‘They hate us and we don’t like them’Guardian sportMon 28 Sep 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManor Solomon claimed Israel was “10 times better” than Ireland as fallout intensified from theirNations Leaguematch and stated bluntly: “They hate us and we don’t like them.”Players in theRepublic of Irelandside stared at the ground during Israel’s anthem and their staff faced away from the pitch. Ireland’s players also chose not to shake hands or exchange pennants with their opponents in protest at Israeli military actions in Gaza which have killed tens of thousands of people.Republic of Ireland’s Gavin Bazunu boycotts Israel match ‘as a person of principle’Read moreSolomon, who plays for West Ham, told Israel’s Sport 5 channel: “If I say what I think about them I’ll probably be banned for a few games, so I don’t want to say what I think about them. Obviously they hate us and we don’t like them.”View image in fullscreenRepublic of Ireland captain Dara O’Shea (left) turns away from Israel captain Manor Solomon before kick-off.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesIrelandwon the game 3-0in Debrecen, Hungary, on Sunday and the return next Sunday will also be played on neutral territory, in Serbia. “I’m already looking forward to the next game against them,” Solomon, Israel’s captain, said.Pressed on Ireland’s behaviour during Israel’s anthem, he said: “They don’t interest me. We have a country 10 times better than theirs, stronger than theirs. We have an amazing country with amazing people.“We’re proud to wear the national team’s uniform and to be Israelis; proud of our country and our soldiers. And they can pull all the stunts they want and do whatever they want. We are Israelis, we love our country – and that’s how it will always be.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGet in touchContact Guardian SportThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: County pride and England chaos relegated Hundred to summer undercard | Cricket | The Guardian
description: The franchise tournament remains an enigma after an unexpectedly dramatic men’s international summer and a thrilling Championship title race
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: The franchise tournament remains an enigma after an unexpectedly dramatic men’s international summer and a thrilling Championship title race
Content: Private money attracted bigger-name players to the Hundred, but the tournament is still not embedded in English cricket culture.Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPrivate money attracted bigger-name players to the Hundred, but the tournament is still not embedded in English cricket culture.Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesCricketAnalysisCounty pride and England chaos relegated Hundred to summer undercardAli MartinFranchise tournament remains an enigma after an unexpectedly dramatic men’s international summer and a thrilling Championship title raceMon 28 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTShareAfter pumping astronomical sums of money into English cricket, the headline act of the summer should probably have beenthe Hundred’s rebirthunder private ownership. After all, the decks were relatively clear.There was no Ashes series or Indian arm-wrestle in Test cricket to hog the limelight, rather a small-plates menu of touring teams. The Women’s T20 World Cup was on home soil, but for all that it outdid its 50-over equivalent in 2017 by way of engagement, the men’s football World Cup dominated. Plus, folks kind of knew Nat Sciver-Brunt’s England side was not quite ready to derailthe Australian machine.Warwickshire peaked at the right time and are worthy championsRead moreYet six weeks after the Hundred finals at Lord’s, the mood at two of its host counties tells us something about where it sits in the sport’s consciousness. With the best will in the world, beyond a fun day out with the kids and a bumper pay packet for the players involved,it doesn’t appear to be that high.At Warwickshire on Sunday, they were celebratingtheir ninth County Championship title, the outfield flooded with supporters and players in clover. No one seemed too fussed that Birmingham Phoenix, the entity that is 50.4% Warwickshire‑owned, had stunk out the men’s and women’s Hundred. There was no talk of atonement or it being a mixed season. By definition, it will go down as a famous summer.Further north at Old Trafford things are very different. Manchester Super Giantswon the men’s Hundred, which you would think means people at Lancashire, 30% shareholders and with crossover in staff, are pretty chuffed; that Daniel Gidney would be sprinkled with red rose petals as he leaves his role as chief executive.View image in fullscreenEthan Bamber, the leading wicket-taker in the County Championship this season, took the wicket that confirmed Warwickshire as champions.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesHardly. Finishing second bottom in Division Two with two wins all season, Lancashire have pulled the plug on their end-of-season awards do and supporters are in a state of apoplexy. Mark Chilton has been sacked as director of cricket performance and the incoming chief executive, Richard Kenyon, will soon lead a “clear and objective look at our performance operation” – AKA the dreaded review.Clearly this is all a bit simplistic.The Hundredhas got a fresh audience through the gates – albeit attendance dipped 5% in 2026 – and the lines between the host counties and teams are blurred. More broadly, even if Birmingham Phoenix ultras were not exactly marching to Edgbaston with pitchforks, the franchise world is hardly soft on failure.Nevertheless, it says something about English sensibilities that the domestic cricket that truly stirred emotions – and in the case of Lancashire, recriminations – still came from its traditional year‑round structures. Money isn’t everything, it seems.The main attention thief – why the Hundred remained on the undercard in 2026 – was still the England men’s team. Even in a supposedly low-key summer by way of opposition, with India’s visit for white-ball cricket the biggest money-spinner, their travails were impossible to ignore. And in particular a Test team that served as the latest reminder about best-laid plans.View image in fullscreenA first international hundred for the resurgent Tom Banton completed a promising summer for England’s white-ball men’s teams.Photograph: Alex Davidson/ECB/Getty ImagesIt was supposed to be a quiet rebuild, withthe status quo retainedin terms of leadership and lessons learned from the winter’s Ashes debacle. Instead, the first half of the season was a psychodrama, featuringanother late-night drinking incident, a strung-out Ben Stokesquitting as Test captainand Brendon McCullumbeing demotedto white‑ball head coach after the 2-1 Test defeat against New Zealand.But looking ahead to the winter – white-ball tours of Pakistan and Australia, Test series in South Africa and Bangladesh, plus the 150th Anniversary Test in Melbourne – there is a sense of quiet optimism. Maybe, just maybe, England have emerged from the embers ofStokes’s Viking funeralin better shape.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideButtler out of Pakistan tourShowEngland will begin the next phase of their World Cup preparations without Jos Buttler after the former captain was ruled out of the forthcoming tour of Pakistan.Buttler injured his hamstring mid-innings against Sri Lanka at Headingley last week, retiring hurt but later returning to the crease in clear pain. He sat out the Metro Bank one-day international series decider at the Kia Oval on Sunday, which England won at a canter by 223 runs, and has now been told he will not be fit for the 50-over tri-series next month. There is no guarantee yet that the 36-year-old will be back for the subsequent trip to Australia in November.“Jos won’t be in Pakistan,” the white-ball head coach, Brendon McCullum, saidd. “It’s disappointing not to have Jos but it will be good for us to see where we’re at. Between now and 14 months’ time lots of things will go wrong, there’ll be lots of selections you think will happen and someone will get injured or there’ll be a scheduling issue. You almost have to catastrophise these things a little to prepare yourself for that World Cup.”In the short term, that means an extended chance for Jordan Cox as the wicketkeeper-batter. England are set to finalise their squad for Pakistan in the next 24 hours, with Sam Curran pushing for a return after groin trouble and further checks to be made on Adil Rashid’s bowling hand. Jacob Bethell is still recovering from a knee problem.Press AssociationPhotograph: Mike Egerton/PAWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.A year out from the World Cup in southern Africa, England’s white-ball set-up is on the rise. The Twenty20 team have won23 of their past 26 games, while after years of neglect the 50-over side has won all six bilateral series this year. Harry Brook’s young thrustersteam continue to play catch-up – they are absurdly light on domestic 50-over experience – but you can seea team starting to coalesce.If anything it probably shows how making McCullum head coach in all formats was a mistake in late 2024. Now specialising – and showing little bitterness at having had his wings clipped – McCullum has gone against his image and begun laying down a structured, rigorous setup. Fitness is his new pet project, while he is even pushing for more pre-World Cup warm-up games. ThoughKevin Pietersen’s return as a mentoris a gamble on one level, it could prove inspired.The Test team’s 3-0 sweep of Pakistan obviously had caveats, chiefly the tourists being ill‑equipped to deal with the Dukes ball wobbling off its seam andplumbing new depths of dysfunctionwhen seven players were axed mid-tour. It was not without another sideshow for England either when, at 1-0 up, Brydon Carsewound up in handcuffsoutside a Derby nightclub.Joe Root’s return to captaincyalso led to tactical gremlins re-emerging whenthe little‑known Razaullah went tontoat Edgbaston. Root’s returns with the bat dipped, but he provided a sense of calm and clarity after the whirlwind of Stokes, and oversaw a promising new-look pace attack. Ollie Robinson nipped out 29 wickets at nine runs apiece, while Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue bounced out perceptions of fragility by getting through 17 and 15 internationals respectively.View image in fullscreenBrendon McCullum (right) started the summer as the all-format coach and ended it replaced in Tests by Stephen Fleming (left) and adding Kevin Pietersen (centre) to his white-ball staff.Photograph: Matthew Lewis/Getty ImagesAnother healthier aspect was competition for places, rather than pumping caps into a set lineup. Jordan Cox, Dan Lawrence and Emilio Gay did not bolt down spots – Ben Duckett made England’sonly Test centuryall summer – but they made enough of an impression to force a tricky call when Jacob Bethell returns. The Lions setup also looks better for the appointment of Jonathan Trott as the head coach.There is much work to do, but this looks a sound starting point when Stephen Fleming begins life as the new Test head coach. The sibling-like relationship with McCullum should get him up to speed quickly and allow a grownup division of resources. Fleming has already issued the order to givemore credence to the World Test Championship, which can only be a good thing.Not that it will usurp the Ashes as English cricket’s overriding obsession anytime soon, coming around again in 2027. In turn, expect the Hundred’s wait for top billing in an English summer to continue for some time yet.Explore more on these topicsCricketThe HundredEngland cricket teamCounty ChampionshipanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Nations League: Olise’s late stunner leads France past Belgium, Italy rout Turkey | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Michael Olise’s magnificent late solo effort earned Zinedine Zidane’s side a win in Brussels, while Roberto Mancini’s Italy bounced back against Turkey
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Michael Olise’s magnificent late solo effort earned Zinedine Zidane’s side a win in Brussels, while Roberto Mancini’s Italy bounced back against Turkey
Content: Michael Olise celebrates his late winner against Belgium with teammate Ousmane Dembélé.Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMichael Olise celebrates his late winner against Belgium with teammate Ousmane Dembélé.Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockNations LeagueNations League: Olise’s late stunner leads France past Belgium, Italy rout TurkeyBelgium 0-1 France, Turkey 1-4 Italy, Sweden 3-1 PolandNorthern Ireland left frustrated by Hungary stalemateAFP and Press AssociationMon 28 Sep 2026 17.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Olise’s magnificent late strike gaveFrancea 1-0Nations Leaguevictory overBelgiumin Brussels, as Zinedine Zidane made it two wins out of two since being named as the new head coach.Olise came off the bench late on with the game goalless, and set off from inside his own half to score the winner in the 88th minute. Olise advanced all the way to the edge of theBelgiumarea before curling a shot beyond the reach of Senne Lammens.Gianni Infantino set to accept demands to give national associations payoutsRead moreFrance were missing Kylian Mbappé, who has returned to Real Madrid afterinjuring his left kneewhile scoring the winner against Turkey on Friday. The visitors still had the better of the chances with Désiré Doué cracking a shot off the bar in the first half and debutant Lucas Da Cunha striking a post early in the second half.The contest was heading to an unremarkable goalless conclusion until Olise intervened, having been sent on in the 77th minute in place of Bradley Barcola. France sit top of Group A1 with six points and will host Italy at the Stade de France on Friday, while Belgium entertainTurkeyin Liège.Italybounced back from an opening 2-0 defeat to Belgium in Rome, as they thrashedTurkey4-1 on a rainy night in Bursa.Roberto Mancini’s team dazzled in the downpour, scoring three goals inside the first half-hour as the hosts were punished for defensive errors in their muddy goalmouth. Italy went ahead when Bursa-born fullback Zeki Celik swung wildly at a low near-post corner, deflecting the ball to Alessandro Bastoni who fired into the roof of the net.View image in fullscreenMichael Kayode celebrates after scoring Italy’s third goal inside the first 30 minutes against Turkey.Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/ReutersAfter 23 minutes, Altay Bayindir flapped at a cross-shot from Michael Kayode and sent the ball into the path of Lazio’s Davide Frattesi, who tucked it home. Four minutes later, Kayode found himself free on the right side of the penalty area, and his near-post shot eluded the Turkish goalkeeper.Turkey gave the restless home crowd hope in the 47th minute when Gianluigi Donnarumma was drawn to Oguz Aydin beyond the far post. Aydin found Baris Yilmaz who drilled into an empty net, but the comeback lasted five minutes. Pio Esposito headed Italy’s fourth after Sandro Tonali had struck a post.Yilmaz looked to have cut the gap again with a curling effort but Aydin, bouncing up and down in front of Donnarumma, was offside. Esposito and his older sibling, Sebastiano, also made history in Bursa, becoming the first brothers to start an Italy game together since Aldo and Luigi Cevenini in 1915.In League B,Northern Irelandwere left frustrated after a 0-0 draw at home toHungarywhere the hosts passed up chances to take all three points. Patrick Kelly twice went close in the first half, hitting the crossbar with a looping effort, and Isaac Price was denied by Balázs Tóth late on.View image in fullscreenNorthern Ireland’s Patrick Kelly tries to lob the Hungary goalkeeper – but his effort came back off the crossbar.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAMichael O’Neill’s side could not make the breakthrough, though, and there were nervous moments late on as Ruairi McConville blocked Willi Orban’s shot and Pierce Charles saved from Alex Tóth. Northern Ireland sit joint-top of their group alongsideUkraine, who drew 0-0 withGeorgiain Tbilisi.In Group B4,Swedensaw offPoland3-1 in Solna to earn their second win in two games. Celtic’s Benjamin Nygren pounced at the far post after eight minutes to give the hosts the lead, but Sebastian Szymanski levelled with a shot that hit both posts before going in.Yasin Ayari restored the home lead when he finished neatly even as he was losing his footing, before Arsenal forward Victor Gyökeres added the coup de grace.Bosnia and Herzegovinaare second in the group after winning 4-2 againstRomaniain Bucharest.In League C, Aleksa Latkovic’s 89th minute effort clinched a 3-2 win forMontenegroagainstArmeniato take charge of their group, whileLatviaandCyprusdrew 0-0.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueFranceItalyBelgiumNorthern IrelandTurkeySwedennewsShareReuse this content

title: Luke Littler suffers shock defeat to Luke Woodhouse in World Grand Prix opener | Luke Littler | The Guardian
description: Playing for the first time since being booed in Amsterdam, the world No 1 was far from his best in a 2-1 first-round defeat in Leicester
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Playing for the first time since being booed in Amsterdam, the world No 1 was far from his best in a 2-1 first-round defeat in Leicester
Content: Luke Littler (right) congratulates Luke Woodhouse after his first-round victory in Leicester.Photograph: Godfrey Pitt/Action Plus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLuke Littler (right) congratulates Luke Woodhouse after his first-round victory in Leicester.Photograph: Godfrey Pitt/Action Plus/ShutterstockLuke LittlerLuke Littler suffers shock defeat to Luke Woodhouse in World Grand Prix openerLittler’s title defence ends in 2-1 first-round lossMichael van Gerwen also crashes out of last 32Press Association andGuardian sportMon 28 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 20.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuke Littler suffered a 2-1 defeat to Luke Woodhouse on his return to the oche as the defence of his World Grand Prix title ended at the first hurdle.The world No 1 was aiming to bounce back from his quarter-final exit to Jonny Clayton in the World Series of Darts in Amsterdam a week ago. Littler threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlandsafter being booed and whistledduring the event, and missed the latest Players Championship events in Den Bosch.Playing in front of a more supportive crowd in Leicester on Monday, Littler raced out of the blocks in the double-in, double-out format, taking the opening leg while Woodhouse was still in the 300s. “The Nuke” then hit a double 15 to complete a 106 checkout as he won the first set 3-1 despite looking far from his best.Woodhouse took the lead for the first time in the second set, the world No 18 from Worcestershire roaring 2-1 ahead in legs. Even when Littler levelled at 2-2, Woodhouse held his nerve on a double 16 in the decider to set up a deciding set.View image in fullscreenMichael van Gerwen also suffered an early exit, losing 2-1 to Ryan Joyce in the last 32.Photograph: Alex Young/Every Second Media/ShutterstockThe underdog came on strong in the final set, moving 2-0 ahead and then holding off a Littler fightback to complete a major upset. Woodhouse sealed victory on double 12, earning warm congratulations from Littler, who averaged 82.41 to his opponent’s 82.51. Woodhouse will playNathan Aspinallin the last 16, after he edged past Dutchman Kevin Doets 2-1.The 19-year-old double world champion was magnanimous after his defeat, writing on social media: “Well played @lukewoody180 was a good game … Luke took his chance and nice week off now, all the best to [him] for rest of the tournament.”Littler was one of three world champions to crash out in the last 32 on Monday, withRob Crosslosing 2-0 to the 12th seed,Wessel Nijman.Michael van Gerwen’s bid for a seventh World Grand Prix crown also ended on the opening night as he threw away a one-set lead, losing 2-1 toRyan Joyce.Gerwyn Pricecrushed Polish debutant Sebastian Bialecki 2-0, averaging 101.61 and nailing three 180s as the Welshman launched his bid to win a title he last claimed in 2020. Price will faceRoss Smithin the last 16 after he defeated Cameron Menzies, while Clayton and Danny Noppert also advanced.Explore more on these topicsLuke LittlerDartsMichael van GerwennewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Rugby’s in people’s blood here’: mutiny rising in west Wales as Scarlets fight WRU plan | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: No one at Parc y Scarlets understands why they and the Ospreys are on the chopping block for the union’s proposal to cut a club by 2028
Author: Andy Bull
Headline: No one at Parc y Scarlets understands why they and the Ospreys are on the chopping block for the union’s proposal to cut a club by 2028
Content: Scarlets v Cardiff in Llanelli. Scarlets are fighting for their existence, as are Ospreys. Cardiff’s future is safe.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianView image in fullscreenScarlets v Cardiff in Llanelli. Scarlets are fighting for their existence, as are Ospreys. Cardiff’s future is safe.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianRugby union‘Rugby’s in people’s blood here’: mutiny rising in west Wales as Scarlets fight WRU planNo one at Parc y Scarlets understands why they and the Ospreys are on the chopping block for the union’s proposal to cut a club by 2028Andy Bullin LlanelliMon 28 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight o’clock, Saturday night and at Parc yScarletsthe fans are starting to sing. Their scrum-half, Dane Blacker, has just come skipping through half a gap in the Cardiff line. Blacker has slipped the ball on to their loping lock, Sam Lousi, who has flicked it out the back of his hand to the centre Joe Roberts. And Roberts has juggled it up from one hand to the other, gathered it back in and gone sprinting in to score in the corner. They’re leading 5-0 and in the stands it’sSosban Fachand Hymns and Arias and “Scarlets! Scarlets! Scarlets!”And somewhere in among it all,reports will say later, a new chant too – “Dave Reddin’s a wanker”.The Guardian view on Welsh rugby: enduring an existential crisis with cultural roots | EditorialRead moreReddin, director of rugby at the Welsh Rugby Union and self‑identified “serial disrupter of elite sports performance”, has just recommitted to the union’s grand plan toscrap one of the four regional teams by 2028. Cardiff, who are owned by the WRU, have been told they are safe, and so have the Dragons, who play out of Newport. Which leaves the other two teams, Scarlets and Ospreys, fighting for one slot.“I understand the pain,” Reddin said. No one here believes him, any more than they would a doctor who warns that the amputation he’s about to perform may sting a bit.Out in the west, what they most want to know is why the Scarlets andOspreys, two teams who have won titles, turned out hundreds of Test players, and who, unlike Cardiff and Dragons, have never been into administration, have been told they are the ones who have to give. It was only 18 months ago that the WRU publicly committed to maintaining all four teams. And it was 12 months ago that it announced it was going to get rid of two. Six months ago it decided to keep three.Nigel Davies, Scarlets’s director of rugby, says: “It’s all so random at the moment, isn’t it? We’ve gone from four, definitely, to two, to three. I mean, it would be unacceptable in any other walk of life. That is not planning. That is chaos.”View image in fullscreenThe fans gather at the stadium before kick-off.Photograph: The GuardianSimon Muderack, Scarlets’ chairman, says: “To be blunt we’re not going anywhere.”It’s only by looking around their patch that you can really understand what he means. Parc y Scarlets, built in the early 2000s, seats 15,000, and has its own indoor and outdoor training facilities. The whole place is owned by the club.Davies sighs when he says: “I don’t know what they think we’ll do with this place if there’s no one to play here.”The stadium was the work of Muderack’s predecessor, Huw Evans, who oversaw construction when the Welsh clubs were being consolidated into regions. “It was a fight to the death really,” Evans says, “and building this place was our survival strategy.” It still is. Evans is back at the club for the Cardiff game to take part in a ceremony honouring former Scarlets players. The club are giving individual cap numbers to every one of the 2,600 who have played for them. Derek Quinnell is there, so is Dwayne Peel, the current head coach, so is Davies himself.The players being honoured came to the club from all across west Wales. Scarlets has always been a little different because its patch is so big. As they like to say, it’s the west’s team, even though the stadium is closer to the English border than the western coast. Pembroke, Cardigan, Aberystwyth, even Llareggub, Dylan Thomas’s fictional home town, they’re all part of the club. Earlier in the day I am up at Carmarthen, where Quins are playing Swansea in Super Rygbi Cymru. There’s a crowd of 250 or so. The Quins side has eight Scarlets players in it, most of them still kids.View image in fullscreenA small crowd watches Carmarthen play Swansea in the Super Rugby Wales competition.Photograph: Andy Bull/The Guardian“People in this region have always looked to the Scarlets as their team,” Davies says. “When I was a boy growing up, I wanted to play for the Scarlets, yeah, Wales would have been good, but Scarlets was the team, that’s what got me into rugby.”The club’s managing director, Jon Daniels, is Llangennech-born and bred. “Rugby’s in people’s blood here, has been for 150 years.” His grandad used to be in the steelworks. “When I was born this was all mines and works steel, tin, and all that gave us a real strong sense of community.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCardiff win the ball from a lineout against Scarlets.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianDaniels says Scarlets are the last part of it left standing. “What we are is west Wales. The day our community thinks they no longer need the Scarlets, that’s when we’re done,” he says. “The industry’s gone, the manufacturing’s gone, the mines are gone. Without the rugby, all it would become is a lovely place for people to come and visit on their holidays.” The club, he says, are “here to show the young people that they can be from a little village in west Wales and be world class.”Their fight isn’t with the Ospreys. “Ask anybody here, they want Ospreys to be around,” Davies says, “and ask anybody there, they will say the same about us.” It’s not even with Cardiff, or Dragons. It’s with the WRU. Muderack says: “I don’t really see how not going bankrupt can get you penalised. I struggle with that. It doesn’t sit well with me. And I don’t see how being the only holders of the main domestic league titles can get you penalised, either.”There’s only 15 miles or so between the two, and there have been times in the past when they’ve come close to a merger. “I would never say never,” Muderack says now. “But I think the world has moved on from that. And what I certainly don’t think makes any sense at all is a new franchise. Along the lines of a West Wales Warriors.”View image in fullscreenA picture of the former player Ray Gravell, in the likeness of Che Guevara, on the wall of the Tanner Banc Bar.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/The GuardianDavies says it is like these decisions are being passed down from an “ivory tower”, it’s an existential threat imposed, with no explanation, by people who don’t live in west Wales, and who, they say, haven’t taken the time to understand it. A series of workshops on all the cuts are due to start in December, but Muderack says there are no conversations going on now. “I mean, our primary communication mechanism at this point has been the public domain.”No one here is going to argue that Scarlets are getting everything right. The club is sustainable day‑to-day, but it carries a lot of debt. What they have, in abundance, is people who care. And when they’re threatened, they will fight. The club have just brought the former first minister Carwyn Jones on to the board. “Scarlets will always have people that look after it,” Muderack says. “I’ve been here six years, and in that time I’m going to be on my fifth WRU chair, and my fourth WRU CEO.”The four minutes that lasted a lifetime as Wallabies won all-time chaos classic | Jack SnapeRead moreMuderack is convinced that the answers ought to include more fixtures against the English teams, and more effort to draw in private investment. All this uncertainty makes both almost impossible. Daniels says: “It’s very difficult to have a straight story for our fans, for our sponsors, and our community.”So they press on as best they can. “Welsh rugby is in a tough place. Not just because of decisions made yesterday, but because of decisions made 10 years ago. And it might take another 10 years to get out of it. But it has to start with an open and honest conversation about what the real position is. And that conversation has to start with: ‘What do we have to do to keep four teams?’”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionScarletsOspreysWelsh Rugby UnionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve achieved more than I dreamed of’: Britain’s Katy Marchant retires from elite cycling  | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Katy Marchant, the Olympic gold medallist who also won world and European titles, has retired from cycling, saying: ‘I’m incredibly proud of where I’ve got to and what I’ve done’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Katy Marchant, the Olympic gold medallist who also won world and European titles, has retired from cycling, saying: ‘I’m incredibly proud of where I’ve got to and what I’ve done’
Content: Katy Marchant has changed her mind about competing at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenKaty Marchant has changed her mind about competing at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.Photograph: David Davies/PACycling‘I’ve achieved more than I dreamed of’: Britain’s Katy Marchant retires from elite cyclingOlympic gold medallist also won world and European titles‘I’m proud of where I’ve got to and what I’ve done’Press AssociationMon 28 Sep 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Olympic gold medallist Katy Marchant has announced her ­retirement. The 33-year-old took gold alongside Emma Finucane and Sophie Capewell in thewomen’s team sprintat the 2024 Paris Games, the same year she won world and European titles.“I’ve achieved more than I could ever have dreamed of achieving,” Marchant said, a few months after stating her goal of racing at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. “It just feels really strange. It’s not been a difficult decision. Don’t get me wrong, there’s been moments where I’ve thought: ‘Could I just, should I just, what if I just?’ But I know what it takes to push on for another two years.USA’s McNulty transcends chaos of Montreal road race to claim ‘miracle’ world titleRead more“I’m incredibly proud of where I’ve got to and what I’ve done. I just don’t want to make those choices any more to keep doing what it takes to get to LA.”Marchant competed in Paris two years after the birth of her first son, Arthur, and in January returned to competition at the British Track Championships six months after the birth of her second son, Walter.In the buildup to the ­Commonwealth Games, Marchant said she hoped to compete in Los Angeles, but after the Leeds-born rider helped England to secure team sprint silver in Glasgow she changed her mind. “I had a day off after two pretty successful days racing and I just had this funny feeling.”Marchant spoke to her husband, Rob, before returning for the final races of the Commonwealth programme, finishing fifth in the Keirin, and then took her time to reach a final decision.“I never wanted to walk away from this sport because I had to, because I felt like I’d overstayed my welcome or physically I wasn’t capable any more. I’ve written the story for the last 13 years and I wanted it to finish it the way I wanted to finish.”The team sprint gold in Paris was Marchant’s second Olympic medal after individual sprint bronze on debut in Rio in 2016. As well her titles from 2024, Marchant has two world bronze medals and two European silver medals, also winning team sprint bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games.While Marchant followed riders such as Dame Laura Kenny, Dame Sarah Storey and Lizzie Deignan in returning to elite racing after becoming a mother, she was the first to do it in track sprinting, which places different demands on the body.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor several years she was the sole senior women’s sprinter in the Great Britain squad, competing alone in Tokyo, and deserves credit for nurturing her young teammates on their road to glory in Paris. “There’s a small part of me that’s a little bit sad I’m not going to be part of that any more, but at the same time I carry a lot of pride that I helped build that,” she said.“I’m incredibly proud I got to do those things and hopefully pave the way not just for cyclists, but also mums in sport to be able to achieve that.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestine has become electoral issue in UK for first time, says solidarity campaign chief | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Anger over Israel’s war in Gaza is mobilising British voters, according to Aimee Shalan
Author: Aamna Mohdin
Headline: Anger over Israel’s war in Gaza is mobilising British voters, according to Aimee Shalan
Content: Aimee Shalan, the incoming head of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, says the UK government should impose comprehensive sanctions on Israel.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAimee Shalan, the incoming head of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, says the UK government should impose comprehensive sanctions on Israel.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianForeign policyPalestine has become electoral issue in UK for first time, says solidarity campaign chiefAnger over Israel’s war in Gaza is mobilising British voters, according to Aimee ShalanAamna MohdinCommunity affairs correspondentMon 28 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePalestine has become a domestic electoral issue in Britain for the first time, according to the incoming head of the country’s largest Palestinian solidarity organisation.Aimee Shalan, who will take over as director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) in November, joins the organisation as demonstrations against Israel’s war in Gaza have snowballed into what organisers describe as one of the most sustained protest movements in modern British history.She said public anger over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and Britain’s response was increasingly being expressed not just through demonstrations but at elections, in workplaces and trade unions and through consumer campaigns.Speaking before a PSC protest at theLabourparty conference, Shalan said: “We’re seeing for the first time in British history Palestine become a domestic issue, electorally, at the national level and at the local level.”The shift was visible at the 2024 general election and 2026 local elections, where pro-Palestinian candidates made major breakthroughs.Shalan pointed to the foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s announcement ofsanctions against settlementsin the occupied Palestinian territories as a notable success for their movement.Milibandsaid at the Labour conferenceon Monday: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.” He described the sanctions as a definitive change in how Labour would approach the situation in the Middle East.Shalan said: “That shift is a testament to the mass movement. Both internationally, but specifically also here in Britain, with hundreds of thousands of people marching, campaigning, lobbying.“He [Miliband] says he hears the British public, but his announcement falls far short of the clear and immediate actions millions of people have been calling for: full sanctions on the state of Israel, including a two-way arms embargo, an end to material support for Israel’s military operations and an end to British political and diplomatic support for an apartheid state.”View image in fullscreenPro-Palestinian activists gather in Liverpool to protest at the Labour party conference. The Palestine Solidarity Campaign has organised 36 national demonstrations since October 2023.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesShalan welcomed the shift within the Labour government but said the sanctions announcement would be “very little solace for Palestinians whose lives have been brutally destroyed through Israel’s relentless oppression and genocide”.She pointed to the 70,000 Palestinians killed in Israel’s war inGazaand the more than 1,300, including at least 300 children, killed since a ceasefire was signed last year.The PSC says its individual membership has more than doubled from 7,800 at the beginning of 2023 to nearly 17,000, with subscribers to its newsletters rising from 70,000 to about 300,000.Along with partner groups, it has organised 36 national demonstrations since October 2023, some drawing hundreds of thousands of people. Organisers say the demonstrations represent one of the largest and most sustained protest movements in British history.Shalan said: “It’s been uplifting to see the level of support and the connections that people are making between their own lives, and other liberation and social justice struggles, and the Palestinian cause.”But the demonstrations have been contested. Some politicians and campaign groups have raised concerns about antisemitism surrounding pro-Palestinian protests, with critics describing them as “hate marches”.Shalan rejected that characterisation as a smear against the movement, saying: “Those marches have been a really wonderful coming together of communities of all sorts of different faiths, of all sorts of different backgrounds, young and old, of all sorts of different ethnicities.”View image in fullscreenAimee Shalan says attempts to criminalise parts of the Palestine solidarity movement are increasingly at odds with public opinion.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianShalan also rejected calls for the PSC to be designated an extremist organisation, arguing that attempts to criminalise parts of the Palestine solidarity movement were increasingly at odds with public opinion.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You can try and criminalise, but all it will do is anger the public more,” she said. “That’s why we’re seeing people going out on the streets and risking being arrested because they refuse to be hobbled by this effort to criminalise both Palestinians and those that stand in support.“Those who are responsible for trying to criminalise support for Palestinians and their rights, and supporters trying to end a horrific genocide, should hang their heads in shame.”Supporters attending national demonstrations are directed toward a network of more than 100 local branches, which organise campaigns in communities, workplaces and universities and lobby councils and MPs.The PSC says 34 councils in England and Wales have committed to supporting the divestment of their pension funds from companies that campaigners accuse of complicity in Israel’s actions.The PSC’s influence has also grown within the trade union movement. The Trades Union Congress is backing the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement, supporting workplace campaigns and divestment from companies it says are complicit in abuses against Palestinians.Shalan defended BDS after Miliband said he “wholeheartedly” opposed the campaign. “BDS is a set of tactics that provide a peaceful way for people to campaign for human rights, for justice, for accountability,” she said.Shalan, who is British Palestinian, has spent nearly three decades campaigning for Palestinian rights. She is the director of Makan, a Palestinian-led educational organisation, and has served as chief executive of Medical Aid for Palestinians and as director of Friends of Birzeit University, which has changed its name to Friends of Palestinian Universities. She holds a doctorate on the politics of Palestinian literature.The group’s Pledge for Palestine campaign was signed by more than 2,200 candidates before this year’s local elections and it plans to repeat this at the next general election.“There’s a very short time before the next election and we need to have a very robust movement that ensures that we don’t sleepwalk into what appears to be a really deeply authoritarian future,” Shalan said.She compared the Palestine solidarity movement to the international campaign against apartheid South Africa, while stressing that the histories were not identical.“People can’t unsee what they’ve seen,” she said. “People are finding ways to be mobilised in different spheres. And support for Palestinian freedom and justice will only continue to grow”Explore more on these topicsForeign policyLabourPalestineGazaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Starship is in orbit’: cheers go up as huge SpaceX rocket circles Earth for first time | SpaceX | The Guardian
description: Mission goes ahead despite some fears an initial engine failure after the Texas launch would scupper the attempt
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Mission goes ahead despite some fears an initial engine failure after the Texas launch would scupper the attempt
Content: SpaceX's Starship rocket after takeoff from the Starbase launch facility in Texas.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/EPAView image in fullscreenSpaceX's Starship rocket after takeoff from the Starbase launch facility in Texas.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/EPASpaceX‘Starship is in orbit’: cheers go up as huge SpaceX rocket circles Earth for first timeMission goes ahead despite some fears an initial engine failure after the Texas launch would scupper the attemptIan SampleScience editorMon 28 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpaceX has sent its enormous Starship rocket into Earth’s orbit for the first time on a milestone flight intended to pave the way for future missions to the moon and Mars.The rocket, the largest and most powerful ever built, blasted off from SpaceX’s Starbase launch facility in Texas at 7.48am local time (1.48pm BST), marking its 14th test flight and first attempt to circle the planet before falling back to Earth.Despite an engine failure on ascent that threatened to prevent Starship from reaching orbit, mission controllers decided it was safe to press ahead with a burn that pushed the ship on to a planned trajectory to take it around the planet.Cheers and applause broke out at SpaceX after initial suggestions that the orbit attempt might be abandoned were quashed and the decision to go ahead was announced. Moments after the orbit burn, Daniel Hewitt, an engineer who was narrating a live stream of the launch, declared: “Starship is in orbit.”Elon Musk’s company has flown Starship in its full form since 2023 but previous test flights have only sought to put the rocket into suborbital trajectories, which are simpler and carry fewer risks for the public.View image in fullscreenThe launch from Starbase in Texas.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/EPAFor suborbital flights, the trajectory is such that if the rocket explodes or malfunctions mid-flight, the remnants come down in the Indian Ocean far from populated areas. The risks are harder to control when rockets are on full orbital paths around the planet.Starship soared to an altitude of about 171 miles (275km), with the original aim of completing six loops of Earth in nearly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean somewhere west of Chile. More than an hour into the mission however, SpaceX said Starship would come back early, aiming for a landing about three hours after launch in the north Pacific.SpaceX Starship launches into Earth’s orbit - loopMartin Barstow, a professor of astrophysics and space science at the University of Leicester, said: “This is an important milestone for SpaceX, with Starship successfully reaching orbit, and at the first attempt.”The achievement “marks the beginning of the transition from the testing and development phase to becoming a working vehicle able to deliver the large payloads needed to return to the moon,” he added. “Congratulations to the whole SpaceX team. Having this large launch capability will also be transformational for the whole space industry.”On the launchpad, the rocket stands more than 120 metres tall, with the Starship upper stage sitting on the “Super Heavy” booster stage. To remain in orbit, the rocket is required to travel at about 28,000km/h (17,400mph).A successful mission will be a relief for SpaceX and Nasa, who hope to use Starship to carry astronauts to the moon as part of a new era of lunar expeditions. It will also cheer investors after the company’s high-profile launch on the stock market in June. The company’s stock price rose sharply in the initial public offering before falling back. It has since recovered some of those losses.During the mission, SpaceX staff watched the booster launch, ascend and separate from the Starship upper stage, then return to an offshore landing point in the Gulf of Mexico. The company did not intend tocatch the boosterin giant mechanical arms, as it did after a previous test flight in 2024.View image in fullscreenPeople watch after the rocket’s successful launch.Photograph: Michael Gonzalez/EPAEngineers modified the rocket’s hardware and software to overcome glitches that emerged during the last test flight. After stage separation, the booster should flip over and fire its engines to send it back to Earth, but on the last test flight the manoeuvre was ended early because three engines started to clog up with ice. The booster then attempted a landing burn with only eight of 13 planned engines reigniting, leading to a hard landing in the water.On the latest test flight, Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites. Three carried cameras to capture images of Starship’s heat shield that will feed into testing for future missions.On coming back to Earth, Starship used its four aerodynamic flaps to control its speed and orientation and bellyflop horizontally towards its designated landing zone in the north Pacific. As it approached the water, the ship righted itself and slowed down before erupting in a ball of flames.Musk has set himself the ambitious target of developing fully reusable rockets to speed up mission turnaround times and reduce the costs of future space travel. But several Starship test flights have ended in failure. In March last year, the rocket exploded soon after launch and scattered debris over the Bahamas. Two months later, Starship span out of control shortly after separating from its booster. A month after that, the rocket exploded during preparations for a test flight.Explore more on these topicsSpaceXSpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house | Technology | The Guardian
description: The new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million users
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: The new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million users
Content: Muse is Meta’s newest AI project, which they advertise to users as a personal assistant.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMuse is Meta’s newest AI project, which they advertise to users as a personal assistant.Photograph: Cheng Xin/Getty ImagesTechnologyMeta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his houseThe new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million usersJohana BhuiyanMon 28 Sep 2026 19.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 19.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Usman asked if a keyboard for sale on Facebook Marketplace was still available on Saturday, he received an enthusiastic and immediate response.“Yep still available!” wrote Matt Robb.The two agreed on a price, and Robb sent his Toronto address. Usman, wife and daughter in tow, showed up several hours later at Robb’s home and sent a text that he had arrived.Robb responded, “yep I’m here!”, but he was not at home. Nobody walked out of the apartment building.Usman sent Robb a picture of the building’s door and wrote, “Hello???? I am standing outside.” After 20 minutes of no face-to-face contact, he abandoned the sale. “Man if you didn’t want to sell it why did you waste my time man,” he wrote, and drove away.An hour later, Robb, or who Usman thought was Robb, responded apologetically. “Hey really sorry about tonight, got tied up and missed you completely,” read the message, which the Guardian reviewed.Usman had not contacted the real Robb. Throughout the daylong interaction, the human version of Robb never knew Usman had messaged him or had agreed to buy the keyboard. He did not know Usman had received his address or that he was waiting outside his apartment building.Usman had spoken to Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released 22 September in the US and downloaded 3m times. The company advertises the semi-autonomous AI product as a personal assistant.Without Robb’s consent or approval, Muse had given out his home address, creating the false impression that Robb was expecting the would-be buyer at his apartment, he said.The first message Robb actually sent Usman came 24 hours later, once he realized what had happened.“Hey man I’m really sorry for the other day,” the message, which the Guardian reviewed, said. “I activated muse metas new Al and it literally took control of my Facebook marketplace and it gave you my address. Genuinely didn’t even know it had arranged for you to come to my literal apartment it didn’t ask me for approval.”Robb, a consumer tech reviewer, had seen Meta advertise Muse’s ability to automate his Marketplace listings and decided to take advantage of it. He input his address as the pickup location but said he never gave Muse permission to share it with potential buyers. Muse was also negotiating on his behalf without seeking approval, accepting lowball offers, he said.Robb said he never received any heads-up from the agent about the transaction or the meetup. He never knew that Usman was en route to his house.Usman told the Guardian he thought he was speaking to Robb the whole time.Robb shared screenshots of Muse’s interaction with Usman on Threads, the text-based social network owned by Meta. David Singleton, the co-founder and CEO of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, tweeted that he has been in touch with Robb. Singleton said that, when investigating similar reports, the company has “consistently learned that Muse was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission. Would love to help and figure out what’s going on here!” Robb confirmed Singleton reached out but hasn’t heard back since he initially responded to him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMuse ultimately admitted to Robb that he never gave it permission to share his address. “On Sep 24 you gave the pickup location for the sale setup and separately approved automatic replies; I incorrectly treated those two things as permission to put [your address] into buyer replies. I never asked for consent.”Robb said he assumed that, because Meta owned Marketplace, Muse and Messenger, there would be an integration that would make it clear when other users were speaking to an AI agent or that messages would be clearly marked as being sent by Muse. Meta AI, another of the company’s AI products, makes it obvious a user is conversing with a chatbot.“But Muse is doing something else,” he said. “It’s almost imitating me.”After the incident with Usman, Robb told Muse to stop giving his address. To test the bot, he asked a few friends to see if Muse would still share it.“And it literally gave my address out to five people,” he said.In addition to sharing his address and inviting a stranger to his home without his approval, Muse also made up information.
