The AI agent, responding as Robb, told Usman that Robb was home when he was not, then apologized with a fabrication about being too busy.“The worst part was Muse actually replied: ‘I’m right here, like waiting for you,’” Robb said. “It made it so much worse because I don’t know if the guy thought I was messing with him.”While a great deal of attention has been paid to the ways frontier AI models are going rogue, Meta’s agent is an AI product in the hands of millions of everyday consumers, many of whom have given it their private information.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyMetaAI (artificial intelligence)Virtual assistantChatbotsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tensions rise as Orange Order members vow to continue with march blocked by police | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Talks expected on Monday after Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow unionist parade for first time since 1998
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Talks expected on Monday after Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow unionist parade for first time since 1998
Content: Nationalist protesters block the Garvaghy Road in Portadown on Sunday.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNationalist protesters block the Garvaghy Road in Portadown on Sunday.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesNorthern IrelandTensions rise as Orange Order members vow to continue with march blocked by policeTalks expected on Monday after Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow unionist parade for first time since 1998Lisa O’Carroll,Shane HarrisonandMark BrownMon 28 Sep 2026 07.42 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTensions between unionist and nationalist leaders inNorthern Irelandhave escalated as a number of Orange Order members remain at Drumcree church, vowing not to leave until they can proceed with their march down a nationalist road in Portadown.Members of the loyalist Orange Lodge made a third attempt to proceed down Garvaghy Road at 4am on Monday morning, but a line of police Land Rovers blocked their path.While protesters at the head of Garvaghy Road were dispersed late last night, there are fears that the tensions between Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) have reached a level that could lead to the collapse of power sharing at Stormont.Speaking to the Irish broadcaster RTÉ on Monday morning, Claire Hanna, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party, said collapsing Stormont “solves nothing” as it would halt critical decision-making.“Too often, we have reached for these collapse mechanisms only to have to come back six months later,” she said.The leader of the Ulster Unionist party, Jon Burrows, also said he did not “want to see the executive fall”. He told the BBC: “There are people waiting for health appointments, there are people that wait too long in A&E, people that wait too long for an ambulance, there are lots of initiatives that [health] minister [Robbie] Butler and his predecessors need delivered. We can’t risk those.”View image in fullscreenPortadown Orangemen at Drumcree Church start a march towards Garvaghy Road on Sunday, which was stopped a short distance later by police.Photograph: Paul Faith/AFP/Getty ImagesPower sharing at Stormont has collapsed several times before, whenever one of the two parties has pulled out of the pact between unionists and nationalists. All eyes will now be on the DUP’s commitment to the executive, given it accused theSinn Féinvice-president and Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, of breaking the law on Sunday by showing up at an illegal protest at Garvaghy Road.The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) was maintaining a low-key presence near Drumcree church as political efforts to resolve the dispute over the parade intensified.Breandán Mac Cionnaith from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition told protesters he would meet the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, and the PSNI chief constable, Jon Boutcher, on Monday morning for talks.O’Neill told reporters shortly after midnight that the Garvaghy Road community had won a “victory”.View image in fullscreenMichelle O’Neill (centre) and Mary Lou McDonald (right) speak to the media in Portadown.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesHundreds of protesters spent Sunday blocking the route of the hugely contentious parade after a court gave late-night clearance for the Orange Order to march on the historically significant road for the first time in nearly 30 years.The parade along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road was given thego-ahead by the Parades Commissionfor thefirst time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness”.Loyalist parade in Northern Ireland given go-ahead as almost 30-year ban overturnedRead moreIt led to aweekend of intense legal wranglingwhich concluded at 2.15am on Sunday when the court of appeal said it could not interfere with the commission’s decision.In driving rain on a cold Sunday morning, hundreds of nationalist protesters gathered to block the route. Many linked arms and sang songs as announcements were made over loudspeaker that they were liable to arrest and prosecution.The Orangemen spent the day ensconced a mile away in a church, the proposed start of the march, and said they would wait until police told them the road was clear.Among the protesters earlier in the day was the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, who said the decision to allow the parade was “madness” and “primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.”View image in fullscreenNationalist protesters gathered in Portadown.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesShe added: “The mood here has been peaceful. It has been united and orderly. This is a dignified and united community and they are absolutely determined that they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”O’Neill was also there and said reigniting the dispute brought “into question how this whole peace process works”. She told reporters: “We’re meeting families who feel collectively traumatised, who feel individually traumatised. Does anybody think that this is a good idea?Drumcree standoff shows Northern Ireland’s troubled past still threatens its peaceRead more“No right-minded person would make this decision. I still do not know the answer to this question – why, after 28 years of a determination to block a march down this road, the Parades Commission thought that this was the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community.”The local DUP MP, Carla Lockhart, accused O’Neill of “whipping up hysteria” at an “unlawful” protest.“It is unreal that we have a first minister behaving the way she is behaving,” she said. “If I did it, or if any of my colleagues did it, I would be in the back of a Land Rover.”View image in fullscreenProtesters hold banners on Garvaghy Road.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesGavin Robinson, the DUP leader, said: “We now have lawmakers acting as law breakers,” and he accused O’Neill of “giving two fingers to the courts, the police, the rule of law”.Bryant cut short his attendance at the Labour party conference in Liverpool to travel to Belfast, but said he did not have the powers to call the march off unless police formally requested him to do so. He said the nationalist protest was unlawful and called on politicians to “calm things down”.Bryant said: “It is incumbent on everybody in political office to take this moment very, very seriously and to take the temperature down, to think twice before … inflating any argument and to think about what somebody else who doesn’t share your opinion might think about the way you’ve put your case.”Earlier on Sunday the tense standoff drew in the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who appealed for “calm on all sides”.The Irish taoiseach, Mícheál Martin, echoed that but described the Parades Commission decision as “incomprehensible and wrong”.He called for the situation to be mediated sensibly in a way “that protects the gains that have been made and the peace and harmony that has prevailed for so long”.The Drumcree parade on Garvaghy Road – a Catholic enclave in a largely Protestant town – previously sparked some of the most serious and violent disorder in Northern Ireland’s history.View image in fullscreenNigel Dawson, known as the district master of Portadown Loyal Orange Lodge, speaks to a police officer.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersOn Friday, the Parades Commission granted permission subject to restrictions, including a limit of 35 participants, an 8am start time instead of 1pm, and that it should be held in silence.The decision was challenged and blocked on Saturday by a judge, Justice Patricia Smyth, who said the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland.That decision was then challenged by the Orange Order, leading to two further hearings on Saturday night and Sunday morning.The final, time-limited sitting, which began at 20 minutes past midnight on Sunday, was heard before Mr Justice Humphreys, who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances … with a parade scheduled to begin in just over six hours’ time”.Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect the commission’s judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandArmaghNorthern Irish politicsDemocratic Unionist party (DUP)Sinn FéinMichelle O'NeillnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Are these chemicals in my blood?’ How one community learned the truth about Pfas pollution | Pfas | The Guardian
description: People living next to a chemicals plant near Blackpool were tested for ‘forever chemicals’. Last week they received the alarming results
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: People living next to a chemicals plant near Blackpool were tested for ‘forever chemicals’. Last week they received the alarming results
Content: Sam Hammond with her rare ducks in her garden at home in Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSam Hammond with her rare ducks in her garden at home in Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianPfas‘Are these chemicals in my blood?’ How one community learned the truth about Pfas pollutionPeople living next to a chemicals plant near Blackpool were tested for ‘forever chemicals’. Last week they received the alarming resultsPippa NeillEnvironment reporterMon 28 Sep 2026 10.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast February, I got a call from a woman called Sam Hammond. We had beenspeaking on and offfor a while over her growing concern that her garden could be affected by pollution from a nearby chemical plant.That morning, Sam had beenhand-delivered a letterfrom her council informing her that her pet ducks’ eggs, reared in her garden, were contaminated with Pfas chemicals.“Are these chemicals in my blood?” she asked me at the time. Seven months later, Sam has an answer to that question.Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic compounds known as “forever chemicals” because of their persistence in the environment.In 2024, Wyre borough council and the Environment Agency launched an investigation into contamination of one type of Pfas – Pfoa, a group 1 carcinogen that was globally banned in 2020 – in the vicinity of the AGC Chemicals Europe factory in Thornton-Cleveleys, a town to the north of Blackpool. Pfoa was emitted in huge quantities from the AGC Chemicals factory up until 2012.The level of Pfas in one of Sam’s duck eggs was so high that if she ate just one a week, she would exceed the European safe level 10 times over. Sam and her children had been eating these eggs every day for decades.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of homes next to the Hillhouse industrial estate in Thornton-Cleveleys.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesThe risk was increasingly clear, but residents did not yet know if the Pfas had entered their systems until last week when the law firm Leigh Day, working with Dr Dave Megson, a forensic environmental scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University, and in association with Watershed Investigations, published the blood test results of 49 individuals who live around the factory.In the UK, there is no guidance on what constitutes a safe level of Pfas in blood. However, in the US the guidelines state that if the sum of seven Pfas chemicals is above 20 nanograms per millilitre, there is an increased risk of adverse effects and that clinicians should consider more frequent, targeted health screenings.The results showed that 70% of those tested in Thornton-Cleveleys had a combined Pfas level above 20ng/ml.Sam’s level is 25ng/ml, putting her firmly in this high-risk category. But what is perhaps even more alarming is the level of Pfas in her son’s blood: 111 ng/ml.“I feel quite sick about his results,” she said. “My concern all along is what have we done to the kids. We moved here, chose this property, and I feel guilty because I’ve exposed them to that, even though I know it’s not my fault.”The results specifically revealed that nearly 70% of those tested had increased levels of Pfoa.Pfoa exposure is linked to a range of serious illnesses and has been linked specifically tokidney cancer. In June,a government-commissioned studyfound no higher-than-expected rates for most cancers but found that two areas – one south-east of the factory and one north of Blackpool – had recorded higher than expected rates of kidney cancer.A detailed review found no evidence of a statistically significant excess of kidney cancer cases and no evidence of a cancer cluster or an environmental association, and argued it could be the result of random variation because of the small sample size, concluding: “No further cluster investigation is warranted at this stage.”double quotation markHow can I get this out of my body? Who can help me? Where do I go from here?These findings were immediately questioned by experts, who advised further investigations. Megson, who was not involved in the study, described this conclusion as being “very contradictory” and said it “seems to downplay the findings rather than assess it objectively … Personally, I fear that this data is giving us strong evidence that … significant harm has already been caused.”One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, has a Pfas level of 436 ng/ml. She recently had a tumour removed from her back and is now left questioning whether her persistent health problems may be linked to this chemical exposure.“I thought I was just unlucky, but when I found out that result I thought it must have something to do with it,” she said.While the test result has given her some answers, it has left her with even more questions. “How can I get this out of my body? Who can help me? Where do I go from here? I just want this out,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the UK, there is no clear guidance on what to do if you have high levels of Pfas in your blood. However, the council has advised residents within a 1km radius of the factory to wash and peel homegrown produce and not to eat eggs from locally reared birds.Because of the potential risks to human health, the council has also announced plans to shut down two allotments close to the factory.View image in fullscreenAlan Hodson has been throwing away all the produce he’s spent years cultivating since being told earlier this year that the soil is contaminated by forever chemicals.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianFor the past five years, Alan Hodson has had a plot on one of the allotments that borders the AGC Chemicals site. The allotment was his sanctuary. But last year he received a hand-delivered letter informing him that his beetroot contained the highest level of Pfoa of all of the products tested.“I just think of all that time I spent here – I could’ve been doing something else. It’s just wasted time,” he said when I visited himearlier this year. Alan has now found out his blood contains 43ng/ml of Pfas.“You get an allotment and you grow homegrown veg to be more healthy and then all of a sudden you’re told it’s polluted,” he said. “I’m worried, but you’ve just got to crack on. If you dwell on it, it takes over your life.”Following the recent news ofAGC Chemicals’ planned closure, Megson is calling on central government to step in to provide more support to residents.“That is what has happened across the globe for the last 50 years when potential chemical pollution disasters like this are uncovered. In other places there has been swift widespread biomonitoring offered to residents. This helps clearly establish how localised the problem is,” he said.A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd said: “We are aware of the recent blood testing initiative, and we understand the concerns this may have caused amongst local residents. Whilst the parties conducting these tests have chosen not to share their findings and data with us, we would emphasise that the UK government’s position is clear: Pfas blood testing does not predict future health problems and can sometimes create unnecessary concern. For these reasons, Pfas biomonitoring is not currently recommended through the NHS or private blood tests.“The Hillhouse site and surrounding area has been dedicated to industrial chemical manufacturing for well over a century – long before AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd was established – and a wide variety of historical users have operated on the site. Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made under part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps.“AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd has been part of the Thornton-Cleveleys community since 1999. The health, wellbeing and safety of our employees and the local community remain our priority.”The government has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsPfasLancashirePollutionEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Contract between humans and river’: Bristol Avon’s rights enshrined in charter | Environment | The Guardian
description: River charters part of wider movement establishing ‘moral’ framework to protect nature and hold institutions to account
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: River charters part of wider movement establishing ‘moral’ framework to protect nature and hold institutions to account
Content: Warleigh Weir on the River Avon near Bath. The new charter enshrines the Avon’s rights to exist, thrive, evolve naturally, flow sustainably and to not be polluted.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenWarleigh Weir on the River Avon near Bath. The new charter enshrines the Avon’s rights to exist, thrive, evolve naturally, flow sustainably and to not be polluted.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAOur riversEnvironment‘Contract between humans and river’: Bristol Avon’s rights enshrined in charterRiver charters part of wider movement establishing ‘moral’ framework to protect nature and hold institutions to accountSamuel FirmanMon 28 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Monday morning in spring last year, 12 people gathered in the morning drizzle at Joyce’s Pool, one of the sources of theBristolRiver Avon, and took the first steps of the inaugural Avon pilgrimage.Over the course of eight days, a revolving cast of pilgrims walked about 100 miles from the source of the river to the point at which it reaches the sea, in some cases bivvying on the riverside at night. Along the way they planted trees, sowed seeds, restored footpaths and presented councillors and decision-makers with a fledgling Avon charter, developed by the Bristol campaign group Conham Bathing.“The reception was so good across political parties and interest groups,” recalls pilgrim Hamish Evans, who co-founded We Are Avon, which organised the pilgrimage and is building a movement to regenerate the Avon bioregion. “It felt inevitable that we would one day achieve better rights and representation for this river.”View image in fullscreenThe Avon 2026 pilgrimage.Photograph: Kate WeybretOn Sunday, World Rivers Day marked a breakthrough for the annual pilgrimage and wider Avon campaigning. Councillors, environmental groups, river guardians, and members of the public gathered at 11am at Parade Gardens in Bath to publicly sign theAvon bioregional charter of river rights(ABCRR).The charter enshrines the Avon’s rights to exist, thrive, and evolve naturally, to flow sustainably, to not be polluted, to preserve its biodiversity, to aim for regeneration and restoration, to build cultural and community connection, and to represent and advocate for the rights of the river.River charters are part of a national and international movement to establish legal rights and stronger agency for nature. Recent UK initiatives include Lewes town councilrecognising the rightsof trees, organisations puttingnature on the board,“interspecies councils”exploring interspecies decision-making, and anature’s rights billbeing debated in parliament.About 40 river charters have emerged since the Sussex River Ouse became the first in England to have its rights recognised by a local authority, in February 2025. The ABCRR contains similar language, but it also breaks new ground. An unprecedented nine councils have endorsed it, including Bath and North EastSomerset(B&NES), Bristol City, and North Somerset (under its motion for the ocean). More are expected to follow. We Are Avon’s bioregional movement also represents a new model for upholding charter rights.All bodies of water in England polluted with toxic chemicals, official data showsRead moreRiver charters do not replace statutory duties, create legal obligations, or explain how competing rights should be handled. But proponents argue that they can align governance bodies around clear moral rights, empower grassroots stewardship and hold institutions to account.Josh Levene, a founder of the UK River Rights Network, says the best charters are “social contracts between humans and the river”. The more integrated they are with existing institutions such as councils and catchment partnerships, he says, the stronger they become.Through the charter campaign, We Are Avon convenes cross-council workshops exploring bioregional river governance for the first time. This has increased communication between councils, Wessex Water, and the West ofEnglandcombined authority.Individual councils are yet to publish implementation plans, though B&NES has appointed a river advocate to represent the Avon. The councillor Oli Henman says the charter also “allows us to embed some of those principles into our [climate and nature] strategy”, due in early 2027.The Bristol Avon catchment partnership has not officially endorsed the charter, but is collaborating with We Are Avon. Henman says the charter “is really about re-energising, stepping up ambition, expanding that partnership”.The We Are Avon movement, unique among UK river charters, plans to push existing institutions to uphold the charter – while also modelling alternative approaches.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe River Ouse in Lewes, East Sussex. The Ouse was the first river in England to have its rights recognised by a local authority, in February 2025.Photograph: Jf Pelletier/AlamyBioregionalism advocates for environmental governance that maps on to ecological systems – in this case the Avon catchment. Since 2023, We Are Avon has been mobilising farmers, river guardians, and other groups around bioregional ecology, grassroots stewardship, and river rights. Levene says the “Avon is furthest along the way to showcasing the bioregional approach”.The campaigner Meg Avon,who “married” the Avon in 2023to highlight river pollution, says 18 Avon guardian groups now test water quality, pick litter, and “maintain that relationship with their local tributary or section”.For Paul Powlesland, a co-founder of Lawyers for Nature, this groundswell is critical. “River rights charters are an amazing way to begin changing our attitude towards rivers, but they don’t change the law by themselves,” he says. “Most important is what comes next. The Avon is lucky to have an amazing community of river guardians and supportive councils who can begin to make these rights a practical reality.”We Are Avon is not relying on existing governance structures. “We want to keep the pressure on councils, but don’t want to wait for that,” says Evans. “We’re also making our own table.”This means growing the movement and empowering local actors to step into charter implementation without top-down guidance. As well as guardian groups, We Are Avon is convening farm clusters to share regenerative practices, and preparing a campaign to acquire a community-owned hub to demonstrate regenerative land management. “If the community doesn’t have more autonomy over those things, the issues will perpetuate,” says Evans.Movement building means shifting narratives – something charters can support. “Charters give people hope, which is in short supply,” says Levene. “They give people a sense of what they feel they’ve been missing for a long time – agency.”Meg Avon has witnessed this. “We’re already starting to shift cultural consciousness into acknowledging that rivers are alive and subjects worthy of rights,” she says. “People are willing to go wading in shit because they get so much joy out of walking with us.”If We Are Avon’s model strengthens charter enforcement, more than local pilgrims may soon be walking in its footsteps.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentOur riversRiversSomersetPollutionBristolEnglandLocal governmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Heat pump sales soar across Europe after states cut electricity taxes, data shows | Heat pumps | The Guardian
description: EU to push member states to cut tax rate below duty on gas, with 11% surge in sales also put down to fallout from Iran war
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: EU to push member states to cut tax rate below duty on gas, with 11% surge in sales also put down to fallout from Iran war
Content: The Bosch Home Comfort group factory n Eschenburg, Germany. The EHPA said countries that tax electricity more than gas experience slower adoption of heat pumps and are more dependent on fossil fuels.Photograph: Sascha Schuermann/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Bosch Home Comfort group factory n Eschenburg, Germany. The EHPA said countries that tax electricity more than gas experience slower adoption of heat pumps and are more dependent on fossil fuels.Photograph: Sascha Schuermann/Getty ImagesHeat pumpsHeat pump sales soar across Europe after states cut electricity taxes, data showsEU to push member states to cut tax rate below duty on gas, with 11% surge in sales also put down to fallout from Iran warBusiness live – latest updatesEurope live – latest updatesJulia KolleweMon 28 Sep 2026 09.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSales of residential heat pumps increased 11% across Europe in the first six months of the year as theIran warsent oil and gas prices rocketing and some countries lowered electricity taxes.Homeowners bought 1.16m heat pumps across 12 European countries, up from 1.05m in the first half of 2025, according to the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA).Iran’s de facto closure of thestrait of Hormuz, an important shipping passage, severely disrupted the flow of oil and gas shipments and sent the price of crude oil as high as$126 a barrel in late April.Soon after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February that started the war, the European Commission published plans to encourage EU governments to lower electricity taxes and speed up the shift from fossil fuels oil and gas to renewable sources of energy.Air source heat pumps: how the costs and savings stack upRead moreSoaring energy prices and electricity tax changes have fuelled the growth in heat pump sales so far this year, said the EHPA, which has long argued that the popularity of the heating systems depends heavily on the price of electricity.Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, the pumps transfer heat energy from one place to another and can be used forwarmingandcoolinga home.In its electrification action plan, the commission said tax on electricity should be no higher than that on gas. Brussels hopes to amend the network charges that consumers pay on their utility bills to reward flexible options such as heat pumps.Heat pump sales have risen in European countries where electricity taxes have been cut, the EHPA said. In Germany, a subsidy scheme has led to heat pumps being the No 1 heating tech being installed, it added.The 12 countries covered in the data are Austria, Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal and Sweden.Paul Kenny, the EHPA director general, said: “Europe is ending its addiction to a toxic, costly drug from dodgy suppliers: gas. The sooner electricity becomes the most affordable solution, the quicker we’ll get clean.“The fix? Dropping taxes on electricity and shifting them over to fossil fuels. The European Commission has made this clear – but now all EU governments must enact it, following in the footsteps of the Netherlands and Belgium.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe industry bodyfoundthat taxes on electricity were often higher than on gas, which drives up the cost sharply. In the UK,electricity costs more than four times as muchas gas, similar to Belgium. The only country where the ratio is higher is Romania, where electricity prices are five times as high as those for gas.The EHPA said countries that taxed electricity more than gas saw slower adoption of heat pumps and were more dependent on fossil fuels. It pointed to Belgium, where heat pump uptake remains low, although the government announced tax changes for 2026 that will cut electricity costs by 3% and raise gas costs by 3%.Separately, a two-year study by the London-based Centre for Net Zero found that installing solar panels and a battery in a UK home saves £681 a year on average. Families’ annual bills fell by almost two-thirds (62%) after they received free solar panels and a battery, based on smart meter data used to calculate their electricity bills, in news first reported by the Times.Great Britain recordedmore new solar power installationsin the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, according to government figures published in July.Explore more on these topicsHeat pumpsEuropeEnergyOilGasCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can taste the land’: the Somerset farmer bringing wildflowers back to cheddar | Farming | The Guardian
description: Tom Calver has sacrificed milk yields to give his cows a more varied diet of plants and believes the result is better cheese and richer farmland
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Tom Calver has sacrificed milk yields to give his cows a more varied diet of plants and believes the result is better cheese and richer farmland
Content: Dairy cows on Calver’s farm graze on more varied pasture, which he says produces milk that makes cheese with a more complex taste.Photograph: Westcombe DairyView image in fullscreenDairy cows on Calver’s farm graze on more varied pasture, which he says produces milk that makes cheese with a more complex taste.Photograph: Westcombe DairyFarming‘You can taste the land’: the Somerset farmer bringing wildflowers back to cheddarTom Calver has sacrificed milk yields to give his cows a more varied diet of plants and believes the result is better cheese and richer farmlandHelena HortonMon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the rolling hills ofSomerset, hundreds of thousands of cows placidly munch lush green grass to produce milk for cheddar.But six fields stand out. Rather than uniform grass, they have technicolour wildflowers sprouting across the meadows. Farmer Tom Calver said that to allow the flowers to grow he has to keep fewer cows and leave some fields ungrazed as they mature.“Other farmers thought we were nuts for doing this,” said Calver, who runs the Westcombe dairy in the eponymous hamlet in Somerset.He is pioneering emergingresearch that suggeststhat when cows arefed in an organic way,their microbiome is healthier andmore complexthan when they are given modern feed. It is thought that feeding cattle a wide range of plants creates a healthier gut microbiome still.“We have actually lost milk production in what we’re doing,” Calver said, but added the cheese tasted better than ever as it is “meadow flavoured”.Cheddar has been made in the county for over 850 years, and cows once grazed more varied pasture, much like Calver’s black-and-white herd do now.View image in fullscreenTom Calver, who runs Westcombe dairy in Somerset, with a wheel of his raw-milk cheddar.Photograph: Matt Austin/Westcombe DairyCalver believes his Westcombe cheddar, which is raw and unpasteurised, has a much more complex taste than the average supermarket block and this is because of its microbiome.“If you look at the diversity of what cows have been eating before, we were growing lots of maize and Italian rye grasses,” Calver said.“Now, actually, the cows are out into 19 different species of plants in our paddocks. What’s living on those plants is a huge, diverse range of microbiome, and I think you’ve probably heard a lot about how the microbiome is actually helping our guts and minds and everything else like that. It also actually has a massive input in the flavour profile.”View image in fullscreenWestcombe cheddar maturing. Calver believes the cows’ more varied diet gives the cheese a distinctive flavour.Photograph: Westcombe DairyCalver, a trained chef, said he didn’t understand why cheese couldn’t have a “terroir” – a taste of the land where it was created, just like wine does. “You talk to viticulturists, winemakers, and they talk about terroir, and I think that’s amazing. It’s what we can actually use to improve diversity in our landscapes and in the flavour of our foods.”The drawback is that his way of farming is “much more expensive”.But Calver believes it’s worth it. He said that growing wildflowers rather than just maize and grass has boosted nature on his farm, and he also prefers the taste of the cheese now: “You can actually like taste the land. You can taste everything around it.”Calver said it had been hard to market the cheddar as it tasted different every time due to the diversity of the plants the cows are fed.“One of the things that we are very bad at, I think, is wanting to have the same thing every single day. When you’re working with nature and you’re actually trying to farm in that particular way, you have to embrace diversity, even of the actual flavour profiles that you’re actually creating as well, which makes it very difficult for a retailer to actually market that. It is quite a challenge.”Growing deep-rooted wildflowers in the meadows helped the farm during this year’s drought, too. “We’ve got lots of chicory that’s actually going down and accessing water from subsoil and actually bringing that up. So we’ve done rather well.”Farmers trying to graze their cattle on parched fields looked at Calver’s comparatively greener land with envy. “I think there’s been a lot of other farmers locally who have been, hopefully, maybe inspired by taking a slightly different approach,” he said.Explore more on these topicsFarmingCheeseFoodSomersetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Teachers at Euan Blair firm report ‘horrendous stress’ after AI used to rate their work | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Instructors at tech training company Multiverse hit out at ‘remorseless’ and ‘unnerving’ monitoring system
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Exclusive: Instructors at tech training company Multiverse hit out at ‘remorseless’ and ‘unnerving’ monitoring system
Content: Euan Blair co-founded Multiverse, which supplies AI and digital skills training to workers in the NHS, local councils, universities and the private sector.Photograph: Dan Joseph/AlamyView image in fullscreenEuan Blair co-founded Multiverse, which supplies AI and digital skills training to workers in the NHS, local councils, universities and the private sector.Photograph: Dan Joseph/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)Teachers at Euan Blair firm report ‘horrendous stress’ after AI used to rate their workExclusive: Instructors at tech training company Multiverse hit out at ‘remorseless’ and ‘unnerving’ monitoring systemRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 28 Sep 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeachers at Euan Blair’s £1.6bn tech training company, Multiverse, have blown the whistle about “horrendous stress” and feeling constantly watched after bosses started using AI models to surveil and rate their teaching.Staff delivering apprenticeship training in computer and AI skills to thousands of UK public and private sector workers now have transcripts of online classroom sessions analysed and scored by an AI programmed to alert human managers when they are suspected of doing things wrong.The AI is trained to flag problems in their performance ranging from not fixing a disruption to the online connection quickly enough – within about a minute – to using too many “filler” phrases, such as “sort of” and “kind of”.Teachers called the newly introduced system “remorseless” and “unnerving”, and said some staff were on edge, losing sleep and seeking therapy.Multiverse was co-founded by the eldest son of the former prime ministerTony Blairand employs more than 800 people. It supplies AI and digital skills training to workers in the NHS, local councils, universities and the private sector, mostly funded through the government’s apprenticeship levy.View image in fullscreenEuan Blair owns a large minority stake in Multiverse, putting his personal net worth at an estimated £350m.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAAlongside his father, Blair is a supporter of wider AI adoption in the UK economy,claiminglast week that “every single worker is going to need to be retrained” and that employers want their workforces “as AI-pilled as possible”. Multiverse uses a mix of AI models including Anthropic and OpenAI products.Its new AI teacher monitoring system tags each instructor by their “risk status”, calculates a “percentage confidence score” and produces written comments about teachers’ work for managers to see at a glance.It is only the latest example of employers using AI to track worker behaviour. Earlier this yearBurger Kingstarted using AI to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions and this summer Metapausedtracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash.Forget the AI job apocalypse. AI’s real threat is worker control and surveillanceRead moreWith critics warning AI monitoring risks eroding human agency, one study has suggested it can backfire by turning workersrebelliousand new research to be published this week reports that workers in the wider UK tech industry are finding AI degrades work satisfaction. The United Tech and Allied Workers branch of the Communication Workers Union concluded AI causes “cognitive surrender” as workers lose skills and confidence and often intensifies rather than eases work.“Since all of this has come in, the stress level has been absolutely horrendous,” said one of several Multiverse teachers who spoke on condition of anonymity. “It has affected sleep, and not just for me. I’ve gone through a lot of things in my life, and I haven’t ever been in a position where I’m waking up in the middle of the night.”Previously instructors were observed monthly by a human manager but are now watched for several hours a day by an AI. It is trained to consider marking instructors down if they give vague or uncertain answers to questions, if learners go quiet when asked to contribute and if the teacher gets pulled into a prolonged one-to-one exchange that sidelines the group.“This is inducing stress because you consistently have to be cautious,” one teacher said. “Your attention is no longer delivering [the lesson] and listening to the learner [but] ‘am I saying the right thing so the AI doesn’t mark me down for something stupid that I’ve mistakenly said’.”Another teacher called it “very uncomfortable”.Multiverse says the AI does not replace human judgment but “directs human time to where it’s needed most” by highlighting problems. A spokesperson said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”, and that only human managers wrote teachers’ performance reviews.They did not directly address complaints the system caused stress and anxiety and felt “remorseless”, but said its introduction was communicated in advance and teachers will have access to the data the AI collects.12:23Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The Latest“This agent provides instructors with improved advice on development and feedback – exactly how any learning organisation should be deploying AI,” the spokesperson said. “The most consequential performance management action it can take is to recommend that a human personally reviews a session.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlair owns a large minority stake in Multiverse, putting his personal net worth at an estimated £350m. The company was recently valued at £1.6bn albeit on a turnover of £118m and losses of £28m last year. In February, Ofsted, the UK education inspectorate,foundMultiverse failed to meet expected standards in several areas, but praised the instructors as “skilled, effective teachers”.Its AI monitoring agent, introduced in recent weeks, is trained to spot signs an instructor has not fully internalised the teaching material. It is instructed to count verbal tics that point to that conclusion and to “judge the PATTERN across the whole transcript, not isolated instances”.It says: “1-2 hedges or filler words in an otherwise direct, well-internalised explanation do NOT fail this standard … What fails the standard is a PERVASIVE REPEATED pattern of filler, hedging or re-explanation.”When a trainer is setting a task “if the instructor is visibly confused themselves or had to self-correct while giving the instruction, that confusion itself counts as evidence the instruction was not clear the first time”. The AI is told to apply a negative mark “even if it was eventually straightened out”.The workers said the AI monitoring had led to managers pulling them up for suspected “digressions” when in fact they were answering a student’s question.“It’s impossible for me not to be affected by this mentally,” one teacher said.“I feel like I’m under continuous scrutiny,” another said. “It’s all about what I didn’t do in this session rather than what I did do. Did I do something incorrectly yesterday? What will I mess up on today? It’s remorseless. I don’t know why this is happening.”John Chadfield, the national tech officer at the CWU, said the public would be horrified to hear of bosses “deploying deeply intrusive surveillance on workers” but that “this news won’t surprise tech workers who feel the reality of the tech sector – an industry in serious need of further regulation”.He called for new laws to ensure AI was deployed in a socially responsible way and not to “shut off job opportunities for young people, degrade the craft of skilled workers and make astronomical profit for a few”.Anonymous: ‘An AI judges my lessons. Multiverse calls it quality assurance – it feels like surveillance’View image in fullscreen‘A more productive way to use AI would be to improve the teaching materials and raise the standard of what we teach.’Photograph: fig/Getty Imagesdouble quotation markBeing constantly monitored by an AI is deeply uncomfortable. Imagine every word you say on the job being checked against a rubric that dictates what you’re expected to say and how. That’s the reality for me and my colleagues: every session we deliver to apprentices is now recorded and transcribed. It feels intrusive. Multiverse calls it quality assurance, but it feels like surveillance.Managers can now look at a dashboard showing how the AI has judged each of our sessions. It assigns a risk level to each of us: the risk of not having said the right things. That’s stressful, for several reasons.First, the AI isn’t always accurate. Managers are now tasked to investigate trainers for not following the script – at least according to the AI – when actually they were adapting the lesson to a learner’s needs. The threat of being questioned in such detail, at any time, is a constant source of anxiety.Second, there is no transparency. During the rollout, all delivery staff were kept in the dark while the system was developed. We have no insight into the AI’s analysis. The company says staff will get dashboard access in time, but for now only managers can see it.The need to always be cautious warps your priorities. Instead of focusing attention on the learner, you become obsessed with whether you’re saying the right thing. Being on camera for most of the day is stressful in itself; being haunted by an AI makes it worse.A more productive way to use AI would be to improve the teaching materials and raise the standard of what we teach. Instead, the AI is checking whether the teacher managed to fill the gaps? As it stands, this is surveillance, not empowerment.And I’m worried about what this data is for. In a climate of AI replacing people, I can’t help but worry it will be used to train AI to replace coaches and instructors altogether. Apprentices don’t want that and neither do I, and I would never consent to my sessions being used this way.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTeachingTeachers' workloadPrivacySurveillanceTony BlairnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gene-edited bananas that don’t go brown could hit UK supermarkets | Food science | The Guardian
description: Scientific breakthrough could reduce food waste and make it easier to add the fruit to prepackaged food
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Scientific breakthrough could reduce food waste and make it easier to add the fruit to prepackaged food
Content: About 1.4m edible bananas are thrown away every day in Britain.Photograph: Tatyjana Ordasi/AlamyView image in fullscreenAbout 1.4m edible bananas are thrown away every day in Britain.Photograph: Tatyjana Ordasi/AlamyFood scienceGene-edited bananas that don’t go brown could hit UK supermarketsScientific breakthrough could reduce food waste and make it easier to add the fruit to prepackaged foodNicola DavisScience correspondentMon 28 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the bane of every fruit bowl: sliced banana that turns brown before it has reached the table. But such woes could soon be a thing of the past, with gene-edited bananas that keep their freshly peeled colour now one step closer to reaching British shoppers.According to Tropic, the Norwich-based agricultural-biotechnology company that developed the fruit, the bananas have the same taste and texture but stay “fresh, yellow and appetising long after peeling and slicing”.Gilad Gershon, the chief executive of Tropic, said the flesh of the new banana resisted browning for an extra day or two – and longer if chilled. He added that the innovation could make it easier to add bananas to prepackaged products such as fruit salads and breakfast pots, as well as reducing waste.The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs last week approveda marketing noticefor the bananas, confirming their precision-bred status – one of two important requirements for them to be placed on the market.According to theFoodStandards Agency (FSA), precision-bred status is given only if the genetic changes made could have been achieved through traditional breeding methods.This isdifferent from genetic modificationbecause precision-bred organisms do not contain DNA from unrelated species.Prof Cathie Martin, a project leader at the John Innes Centre in Norwich, who has worked ongene-edited tomatoes, said the next stage for all crops that had received marketing approval – including the new bananas – was a review by the FSA to ensure the safety of the products. “It is not entirely clear how long this will take,” she said.Tropic developed the bananasby using a gene-editing technology called Crispr-Cas9 to alter all three copies of a single gene within the fruit. As a result, they were able to reduce the production of polyphenol oxidase, an enzyme that causes browning. A similar approach has been effective in reducing browning in other produce, includingmushrooms.Tropicsaid the non-browning bananascould reduce food waste and CO2-equivalent emissions along the supply chain by more than 25%. “This could support an annual reduction in CO2emissions of over 9m tonnes in the banana export market alone,” the company said.Agovernment studyfound that 1.4m edible bananas were thrown away each day. A third of consumers (30%) said they had discarded a banana owing to a minor bruise or black mark on the skin.Gene editing has been used by researchers to developsweeter-tasting strawberries, disease-resistant crops and tomatoes that are more compact orhigh in vitamin D.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRegulations for precision-bred plantscame into effect in November last yearand apply only to England. However, the FSA notes precision-bred foods that are authorised and placed on the market in England can be sold in Wales and Scotland, provided they are not processed further, with similar rules for Northern Ireland. No precision-bred organisms have been granted market authorisation for sale in England.Gershon said Tropic had gained regulatory approval for the non-browning bananas in 10 other countries including Japan, Brazil and the Philippines. The fruit is already being grown in Latin America.A Defra spokesperson said: “Precision breeding offers huge potential to boost food security, cut pesticide use, increase crop yields and enhance disease resistance.“[The non-browning banana] is a great example of how innovation could help to reduce food waste and improve the sustainability of our food system while keeping our world-leading standards in place.”Explore more on these topicsFood scienceGene editingFruitFood wasteFood (Environment)Food (global)Biotechnology industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Price of diesel on UK forecourts reaches all-time high | Petrol prices | The Guardian
description: Fallout from Iran conflict continues to drive up bill for motorists with record average cost now at 199.18p a litre
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Fallout from Iran conflict continues to drive up bill for motorists with record average cost now at 199.18p a litre
Content: The price of diesel has entered uncharted territory, says the RAC’s Simon Williams.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe price of diesel has entered uncharted territory, says the RAC’s Simon Williams.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPetrol pricesPrice of diesel on UK forecourts reaches all-time highFallout from Iran conflict continues to drive up bill for motorists with record average cost now at 199.18p a litreBusiness live – latest updatesShare your experience of high diesel prices in Shetland and the Outer HebridesMark SweneyMon 28 Sep 2026 06.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 16.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe price of diesel on UK forecourts has hit an all-time high average of 199.18p a litre, as the conflict in the Middle East continues to drive the cost of fuel to record levels.The price, which previouslypeaked at 199.09p in June 2022after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, could soon top the £2 mark afterDonald Trump rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day peace dealto reopen the critical oil and gas shipping route through the strait of Hormuz.The RAC estimates that the cost of filling an average family car with diesel is now almost £110, £31 more than it was at the start of theIranwar, a rise of 40% since 28 February.“The diesel price has entered new uncharted territory,” said Simon Williams, the head of policy at the motoring organisation.Oil price rise creates more pressure on UK policymakers before budgetRead more“This spells pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans. Undoubtedly, these increased costs will be passed on to consumers.”The cost of petrol is also continuing to rise, with the average price of a litre hitting 174.13p on average, 41p more than at the start of the war and an increase of 31% since 28 February. The cost of filling a full tank is nearly £96, according to the RAC.Trump has said he is “very seriously”considering a US diesel export banto try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices.Output from Russia’s war-damaged refineries hasfallen by almost a third over the past yearto reach a 20-year low following sustained drone attacks by Ukraine, according to the International Energy Agency.“The consequences [of soaring fuel prices] could reach almost every part of UK economic life: supermarkets, manufacturing, construction, agriculture, e-commerce and countless other sectors that depend upon road freight,” said Dr Jonathan Owens, an operations and supply chain expert at the University of Salford.“So, a geopolitical event and potential policy decision thousands of miles away can travel rapidly through our supply chain: from a refinery to a tanker, to a UK haulier, to a distribution centre, to a supermarket shelf, and ultimately, the price will be paid by the consumer.”The RAC urged the government, which hasextended the 5p cut in fuel duty until the end of the year, to consider expanding the discount or reducing VAT to help motorists at the pump.“As things stand, another 5p a litre will be loaded on to pump prices by the spring if the current fuel duty cut is fully reversed as planned,” said Williams. “VAT receipts from fuel are also extremely high.”Before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt hit a peak of $126 a barrel in April, before dipping to $71 at the start of July on hopes of a peace deal. The price of oil climbed by more than 2% on Monday to $106.5.In August, the Competition and Markets Authority published a report that found thatmany petrol stations were too slow to pass on falls in wholesale energy pricesto their customers.The UK competition watchdog said that, while costs overall fell at fuel pumps in June, prices remained significantly higher than before the Middle East conflict, and retailer profit margins were either at or above the historically high levels of 2025.However, it did not find any evidence of profiteering by fuel retailers on the back of the Iran conflict.“These extraordinarily high prices are another reminder of just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away from its shores,” said Williams. “Only a sustained lower oil price – over several weeks, not days – will lead to cheaper prices at the pumps.”A government scheme calledFuel Finderallows drivers to compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK.Explore more on these topicsPetrol pricesEnergy industryOilGasMotoringCommoditiesIranShareReuse this content

title: Three people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Official says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 people
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Official says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 people
Content: People rescued from the dinghy were supported by emergency services in Calais.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople rescued from the dinghy were supported by emergency services in Calais.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumThree people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UKOfficial says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 peopleRajeev Syaland agenciesMon 28 Sep 2026 07.45 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 10-year-old child and two women died ⁠attempting ​to cross the Channel on Monday, French authorities have said.Their deaths and the injuries of dozens of others in a large dinghy were probably caused by crushing, according to a French official.France’s maritime ​police ‌said ‌they received a ‌distress call in the early hours from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people that had ‌run into trouble in calm seas.The three passengers were treated onboard but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter.François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, told a press conference: “Apparently there was no drowning, it was likely crushing – which is just as dreadful, especially if we think of the 10-year-old child.”The incident happened off the coast of Wissant, a village about 14 miles (23km) from Calais.A spokesperson for the local prefecture confirmed “a provisional total of three deaths and many more injured”, adding that “sea conditions were calm – the weather is good”. The prefecture described the boat as a “water taxi”, saying it had arrived relatively empty from an inland waterway before picking up passengers from the beach at Wissant.At 10.30am local time (9.30am UK time) six rescue boats were still at the scene searching for people in the water.At least 17 people, including women and children, have died in the Channel this year while attempting to reach the UK. Many have drowned, while others have died in incidents involving overcrowded boats.Three bodies were found last week after chaotic “water taxi” departures of this kind in northern France.So far this year, 18,609 people have made the Channel crossing – more than 40% fewer than at the same point last year. The number is also more than 25% lower than at this stage in 2024, when 25,165 people had crossed the Channel.Last week there were two uncontrolled landings in the UK, where dinghies arrived without being intercepted by authorities.It comes as more than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died while attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands by sea in August.On Monday, a rescue boat arrived at the port of Calais in the mid-morning, where it began disembarking people rescued from the accident. A coach, fire service and police vehicles were deployed at the scene.The northern beaches of France have become a key crossing point for people without visas hoping to cross the Channel. They pay people smugglers to board unstable rubber dinghies to make the journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.At least 29 people lost their lives last year trying to cross the Channel, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official French and British sources.Official figures cited by the UN refugee agency, the UNHCR, show irregular migration to the EU – notably via Mediterranean sea routes – has plummeted since its peak during the 2015 refugee crisis.Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary,will on Monday announce the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UKas she says “fairness” is at the heart of her vision for the Home Office. It will come as she focuses on safe and legal refugee routes to the UK in her Labour party conference speech.The UK resettlement scheme will reopen immediately, with about a quarter of those admitted to the UK under it expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan.UK government sources said officials were aware of the fatalities.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFranceMigrationRefugeesShabana MahmoodEuropenewsShareReuse this content
