title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says
Content: Health workers at an Ebola treatment centre in Butembo, where mistrust of the response to the outbreak has fuelled a series of attacks.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersView image in fullscreenHealth workers at an Ebola treatment centre in Butembo, where mistrust of the response to the outbreak has fuelled a series of attacks.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersEbolaDRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreakMarie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party saysCarlos Mureithiin Nairobi and agenciesMon 28 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of theEbolavirus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in westAfrica, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has beenintensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoWorld Health OrganizationGlobal healthHealthAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Foie gras, live dolphins and toasters: China and US cut reciprocal tariffs on $30bn each of goods | Tariffs | The Guardian
description: World’s biggest economies release lists of products in latest move away from trade war – but no strategic goods are included
Author: Rebecca Bailey
Headline: World’s biggest economies release lists of products in latest move away from trade war – but no strategic goods are included
Content: Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met last week in Washington for an optics-driven summit aimed at stabilising the two sides’ relationship.Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenXi Jinping and Donald Trump met last week in Washington for an optics-driven summit aimed at stabilising the two sides’ relationship.Photograph: Win McNamee/Getty ImagesTariffsFoie gras, live dolphins and toasters: China and US cut reciprocal tariffs on $30bn each of goodsWorld’s biggest economies release lists of products in latest move away from trade war – but no strategic goods are includedRebecca BaileyChina correspondentMon 28 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US andChinahave released reciprocal lists of goods worth about $30bn each on which they plan to cut tariffs, ranging from consumer electronics and agricultural products to artificial flowers and live dolphins.The announcements are the latest tack away from the intense trade war between the world’s two largest economies that dominated much of last year, though major strategic products are not included and no timeline has yet been given for the reductions.The US list includes 77 categories of Chinese products including bed linen, garden umbrellas, toasters, fish hooks and billiard balls. The reciprocal Chinese list features 1,619 types of US product including a broad range of food such as butter, offal, lobster and foie gras.It also includes coal, scientific devices such as MRI systems, rabbit hair and several types of animals for breeding.Han Lin, the China country director at The Asia Group, a strategic advisory firm, said: “The animal list is certainly eye-catching: donkeys, mules, horses, whales, dolphins and dugongs. But I’d read it less as an exotic trade story than as evidence of how granular tariff codes can be.”The news comes days after Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met in Washington for anoptics-driven summitaimed at stabilising the two sides’ volatile relationship.Zhu Tian, a vice-president and co-dean at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) in Shanghai, said: “It is a positive step, but not a major breakthrough.” He noted that the reductions covered a relatively small share of US-China trade, and that other tariffs on more strategic goods remained in place.“Still, it is significant that the two sides are moving from simply avoiding further escalation to actually reducing some tariffs,” he added.The agreement has been brokered through the US-China Board of Trade, set up duringTrump’s visit to Beijing in May.The US trade representative Jamieson Greer said each side had recommended $30bn of non-sensitive trade that “could benefit from more favourable tariff treatment in the future”. The list represented “improved market access for about 30% of US exports to China”, he added.The Chinese commerce ministry said levies on more than 90% of the products would be subject to “most favoured nation” levels, according to state media.Sensitive product categories such as semiconductors, batteries and electric vehicles are not covered in the $30bn tariff cut lists.US whole soya beans imports – which became a Chinese target during 2025’s trade war – are not on Beijing’s tally, Reuters news agency noted, meaning they still face an additional tariff of 10%.Meanwhile, the Xi-Trump meeting last week yielded only a two-month extension to a wider trade truce first established by the two leadersin Busan, South Korea, last year.Lin said: “Both sides are carving out non-sensitive trade where cooperation is still possible. It’s managed stabilisation, not a trade reset.”Explore more on these topicsTariffsTrump tariffsChinaUS foreign policyUS economyEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Aldi to invest £900m in UK and open 40 more stores next year | Aldi | The Guardian
description: Supermarket chain declares ‘increasing confidence’ in its growth plans after posting record annual revenue of £19bn
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Supermarket chain declares ‘increasing confidence’ in its growth plans after posting record annual revenue of £19bn
Content: Aldi has struck a deal with Deliveroo for the delivery of groceries bought through its app.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenAldi has struck a deal with Deliveroo for the delivery of groceries bought through its app.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersAldiAldi to invest £900m in UK and open 40 more stores next yearSupermarket chain declares ‘increasing confidence’ in its growth plans after posting record annual revenue of £19bnBusiness live – latest updatesSarah ButlerMon 28 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAldi says it is stepping up investment in the UK with plans to spend £900m and open more than 40 stores.The company, which operates 1,092 budget supermarkets in the UK and Ireland, revealed sales rose 5% to a record £19bn last year. It opened 40 stores but profits slipped by £2.6m to £433m as it cut prices despite cost inflation.Giles Hurley, the boss of Aldi’s UK and Irish arm, said the German-owned business had “increasing confidence around growing our business”, claiming it already was the third largest UK supermarket in terms of items sold and customer numbers.Asda is classed as the UK’s third largest supermarket by value of sales, just ahead of Aldi. Leeds-based Asda is less than one percentage point ahead of its rival, with a market share of 10.6% in mainland UK, according to the latest data from Worldpanel.Aldi will open 42 stores this year, with 30 opening in the next 10 weeks. It plans a similar number next year, stepping up investment by about £100m to £900m. In the longer term it is aiming for 1,500 outlets in the UK and Ireland.“We could probably grow faster but we need to find the right sites in the right locations and have to go through a planning process which can, at times, be challenging,” Hurley said.He said consumers were “feeling the pinch” against a backdrop of persistent inflation, and the “continuity and clarity” of Aldi’s range of cheap groceries had attracted 425,300 more customers.He said the outlook for grocery inflation, which stood at 2.8% in August, according to the British Retail Consortium, was difficult to assess until the impact of drought and extreme heat on UK crop yields was clear.He said the industry was “not seeing systemic food shortages” but the climate crisis was creating “a real challenge” for food producers. He urged the government to treat the UK’s food system as “a national strategic priority” because “relying on imports leaves us exposed”.Hurley claimed Aldi was the only grocery chain reducing prices. He said the loyalty discount schemes offered by many rival chains, including Tesco and Sainsbury’s, were “definitely a roll of the dice for customers and questions remain about how much of the value [they offer] is perceived rather than real”.He said Aldi was winning over customers because it remained the cheapest place to shop in the market and it would continue to invest to maintain that position by cutting prices.However, Aldi does not reveal sales performance in established stores – those open for more than a year – making it difficult to gauge how much growth is just the result of expansion.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAldi’s growth is much slower than than that of its rival Lidl, which is gaining market share with a loyalty scheme while allowing shoppers to order online and pick up in a store.Aldi has signed a deal withDeliveroo under which the courier firm’s workers will pick, pack and deliver Aldi groceries sold through its app.The supermarket chain said it had committed to sourcing at least half its products through long-term supplier agreements by next year, giving its producers and manufacturers greater confidence to invest and make Britain’s food system less reliant on imports.Aldi said it spent £14bn with British suppliers in 2025 and about 80% of its sales came from them.Explore more on these topicsAldiSupermarketsRetail industryFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Avanti West Coast to be renationalised in March as ministers float public ownership of new trains | Rail industry | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham hails nationalisation of much-criticised service between London, Birmingham and Glasgow
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Andy Burnham hails nationalisation of much-criticised service between London, Birmingham and Glasgow
Content: Avanti has among the highest proportion of train cancellations in Britain, at 7.1% from April to June this year.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAvanti has among the highest proportion of train cancellations in Britain, at 7.1% from April to June this year.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRail industryAvanti West Coast to be renationalised in March as ministers float public ownership of new trainsAndy Burnham hails nationalisation of much-criticised service between London, Birmingham and GlasgowLauren AlmeidaandGwyn TophamMon 28 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 03.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s biggest intercity rail operator, Avanti West Coast, will be renationalised in spring, ministers have announced, while new trains could also be publicly owned under plans to reduce costs paid to private firms.Avanti, which has been one of the worst rail firms in the country for train delays and cancellations, will come under public ownership from 7 March when its contract ends.Andy Burnham said “enough is enough” for passengers who had put up with a rail service “that has failed them time and time again”.The Labour government has been nationalising passenger rail services across the country as their contracts have expired, as the public bodyGreat British Railways prepares to take full oversight in 2027.The transport secretary,Heidi Alexander, formally announced the decision to nationalise Avanti at the “earliest opportunity” in her speech at the Labour conference on Tuesday afternoon, and said the government would also explore bringing trains into public ownership.Train operators currently lease trains from private rolling-stock companies (Roscos) at the cost of several billion pounds a year. Alexander said the practice since privatisation meant train operating companies “saved money upfront, but it also brought significant long-term costs”.“In 2024, franchised train operators spent over £4bn leasing and maintaining trains they didn’t own – £4bn, that is about a third of the total day-to-day running costs of operating railway services.“Every Rosco contract includes financing and transaction costs and investment returns, costs which are ultimately borne by taxpayers and passengers.“So, as we set up Great British Railways, we will explore whether the state can directly own the new trains we order.”She added: “If GBR owning trains would best serve taxpayers and passengers, then we should do it.”View image in fullscreenAn Avanti West Coast train at Glasgow Central station. Its connect the north and south of England, and on to Wales, Glasgow and Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianUnions welcomed the news. The RMT’s general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said Roscos were “sucking much-needed money out of the railways and into offshore bank accounts”, adding: “This should be the start of a process of winding up the rolling stock racket once and for all.”Dave Calfe, the general secretary of Aslef, the train drivers’ union, said it was “a big step forward for our railway”, adding: “Billions of pounds haemorrhage from the network in profits and dividends which could – and should – be invested in our railway and help keep fares for passengers down.”However, the government said that owning new trains would happen on a “case-by-case basis”, and a rolling stock firm director who had been briefed indicated there was no question of nationalising existing trains.For now, the confirmed nationalisation date of Avanti brings into public ownership a service which had beennotoriouswith unions and passengers –including the prime minister.The company connects the north and south ofEngland, with its service running from London to Manchester and Liverpool. It also runs services through the north-west of England and on to Wales, Glasgow and Edinburgh.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMost of Great Britain’s major rail operators are back in public hands – is it working?Read moreThe prime minister has previously complained about high prices on Avanti, with tickets for peak-time returns from Manchester to London costing as much as £300.Burnham wrote on social media that “for years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again”.“So my Labour government is bringing Avanti West Coast into public ownership at the earliest opportunity in March next year. That means passengers, not shareholders, will come first.“More investment, fewer delays, and a renewed focus on getting the basics right. We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.”Avanti has theworst punctuality rating for any large rail company in the UK.Andy Mellors, the managing director at Avanti West Coast, said: “We’re proud of what we’ve achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before.”He said the improvements had given “customers greater choice, more capacity and better connectivity, while we’ve continued to innovate to shape the future of the west coast and wider rail industry”.Earlier this month, Chiltern Railways became the latest train operator to enter public ownership, becoming the sixth to benationalised under Labour, with the remaining four to follow by the end of 2027. The next operator to transfer into public ownership is scheduled to be Great Western Railway in December.East Midlands Railway is scheduled to be nationalised between this winter and mid-2027, and the last is CrossCountry, in autumn 2027.Explore more on these topicsRail industryRail transportAndy BurnhamTransportNationalisationPublic transportHeidi AlexandernewsShareReuse this content

title: Boss of Beaverbrooks urges government to give businesses ‘a bit of a break’ | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Jeweller reports flat sales and fall in underlying operating profit as retailers anticipate October budget
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Jeweller reports flat sales and fall in underlying operating profit as retailers anticipate October budget
Content: Beaverbrooks, which operates 56 of its own stores, reported a slight fall in sales to £217m.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenBeaverbrooks, which operates 56 of its own stores, reported a slight fall in sales to £217m.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverRetail industryBoss of Beaverbrooks urges government to give businesses ‘a bit of a break’Jeweller reports flat sales and fall in underlying operating profit as retailers anticipate October budgetBusiness live – latest updatesSarah ButlerMon 28 Sep 2026 05.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 05.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of the family-owned jeweller Beaverbrooks has called on the government to give business “a bit of a break” by halting cost increases amid flat sales and falling profits.The retailer, founded in 1919, revealed a 9% fall in underlying operating profit to £7.8m last year after an increase in employer national insurance contributions (NICs) and the legal minimum wageintroduced by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves.Anna Blackburn, the managing director of Beaverbrooks, said she was positive about the performance against the backdrop of a challenging retail market: “Everything we hear in the jewellery industry [suggests] this is a pretty strong performance,” she said.Total sales slipped 0.1% to £217m at the group, which operates 56 Beaverbrooks and four Loupe stores as well as 22 outlets for specific brands including watchmakers Omega, Breitling, Tudor and TAG Heuer.Blackburn said she wanted to see the government help boost consumer confidence and provide stability by tackling unemployment and inflation and not adding new taxes in next month’s budget as retailers prepare for Christmas.She said: “[The government] can’t increase business costs much more. Give business a bit of a break and stimulate some growth and confidence. A long-term, joined-up strategy is critical.”Blackburn said Beaverbrooks was outperforming its rivals in tough conditions as it continued to invest in its stores and staff, modernising its online operation and developing new products.“Our business has remained strong for 107 years because we believe in the high street and the importance of exceptional products and customer service.”The group has just opened its fourth Loupe watch boutique, in Sheffield, and is investing in revamping its outlets in Manchester’s Trafford Centre and Lakeside in Essex in the year ahead.Blackburn’s comments come after thesince-departed boss of the John Lewis department storechain, Peter Ruis, said the chancellor’s budget would come at a “critical period” for retailers and hewanted to see more help on business rates.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe boss of fellow retailer JD Sports has also said Reeves’s move to increase employer NICs at the same time as a chunky rise in the legal minimum wage had been “really a wrong movement” and pushed retailers to use more technology and hire fewer young people.The government faces a tricky budget as the high price of oil and government borrowing put the squeeze on its finances – and on household bills.The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly considering shifting more green subsidies from energy bills into general taxation, examining fuel duty and targeting help at the poorest households.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryConsumer spendingLuxury goods sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve never watched a whole episode of Peep Show’: Matt King on surviving a stroke and reviving Super Hans | Peep Show | The Guardian
description: The actor is returning to his character in the cult Channel 4 sitcom with a new autobiography – despite barely watching the series. He talks about his ‘terrifying’ hospital stay and why strangers still shout at him about crack being ‘moreish’
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The actor is returning to his character in the cult Channel 4 sitcom with a new autobiography – despite barely watching the series. He talks about his ‘terrifying’ hospital stay and why strangers still shout at him about crack being ‘moreish’
Content: You need Hans … Matt King as Peep Show’s king of chaos.Photograph: Kenny McCrackenView image in fullscreenYou need Hans … Matt King as Peep Show’s king of chaos.Photograph: Kenny McCrackenPeep Show‘I’ve never watched a whole episode of Peep Show’: Matt King on surviving a stroke and reviving Super HansThe actor is returning to his character in the cult Channel 4 sitcom with a new autobiography – despite barely watching the series. He talks about his ‘terrifying’ hospital stay and why strangers still shout at him about crack being ‘moreish’Rich PelleyMon 28 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuper Hans is back! What’s he been up to since we last saw him?Splitting up withMolly, the twins, themoped-rental business inMacedonia…Well, Super Hans finds a legal loophole in the marriage certificate, which means it’s null and void and … hang on … I’m basically telling you the whole plot of the book!Is the book just you, Matt King, writing on behalf of Super Hans? Or does your inner Super Hans just come out and write it for you?It’s neither. He comes around my house every morning. I put the kettle on, he borrows my computer and off he goes. I don’t know what he gets up to. I usually try to get out of the way, go for a nice walk.Is Super Hans your golden goose – or the albatrossround your neck?Well,Peep Showended in 2015. It started 23 years ago as an acting job, for want of a better term. A lot has happened since then, including having a stroke in April this year, which often means I totally lose the thread of what I’m saying, as you may have noticed.double quotation markI’ve seen Bake Off now I’ve been on it, but never watched a whole episode of Peep ShowHaving a stroke must have been awful. Even so, you seemed to be very good-humoured about it on social media from the get-go.I mean, initially it was absolutely terrifying because I was paralysed for 36 hours. I don’t remember the ambulance ride, or the first day and a half. I woke up on the stroke ward at Royal Sussex County hospital. But yes, I think I was quite good-natured about it. I had a very rare type of stroke, quite low down on the spinal cord. The doctors told me that I could have ended up in a wheelchair, or worse. I was very lucky, so I spent most of my time in hospital feeling very grateful. Cognitively, I’m quite a bit different from how I was before the stroke, although I am improving. I still had around a quarter of the book to write when it happened. In a weird way, my brain jumping all over the place helped on the home stretch.Could we see a Super Hans spin-off TV show?I would be more interested in a film based on this – the first of many books. I’m not going to be able to get away with playing him for much longer. I was talking to David Mitchell when we did The Great Peep Show Christmas Bake Off last year. We both remember [Peep Show creators] Jesse [Armstrong] and Sam [Bain] saying to us on the last day of filming: “See you in 10 years.” Ten years came and went, and none of us got the call. Maybe it’s because Jesse had some show called Succession going on.View image in fullscreenLift off … Matt King in the season nine Peep Show episode The William Morris Years.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyPerhaps the most surprising thing you revealed while appearing onThe Great Peep Show Christmas Bake Offwas that you’d never seen Bake Off – or, indeed, Peep Show.I have seen Bake Off – now that I’ve been on it. But it’s true that I have never watched a whole episode of Peep Show.Does that make it more difficult dealing with obsessive fans – and needy journalists – who can quote every episode word for word?For example,how many of the bands you and Jez were in can you name?The Hair Blair Bunch, Curse These Metal Hands, Coming Up for Blair, Various Artists …Have you heard about the now-annualAccidentally Run to Windsor, where people actually run from Croydon to Windsor, inspired by Super Hans giving up all his vices but becoming addicted to endorphins?Yes. I was meant to be at the finish line last year, but I was unwell. This year, I think I’m going to be firing the starter’s pistol.Why are you not the pacemaker for the first, say, 13 miles?I think the answer to that would be evident from looking at me. But that’s not to say that I’m not going to run across the finish line first. I’ll just be getting in the van the other 25 and a half miles.double quotation markTwo years ago, my daughter came home from school and went: 'It’s happened. Everyone is watching Peep Show, and they all know you’re my dad'What do people shout the most at you when they see you?“That crack is really moreish”, from the other end of a tube compartment. If they go too niche, I’ve no idea what they’re talking about. Often, I’ll have no recollection of saying it, so I get a disappointed response when they have to explain that it was in season seven, episode four, or whatever.Peep Show seems to be bigger now than when you finished making it.Why do you think it keeps finding new generations of fans?Obviously, it’s brilliant. Obviously, it’s endlessly quotable. Obviously, it’s funny. But there aren’t any other shows from that era that are still watched by ever-changing generations. My daughter is 17. About two years ago, she came home from school and went: “It’s happened. Everyone at school is watching fucking Peep Show, and they all know that you’re my dad.” My son, who’s 22 now, had gone through the same thing. The wave just keeps going.Has Super Hans somehow become timeless, then?More people come up to me now than they did 10 years ago. I was in an underground swimming pool in Morocco and there was another geezer doing lengths next to me. When I got out of the pool, he said: “Do you mind if I just interrupt you?” Turns out, he had gone to Sandhurst. He said they all used to watch it and that the box set belonged to Will. I said: “Who’s Will?” “Prince William.” There’s footage of David Bowie being interviewed in his house, and he’s got the box set of all nine series of Peep Show on DVD behind him. Between that and builders shouting it from scaffolding, it’s got every colour of the rainbow, every type of humanity.Is it hard to know where Matt ends and Super Hans begins? What are your views on Coldplay, for example?Let’s just say, my views on Coldplay are even more extreme than his!Moreish: My Mad Autobiographyby Super Hans is out now published by Mudlark.Explore more on these topicsPeep ShowTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Should have garnered the actor an Oscar’: why Liar Liar is my feelgood movie | Jim Carrey | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers paying tribute to the films they watch when they need a lift is an appreciation of Jim Carrey’s manic 90s comedy
Author: Rob LeDonne
Headline: The latest in our series of writers paying tribute to the films they watch when they need a lift is an appreciation of Jim Carrey’s manic 90s comedy
Content: Jim Carrey and Jennifer Tilly in Liar Liar.Photograph: Moviestore Collection/REXView image in fullscreenJim Carrey and Jennifer Tilly in Liar Liar.Photograph: Moviestore Collection/REXMy feelgood movieJim Carrey‘Should have garnered the actor an Oscar’: why Liar Liar is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers paying tribute to the films they watch when they need a lift is an appreciation of Jim Carrey’s manic 90s comedyRob LeDonneMon 28 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo be completely honest, whenever anybody asks what my favorite movies are, my list has some typical standbys: Goodfellas and It’s a Wonderful Life among them. The holiday classic National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation is another. But there’s one feelgood fave on my list that always surprises people: Jim Carrey’s 1997 blockbuster Liar Liar.‘Still feel a jolt of joy’: why Dirty Dancing is my feelgood movieRead moreThe movie (for the lack of a better word) lies on the bedrock of a simple premise: a lawyer and doting father is physically unable to tell an untruth due to a birthday wish. In the hands of a less competent creative team and cast,Liar Liarwould have been yet another forgettable piece of 90s comedy junk; destined for the bottom of a discount VHS bin, forgotten as the years trudged on. But largely thanks to an unbelievable performance courtesy of Carrey, who was working with a smart and peppy script, the film ascends into rarefied air.The bellylaugh-o-meter breaks its springs on a regular basis throughout its brisk 86-minute runtime. In fact, it’s on par, or even surpassing, fellow comedy powerhouses such as Airplane! and The Naked Gun when it comes to the sheer volume of gags, set pieces and jokes. Tom Shadyac, the director, who previously directed Carrey in his 1993 breakout Ace Ventura: Pet Detective, wisely unleashes Carrey, who spins out and around the scenery like the Tasmanian Devil, remarkably combining such a manic and energetic performance with one grounded in pure emotion.At the center of Carrey’s character, Fletcher Reede, is love for his son; with themes of fatherhood and parenthood the beating heart of the film. There’s inherent likability inside the hamminess, a trick Carrey delivers as if that combination is almost totally impossible. What Carrey pulls off is a performance that, in a fair world, should have garnered the actor an Oscar. Comedic turns, and comedy films in general, are arguably much more difficult to pull off as opposed to the understated and moody dramas the Academy likes to honor.However, it was quickly proven that even when Carrey transformed himself into a formidable dramatic actor with 1999’s Man on the Moon, the Academy snubbed that too. (Thankfully, he was indeed nominated for a Golden Globe for Liar Liar).What defines a feelgood movie, along with being a comfy joy to experience, is its bevy of rewatchable scenes: the kind that make you stop in your tracks when flicking through TV channels. (The Ringer’s Bill Simmons devised a whole delicious podcast about this). Liar Liar serves up can’t-miss-’em scenes in spades. In one of them, Carrey, realizing he’s cursed to tell the truth, tries to say that a blue pen is red but can’t bring himself to, later revealing he put himself through a physical wringer. (He latersaidthe entire self-tussle had one simple direction: Fletcher “beats himself up”). Who can also forget Carrey’s epic meltdown after he’s baited into joining a stuffy meeting at the law firm and roasts everybody in sight? “You’ve got your head so far up Mr Alan’s ass, I can’t tell where you end and he begins!” The final courtroom showdown is another gem, rivaling any scene in A Few Good Men.I vividly remember watching its epic LAX-set grand finale where Carrey’s Reede hijacks a mobile airplane stairway as his son Max is about to fly out of California and wowed by the hilarious spectacle of the stunt in a movie that, up until that point, consisted of scenes in courtrooms, offices and homes. But by the time we wrap things up with Carrey battered and bruised, albeit with his son back, the bloopers inserted at the end of the film demonstrating the insanity Carrey unleashed on set, were the cherry on top of the whole shebang, and stand as one of the rare cases of a gag reel being actually funny as opposed to a series of awkward flubs.A cozy rewatch also reminds one of how a film with as many pure chuckles as Liar Liar is a nonexistent entity at theaters in the modern era. It’s almost as if recent studio comedies such as One Night Only and Anyone But You forgot they were supposed to elicit laughs, instead of subtle smirks at best. It’s also the type of movie one can take away lessons from at any point in one’s life. When I was 10 and watched Liar Liar, I obviously gravitated towards the kid’s perspective. But as the decades roll on, you can glean something from it at every stage of life.It’s an underdog of a feelgood movie, and one that gets lost in the hubbub of fellow Carrey classics such as Dumb and Dumber. But whether the headlines got you down, it’s a rainy night or the family’s simply getting together, one can’t go wrong with popping on Carrey’s unreal tour de force in Liar Liar. And that’s the truth, so help me God.Liar Liar is available on Netflix in the US, NOW TV in the UK and Paramount+ and Binge in AustraliaThis article was amended on 28 September 2026. An earlier version said that in Liar Liar Jim Carrey tries to say that a blue pen is black; in fact, he says it is red.Explore more on these topicsJim CarreyMy feelgood movieLiar LiarComedy filmsComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pandora’s Legacy review – fascinating profile of silent film legend GW Pabst | Movies | The Guardian
description: Through intimate letters and family interviews, this probing documentary about the Austrian film-maker reveals a complicated figure
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Through intimate letters and family interviews, this probing documentary about the Austrian film-maker reveals a complicated figure
Content: Wealth of archive material … Pandora’s Legacy.Photograph: Max BernerView image in fullscreenWealth of archive material … Pandora’s Legacy.Photograph: Max BernerMoviesReviewPandora’s Legacy review – fascinating profile of silent film legend GW PabstThrough intimate letters and family interviews, this probing documentary about the Austrian film-maker reveals a complicated figurePhuong LeMon 28 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtitan of silent cinema, Austrian director GW Pabst left behind a treasure trove of classics. Working in WeimarGermany, Pabst gave Greta Garbo her second ever lead role in The Joyless Street (1925), and propelled Louise Brooks to international stardom with Pandora’s Box (1929) and Diary of a Lost Girl (1929). Attentive to the marginalised elements of society, these early triumphs exemplified the kind of free-spirited film-making that flourished before the rise of the Nazi regime. Faced with this colossal legacy, Angela Christlieb’s probing documentary takes a more winding path through Pabst’s personal archive. Through intimate letters, family albums, and interviews with his descendants, the film foregrounds the man behind the images, while bringing another figure into the spotlight: Gertrude Pabst, the director’s wife of more than 40 years.Far from a hagiographic portrait, Christlieb’s film reveals Pabst to be a complicated and patriarchal figure. His grandchildren – Marion, Daniel and Ben – describe the great film-maker as a distant figure, who instilled fear rather than love in his two sons. Pabst’s films have been praised for their modern and strong-willed female characters, yet in private he forbade Gertrude from pursuing her own acting aspirations. She also reluctantly underwent numerous abortions – seven in total – so as not to derail her husband’s career.Christlieb often uses scenes from Pabst’s films to illustrate these family frictions, an approach that feels strained and contrived; these sequences showcase the brilliance of the director’s filmography, but risk drawing a simplistic biographical link between his work and his life, undermining both the richness of his creative visions and the difficulties endured by those in his orbit. Meanwhile the detours into Marion, Daniel and Ben’s careers are interesting, but they distract from Gertrude’s story, which could have merited more screen time. These structural missteps aside, the wealth of archive material is fascinating to behold, revealing a hidden side to a much-discussed film legend.Pandora’s Legacy is on True Story from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsSilent filmGermanyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Crushed review – Steve Oram is priestly lead in harrowing Bangkok-set child-abduction thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: A priest investigates his daughter’s kidnapping in Thailand in this Paul Schrader-esque inquiry into spiritual nihilism
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: A priest investigates his daughter’s kidnapping in Thailand in this Paul Schrader-esque inquiry into spiritual nihilism
Content: Lofty ideals … Steve Oram as Father Daniel and Margaux Dietrich as Olivia in Crushed.Photograph: GrimmVisionView image in fullscreenLofty ideals … Steve Oram as Father Daniel and Margaux Dietrich as Olivia in Crushed.Photograph: GrimmVisionMoviesReviewCrushed review – Steve Oram is priestly lead in harrowing Bangkok-set child-abduction thrillerA priest investigates his daughter’s kidnapping in Thailand in this Paul Schrader-esque inquiry into spiritual nihilismPhil HoadMon 28 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘He’s American, a little bit overweight, sweaty, a little bit camp, creepy.” As far as descriptions of border-hopping paedophiles go, this seems a little on the nose. So it’s not surprising when the man who was enquiring, priest Father Daniel (Steve Oram), responds: “Are you making this up?” Featuring a seedy child-abduction situation in Bangkok, Simon Rumley’s thriller comes close at times to bugged-out exploitation flick territory – but lets its fleet and fresh manner carry it towards a Paul Schrader-esque moral calvary.Pastor to a mixed Anglo-Thai congregation, Father Daniel has a young daughter, Olivia (Margaux Dietrich), with wife May (Nattapohn Rawddon). At a sleepover, Olivia is traumatised when her friend’s older brother shows her a“crush” videoof a kitten being stomped by a scantily clad floozy. So when her own cat Missy goes awol, she is convinced the same lady is responsible, and asks her dad how God could let it happen. The family mobilise to track down Missy, but Olivia in turn disappears one day after school, kicking off Father Daniel’s own test of faith.There could have been a very different version of Crushed, if Liam Neeson had signed on with his special set of ecumenical skills. But Rumley holds the vengeance angle at bay, subtly foreshadowing Olivia’s ordeal with the implied horror of the squashed furballs filtering through her nightmares, and using clever juxtaposition to slyly compare and contrast her father’s lofty ideals with the surrounding scrappy reality. At one point, after refusing to play the Beatles’ profane songs, Father Daniel’s acoustic guitar version of All Creatures Great and Small soundtracks Olivia’s pet search on the streets.The film’s almost new-wave alertness lifts it above lurid payback fodder, but its inquiry into the feasibility of forgiveness wavers. While Rumley has an understandable tendency to euphemistically cut away from hotel-room horrors, it also gives the impression that these are disposable plot points rather than unbearably squalid confrontations with spiritual nihilism. When Father Daniel and May separately interrogate the paedophile’s South African fixer, Rumley’s use of split screen again makes the inquest seem superficial.In fact, the fixer – an increasingly harrowing performance from Christian Ferreira – undergoes more of a moral crucifixion than Oram’s Daniel, whose complacent mildness makes him something closer to a satirical stooge. But if the clergyman finally goes all the way when the film itself can’t quite, Rumley’s limber style keeps things consistently interesting.Crushed is available on digital platforms from 5 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsCrime filmsThailandreviewsShareReuse this content

Content: Lit chit-chat … Barack Obama.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty Images for NetflixView image in fullscreenLit chit-chat … Barack Obama.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty Images for NetflixBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioObama and Tom Hanks have an inspirational chat: best podcasts of the weekDaring to defy the norms of political lobbying, the ex-US president is becoming a podcast mainstay – and is opening up about the books that inspired him. title: Paraorchestra; Sinfonietta/Jonny Greenwood review – Reich’s kaleidoscopic music bursts into life | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Paraorchestra’s immersive performance of Music for 18 Musicians was immaculate and exhilarating; London Sinfonietta and the Radiohead guitarist’s vibrant tribute to the almost 90-year-old composer followed
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Paraorchestra’s immersive performance of Music for 18 Musicians was immaculate and exhilarating; London Sinfonietta and the Radiohead guitarist’s vibrant tribute to the almost 90-year-old composer followed
Content: ‘Grins on faces’ … Paraorchestra get the Steve Reich party started.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorView image in fullscreen‘Grins on faces’ … Paraorchestra get the Steve Reich party started.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorClassical musicReviewParaorchestra; Sinfonietta/Jonny Greenwood review – Reich’s kaleidoscopic music bursts into lifeSouthbank Centre, LondonParaorchestra’s immersive performance of Music for 18 Musicians was immaculate and exhilarating; London Sinfonietta and the Radiohead guitarist’s vibrant tribute to the almost 90-year-old composer followedClive PagetMon 28 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo birthdays were celebrated at Southbank Centre’s Steve Reich-fest. First,the composer himself, a supremely influential artist who has shifted the classical music dial over decades with his evolving yet instantly recognisable soundworld. He turns 90 on 3 October. And then there was Music for 18 Musicians, one of his signature works, which notches up a half-century this year. An immersive performance of the latter invited the audience to mingle with an ensemble dotted around the Clore Ballroom, the collective grins on faces proof positive of the work’s enduring power to raise the spirits.View image in fullscreen‘Clean-as-a-whistle technique’ … Jonny Greenwood alongside the London Sinfonietta.Photograph: seb.gardner/seb gardnerDoing the honours wasParaorchestra, Charles Hazlewood’s enterprising collective of disabled and non-disabled musicians, who brought Reich’s kaleidoscopic music to life with ironclad discipline. Freed from fixed seats, the itinerant audience peered at musicians on podiums as if they were objects in an exhibition, marvelling at the precision of polyrhythmic marimba players, or grooving in a central mosh pit with a flexuous quintet of dancers who persuaded children and grandparents alike to go with the flow. Line dancing, disco lights – this exhilarating performance had it all.Twenty minutes to catch the breath and it was upstairs to the Festival Hall for the London Sinfonietta and guitaristJonny Greenwood. If the formal atmosphere was more subdued and the hall less intimate, the playing, under conductor Chloe Rooke, was crisp and controlled. Pulse, written in 2015, saw canonic wind and string melodies spun out over piano-led ostinatos in one of the composer’s more relaxed works. Greenwood played electric bass, providing a neat link with Radio Rewrite, a Sinfonietta commission from 2013, in which Reich partly absorbs and partly riffs on a pair of songs by Radiohead.Opening the second half, Greenwood brought clean-as-a-whistle technique and a distinctive personality (not always associated with this composer’s music) to Electric Counterpoint. A tenacious performance pitted live electric guitar against his own pre-recorded version of Reich’s original backing track. To finish, the Sinfonietta gave a gritty account of City Life. Sampling keyboards introduced urban sounds, from car horns and door slams to heartbeats and police sirens, into the orchestral mix in a kinetic tribute to Reich’s native New York.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicSteve ReichThe London SinfoniettareviewsShareReuse this content

title: I Can’t Tell You But I Will by Magda Szubanski review – an insightful, elegant, anti-celebrity memoir | Magda Szubanski | The Guardian
description: Szubanski’s latest book delves into both her mother’s decline, and her triumphant fight for marriage equality
Author: Tim Byrne
Headline: Szubanski’s latest book delves into both her mother’s decline, and her triumphant fight for marriage equality
Content: In her latest memoir, I Can’t Tell You But I Will, Magda Szubanski ‘writes about her life with such emotional precision, like a forensic pathologist wielding a scalpel’.Photograph: Darren JamesView image in fullscreenIn her latest memoir, I Can’t Tell You But I Will, Magda Szubanski ‘writes about her life with such emotional precision, like a forensic pathologist wielding a scalpel’.Photograph: Darren JamesAustralian book reviewsMagda SzubanskiReviewI Can’t Tell You But I Will by Magda Szubanski review – an insightful, elegant, anti-celebrity memoirSzubanski’s latest book delves into both her mother’s decline, and her triumphant fight for marriage equalitySupported byAbout this contentTim ByrneMon 28 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a certain tension in the celebrity memoir between what is confessed and what is withheld. We want to know the things the celebrity isn’t telling us, and comb through what they do say looking for secrets, the flaws or inconsistencies, the myopic and self-serving. Most celebrities try to thread their stories through this needle, giving us the sense of candidness without revealing too much of anything. After all, there are reputations to uphold.Magda Szubanski doesn’t write those memoirs. She writes about her life with such emotional precision, like a forensic pathologist wielding a scalpel; never aiming for amiability nor belly laughs, but a kind of equilibrium of understanding instead. She processes the tectonic forces in her life in order to stand on firmer ground, like building a mound on which to better survey the topography. I Can’t Tell You But I Will is the follow-up to her 2015 memoir Reckoning, about her father and the scars of war; this memoir turns the attention away from him and on to her mother, Margaret.Always a joker: Magda Szubanski reveals Heath Ledger asked to play her stalker on Kath and KimRead moreMother-daughter relationships often make for fascinating reading, as we saw recently withArundhati Roy’s Mother Mary Comes to Me.There’s something about the intensity and ruthlessness of familial female dynamics that feels particularly brutal and bruising, and Szubanski doesn’t shy away from the ways in which mothers can get under the skin and into the fibres of our being. Margaret is a flinty Scotswoman with a mean streak – Szubanski often emphasises the word “mean” in a way that lets you feel every slight and insult – but she’s also complex and loving. I Can’t Tell You is less a reckoning and more a painfully earned benediction.That seems appropriate, given a key theme in the memoir is Szubanski’s religion. Raised Catholic, she struggled with the strictures and the doctrine of Christianity while finding comfort in its rituals (“Rituals matter more than clever secular people like to admit,” she writes) and sense of tribalism. Being a lesbian made this relationship with the church untenable while opening her to a new tribe; witnessing friends in beautiful same-sex relationships, she realised the dogma was plain wrong. When she first had sex with a woman, “I knew, despite what I had been told my whole life, that this was not an unnatural act. That while it might be a sin against the Church it was definitely not a sin against nature.”I Can’t Tell You employs and entwines two narrative arcs: Margaret’s long, awful decline and death, and Szubanski’s public activism in the fight for marriage equality. Ambivalence runs through both. It’s fascinating to learn of the doubt and insecurity Szubanski felt as the voice of the Yes campaign – and appalling to learn of the hatred and vitriol she endured – given her status as one of Australia’s most beloved people, with an Order of Australia to her name: “This is an ideological gun fight, and I have come armed with a butter knife. My ‘popularity’.”Szubanski’s reticence about getting involved with activism of any kind stems from her time working at a women’s refuge, where she experienced the remorseless consequences of domestic violence as well as the excruciating internal politics of the feminist collective that ran it. She may have found the experience traumatising, but it presumably helped in the latter campaign, which culminatedwith an appearance on Q&Athat made her opponents seem petty and the Yes campaign dignified and warm.Contrasting with the victorious story of Szubanski’s return to activism – told without a hint of triumphalism, but rather a weary sense of accomplishment – is Margaret’s decline and her daughter’s profound experience in caring for her at the end of her life. It’s sometimes embittered but also honest and generous, a portrait of people loving imperfectly but passionately and without regret.View image in fullscreenThere is a sense over the course of these two memoirs that Szubanski is exorcising the spirits of her mother and father – and of ennobling them in the act of writing them down – in order to better understand herself and her place in the world. “Both my parents had such powerful personalities that I had always needed to fight for psychic space, even within my own head,” she writes.Two things are missing, or at least touched on so briefly they leave a gap or ellipsis. Given half the book is dedicated to Australia’s vote in favour of same-sex marriage, the single mention of the subsequent Indigenous voice to parliament vote and the racism it fostered feels slightly avoidant. Perhaps Szubanski didn’t feel she could speak to that. The other is her cancer diagnosis last year, which she most likely doesn’t feel like discussing right now, even while in remission.It could be argued that Szubanski’s new book isn’t a celebrity memoir at all. The handful of famous names that crop up aren’t emphasised or mined for their reflected glamour; the heroes are named Clint or Narelle, and backstage stories from her hit shows are completely absent. If anything, it is anti-celebrity, keen to highlight the expansiveness and grit of anonymous people dedicated to “unhistoric acts”. I Can’t Tell You But I Will is, like Reckoning, an insightful and deeply elegant window into aspects of Szubanski we rarely get to see, even if they’re not the ones we may have been expecting.I Can’t Tell You But I Will by Magda Szubanski is out now in Australia(Text Publishing, $55), with wider release to followExplore more on these topicsMagda SzubanskiAustralian book reviewsAutobiography and memoirCelebrityAustralian booksMarriage equalitySame-sex marriage postal surveyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Deep into the Sixties: Britain 1965-66 by David Kynaston review – a tour de force of popular history | History books | The Guardian
description: From the Beatles and the World Cup to racism and homophobia, the latest instalment in Kynaston’s series captures a society in the throes of change
Author: Blake Morrison
Headline: From the Beatles and the World Cup to racism and homophobia, the latest instalment in Kynaston’s series captures a society in the throes of change
Content: Beatles Fans.R0JEMN Police try to hold back Beatles Fans.Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenBeatles Fans.R0JEMN Police try to hold back Beatles Fans.Photograph: Album/AlamyBook of the dayHistory booksReviewDeep into the Sixties: Britain 1965-66 by David Kynaston review – a tour de force of popular historyFrom the Beatles and the World Cup to racism and homophobia, the latest instalment in Kynaston’s series captures a society in the throes of changeBlake MorrisonMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 02.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February 1965, the civil rights activist Malcolm X visited Smethwick, in the Midlands, where the Conservative-run council was planning to buy up houses to stop the area becoming a “coloured ghetto”. He wanted to see how bad the racism was and he experienced it first-hand when refused service in a pub. White residents thought his visit a “disgusting” intrusion. Nine days later, back in the US, he was shot dead.Britain in the mid-60s is associated with Carnaby Street, the Beatles and miniskirts, not racism. But what Black people endured, from a colour bar on property to the abuse of Leeds United winger Albert Johanneson as a “golliwog”, is no less a period marker than Harold Wilson’s pipe, Twiggy’s haircut, Mary Whitehouse’s clean-up TV campaign and Bob Dylan’s use of an electric guitar. David Kynaston doesn’t underplay the excitements of the period. But he rightly emphasises that the rotten old 50s – patriarchal, homophobic, class-divided and bigoted – wouldn’t just fade away.His mammoth project, a history of Britain from 1945‑79, is now past halfway. He originally expected this volume to continue to 1967. In the event it covers just 18 months, from February 1965 to July 1966, and (with notes) runs to nearly 700 pages. The challenge is to balance an in-depth account of politics, economics, industry, education and culture with personal stories of what it was like to be there: the food you ate, the clothes you wore, the films you saw. The sources he draws on range from statistical surveys and sociological reports to political biographies, personal diaries and the grouchy letters of Philip Larkin. No living historian is as comprehensive.With much to accommodate, he relies on the semicolon for day-by-day narration: “At a Monday morning cabinet session…;” “later that afternoon …;” “on the box the same evening …;” “next morning in Manchester … ;”and so on. The sentences are long but full of humour and never dull. The high point comes with a “freewheelin’, mid-60s play list” (duly abbreviated here) that takes up five pages:Multi-flavoured Golden Wonder crisps displacing Smith’s plain; one-third of new marriages now civil marriages; pubs reluctantly installing fruit machines; Jimmy Hill’s Sky-Blue revolution at Coventry City; AA patrols no longer required to salute; picture rails, seen as dust traps, removed en masse from Victorian and Edwardian houses; Boots from 1965 at last consenting to sell condoms; arrival of open-plan offices; arrival, too, of the hot drinks vending machine; no car more iconic of modernity than the Mini Cooper …As well as giving us snippets from daily life and reminding us how nasty the 60s could be (Ian Brady, Myra Hindley and the Kray brothers), Kynaston devotes chapters to larger-scale cultural shifts, chief among them in education. Harold Wilson dreamed of “a Britain in which anyone can get to the top on merit and ability, not on social or family connections”, and the shift to comprehensive schools was integral to that. Grammar schools resisted, public schools clung on to their independence, and refusenik local authorities caricatured the change as a Nazi-like conspiracy designed to “tyrannise the minds of the young” and create “animal farms” run by state commissars. But Anthony Crosland pushed hard for the reform and it did Labour no harm in the March 1966 general election, which kept them in power with a majority of 97 seats.Polytechnics arrived too – 30 of them over the following eight years, along with the Open University. This wasn’t quite the age of social mobility it’s cracked up to be. Most children still left school at 15. Whereas 50% of high-school graduates in the US went on to university, it was still less than 6% in the UK. But expansion was under way. And many of the era’s famous names – David Bailey, Albert Finney, Michael Caine, Jean Shrimpton, Harold Evans, Terence Stamp, Cilla Black and Lulu – had working-class roots.Kynaston also explores the rebuilding of cities: slum clearances, tower blocks and (in the words of the song by pop band Unit 4 Plus 2), concrete and clay. It was a peak time for high rises, with whole streets destroyed (as if wartime bombing had resumed) and millions of people displaced to new estates. Some were grateful to escape the damp and squalor of the houses they’d been in; many were not: “I’d rather have a tent on the moors.” Kynaston detects “a certain residual arrogance” in the architects and planners. The pendulum would gradually swing against a “dim-witted adulation of Le Corbusier”, but until then the vogue was for streets in the sky.Happily, there was also a vogue for liberalisation: of birth control, abortion law, consensual sex between men, and greater opportunities for women. All were much needed: homosexuality was widely vilified; the Factories Act forbade women to do night shifts and only 80 of 1,707 candidates at the election were female; family planning clinics wouldn’t see young, unmarried women, one of whom asked agony aunt Marjorie Proops: “If a girl has intercourse, and then has nothing to do with boys for a year, can she have become a virgin again?” More surprising is to find that half the workforce in 1966 was already in the service industry and that the City of London was a hub of global power long before the 1980s.The book’s likeliest readers will be those alive at the time, whose memories will be triggered by what was new (the Post Office Tower, microwaves, Laker Airways), what needed phasing out (bottom-pinching, outdoor loos, “the brain-damaging heaviness” of leather footballs) and what songs, plays, films and television programmes had to say about contemporary life. Kynaston quotes generously from reviews, many of them more robust than you find today (“pretentious bunkum”, “inane, asinine, witless”); the BBC’s brilliant Wednesday Play series infuriated audiences and even the Beatles were denounced when awarded MBEs: “All they do is exploit a basic jungle rhythm for money.” A younger audience may be struck by the parallels between then and now: a Labour prime minister from the north, economic strife, the US in a pointless war, hostility to immigrants. We’re not facing devaluation of the pound, as Harold Wilson was. Still, the continuities stretch forward as well as back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe last section of the book is a tour de force, interspersing Kenneth Wolstenholme’s commentary on the World Cup final (“Four minutes now left to play and the crowd biting fingernails down to the knuckles”) with the reactions of those watching on television, among them young Laurence Marks, the finest of the diarists quoted in the book, who stood to lose £2/12 shillings on a bet if England won, and Kynaston himself, on his 15th birthday: “I retreat upstairs to my bedroom and play a side of a Nancy Sinatra album, reckoning it will see both me and England through.” It did. The match was a triumph and so is the book. But spare a thought for the 6,000-strong crowd in Devon who’d paid to see the Kinks perform that night. The band stayed in London till the match was over and, arriving two hours late at 11.45pm, were allowed to play for just 10 minutes.Deep into the Sixties: Britain 1965-66 by David Kynaston is published by Bloomsbury (£35). title: Range by Dorthe Nors review – an astrophysicist at odds with reality | Fiction | The Guardian
description: In the Danish writer’s latest novel, an eminent scientist withdraws to the countryside
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In the Danish writer’s latest novel, an eminent scientist withdraws to the countryside
Content: Dorthe Nors.Photograph: Lea MeilandtDorthe Nors.Photograph: Lea MeilandtFictionReviewRange by Dorthe Nors review – an astrophysicist at odds with realityIn the Danish writer’s latest novel, an eminent scientist withdraws to the countrysideCaleb KlacesMon 28 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Gunn Haven, an eminent professor of astrophysics at an urban university, moves to rural Denmark, she tells a local newspaper: “It’s to do with the sky.” From the outset of Range, Danish author Dorthe Nors’s fifth full-length novel, it is apparent this is not the whole truth. Soon after arriving, Gunn is compelled to trespass along a nearby track to look at a farmhouse with collapsed gable walls, her curiosity driven by personal interest rather than scientific inquiry. A woman pulls up in a dark blue BMW. She is dressed in “hunter’s camouflage, fleshy-faced. And ponytailed. Weapon raised: a phone, filming Gunn.” Gunn reluctantly retreats.Gunn is distracted by this woman, Krista, who works at the local potato flour factory. Gunn should be working ona general introduction to astrophysics, “the Work”. Instead, the Professor finds herself wondering what “Gable Woman” would do if she came to “the Institute”, where Gunn researches “light from the oldest galaxies”. She would draw a dick on a blackboard, Gunn imagines, “with a small titillated smile”. Gunn is more generous to promising young scientists. She pays for a former student to travel to America. Closer to home, she begins to help Jenny, the teenage daughter of her hairdresser, with a school project on black holes. Jenny is an “uneducated creature” who smells “faintly of iron”, with a “faint red to the cheeks, from shyness or cold. Oddly sexless, and she had been here before, but with her mother.”The construction of that sentence – from fragments and obtrusive conjunctions – is typical of Caroline Waight’s English translation of Range. The novel’s imagery is equally difficult to understand. During a lecture, Gunn thinks: “I’m coated in saliva.” Speculating on how a colony on Mars might develop, she says: “second generation: identical glasses and spit”.double quotation markThe scenes of awkward intimacy between Gunn and Jenny are the tender heart of Range, but they are wrapped in a predictable plotNors’s previous novel translated into English,Mirror, Shoulder, Signal, is also about a woman whose interior world is at odds with external reality. The novel, shortlisted for the 2017 International Booker prize, follows Sonja, a middle-aged translator of Swedish crime novels, as she embarks on driving lessons. Sonja makes a living finding just the right words for acts of graphic violence. The novel’s subtle humour comes in the juxtaposition between the details of this violence and the mundane challenges of Sonja’s life, such as learning to use a gated stick shift. In Range, the incongruity between Gunn and those around her feels darker and more cryptic. Gunn receives a dead bird in her post box and a “For Sale” sign is moved close to her house. These hostile acts trigger memories of Gunn’s early life, which filter through her studies of the universe’s earliest light. Gunn’s mother died in a traffic accident. Her childhood with her father was poor but loving, with “moments of equations so long they went beyond any greasy cooker hood”. This might explain why, in adult life, Gunn is so concerned with the celestial that she fails to understand more local phenomena, such as other people.Gunn’s thinking, however, is improbably imprecise. “The Work” is jumbled and vague. Gunn imagines evolution will soon mean “we’ll be born with Vaseline glands”. If this construction is distracting, the following description is dismaying: “But she didn’t get that far: she heard the car before she saw it. Rather like with thunder, and she turned back to the living room, crouched.” Gunn, an astrophysicist so renowned that her moving house is reported in the local newspaper, seems to believe that thunder is heard before lightning is seen.Gunn is interested in Jane Austen’s novel Persuasion because “the word was nice”. She buys a copy of a Danish translation and is disappointed to find a glaring mistake on page one (“1810” had become “1801”). “Such sloppiness was unforgivable, and the sentences trickled on and on, riddled with mistakes no doubt.” She impatiently flips to the end of the book and decides that the story’s moral is “to listen to Lady Russell”, a “seemingly childless” widow who is “like a mother” to the central character, Anne. There is an obvious parallel between Lady Russell and Gunn, who we learn is both mentor and mentee, taken in by the woman from whom she inherited the house. The scenes of awkward intimacy between Gunn and Jenny are the tender heart of Range, but they are wrapped in a predictable plot, leading to an unconvincing altercation with “brutish” Krista that confirms Gunn’s prejudices about rural life. I kept thinking of a line from Mirror, Shoulder, Signal, in which Sonja comments on the many people who feel forced to move from the countryside to Copenhagen: “Shaming the provinces is just a covert form of deportation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
