title: The First Year (of the Gaza Genocide in the Media) review – bold but uneven focus on Palestinian voices | Stage | The Guardian
description: Passionate production based on testimonies from Gaza poses many questions regarding Israel’s actions but gets overwhelmed by fact-delivery and form-switches
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Passionate production based on testimonies from Gaza poses many questions regarding Israel’s actions but gets overwhelmed by fact-delivery and form-switches
Content: ‘Should be admired for its ambition’ … The First Year.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreen‘Should be admired for its ambition’ … The First Year.Photograph: Alex BrennerStageReviewThe First Year (of the Gaza Genocide in the Media) review – bold but uneven focus on Palestinian voicesNew Diorama theatre, LondonPassionate production based on testimonies from Gaza poses many questions regarding Israel’s actions but gets overwhelmed by fact-delivery and form-switchesArifa AkbarMon 28 Sep 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do news outlets cover war in a region where independent foreign journalists are blocked entry? What to make of the reports of theIsrael-Gaza warby the western press in relation to the livestreamed footage on our phones?These are some of the questions that come to mind when thinking about Israel’s actions in Gaza, triggered by Hamas’s attack on 7 October 2023, and bringing apocalyptic brutality and death tolls. This 90-minute production by British-Romanian collectiveBÉZNĂ theatreasks many more in its polyphony of satire, song, graphics, snatches of history, absurdism and sincerity. The four-strong cast – comprising Maryam Abu Khaled, Sara Masry, Luca Kamleh Chapman and Sofia – juggle it all in a series of mini lectures, dramatised dialogue, poetic monologues and meta theatre.Written and directed by Sînziana Cojocărescu, it is a production of utmost integrity, centring Palestinian voices, including short excerpts from works by playwrights Ahmed Masoud and Hannah Khalil, and anonymous writings. They hint at the difficulty in bringing this show to a stage, mentioning two PR companies that shied away.For a play that questions the framing of facts and stories, there is formal innovation around the presentation of these here. But the drama is beached by its own welter of facts and its experimental switches in form. The latter leave you stranded, some scenes so elliptical you are unsure of who is talking and what is happening, with the tone wobbling between plaintive laments, comedy and justified outrage.The trigger warnings, spoken into a microphone, go on for quite a while, and the dramatised material, when it comes, is horrific, such as the report of an Israeli strike first from the point of view of a western marine rescuing a hostage who relays a narrative of squeaky-clean heroism, followed by a report of the same event from the point of view of Palestinian civilians who witness a massacre around them, air-bushed out of the first report. An actor climbs into a glass box beneath the stage, in Jida Akil’s set design (immensely atmospheric, if underused, with mounds of earth) as if hiding from war terror. “I woke up this morning to nothing and fled to nothing,” says one character. We hear thestory of a Palestinian man with Down’s syndrome, mauled by an Israeli army dog and locked in a room by IDF soldiers, whose body was found decomposing by his family.These moments are powerful, bringing the play to life, but it is a shame that there is not enough of them and it seems less a drama than a static narration, despite the (sometimes abstruse) movement. A blizzard of facts and figures including the daily death tolls of journalists and of Palestinians are projected on the walls, as well as context that conveys the actions of the Israeli military. But these come and go in flashes, too fast to absorb or even read. Performers bring verve but are sometimes halting. The overall effect is disjointed and convoluted, with so much hard-hitting material but not enough clear-sighted focus.So its power is drowned out, yet still this is a production that should be admired for its ambition to say something profound in a fresh and radical way. It feels like a show still finding its centre, playing out prematurely. It is one I would like to see, in due course, containing just as much dimension and depth but with greater clarity and rigour alongside it.AtNew Diorama theatre, London, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatrePolitical theatreIsrael-Gaza warreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Happy Days review – Beckett’s bewitching heroine buries her existential fears | Stage | The Guardian
description: In what feels now like a premonition of the climate crisis, Siobhán Redmond is compelling as the everywoman putting on a brave face in an unforgiving landscape
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: In what feels now like a premonition of the climate crisis, Siobhán Redmond is compelling as the everywoman putting on a brave face in an unforgiving landscape
Content: A twinkle in her eyes … Siobhán Redmond (Winnie), with Forbes Masson (Willie) in the background, in Happy Days at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenA twinkle in her eyes … Siobhán Redmond (Winnie), with Forbes Masson (Willie) in the background, in Happy Days at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanStageReviewHappy Days review – Beckett’s bewitching heroine buries her existential fearsPitlochry Festival theatreIn what feels now like a premonition of the climate crisis, Siobhán Redmond is compelling as the everywoman putting on a brave face in an unforgiving landscapeMark FisherMon 28 Sep 2026 08.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSamuel Beckett’s play is always staged with a radiant brightness. It is hot enough to set a parasol alight. If, on its premiere in 1961, that resonated with audience anxieties about nuclear Armageddon, in 2026, it feels like a premonition of the climate crisis. Is this how it ends?Emma Bailey’s set is a dune of bleached-white sand, clumps of sea grass forcing their way through into a scorched environment, baked by Colin Grenfell’s lighting. When Forbes Masson crawls out of his hole as Willie, keeping his back to us, he reveals nothing more than his neck and shoulders, raw and sunburnt, his scarred head protected by a handkerchief (used).View image in fullscreenTremendous vocal range … Siobhán Redmond.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanNot that Siobhán Redmond would admit to such discomfort. As Winnie, she is irrepressibly cheery, a woman incapable of entertaining a negative thought without batting it back with a positive spin. Even when she talks about a “black night without end” in a second half of even greater bleakness, she maintains a genteel smile and a twinkle in her eyes.By that point, twinkle is pretty much all her eyes can do. Buried deep and then deeper still in this unforgiving landscape, she is deprived of movement and not totally unwillingly: Willie’s carnal grunts are uncouth, humanity at its most base and fundamental, where she is all bodiless elegance. She needs him as an audience – an actor is nothing if she is not seen and heard – but is faintly alarmed by his physical presence.With eyeshadow to match her turquoise ballgown, her crystal earrings and black fascinator in check, even if her blonde bob is dishevelled, she is a figure in denial of her circumstances. She would never mention the arrival of a migraine, but celebrates its passing with elan, an everywoman putting on a brave face in preference to existential despair.Showing tremendous vocal range, from girlish singsong to notes of dark resonance, Redmond is compelling in Roxana Silbert’s carefully controlled production. In a play that lands somewhere between the time-watching of Waiting for Godot and the mutual dependency ofEndgame, she is a bewitching metaphor for the futility of existence and the urgency to carry on regardless.At Pitlochry Festival theatre until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatrePitlochry Festival theatreSamuel BeckettreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Painting the French Riviera review – about as erotic and glamorous as a wet day in Margate | Art and design | The Guardian
description: They’ve marginalised Matisse and given Picasso the cold shoulder – and what’s left seems more informed by pedantic geography than sensual art
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: They’ve marginalised Matisse and given Picasso the cold shoulder – and what’s left seems more informed by pedantic geography than sensual art
Content: Obscure eroticism: Paul Cézanne’s Bathers, oil on canvas.Photograph: Saint Louis Art Museum, Funds given by Mrs. Mark C. SteinbergView image in fullscreenObscure eroticism: Paul Cézanne’s Bathers, oil on canvas.Photograph: Saint Louis Art Museum, Funds given by Mrs. Mark C. SteinbergArt and designReviewPainting the French Riviera review – about as erotic and glamorous as a wet day in MargateRoyal Academy of Arts, LondonThey’ve marginalised Matisse and given Picasso the cold shoulder – and what’s left seems more informed by pedantic geography than sensual artJonathan JonesMon 28 Sep 2026 07.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French Riviera is not a place. It is a dream of paradise, one of those Arcadias we long for – timeless, perfect worlds saturated with light. In the modern age, artists found theirs in the south of France. Yet this exhibition misses the point entirely. Instead of the modern myth of the Med, what we get here is a pedantic obsession with the geography of France’s southern coast. Artists get rewarded for which bit of it they painted. This leads to some serious distortions.The neo-impressionists – the dot-fixated movement led by Paul Signac – and their paintings of the Côte d’Azur get a grand, spacious setting. That’s OK; though when you’ve seen one pixelated shoreline, you’ve seen them all. What’s baffling is that Henri Matisse and the Fauves have been squeezed into a smaller, less weighty adjoining display. The revolution that Matisse and his friends enacted at the seaside town of Collioure, replacing nature with the colours in their heads, was far more radical, exciting and visually brilliant than Signac and co. I couldn’t fathom it.View image in fullscreenMonet’s Morning at Antibes, 1888, oil on canvas.Photograph: Philadelphia Museum of Art: Bequest of Charlotte Dorrance WrightThen I looked at a map. Collioure is on the far west of Mediterranean France, close to the Pyrenees. The Côte d’Azur to the east is the Riviera proper, including all your favourites: Nice, Cannes, Antibes, Saint-Tropez. The Fauves are punished for straying from it.This is ridiculous. In fact there seems to be a grudge against poor Matisse. A mere handful of his 1920s paintings that linger adoringly on women in Nice hotel rooms have to share space with cosy Raoul Dufy who was at best a Matisse imitator. Then at the end a single late Matisse cut-out, a serpentine white line through aquatic blue called The Wave, is juxtaposed with a lot of blue imprints of bare-naked ladies by the showboating 1960s artist Yves Klein.Yet it is Matisse who defines with one captivating work what Painting the French Riviera should have been about. His 1904 Study for Luxe, calme et volupté, in the little Fauve room, depicts a seaside Eden with unfettered passion and hedonism. Gold, green and violet dots, much freer than the neo-impressionists’ pedantic fields, fleck this little canvas in which Matisse experiments with a group of female nudes, gracefully posing by the shore, that he would finalise in the completed version of Luxe, calme et volupté in the Musée d’Orsay. “Luxury, peace and pleasure” – the title comes from Baudelaire – is Matisse’s ideal. It’s 1904, the new century is full of nationalists, revolutionaries, discontent, but he dreams of a perfect day by the sea surrounded by beautiful beach bodies.View image in fullscreenPainting the French Riviera at the Royal Academy of Arts brings together over 120 paintings, sculptures and drawings.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockThe fascination of this study is its rawness: these might just be actual women on a beach. They haven’t yet become the mythic beings of the final version. Matisse stares at real life bathers until they become goddesses – it’s the essence of the Riviera in French modern art, both a mythological Arcadia and a place you can get to on the Blue Train.Picasso’s backcloth for the Ballets Russes production The Blue Train hangs here. It is not actually by him but an enlarged copy by a scene painter of his small intense 1922 original Two Women Running on the Beach. Exciting, if you didn’t recently see it at V&A Storehouse East. Yet the show’s choice of Picasso is even more dispiriting than its meanness with Matisse.Much stress is placed on how Picasso saw the Riviera through a classical lens, from sculpture-like women to flute-playing fauns. But that’s a children’s book. For Picasso, as for Matisse, the Riviera meant sex. This show leaves out Picasso’s outrageous multi-orificed beach volleyball players, his prints of voluptuous women laid out for the eyes of artists and fauns, his erotic reveries over Marie-Thérèse Walter. Only one work captures his equation of sun, sea and lust: a witty woman-shaped vase from 1961 with a bikini painted on its pink terracotta form.Why am I banging on about Picasso and Matisse? It’s because any exhibition about the Riviera worth its salad niçoise would put them at its heart: it would be Matisse-Picasso, the Rematch. So many of their dazzling creations feast on this paradise – and reveal its dark side.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHenri Matisse’s Interior at Nice (Room at Beau-Rivage), 1917-1918, oil on canvasPhotograph: Joseph Hu/Philadelphia Museum of Art; AE Gallatin CollectionInstead of a dive in that sea, this is a collection of dry little diversions. It gives more space to Monet than Cézanne, which is tomfoolery. Monet’s views of Antibes are lovely but this Normandy-born artist is not southern in the same way as Cézanne, who sees his native Provence with painful intensity, burning his eyes at midday. In his painting Bathers, a group of near-nude young men pose against sky and water that seem to be baked rock hard by the sun. You instantly recognise the dream of the Med, the reverie, the obscure eroticism: pink flesh, dark blue sea, light blue sky.Then more detours. You linger with Bonnard and wonder what Picabia is doing here. Meanwhile, you have to ask why they didn’t include van Gogh, who did paint southern beaches, and owned the sun.The Riviera is left looking about as sublimely erotic and glamorous as a wet day in Margate. Tender Is the Night this is not. I don’t know whether the problem is pretension or, more depressingly, pandering to visitors the RA thinks want nice sunsets without the disturbing desires. If you go to this beach, leave your brain behind.At Royal Academy, London, from 2 October to 31 January 2027Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtRoyal Academy of ArtsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stevie Wonder releases four unheard songs from Songs in the Key of Life sessions | Stevie Wonder | The Guardian
description: Previously unreleased material comes as Wonder marks 50th anniversary of album with arena tour
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Previously unreleased material comes as Wonder marks 50th anniversary of album with arena tour
Content: Stevie Wonder in 1973.Photograph: David Reed/RedfernsView image in fullscreenStevie Wonder in 1973.Photograph: David Reed/RedfernsStevie WonderStevie Wonder releases four unheard songs from Songs in the Key of Life sessionsPreviously unreleased material comes as Wonder marks 50th anniversary of album with arena tourBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 28 Sep 2026 09.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStevie Wonder has expanded the scope of what was already the most epic studio album in his catalogue, 1976’s Songs in the Key of Life.Four unheard songs from the recording sessions have been released today as a new EP of the same name, marking the 50th anniversary of an album which won album of the year at the Grammys and contains a number of Wonder’s landmark tracks including Sir Duke, As and Isn’t She Lovely.“We’ve lived with Songs in the Key of Life for 50 years, but there’s still more to hear,” Wonder said in a statement. “We didn’t add these songs to the album, but they were part of what I was feeling and discovering as we made it. They bring me back to that time in my life, and now they get to become part of yours.”The songs are suffused with the style Wonder had crafted during the 1970s, and which arguably reached its apotheosis on that 21-track double album: a sunlit, spiritually attuned type of soul and R&B, celebrating love and the richness of existence while acknowledging emotional strife and social struggle.The album’s backings are gorgeously detailed, instantly recognisable psychedelic soul arrangements with funk and jazz detailing, bringing in the futurist sound of keyboards and synth bass but fleshing everything out with a huge range of organic instrumentation.The unheard tracks continue in that vein: It’s Easier is a shimmying, bossa nova-esque number that questions whether to walk away from the very concept of love; My Life Story of Love is quintessential Wonder with the singer using bucolic imagery (“let her bloom into my flower of love”) on a tale of a blossoming relationship; I Can See the Sun in Late December is a slow jazz ballad about determined optimism and self-discovery; and I’m Into Livin’ is a squelchy funk track as Wonder renounces his old partying and womanising ways and pledges himself to a single lover.All four are written and produced by Wonder, though My Life Story of Love features a co-writing credit for former Supremes member Susaye Greene, who also co-wrote Michael Jackson’s I Can’t Help It with Wonder. The original recording and mixing engineers, John Fischbach and Gary O Adante, recently mixed the tracks for release.The voices of two future stars – Thelma Houston and Deniece Williams – can be heard as backing vocalists on I’m Into Livin’, along with Shirley Brewer, who features on Songs in the Key of Life’s Ordinary Pain.The new EP comes as Wonder prepares to play Songs in the Key of Life in full on an arena tour, which begins 13 October in Birmingham, UK. Wonder then tours across Europe before returning to the UK for three more dates in London, Manchester and Glasgow, then plays five US cities: New York City, Chicago, Washington DC, Detroit and Los Angeles.Stevie Wonder – every studio album ranked!Read moreWonder’s most recent new material was the single Can We Fix Our Nation’s Broken Heart, released in 2024, though he hasn’t released a new studio album since 2005’s A Time to Love.In 2020 he announced a new “project” entitled Through the Eyes of Wonder, though no further news on its status has been released since.Explore more on these topicsStevie WonderPop and rockR&BSoulnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatre | Stage | The Guardian
description: The actors are working together for the first time ever, in Noël Coward’s comedy Hay Fever. Backstage, there’s no stopping their tales of skinny-dipping, fat-shaming and warring co-stars
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: The actors are working together for the first time ever, in Noël Coward’s comedy Hay Fever. Backstage, there’s no stopping their tales of skinny-dipping, fat-shaming and warring co-stars
Content: ‘It’s camp that’s elegant’ … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski star in Hay Fever.Photograph: Oliver RosserView image in fullscreen‘It’s camp that’s elegant’ … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski star in Hay Fever.Photograph: Oliver RosserDouble actsStage‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatreThe actors are working together for the first time ever, in Noël Coward’s comedy Hay Fever. Backstage, there’s no stopping their tales of skinny-dipping, fat-shaming and warring co-starsRyan GilbeyMon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard EGrant: Despite our vast combined vintage, our paths have never crossed before, have they?Christine Baranski: Regrettably not. We could have had some good fun a few decades ago. A girl could have got into some real trouble. But here we are, and now we’re the veterans. You’re among the great character actors, popping up delightfully in so many things and always being spot-on.REG: My late wife said I’m in the condiment years, where you’re added to the meal in these cameo roles like vinegar or ketchup or mustard, spice or pickle or whatever. I think that’s absolutely accurate.CB: It makes for an interesting and varied career. You have a shelf life certainly if you’re a leading lady. It’s a harder perch to descend from, which is sort of what Hay Fever is about. My character, Judith Bliss, can’t quite accept that she’s not up there doing it any more. I’ve had a long career because I was comfortable being the supporting actress. I did The Real Thing by Tom Stoppard on Broadway in 1984 [for which she won the first of two Tony awards]. My character in that, Charlotte, is so bitingly witty and she has this marvellous repartee with Henry, played by Jeremy Irons. I’d do my scenes, then go up to my dressing room, and people would say: “Oh, we wanted you to come back!” They’ll have their fill of me with Hay Fever. It’ll be more like: “When is she going to leave the stage?”View image in fullscreenGrant and Baranski in rehearsals for Hay Fever.Photograph: Marc BrennerRyan Gilbey: Judith in Hay Fever has been played by everyone fromEdith EvansandCelia JohnsontoJudi Dench,Penelope KeithandLindsay Duncan. Why is the part such a magnet for great performers?CB: Well, she’s an ageing actress, and how delicious to play that in your later years. It’s all about the vanity and vulnerability of ageing. There’s a poignancy to it; I really find her rather dear. You don’t have to be an ageing actress to feel that way as a woman, particularly in our culture. We cling to youth for dear life. You could say it all borders on the camp, but because it’s Coward and he’s writing affectionately as well as cynically about theatre people, it has a sweetness to it – it’s camp that’s elegant. He wrote it at 24, so even as a young man he had that sense of something behind all the fame and glamour.Christine, this is your first time in the West End but your fourth Coward play. What’s the secret to mastering him?CB: If you find out, will you please tell us? Speed, facility, lightness of tone. He uses words as weapons. I really want people to sit up and listen because we don’t use language like that any more, do we?Judith and her husband,David, played byRichard, are decidedly poor hosts. What makes a good host and a decent party?REG: My late wife said that everyone there should know a minimum of two people. It’s foolproof, and it means that you as the host can let people get on with it. If nobody knows anybody, you’re buggered. I’ve found that whenever a party has been awkward, it’s because there’s not enough social glue to begin with.CB: We had the most wonderful party at Richard’s house on the first weekend I was here in London. It’s the most enchanting, magical house. You can describe it for me, Richard.REG: Maximalist.CB: Sitting around, having drinks and laughing were Steve Martin and Martin Short, Helena Bonham Carter, Gary Oldman, various spouses and Richard’s daughter and son-in-law. It was so relaxing despite the extraordinary pedigrees of all these talented people with big egos.REG: There were 12 of us, so you could still hear someone at the other end of the table and you didn’t feel cut off. Christine already knew Steve, Marty and Helena but not Gary. Gary knew Helena but not Steve and Marty. There was enough glue.View image in fullscreenGrant (left) and Paul McGann in Withnail and I.Photograph: Handmade Films/Kobal/ShutterstockYou and Gary Oldman have worked together a few times, haven’t you, Richard? Including on one of your first credits,Les Blair’s BBC film Honest, Decent and True.REG: Yes, that was 1985. The day I landed here when I emigrated from Swaziland in 1982, I went to see Gary in the play Summit Conference with Glenda Jackson as Eva Braun and Georgina Hale as Clara Petacci, the mistresses of Hitler and Mussolini. That was where I first met him. We each got married at the same time – well, Gary’s been married five times – and my daughter was born around the same time as his first child. When I had to lose weight for Withnail and I, I asked Gary how he’d done it for Sid and Nancy. I had just spent almost a year when I was unemployed trying to gain weight because I’d read in a magazine that if you’re six foot, you should weigh 12 stone. Now, I’d never weighed 12 stone in my life, so I was doing all the weight-gain powder and the gym and all that. Then Bruce Robinson, the director of Withnail, said, “Could you lose a stone?” So I called Gary, who I think had eaten nothing but tuna and melon; he even ended up hospitalised at one point. I went to Boots instead and got weight-gain-off powder, and my year’s work disappeared within a week.Before that, didn’t Bruce say you looked like “a fat Dirk Bogarde”?REG: He did. He still calls me Fatty.As you were going in to audition for Withnail, you passedBill Nighycoming out.REG: Bill Nighy. Kenneth Branagh. A whole bunch of people went up for it. I had to read the kitchen scene at the start of the film. Bruce told me: “Drop the Noël Coward. The character is not as affected as you’re thinking. Read it with more rage.” I’d been unemployed for nine months so that rage was very easy to tap into.Christine, do you host?CB: I have a marvellous house on a lake in Connecticut and I’ve hosted some very famous actors there. It has a very long dock that has been “grandfathered” in, as in they don’t allow a dock that long to be built any more, but this is about 100 years old. You sit in the living room in summer and watch the sun set, and then go out into the evening and skinny dip in the lake. When I did Boeing-Boeing for nine months on Broadway with Mark Rylance, he became a great pal – he’s a godfather to my third grandson – and we’d be out there howling at the moon at four in the morning. So much fun.REG: Have you ever had anybody who won’t take their clothes off?CB: Oh, it’s not a prerequisite. I encourage people only if they’re comfortable and if it’s pitch dark. Although one actress I adore insisted on sunbathing stark naked in the middle of the afternoon. In fact, she would spend all night on the dock, fall asleep on there and then wake up at dawn and there she was!You won anEmmyin1995for the sitcomCybill, where you playedCybill Shepherd’s divorced best friend. But you’d been reluctant to do TV, hadn’t you?CB: Absolutely. Mainly because I didn’t want to live in Los Angeles. I also had a very active theatre career, going from play to play; I loved it. It just became a question of raising two kids and having tuition bills to pay. So at 41 or 42, I began my television career with the caveat that I would commute. I never bought real estate in LA. I lived in a hotel and was on the first red-eye back to the kids. Winning the Emmy gave me this visibility. I’d worked with Mike Nichols on The Real Thing, but it was because of the Emmy that he cast me in The Birdcage. Most of my film and television stuff happened after the age of 40.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve had a long career because I was comfortable being the supporting actress’ … Baranski in Cybill.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/Getty ImagesREG: I read yesterday that there was an unprecedented number of Emmys going to female actors over 50 this year.CB: It’s about time.Christine and one of this year’s winners,Jean Smart from Hacks, playedbiker chicksinThe Odd Couple II.CB: Well done! Yes, Jean danced with Jack Lemmon and I got to dance with Walter Matthau. It was not a good movie, but to work with those guys at the end of their careers … oh, I adored them. Lemmon was the consummate professional, always the first one on set, and Matthau was this curmudgeonly, lovable old woolly bear.REG: Talking of Mike Nichols, I had dinner with Mike 22 years ago, the night before I went to Africa to make the only film I’ve directed, Wah-Wah. I asked him for advice and he said – apart from getting good caterers – that actors can always act faster than they think they can. He said: “Do the takes that you’re happy with. Give the actors the takes they’re happy with. And then tell them: ‘Let’s do one for Mike.’” It’s amazing, the speed and effectiveness when people aren’t pausing and breaking … up … lines … all … the … time. Because we don’t do that in life, do we? It was great advice.CB: It was. He couldn’t tolerate indulgence. He was so fiercely intelligent and he loved clarity. Richard, did you have a wonderful time working with Robert Altman?REG: I did. I worked with him on The Player and Gosford Park and a terrible film called Pret-a-Porter. Whereas the other two had scripts, Pret-a-Porter was like this: “Ryan, Christine and Richard meet in a small room. She spills the water. They argue. Improvise.” It had no structure and it was a car crash as a result. If you’ve got a good script, you can embellish and add stuff, but this was a free-for-all. There was one insane day when Danny Aiello completely lost the plot. Sophia Loren was supposed to have fainted, and he infiltrated the scene and started taking it over: “I’ll give her mouth-to-mouth resuscitation!” He called Lauren Bacall “a left-wing Commie bitch”. Then he insulted Rupert Everett for being English and for being …View image in fullscreenGrant in rehearsals for Hay Fever.Photograph: Marc BrennerCB: Oh dear. Did Lauren eat him up and spit him out?REG: She took no prisoners. She ripped him five new ones. It was more dramatic than anything that happened in the actual film. None of the cast would talk to Danny after that; they sent him to Coventry.CB: We all have our stories.Christine, have you ever worked the way Altman did, with multiple cameras and the actors not always knowing for sure if they are in shot?CB: A little bit on television. I think it’s a great way of keeping actors on their toes. Sitcoms can be harrowing, though. If the studio audience doesn’t laugh, the writers go away and come up with a different joke there and then. They’re always adjusting and you’ve got to nail those one-liners. You know you’ve got to get that laugh because it’s your job. It’s a wonderful discipline. After all that comedy, I told my manager: “It’s time for me to do a dramatic role.” Be careful what you wish for, because if The Gilded Age goes for a fifth year, that’ll be 18 straight years of television work, after The Good Wife and The Good Fight.With you inThe Gilded Age, and Richard inGosford ParkandDownton Abbey, you’re both part of theJulian FellowesDramatic Universe.REG: Yes, but we’re not as rich as Julian Fellowes. Well, Christine probably is, but I’m not.I noticed a few other similarities on your CVs. You both appeared in great Steve Martin comedies: Richard in LA Story, Christine inBowfinger.CB: Underrated, I think. It’s certainly got some of Eddie Murphy’s greatest work. He was huge then. His first day on set, I had to walk across the street and assault him. He’s a really intelligent actor. And God, does he have comedic instincts! He’s also a very private person.View image in fullscreenBaranski with Walter Matthau and Jean Smart in The Odd Couple II.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyREG: So he won’t be skinny-dipping in Connecticut?CB: No skinny-dipping with Eddie Murphy.Early in your careers, you also each appeared in a scandalous erotic movie. Richard was inHenry & June, the film for which the controversialNC-17rating (the highest age rating)was created in the US.REG: That’s right. It has a lot of bonking and brothel scenes.CB: We’re notknownfor the erotic works, I should say. But yes, mine was 9½ Weeks. I played Kim Basinger’s friend. I have a dinner scene where I balance a teaspoon on the end of my nose. And I can drink while it’s sort of hanging there.REG: You should do that during the breakfast scene in Hay Fever.CB: And upstage you, my darling?Hay Fever is atWyndham’s theatre, London, until 12DecemberExplore more on these topicsStageDouble actsTheatreRichard E GrantTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: MTV VMAs 2026: Taylor Swift and Madonna win at awards dominated by female artists | MTV Video Music Awards | The Guardian
description: Madonna and Swift take home four of six prizes given out during ceremony telecast, alongside K-pop star Lisa and British newcomer Sienna Spiro
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Madonna and Swift take home four of six prizes given out during ceremony telecast, alongside K-pop star Lisa and British newcomer Sienna Spiro
Content: Taylor Swift and Madonna at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards (VMAs). The two artists won four of the six awards given out during the telecast.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTaylor Swift and Madonna at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards (VMAs). The two artists won four of the six awards given out during the telecast.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesMTV Video Music AwardsMTV VMAs 2026: Taylor Swift and Madonna win at awards dominated by female artistsMadonna and Swift take home four of six prizes given out during ceremony telecast, alongside K-pop star Lisa and British newcomer Sienna SpiroMTV VMAs 2026 red carpet: Taylor Swift, Charli xcx, Troye Sivan and more – in picturesMTV VMAs: full list of winnersAdrian HortonSun 27 Sep 2026 23.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMadonnaandTaylor Swifttriumphed at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards, with the former winning three trophies and the latter winning the night’s top honor, extending her run as the most-awarded artist in VMAs history.In a ceremony that largely awarded female artists,Madonnaentered the evening as the most nominated artist of the year with 13 nods and won seven, including three during the telecast: for best collaboration (with Sabrina Carpenter), best dance, and artist of the year.MTV VMAs 2026 red carpet: Taylor Swift, Charli xcx, Troye Sivan and more – in picturesRead more“Most of you were probably not born when I performed at the very first VMAs 43 years ago,” the 68-year-old said while accepting the award for artist of the year, which she won over Swift, Carpenter, Ariana Grande,Bruno Marsand Morgan Wallen.After recalling how she fell and accidentally exposed her rear, threatening her nascent career in a very different media landscape, Madonna ended on a more serious note. “I spent the last year and a half finding myself, believing in myself and really making the music that I wanted to make,” she said. “My hope for all of you here tonight is that you … do the same. Find yourself and believe in yourself.”View image in fullscreenSienna Spiro accepts the best new artist award.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesMadonna, whose provocative performances in the 1980s helped cement the VMAs as a can’t-miss cultural event, opened the show at the Peacock theater in Los Angeles with her first VMAs performance in 23 years, the first since her infamous onstage kiss with Britney Spears in 2003.She performed two songs from this summer’sConfessions II: Bring Your Love with Carpenter, and a intricate, lively rendition of Danceteria, her tribute to New York’s 1980s club scene, with Charli xcx and a who’s who of background dancers including Julia Garner, the actor who was cast to play Madonna in a long-gestating biopic that wascancelledafter a “falling out” with Universal Studios.Taylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore review – flashes of humanity and bafflingly vindictive love songsRead moreSwift won three categories, including the night’s top honor – video of the year – for The Fate of Ophelia, and the inaugural artist director honors. The new award, to celebrate “groundbreaking music artists whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video”, honored Swift’s status as the most-decorated music video director in the show’s history, as well as itsmost-awarded solo artist.Swift dedicated her win to “the ultimate showgirl” Dolly Parton,who died last month at 80 after being diagnosed with cancer.“Listening to her songs, it’s like watching the best music video you have ever seen in your life, every single time you hear what she’s written,” she said. “And she handled this thing with such grace and joy and love and gratitude for the fact that she got to do this, and everything that happened in her life or her career, she channelled back into love and gratitude and appreciation for her fans.“I’m lucky I got to be one of them, and I’ll always be one of them. I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time.”View image in fullscreenKacey Musgraves pays tribute to Dolly Parton at the VMAs.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesAfter reflecting on her 20 years of making nearly 60 music videos, 18 of which she wrote and directed, Swift premiered her new video for Patient Zero, the lead single fromThe Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, her four-track addition to last year’scritically maligned album. The new video sees her twinning with actor Dakota Johnson in a showdown with a mutual ex played by Colin Farrell.Country singerKacey Musgravespaid tribute to Parton by harmonizing with archival video of the late singer performing her hit I Will Always Love You, to a visibly moved crowd. Later on, Sombr, Raye, Teddy Swims and Adam Lambert performed hits from George Michael’s Faith tour, 10 years after the English singer’s death aged 53.Madonna and Swift’s dominance – the duo won four of the six awards handed out during the two-and-a-half-hour telecast, which was delayed by more than 20 minutes by an NFL game – injected some much-needed star power in a show that has struggled to find its identity in the streaming era.Presided over by a largely absent, if reliably chill first-time host, Snoop Dogg, the 2026 VMA telecast was once again dominated by female artists. K-pop star Lisa won best pop for her song Dream, while British newcomer Sienna Spiro was named best new artist after fans voted throughout the show.View image in fullscreen(L-R) Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear of Nirvana accept the video vanguard award.Photograph: Rich Polk/Billboard/Getty Images‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the yearRead moreThe Michael Jackson video vanguard award, a honorary lifetime achievement prize, went toNirvana, for the influence of the era-defining grunge band’s music videos. The visual concepts for Smells Like Teen Spirit, Come As You Are, In Bloom, Heart-shaped Box and All Apologies “came out of the vision of one of the greatest artists of all time, Kurt Cobain,” said Krist Novoselic, the band’s bassist, speaking on behalf of drummer Dave Grohl and guitarist Pat Smear, who joined the band on tour beginning in 1993.Cobain, who took his own life in 1994, was “one of one” he added, noting that the band’s music still resonates because “people are still hungry for authenticity, for something real, something uncompromising … Kurt would have loved that legacy.”In categories not included in the telecast, K-pop group BTS won best group and best K-pop and song of the year for their hit Swim, Bruno Mars won best R&B for I Just Might, Cardi B and Kehlani won best hip-hop for Safe, Bad Bunny won best Latin for NUEVAYoL, Olivia Rodrigo won best alternative for The Cure, and Ella Langley won best country forher record-breaking hitChoosin’ Texas.Explore more on these topicsMTV Video Music AwardsMTVMadonnaAwards and prizesTaylor SwiftKacey MusgravesNirvananewsShareReuse this content

title: Sanjana Modha’s quick and easy recipe for baked beans butter masala  | Food | The Guardian
description: Transform two tins of baked beans into this creamy curry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Transform two tins of baked beans into this creamy curry
Content: Sanjana Modha’s baked beans butter masala.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenSanjana Modha’s baked beans butter masala.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.Quick and easyFoodSanjana Modha’s quick and easy recipe for baked beans butter masalaTransform two tins of baked beans into this creamy currySanjana ModhaMon 28 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMasala baked beans, tadka baked beans, curried baked beans, spicy baked beans; all avatars of spice-laced baked beans are a mainstay of British Asian kitchens. We were raised on this stuff – use as a toastie filler, to smother jacket potatoes, or scoop them up with roti. Enter baked beans butter masala. With a sharp sweetness, a versatile tin of baked beans already has all the foundations required to build a brilliant butter masala, so all we’re doing is dressing them up. I like to think of it as though the beans are donning a frock made of all the good stuff: butter, cream and spices.Baked beans butter masalaThis creamy, dreamy baked bean curry is delicious with naan or served as any of the suggestions mentioned above. To make this vegan, use your favourite plant-based butter and an oat- or soya-based cream. Coconut milk also works in place of cream.Prep15 minCook20 minServes42tbsp salted butter, plus a little extra to garnish (optional)1 small brown onion, peeled and finely chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped1tsp minced ginger1tbsp tomato puree2410gtins baked beans½tsp ground turmeric1tsp kashmiri chilli powder4 greencardamom pods, smashed open and seeds finely ground3tsp garam masala1 small pinch salt150mlsinglecream2tsp dried fenugreek leaves2tbsp chopped coriander, including stalks, to garnishMelt the butter in a medium saucepan, then add the onion and saute for three to five minutes, until soft and translucent. Add the garlic, ginger and tomato puree, and cook for another minute, until aromatic.Add all the baked beans, along with all the sauce from the cans, stir in the turmeric, chilli powder, ground cardamom, garam masala and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.Stir in the cream (reserve a few tablespoons to serve), cover the pan with a lid and leave the curry to come to a simmer over a low heat for 10 minutes, stirring often to stop the beans sticking to the base of the pan.Take off the lid and add the dried fenugreek leaves, rubbing them between your palms to break them into a fine powder. Swirl in the reserved cream and, if using, the extra butter, garnish with the coriander and serve.This recipe is an edited extract from Modern Masala, by Sanjana Modha, published by Quadrille at £25. title: Rice ‘polenta’ with sausage sauce and rice with pork, lemon and saffron: Pasta Grannies’ Italian rice recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Spoons at the ready for 83-year-old Maria’s rustic risotto with pork and saffron, and Rita’s polenta-style rice with a punchy sauce
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Spoons at the ready for 83-year-old Maria’s rustic risotto with pork and saffron, and Rita’s polenta-style rice with a punchy sauce
Content: Pasta Grannies’ Sardinian rice with pork and saffron.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenPasta Grannies’ Sardinian rice with pork and saffron.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodRice ‘polenta’ with sausage sauce and rice with pork, lemon and saffron: Pasta Grannies’ Italian rice recipesSpoons at the ready for 83-year-old Maria’s rustic risotto with pork and saffron, and Rita’s polenta-style rice with a punchy sauceVicky BennisonMon 28 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf I were to say “Italian rice”, you might well think “risotto” and “the Po Valley”. However, these two recipes come from Sardinia and the Marche, mainly because I wanted to share a few easy, not-laden-with-rules Italian rice dishes.Maria’s riso con maiale e zafferano (rice with pork and saffron)Eighty-three-year-old Maria was widowed young and, to make ends meet, set up an agriturismo dining space in her home near Oristano in Sardinia’s rice-growing heartland. This rustic risotto with a wonderful combination of flavours was one of her customers’ favourites, and it’s a great recipe if you are nervous about making a classic risotto with all its rules.Prep20 minStock2 hr+(optional)Cook1 hr 20 minServes4For the stock (optional)1kg pork bones1 sun-dried tomato, or ½ tsp tomato puree1 onion, peeled2 celery sticks1 carrotFor the riceExtra-virgin olive oil1 carrot, dicedSea salt andblack pepper500gpork shoulder steak, or other stewing pork, cut into 1cm chunks1 onion, peeled and chopped1 sprig fresh rosemary1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed1 sun-dried tomato, minced (optional; see method)3½ tbsp white wine(vernaccia, if you can find it, otherwise any dry white wine)100gpassata750ml hot meat stock, homemade (see above and method) or bought in250garborio riceZest of 1 lemon, ½ finely grated, the rest pared off in strips and julienned20.1g sachets saffron powder, or 1 pinch saffron threads soaked in hot water or stock50gpecorino, grated, plus extra to serveIf you’re making your own stock, simmer the pork bones in plenty of water with the tomato, onion, celery and carrot for several hours, until deeply flavoured. Strain and keep hot if you are going to use it immediately.Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pan, then fry the diced carrot with a pinch of salt until it starts to soften. Add the diced pork, fry, stirring, until browned all over, then add the onion, rosemary and garlic, season well and cook for five or so minutes, until the onion is translucent.If you didn’t use a sun-dried tomato in your stock, add the minced one now – it’s Maria’s secret for boosting umami. Pour in the wine, let the liquid evaporate, then stir in the passata. Add a ladle of hot stock and simmer gently for anything between 20 and 40 minutes, depending on your cut of pork: you want the stew to have cooked properly before making a risotto with it. Indeed, you can make it the day before to improve its flavour; just reheat first.When the stew is ready and bubbling and the stock is keeping hot in another pot next door, add the rice to the stew, stirring to coat it in the sauce. Add more hot stock a ladleful at a time, stirring frequently until absorbed. Tasteand add salt if necessary. When the rice is about halfway cooked, stir in the grated lemon zest and julienned peel.Dissolve the saffron in a little hot stock, then stir it through the rice. Keep cooking, stirring and adding stock as needed, until the rice is tender but still has some bite; the finished dish should be more like a pilaf than a creamy northern Italian risotto, and the whole process will take about 20 minutes.To finish, stir through the grated pecorino and serve with extra cheese at the table.Rita’sfrascarelli con sugo di finocchietto e salsiccia(rice “polenta” with wild fennel and sausage sauce)View image in fullscreenPasta Grannies’ rice polenta with fennel and sausage sauce.Rita, Adriana and Brunhilde are the bustling heart of my home town, Cingoli inLe Marche,where they organise asagra, or food festival, at which they serve this rice “polenta” that has sustained families in the region for centuries. Frascarelli was traditionally served plain to invalids and new mothers, because it was considered nourishing and easy to digest, but when dressed with a spicy, robust sauce, it becomes a hearty meal for the whole family. It was originally served on a communal polenta board, because in the old days people didn’t have individual crockery, andour Instagram post of the three friends demonstrating thiswent viral (some viewers were horrified); of course, these days, everyone uses plates or bowls.Prep10 minCook45 minServes6For the sauce1 bunchwild fennel fronds, or 1 tsp freshly ground fennel seedsExtra-virgin olive oil½ tspdried chilli flakes, or to taste1 splash white wine3 large, meaty Italian sausages1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed (optional; see method)400ml passata1tspcastersugarSalt, to tasteFor the frascarelli400garborio rice50gplainflour1 generous pinchsaltBegin by making the sauce. Pick through the fennel fronds for the tenderest pieces and wash thoroughly; otherwise, use freshly ground fennel seeds, or substitute with chervil or parsley. Heat a generous amount of oil in a large pan on a medium heat. Add the fennel, chilli flakes and white wine, and cook gently for a few minutes, to release the aromatics. (Adriana says the older the herb, the longer it will need to simmer, and that you should cook it for at least 10 minutes.)Skin the sausages, crumble the meat into the pan and cook, stirring frequently, until it begins to brown and release its fat (if your sausages aren’t Italian, add the crushed garlic clove at this point and fry for an extra minute). Add the passata, rinse out the jar with a little water to capture every drop, and add that, too. Stir in the sugar to balance the acidity of the tomatoes, then simmer gently for at least 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Check the seasoning and keep warm.For the frascarelli, bring two litres of water to a gentle simmer in a large, heavy-based saucepan. Add the rice, stir well and season with a good pinch of salt. Keep the heat moderate, to prevent the rice boiling over – Rita is vigilant about this – and cook, stirring regularly to prevent the rice sticking to the bottom of the pan. After about 10 minutes, when the rice is nearly tender, the mix will still be liquid. Gradually whisk in the flour to thicken it to a soft, polenta-like consistency; the texture should be creamy but not too thick.Spoon the frascarelli into warmed bowls, top generously with the fennel and sausage sauce and serve immediately.These recipes are edited extracts from Pasta Grannies: Eat Everything – Pasta and Beyond for the Good Life, by Vicky Bennison, published by Rizzoli at £29.95. To order a copy for £26.95, go toguardianbookshop.comThis article was amended on 28 September 2026. The headline of an earlier version said these were both Sardinian recipes, but the second one hails from the Marche.Explore more on these topicsFoodRiceItalian food and drinkMain coursePorkMeatVegetablesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Dennis the terrier – who once farted on Jilly Cooper’s sofa | Life and style | The Guardian
description: It seemed like a good idea to get a puppy with my partner, but then he left me. Single life was hard at first but my disobedient dog made me laugh again
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It seemed like a good idea to get a puppy with my partner, but then he left me. Single life was hard at first but my disobedient dog made me laugh again
Content: Puppy love … Dennis the lovable menace.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenPuppy love … Dennis the lovable menace.Photograph: PRThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Dennis the terrier – who once farted on Jilly Cooper’s sofaIt seemed like a good idea to get a puppy with my partner, but then he left me. Single life was hard at first but my disobedient dog made me laugh againSophia Money-CouttsMon 28 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the spring of 2024, my boyfriend and I lay in bed scrolling through photos of puppies. What about this one? Or that one? We had only been dating for six months or so, but had become besotted quickly, making long-term plans and talking about our future.Then I found the one: a scruffy, small terrier with black and brown markings on his back that looked like the world map and eyes like Galaxy Minstrels. We named him Dennis to connect him to my mum’s terrier, Beano, because she was ill at the time and I’d failed to provide her with a grandchild. A puppy was the consolation present.Within three months of sleepless nights (me) and accidents on the carpets (Dennis), my boyfriend decided to leave. I was left holding the baby. Whoops, I mean puppy. This had not been the plan.Single life with a puppy was harder than expected. Dennis and I took to marching around the park and nearby woods, endless walks as I stomped through heartbreak and made futile attempts to train him. But I was distracted from my sadness by this small, bouncy, intensely disobedient dog. He raced after every squirrel, made enemies with the park geese and flung himself into the algae-covered lake with all the glee of a small child jumping into a swimming pool.Dennis was on continual alert for foxes and once chased one into a building site, only reappearing after nearly an hour, plastered with mud, during which time I wondered a thousand times over whether getting a goldfish might have been more sensible.If I left my foam earplugs on my bedside table he ate them. He also devoured spiders and the odd stray sock. All the wastepaper bins in my flat had to be lifted on to the nearest table or windowsill to prevent Dennis from rifling through them and eating a tissue or an old toothbrush.And then I started dating, another interesting experiment when you have a young puppy. During an amorous moment in my bedroom, my date suddenly froze and looked uncomfortable. “Dennis is licking my leg,” he said. Dennis was, briefly, banished to his crate in the sitting room. Fortunately that guy wasn’t put off.In Tony Parsons’ new book, Man & Dog, about his late spaniel, Stan, he writes that life is so much better with a dog but easier without. I laughed in recognition when I read that line. Without Dennis, there’d be no logistical stress, no vet dramas, no worrying about him eating yet another sock or pair of pants, but my life is also immeasurably improved by him.View image in fullscreenDennis travels with Sophia everywhere.I talk to Dennis almost constantly, since, as a journalist, I work alone. He comes with me to interviews and always, even with the frostiest of celebrities, helps break the ice. Although he did once fart on Jilly Cooper’s sofa. “It doesn’t matter a bit, does it darling?” cried Jilly, clutching him closer to her. “He can do whatever he likes.” That definitely seems to be Dennis’s general policy and I love him for it.The Year of the Dog by Sophia Money-Coutts is out now and is published by HQ (£9.99). title: Should you lock into a fixed-rate savings account paying 5.25%?  | Savings | The Guardian
description: Savers face a dilemma: lock down the deals now or wait, with offers tipped to ‘get even better’
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Savers face a dilemma: lock down the deals now or wait, with offers tipped to ‘get even better’
Content: The data provider Moneyfacts says fixed savings rates are at ‘multiyear highs’.Photograph: Viktoria  Rodriguez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe data provider Moneyfacts says fixed savings rates are at ‘multiyear highs’.Photograph: Viktoria  Rodriguez/Getty ImagesSavingsShould you lock into a fixed-rate savings account paying 5.25%?Savers face a dilemma: lock down the deals now or wait, with offers tipped to ‘get even better’Britain’s low-paid urged to sign up to savings scheme offering cash bonusRupert JonesMon 28 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 04.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReturns on the top fixed-rate savings accounts are at their highest level in years and still climbing, with some now paying up to 5.25%.It leaves those with money to put away facing a choice: lock into some of the best interest rates on offer in several years or hold your nerve in the hope they get even better?While new fixed mortgage rates have jumped in recent months – dealing a blow to many homebuyers and those aiming to remortgage – their pain has been savers’ gain.This month, the data providerMoneyfactssaid fixed savings rates were at “multiyear highs”, fuelled by strong competition, and this trend has continued: on Thursday the average new one-year fixed savings bond rate was 4.41%.With a fixed-rate savings bond, you typically have to tie up your money for between six months and five years, and they provide a clear, guaranteed return. The one-year version tends to be popular as many people do not want to tie up cash for long periods.The top-paying accounts are offering a fair bit more than that average: at the time of writing, GB Bank had a one-year fixed-rate bond paying 5.05%. Meanwhile, Kent Reliance had a 13-month account offering 5.06%. (With both, the minimum deposit is £1,000.)View image in fullscreenReturns on the top fixed-rate savings accounts are at their highest level in years.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesThe best-buy rates are even higher if you tie up cash for longer. This week, GB Bank, Shawbrook Bank and Vanquis were among those paying 5.25% on a five-year fixed bond.However, some savers will recall that as recently as late 2023 there were fixed bonds paying 6%, and if and when the Bank of England base rate goes up, that could push returns on savings higher than they are now.Many economists predict the Bank will lift the base rate before the end of this year, with further rises thought likely next year.Rachel Springall at Moneyfacts expects the deals on offer to savers “to get even better”. However, she cautions that we do not know the path interest rates will follow, and that anything could happen in the next few months or so.double quotation markSome fixed-rate savings bonds will let you drip-feed cash inThose with cash to stash may want to hedge their bets by putting some into a competitive fixed-rate bond now and keeping another chunk in a high-paying easy access account. There are easy access accounts paying up to 5%.Some fixed-rate savings bonds will let you “drip-feed” cash in – for example, some will let you add money while the account is still open to new customers, while others have a specific “funding window”, which might be a few weeks but can be just a few days.The cost of living is still a big issue, with many worried about the prospect of higher energy bills this winter – so it could be a mistake to put all your savings cash out of reach. Springall suggests spreading your money across fixed-rate products and accounts that are accessible, plus also making use of tax-free cashIsas.View image in fullscreenDo you have an Isa?Photograph: Leonora Oates/AlamyIf you are aiming to put some money into savings or switch providers and are not using your Isa allowance at all, you are missing out on valuable tax benefits.Rates on fixed cash Isas are often slightly lower than for similar non-Isa accounts, although not always: Shawbrook Bank’s five-year fixed savings bond and five-year fixed cash Isa pay 5.25%.Every tax year you can save up to £20,000 in Isas, but from April 2027, the rules will change for anyone under 65. Instead of being able to put all of the money into a cash Isa, that elementwill be capped at £12,000. If you are 65 or over, all £20,000 can still be put into a cash Isa.Explore more on these topicsSavingsSavings ratesBanks and building societiesIsasCash IsasInterest ratesBondsnewsShareReuse this content

title: TfL’s bailiffs are chasing me for a stranger’s unpaid Ulez fines | Low emission zones | The Guardian
description: Now TFL is threatening to seize goods for four penalties for a car I’ve never owned
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: Now TFL is threatening to seize goods for four penalties for a car I’ve never owned
Content: Caught on camera and chased for fines for a car owned by a complete stranger.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenCaught on camera and chased for fines for a car owned by a complete stranger.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAConsumer championsLow emission zonesTfL’s bailiffs are chasing me for a stranger’s unpaid Ulez finesNow TFL is threatening to seize goods for four penalties for a car I’ve never ownedAnna TimsMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBailiffsturned up at my home to seize goods over four unpaid Ulez fines issued byTransportfor London (TfL) that have nothing to do with me.The saga began two months ago when I received four enforcement notices from CDER Group relating to a vehicle I have never owned.I was told my address had been obtained from theDVLA, but the DVLA confirmed that the vehicle has never been registered to me or my address. I sent this confirmation to CDER, but they nevertheless ordered bailiffs to come to my house and told me enforcement could not be stopped.I complained toTfL, which referred me back to CDER. CDER then informed me that TfL had rejected the evidence I had supplied.For more than 25 years I have been repeatedly mistaken for another individual with the same name, resulting in debt collection activity by numerous organisations. I have spent years proving my identity and correcting mistakes, only for the same problems to happen again.CW,BlackpoolIt seems that the original penalty charge notices (PCNs) were sent to the address of the offending driver and, when they ignored them, tracing agents trawled citizens with the same name and decided you were a good fit.Your labours to prevent bailiffs confiscating your belongings, including sending CDER 13 years of payslips and eight years of bills, took such a toll that you had to be signed off work.I paid my Ulez charge, but I am still receiving threats from TfLRead moreMost gobsmacking of all is an email from TfL to CDER rejecting the DVLA’s written confirmation that the offending vehicle has never belonged to you.“We cannot consider the evidence as valid,” TfL wrote, and it instructed CEDR to continue enforcement action.In the meantime, you discovered that the credit reference agency TransUnion had incorrectly merged a stranger’s credit report with yours. This, it turned out, was the third time in three years that it had done so.That explains why tracing agents came to your address because of a debt owed by a man with the same name in Yorkshire. You have now established that your address has, over the years, been given to tracing agents acting for more than 20 creditors, a few of whom have pursued you for debts accrued by your Yorkshire namesake.This blunder by TransUnion does not excuse either CDER or TfL for failing legal obligations to ensure they had the right person before contacting you, and for failing to accept the evidence proving your innocence.TfL, responding also for CDER, belatedly apologised when I intervened.“Our contracted enforcement agents use credit searches to track down the person liable [for unpaid PCNs],” a spokesperson says. “From this search, it wrongly concluded that CW was the owner of this vehicle.”TfL has now cancelled enforcement action, and CDER has paid you £500 in compensation for the “anguish” it now recognises it has caused.TransUnion declined to comment while the Financial Ombudsman Service investigates a complaint you have lodged about its conduct.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually.
