title: ‘The champagne of pale ales’: my search for the perfect kölsch beer in Cologne | Travel | The Guardian
description: ‘Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion’ in Cologne, and it’s only brewed in and around the German city. But which of the many beautiful, storied beer halls serves up the best?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion’ in Cologne, and it’s only brewed in and around the German city. But which of the many beautiful, storied beer halls serves up the best?
Content: Two beer stangen – the narrow glasses designed to be drained quickly, then swiftly replaced.Photograph: Jotily/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenTwo beer stangen – the narrow glasses designed to be drained quickly, then swiftly replaced.Photograph: Jotily/Getty Images/iStockphotoTravel‘The champagne of pale ales’: my search for the perfect kölsch beer in Cologne‘Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion’ in Cologne, and it’s only brewed in and around the German city. But which of the many beautiful, storied beer halls serves up the best?Scott AntcliffeMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a saying in Cologne, repeated with the mild smugness of people who know they’re right: kölsch is the only culture you can drink. It sounds like a line lifted straight from the tourist board’s brochure. Then you spend a day working your way around the city’s traditional brewhouses and realise it’s a statement of fact.Since 1997, kölsch has held a protected geographical indication within the EU, guaranteeing that any beer bearing the name is brewed within 50km of the city and made strictly to the Kölsch-Konvention. That agreement, signed in 1986, defined the style as “a light, highly attenuated, hop-accentuated, clear, top-fermenting ‘vollbier’ [full-beer]”, restricting production exclusively to the local area. It is, in effect, the champagne of pale ales: locally adored and tied to a city that has always insisted on doing things its own way.double quotation markYou never order a second; you never need to. They only stop when you place your beer mat on top of your glassThe delivery is as ritualised as the brewing itself. You sit. Aköbes– the traditionally deadpan, blue-aproned brewhouse waiter – arrives carrying akranz(a circular tray) holding a ring ofstangen, narrow 200ml glasses designed to keep the beer cold and effervescent long enough for you to drain one before the next takes its place. You drink. He marks a tally on your beer mat with a stub of pencil. You never order a second; you never need to. The conveyor belt only stops when you place your beer mat on top of your glass.Ten hours, seven brewhouses and an inadvisable number of tally marks later, I had formed some very firm opinions about Cologne’s legendary liquid culture.Brauhaus Früh am DomView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeThe twin spires of Cologne cathedral are visible from the doorway of this brewhouse. So, unfortunately, is the gift shop and a tour group from Ohio. Früh am Dom, arguably the most internationally recognisable kölsch brand, is housed in a sprawling warren of vaulted dining rooms, cellars and long oak bars. It is enormous and boisterous, yet the kölsch, poured at speed to a rotating cast of daytrippers, lacks the crisp clarity found elsewhere. Being on the cathedral’s doorstep makes this prime real estate, but the footfall turns the room into something closer to a transit lounge, where most visitors drop in for a quick photo with theirstangebefore rushing off.4.5/10,€2.50Brauhaus SionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeFounded in 1912 and heavily renovated since, Sion merges a contemporary interior with old-world charm. The result is the slickest room on this list: warm mood lighting, clean lines and a menu that reaches beyond the usual brewhouse staples of fried pork and potatoes. The kölsch itself is technically flawless and refreshing, though it lacks the rustic bite of the city’s smaller producers. It’s a fine spot for a proper sit-down dinner rather than a session – and even the köbes here shows genuine warmth, a demeanour that feels either refreshing or faintly suspicious depending on how strictly you hold to Rhenish brusqueness.6/10,€2.60Brauhaus PäffgenView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mauritius Images /AlamyBeyond the tourist centre, in the lively and historic Friesenviertel district, is the hallowed Päffgen. Operating on Friesenstraße since 1883, this is one of the lasthausbrauereien(brew pubs) that refuses to bottle for supermarket shelves; if you want Päffgen, you come here or haul a wooden keg home yourself. The beer is tapped straight from wooden barrels on the counter, giving a pour with a floral, grassy hop aroma, a hint of stone fruit and a crisp bitter finish. The room feels untouched by time – look out for the old woodenbeichtstuhl(“confessional”), the elevated booth where the innkeeper once oversaw the floor and counted the day’s takings. One of the köbesse, sliding a freshstangeacross the counter without breaking stride, put it more bluntly than any brochure could: “Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion. And this is the church.” With its gruff, lightning-fast staff and a leafy beer garden out the back, Päffgen is the gold standard of kölsch culture.9.5/10,€2.60Peters BrauhausView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Kolnik/AlamyTucked into the historic old town, Peters is what the cathedral-adjacent halls wish they were. It strikes the finest balance in central Cologne, fiercely popular with local people while remaining welcoming to passing travellers. The interior is gorgeous – stained-glass skylights throwing amber light across scrubbed, decades-old wooden tables, dark wainscoting framing the chatter of the room. The kölsch is beautifully balanced: smooth, clean and poured properly cold. We might have come at a bad time, though, as it wasn’t particularly busy and lacked atmosphere.7/10,€2.50skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrauerei zur MalzmühleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeSitting on the edge of the historic Heumarkt, Malzmühle is the second-oldest brewery in Cologne, operating on this spot since 1858. Destroyed almost entirely in the second world war, only the stone portal survived; you now pass through that same archway into a sprawling hall of rustic brickwork and heavy oak benches. Malzmühle brews Mühlen Kölsch, a pour favoured by the former US president Bill Clinton, who declared “Ich bin ein Kölsch” on a visit in 1999. It is slightly darker and maltier than its peers, with a gentle honey note against a solid bitter backbone. The atmosphere is unapologetically noisy and authentic – a meeting ground where workers in hi-vis vests share benches with executives in suits. We spoke to one of theköbesse, Carl, who told us he’d worked here for 38 years: “This is the place to be. These walls have seen so much and heard so many conversations. I wouldn’t work anywhere else.”8.5/10,€2.50Gaffel am DomView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeGaffel is a heavy hitter among local people, distributed widely across the city’s bars and football stadiums. Its flagship hall, opposite the central station, is handsome and impeccably run, with high ceilings and sweeping arches giving it real metropolitan energy. The kölsch is consistently good – bright, sharply carbonated and noticeably hop-forward, exactly as the Konvention prescribes. Knowing this same beer is sold at the gate in Cologne Bonn airport slightly undercuts the local romance, though; it’s reliable in a high-volume, commercial way. The kitchen redeems it somewhat with a stellarhimmel unääd– crispy black pudding with smooth mash and stewed apples – comfort food good enough to justify the visit alone.6.5/10,€2.50Brauhaus Sünner im WalfischView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeDown a cobbled alley in the old town, Sünner im Walfisch is pure historical theatre. Housed in a striking 17th-century step-gabled building, dismantled and rebuilt brick by brick on its current site, it serves as the old town outpost for Sünner, Cologne’s oldest operating kölsch brewery. Inside, narrow timber-framed rooms and low ceilings transport you back to medieval Rhineland. The beer is fantastic – crisp and dry with a peppery hop finish that makes it dangerously easy to drink – and it’s quieter and more intimate than the echoing halls near the station, its köbesse still delivering drinks with a wink of humour. A favourite for decor and character, if not quite for atmosphere.8/10,€2.50Scott Antcliffe’stravel to Cologne wasprovided byVikingas part ofits8-dayRhine Getaway,from £1,695Explore more on these topicsTravelCologne holidaysGerman food and drinkFood and drinkGermany holidaysEurope holidaysCity breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Did you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: The solution to the seventeenth century stumper
Author: Alex Bellos
Headline: The solution to the seventeenth century stumper
Content: Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleMathematicsDid you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzleThe solution to the seventeenth century stumperAlex BellosMon 28 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier today I set you a puzzle that Isaac Newton posed in 1679 in a latter to Robert Hooke. I mentioned that the answer is counter-intuitive, and also gave you the hint that it might have something to do with figure skating. Here’s the problem again, with its solution.The tower dropThe first known diagram of the puzzle, from Claude DechalesCursus seu Mundus Mathematicus(1674).An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land?slightly to the westslightly to the eastexactly at the bottomSolution2. slightly to the east.The Earth rotates from west to east.Our first thought might be that the object falls slightly to the west, on the grounds that as the object is falling the Earth will rotate slightly to the east.But such an argument ignores the fact that the object is originally – like the tower itself –rotating with the Earth. Our second thought might be that it lands exactly at the bottom of the tower.Again wrong! The object lands slightly to the east because as it falls it spins about its axis slightly faster, by essentially the same mechanism that makes a spinning ice-skater spin faster when they pull in their arms. It is in this way, then, that the object lands slightly to the east.View image in fullscreenIllustration from Wonders in Motion by David AchesonThe effect is small, but not absurdly so. If the Eiffel tower were on the equator the deflection to the east would be about 11cm.In more technical detail, the result follows from conservation of angular momentum, which is a measure of the momentum of an object rotating about an axis.When an object is falling from a tower, gravity is pushing it towards the centre of mass of the Earth. Yet the object is also spinning in a circle around the centre of the Earth.As the object falls its angular momentum stays the same. Which means that the expressionwr2– wherewis the object’s angular velocity andris its distance to the rotational axis (in this case, the centre of the Earth) – stays the same.Since the value ofrdecreases during the fall, the value ofwmustincrease, which means that the object spins faster. If it spins faster than the Earth is spinning it will land slightly to the east of the position directly underneath the tower.Thanks to David Acheson for today’s puzzle. He is the author of a new book,Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics,which among other things explains the background to Newton’s puzzle in more detail.I hope you had fun. I’ll be back in two weeks.Wonders of Motion by David Acheson ison sale at the Guardian Bookshop.I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one,email me.Explore more on these topicsMathematicsAlex Bellos's Monday puzzlePhysicsShareReuse this content

title: Starwatch: Tracking down the faint stars of Pisces | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Below the southern edge of the Great Square of Pegasus lie the fishes, linked by two strings
Author: Stuart Clark
Headline: Below the southern edge of the Great Square of Pegasus lie the fishes, linked by two strings
Content: Illustration: The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: The GuardianStarwatchAstronomyStarwatch: Tracking down the faint stars of PiscesBelow the southern edge of the Great Square of Pegasus lie the fishes, linked by two stringsStuart ClarkMon 28 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars.The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen.Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location.The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars.Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.From the southern hemisphere, Pisces is also well placed in the evening, appearing higher in the sky.Explore more on these topicsAstronomyStarwatchfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A young shieldbug has found a safe place to hide – or so it hopes  | Insects | The Guardian
description: Bedmond, Hertfordshire: Serge Hill Project is a haven for humans and wildlife, and there’s much to find in its collection of drought-tolerant plants
Author: Nic Wilson
Headline: Bedmond, Hertfordshire: Serge Hill Project is a haven for humans and wildlife, and there’s much to find in its collection of drought-tolerant plants
Content: A hairy shieldbug nymph on a Crete scabious seedhead.Photograph: Nic WilsonView image in fullscreenA hairy shieldbug nymph on a Crete scabious seedhead.Photograph: Nic WilsonCountry diaryInsectsCountry diary: A young shieldbug has found a safe place to hide – or so it hopesBedmond, Hertfordshire:Serge Hill Project is a haven for humans and wildlife, and there’s much to find in its collection of drought-tolerant plantsNic WilsonMon 28 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 05.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLooking across a swathe ofgolden oat grassto the Apple House, it seems almost inconceivable that the M25 and M1 motorways are just beyond the treeline. I’m exploring theSerge Hill Project for Gardening, Creativity and Health: a therapeutic resource for local schools, community groups and charities, founded three years ago by Tom and Sue Stuart-Smith.All around me, a diverse collection of drought-tolerant plants is thriving in a six-inch layer of sharp sand in the uppermost section of thePlant Library, despite not having been watered once during our sweltering summer.View image in fullscreenHairy shieldbug adults on sunflower stem.Photograph: Nic WilsonAmong the many plants I’ve not met before,Crete scabiousis the epitome of autumn glory. Its pale lilac flowers have transformed into globular seed heads that quiver in the breeze. Each sphere is a fanfare of tiny trumpets, their flared funnels marked with brown stripes. On closer inspection, I can see that some of these papery alcoves harbour hairy shieldbug nymphs,Dolycoris baccarum.Elsewhere in the garden, troops of adults and juveniles cluster on sunflower stems and wine-red dahlias, but nowhere is the nymphs’ camouflage as successful as on the scabious seed heads. While the adults invite attention with their black and white striped antennae and connexivum (edge of the abdomen), and reddish-brown forewing bases and pronotum (a hardened plate covering the front of the body), the young bugs’ markings shield them from sight. Golden-brown bands on their abdomens and along the connexivum break up their oval outlines, and the colour match between plant and insect helps them sink into sepia obscurity.Their sanctuary – Crete scabious – is one of many Mediterranean species planted in the garden as part of the project’s research into climate-resilient landscapes, so it’s encouraging to see the shieldbugs making themselves at home. So far, almost 350 invertebrates (including five species of shieldbug) have been recorded across more than 2,500 herbaceous perennials, low shrubs and bulbs in the Plant Library.Like the children and adults who come to this inclusive garden to connect with nature, the Serge Hill Project provides wildlife with a safe space to shelter and develop. And all within a mile of the London orbital, Britain’s busiest motorway.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsInsectsCountry diaryPlantsConservationRural affairsDroughtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: We would like to hear your stories of loneliness | Loneliness | The Guardian
description: How has loneliness affected you? Please share your experience
Author: Guardian community team
Headline: How has loneliness affected you? Please share your experience
Content: Have you been affected by loneliness?Photograph: Paul Maguire/AlamyView image in fullscreenHave you been affected by loneliness?Photograph: Paul Maguire/AlamyLonelinessWe would like to hear your stories of lonelinessHow has loneliness affected you? Please share your experienceGuardian community teamMon 28 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe live in an age where we have better tools for communication and connection than ever before, and yet we are in the midst of a loneliness epidemic.In 2025, a World Health Organizationreportidentified that 1 in 6 people globally are lonely. The report defined loneliness as “the painful feeling that arises from a gap between desired and actual social connections.” Perhaps, most strikingly, the age bracket that had the highest levels of loneliness was13–29-year-olds.Social isolation can strike at any age and impacts people of all social statuses, with the stigma of it often worsening the problem. As Olivia Laingwrote earlier this year, to mark the tenth anniversary of The Lonely City: Adventures in the Art of Being Alone: “The pain was intensified, as a broken leg or even a broken heart would not have been, by the fact that my loneliness felt inadmissible, a thing that could not be said for fear of repelling other people.”Loneliness shouldn’t be something to be ashamed of, but rather a set of circumstances to be discussed and explored, so that solutions to this modern quandary may be found.We would like to hear your stories of loneliness: how and when it has affected your life, why you think it happened, what it meant to you, how you have made changes to address it. title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says
Content: Health workers at an Ebola treatment centre in Butembo, where mistrust of the response to the outbreak has fuelled a series of attacks.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersView image in fullscreenHealth workers at an Ebola treatment centre in Butembo, where mistrust of the response to the outbreak has fuelled a series of attacks.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersEbolaDRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreakMarie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party saysCarlos Mureithiin Nairobi and agenciesMon 28 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of theEbolavirus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in westAfrica, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has beenintensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoWorld Health OrganizationGlobal healthHealthAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says | China | The Guardian
description: David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island
Content: Taiwanese soldiers use a variant of the US-made Abrams tanks during drills in July 2025. Donald Trump is said to have offered to sell US weapons to China.Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPAView image in fullscreenTaiwanese soldiers use a variant of the US-made Abrams tanks during drills in July 2025. Donald Trump is said to have offered to sell US weapons to China.Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPAChinaTrump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador saysDavid Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled islandAmy Hawkinsand agenciesMon 28 Sep 2026 06.40 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 20.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”On Monday, Chinese state media praised the “extraordinary level of courtesy” that Trump had shown Xi on theChinese leader’s visit to Washington.The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve anew arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn(£10.5bn), after a record multibillion-dollar deal wasannounced in Decemberlast year.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump and his wife, Melania, hosting Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the White House last week.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesTrump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previouslybeen questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanesRead moreWashington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defendTaiwanin the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take it. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence”, according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.After Perdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times the US had no plans to sell arms toChina, while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”China is a net exporter of weapons. Of the arms that it does import, most come from Russia, but the volume is rapidly falling thanks to advances in China’s own military manufacturing capacity. China’s arms imports fell by 72% between 2021 and 2025 compared with the previous five years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.Before the interview, the Taiwanese deputy foreign minister, Chen Ming-chi, spoke of the severe military threat China posed.“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.View image in fullscreenTaiwanese honour guards during a flag-lowering ceremony at Liberty Square in Taipei, on the eve of Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington last week, during which he urged Trump to oppose ‘Taiwan independence’.Photograph: Daniel Ceng/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOn Sunday, a Taiwanese official, Shen Yu-chung, also pushed back on what he said was an attempt by Beijing to “falsely claim that the Chinese Communist party and the US were allies” in the second world war. A fact sheet released by the White House after the Trump-Xi summit had said China and the US “fought side by side to win” in the war.China’s government during the second world war was the Republic of China led by Chiang Kai-shek. Chiang’s government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, who established the People’s Republic of China in 1949.In recent years Taiwan has sought to emphasise its history of fighting alongside western democratic allies as it hopes to bolster international support against aggression from Beijing.Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.Perdue told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsChinaTaiwanUS militaryAsia PacificUS foreign policyTrump administrationDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bangkok declared a ‘disaster zone’ after flooding, as rainstorms shift direction | Flooding | The Guardian
description: Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island
Content: People shopping in a market still submerged in flood water in Bangkok, Thailand, on Monday.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople shopping in a market still submerged in flood water in Bangkok, Thailand, on Monday.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersWeather trackerFloodingAnalysisBangkok declared a ‘disaster zone’ after flooding, as rainstorms shift directionJames Parrish for MetDeskCapital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big IslandMon 28 Sep 2026 04.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTShareBangkok wasdeclared a disaster zoneby its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions.The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average585mm a year). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall.1:27Bangkok residents navigate streets by boat as flood waters rise – videoOut in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away fromHawaiiwhere it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.Explore more on these topicsFloodingWeather trackerThailandExtreme weatherAsia PacificHawaiiHurricanesanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Corporations claim their fossil fuel emissions are a drop in the ocean. But what if we could count the real cost? | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: A new tool called Carbon Impacts Tracer can be used to estimate climate impact from emissions across eight metrics, including lost food production
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: A new tool called Carbon Impacts Tracer can be used to estimate climate impact from emissions across eight metrics, including lost food production
Content: The Hunter Valley Operations mine in New South Wales, Australia. A new online tool, the Carbon Impacts Tracer, allows users to calculate the impact of carbon dioxide emissions from such projects.Photograph: New South Wales Department of Planning, Housing and InfrastructureView image in fullscreenThe Hunter Valley Operations mine in New South Wales, Australia. A new online tool, the Carbon Impacts Tracer, allows users to calculate the impact of carbon dioxide emissions from such projects.Photograph: New South Wales Department of Planning, Housing and InfrastructureGreenhouse gas emissionsAnalysisCorporations claim their fossil fuel emissions are a drop in the ocean. But what if we could count the real cost?Graham ReadfearnA new tool called Carbon Impacts Tracer can be used to estimate climate impact from emissions across eight metrics, including lost food productionMon 28 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 20.34 EDTShareThe biggest coal project before authorities in New South Wales, theHunter Valley Operations mine, will emit the equivalent of about 809m tonnes of climate-warming carbon dioxide if it wins approval.That number, for most people, will carry little meaning, as might the calculation that adding that amount of greenhouse gas to the atmosphere will cause an extra 0.00036C of global heating.But what if the public was instead told that that amount of carbon dioxide would expose almost half a million people to unprecedented heat, or kill nearly 15 million coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef every time it bleaches, or lead to more than 100 additional deaths from heatwaves in Europe to the end of this century.All those statistics come from a new tool that translates the emissions from burning fossil fuels into estimated real-world climate effects taken from peer-reviewed climate studies.Australia’s renewables transition is well under way – but meeting its 2030 target will be ‘extremely challenging’Read more“Small numbers in global warming can mean catastrophic impacts,” says Prof Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick, a climate scientist at the Australian National University who is part of a team launching theCarbon Impacts Tracer.The NSW Independent Planning Commission is expected to make a decision this weekabout the future of the HVO mine, with the joint owners Yancoal and Glencore hoping to keep digging at the Hunter Valley site until 2045.Plugging the project’s expected emissions into the tracer suggests, for example, the extra heat trapped in the atmosphere by its emissions will reduce crop production every year by an amount that is the equivalent to the minimum dietary requirements of 276,129 people.The tool can be used to estimate the impact of carbon dioxide emissions from any project, company or state – or for any known amount of emissions – across eight different factors including the loss of labour hours due to excess heat, the loss of glaciers, the death of corals or lost food production.Central to the tool is a metric known as Transient Climate Response to CO₂ Emissions (TCRE) – an established calculation that every billion tonnes of CO2causes about 0.45C of global heating.Once an amount of CO2is known – such as from a major fossil project – it’ contribution to global heating can be calculated and, from there, says Perkins-Kirkpatrick, measured against already published studies.“Every tonne of CO2matters and we’ve known this for decades,” she said.“To pinpoint what this means with a high degree of confidence has taken us a long time. This [tool] is to hold big fossil fuel emitters accountable. It is not meant to be a blame game. It just shows that all emissions have impacts and now we can prove it.”All the results are presented as the best estimate within a likely range of uncertainty, with links back to the original scientific studies used for the calculations.3:01What is an El Niño and how could it cause the hottest year on record? – videoPerkins-Kirkpatrick accepts some may be sceptical of the results, but counters “we are not making these numbers up for shits and giggles”.“This is based on the best analysis published in the peer-reviewed literature,” she said.And this is only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the impacts [of fossil fuel burning].”The Carbon Impacts Tracer was developed by scientists at the Australian National University, the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century and the Lethal Humidity Global Council, and was funded by the Minderoo Foundation.Maria Nawaz leads the Australian Climate Accountability Project at the Australian Human Rights Institute at the University of New South Wales – a partner in the tracer project.“One of the major challenges in climate litigation has been establishing a direct link between a government or a corporation’s actions and climate harms and suffering,” she said.“Governments and corporations have argued their emissions are ‘just a drop in the ocean’ and too small to measure.“But we can now refute this defence and show the emissions of any state or corporation can be tied to a global warming figure and then human and ecological harms. It is transformative.”Elaine Johnson, an experienced climate lawyer and director of Johnson Legal but not involved in the work, said there will be governments and corporations that will not welcome the development of the tool.“Fossil fuel companies do not want people to be able to make that connection between their products and, say, deaths from heatwaves.“But now the science is at the point where we can make those connections clearly. That is a story the industry does not want told.”The Guardian approached Glencore, a partner in the HVO mine, for comment, but received no response.Graham Readearn is Guardian Australia’s environment and climate correspondentExplore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisMiningEnergyFossil fuelsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Queensland anti-corruption commission investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints in a year | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Statistics showed there is ‘almost no chance’ a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently, expert says
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Statistics showed there is ‘almost no chance’ a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently, expert says
Content: Both parties in Queensland have backed formation of a police integrity unit to investigate complaints against police but progress has stalled.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenBoth parties in Queensland have backed formation of a police integrity unit to investigate complaints against police but progress has stalled.Photograph: Darren England/AAPQueenslandQueensland anti-corruption commission investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints in a yearStatistics showed there is ‘almost no chance’ a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently, expert saysFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerMon 28 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQueensland’s anti-corruption commission has investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints of suspected corruption in the past year, as the state government comes under renewed pressure to implement a years-late recommendation toend the practice of police investigating police.The statistic was revealed in Queensland’s Crime and Corruption Commission’s annual report, tabled in state parliament on Friday afternoon.It revealed the CCC assessed 6,198 corruption complaints in 2025-26. It referred 4,244 back to the agency concerned, including the police, local government and public service departments.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUniversity of the Sunshine Coast criminology professor Tim Prenzler said the statistics showed the state was still operating a “discredited” approach, “facilitating misconduct through impunity”.Prenzler was one of the key experts who advised thelandmark 2022 commission of inquiryinto police responses to domestic violence.The inquiry considered numerous cases of conflicts of interest and lack of independence in police investigations of its officers. In one case, a police officer was even tasked with investigating their own actions.Subsequent reporting by the Guardian has alsorevealed allegations by former police officers that the QPS covered up its own failures prior to domestic and family violence deaths and that in other casespolicing failures were never properly investigated.The Queensland government promised to put victims first. But it has buried a report from domestic violence survivorsRead moreIt recommended creating a new independent organisation – known as a police integrity unit – to investigate all complaints against policeby May 2024, as one of its “four highest-priority recommendations”.Both parties of government backed the recommendation, butprogress has stalled.Prenzler said the statistics showed there was “almost no chance” a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently.“From the outside, the CCC looks like a powerful independent agency that will thoroughly investigate all allegations and suspicions of public sector misconduct, protect parties, and provide justice,” he said.“In reality, complainants and whistleblowers will have their expectations dashed as their matter is referred back to the agency involved and they will be doubly traumatised by the process.”He said there was no rational justification for delaying the recommendation.“Setting up the police integrity unit must be amongst the easiest things a government could do.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe state’s police minister, Dan Purdie, said police “have got really robust systems when it comes to complaints about police”.“All of those matters are overseen by the CCC. That’s been the case for a long time, and they review all of those matters,” he said.The CCC assessed 6,198 complaints in 2025-26.It retained 20 for its own investigation. It referred 4,244 to the “appropriate agency’”, with 46 referred subject to CCC monitoring, 375 with a requirement for advice on its outcome, and 3,823 referred without any oversight.It also assessed 1,934 complaints as “requiring no further action”.Asked if the unit would be established by the 2028 state election, Purdie referred the question to the attorney general.Unlike New South Wales’s Icac, the CCC is also responsible for investigating crimes such as murder and rape that don’t involve corruption.The CCC held 16 days of corruption hearings in 2025-26 but more than 100 days of crime hearings, its annual report revealed.The annual report revealed the number of corruption complaints has been steadily increasing, up about 47% in the last four years.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandAustralian police and policingQueensland politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Further interest rate hikes could ‘devastate’ property market without easing unaffordability | Reserve Bank of Australia | The Guardian
description: With RBA predicted to lift cash rate for fourth time this year on Tuesday, experts warn a fifth – or even sixth – rise would be ‘overkill’
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: With RBA predicted to lift cash rate for fourth time this year on Tuesday, experts warn a fifth – or even sixth – rise would be ‘overkill’
Content: RBA governor Michele Bullock. An increase in the cash rate to 4.6%, from 4.35%, would add another $100 to the monthly mortgage interest bill on a $700,000 loan.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenRBA governor Michele Bullock. An increase in the cash rate to 4.6%, from 4.35%, would add another $100 to the monthly mortgage interest bill on a $700,000 loan.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPReserve Bank of AustraliaFurther interest rate hikes could ‘devastate’ property market without easing unaffordabilityWith RBA predicted to lift cash rate for fourth time this year on Tuesday, experts warn a fifth – or even sixth – rise would be ‘overkill’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastPatrick ComminsEconomics editorMon 28 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 17.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo or even three more Reserve Bank interest rate hikes would be “devastating” for the property market but still leave housing more unaffordable than ever as higher borrowing costs trump lower prices, experts say.The RBA’s monetary policy board is widely expected on Tuesday afternoon to announcean increase in its cash rateto 4.6%, from 4.35%, in a decision that will add another $100 to the monthly mortgage interest bill on a $700,000 loan.A number of analysts are tipping a further interest rate rise – the fifth this year – on Melbourne Cup day. Financial markets are even pricing in a 60% chance of a sixth rate increase by mid-2027.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereAs petrol prices push towards $2.40 a litre, Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said two or three more rate hikes would be “overkill” given the already weakened state of the economy and families’ finances.A rate hike on Tuesday would push the cash rate to its highest level since late 2011, and a further increase at the next meeting in November would push it to 4.85% – the highest since just before the GFC, Oliver said.Another hike to 5.1% “is going to cause major problems for households with mortgages”, he said, pointing out that debt burdens have become substantially larger over the past two decades.“And it would be devastating for the property market. The higher you go [with the cash rate] the greater the chance you hit a tipping point, and instead of a 10% decline in home prices, you get more like a 15-20% drop.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHalf of young Australian adults now live with their parents – and it’s not hard to see whyRead moreTom Devitt, senior economist atHousingIndustry Australia, said the HIA’s national affordability index hit the lowest in history at the end of June.The silver lining from falling home values is that it makes it easier for first-time buyers to get into the property market.Devitt said he had expected affordability to improve over the second half of this year and perhaps into 2027 – but that was predicated on the RBA not pushing borrowing costs higher.Tuesday’s anticipated rate hike, alongside the prospect of more to come, had changed the calculus.“In this cycle we now don’t see any improvement in affordability at all,” he said.Taylor Nugent, a senior economist at NAB, said the prospect of more interest rate hikes suggested property values would fall further and for longer than anticipated.Beyond prices, Nugent said the fundamental issue with the housing market – too many people chasing too few homes – was evident in anongoing lack of rental properties and climbing rents.“Housing affordability is a challenge not just for people trying to buy, but people renting as well,” he said.Explore more on these topicsReserve Bank of AustraliaAustralian economyHousingInterest ratesMortgage ratesCost-of-living crisisBusiness (Australia news)newsShareReuse this content

title: Marine Le Pen hails RN senate surge as ‘milestone’ towards French presidency | France | The Guardian
description: National Rally and allies gain record 14 seats and can form senate group for first time after indirect vote by local officials
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: National Rally and allies gain record 14 seats and can form senate group for first time after indirect vote by local officials
Content: The National Rally presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, campaigning in northern France this month.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe National Rally presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, campaigning in northern France this month.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersFranceMarine Le Pen hails RN senate surge as ‘milestone’ towards French presidencyNational Rally and allies gain record 14 seats and can form senate group for first time after indirect vote by local officialsAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 28 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTFirst published on Sun 27 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has said her 2027 presidential campaign will be boosted after her anti-immigration party, theNational Rally(RN), and its allies improved to a record 14 seats in partial senate elections this weekend.Le Pen called the results a “historic victory” and a “major milestone” after her party cleared the 10-seat threshold to be able to form a senate group for the first time, after an indirect vote by local officials including mayors and councillors.The party’s progress in the senate will allow it higher visibility and more funding in the second house of parliament before next spring’s presidential election. Le Pen is polling high as Emmanuel Macron prepares to step down after 10 years in office.The French investigative website Mediapartreportedon Monday that the RN party president,Jordan Bardella, allegedly made antisemitic comments in writing in 2013, when he was a young party member.View image in fullscreenJordan Bardella, the National Rally president, with supporters in La Seyne-sur-Mer on Sunday.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesThe alleged comments in a chat, which Mediapart said it had authenticated, included: “The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so.” He was also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”.Bardella responded on X that he “formally” rejected the allegations, which he described as “crude forgeries”, saying he would take legal action.The RN MP Sébastien Chenu called the senate gains “a boost for the presidential campaign” and said there was “no more glass ceiling” for the party. Edwige Diaz, who secured a large senate win for the RN in Gironde outside Bordeaux, told Le Parisien: “This will be very useful for us before the presidential election.”The 348-seat senate is France’s second chamber of parliament alongside the national assembly. Final results on Monday morning showed the senate remained dominated by the traditional right and centre right.The upper chamber’s president of more than a decade, Gerard Larcher, 77, from the rightwing party Les Républicains, is expected to be re-elected next week.Although the RN is now the biggest single opposition party in thenational assemblyand has the largest number of French members of the European parliament, it has until now never had a grouping in the senate, where its presence has been small.Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, in addition to the three who won seats in 2023. The RN ally, Éric Ciotti’s Union of the Right for the Republic party, won two seats.The RN had entered the senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the Front National.The senate has an indirect voting system, with local elected officials choosing new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term.Racist abuse of French judo star Teddy Riner investigated after he spoke about rise of far rightRead moreSunday’s vote by local mayors and councillors reflected the RN’s growth in support in medium towns atthe last local elections in March. It also showed the party has support among independent rural mayors. Bardella called on politicians on the traditional right to join forces with his party.The Socialist senator Laurence Rossignol said a crucial question would be whether the right and centre right in the senate now moved closer to the RN and hardened their own stance on issues such as immigration and welfare benefits. She told Public Sénat TV: “Will there be a republican barrier against RN ideas? That will be key.”The right, the centre and the left’s Socialists remain the three major forces in the upper house.The radical left party La France Insoumise won a senate seat for the first time, with Gabriel Amard elected in the Rhône. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the party’s leader, who is the highest-pollingleft candidate for the presidency, said Amard’s win was a “good omen” for his own 2027 presidential campaign.Explore more on these topicsFranceNational RallyMarine Le PenThe far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Gisèle Pelicot’s daughter launches awareness campaign for potential victims of drugging and sexual assault  | Gisèle Pelicot | The Guardian
description: Campaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attack
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Campaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attack
Content: Gisèle Pelicot and another woman in the campaign led by her daughter, Caroline Darian. The caption on Pelicot’s picture reads: ‘For years, I was ... by my husband.’Composite: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisView image in fullscreenGisèle Pelicot and another woman in the campaign led by her daughter, Caroline Darian. The caption on Pelicot’s picture reads: ‘For years, I was ... by my husband.’Composite: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisGisèle PelicotGisèle Pelicot’s daughter launches awareness campaign for potential victims of drugging and sexual assaultCampaign broadcast across France encourages people to come forward even if they have little to no memory of attackKim Willsherin ParisMon 28 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGisèle Pelicot is the figurehead of a new campaign run by her daughter to encourage people who suspect they have been drugged and sexually assaulted to come forward, even if they have little to no memory of the attack.Caroline Darian, 47, who believesshe was also drugged and assaultedby her father, Dominique Pelicot – her mother’s ex-husband – launched a primetime public information push on Monday across France’s television network, on social media, in the press and on posters.Her 73-year-old mother became an international symbol of courage and resistance when she insisted shame must change sides during the trial of her former husband and dozens of men who raped her while she was unconscious.Video clips featuring Gisèle Pelicot state that in 75% of cases of sexual abuse while drugged, the perpetrator is a relative or friend. She urges those who believe they may be victims to contact theCentre of Excellence on Substance-Facilitated Assaults(CRAFS).View image in fullscreenAnother poster in the campaign reads: ‘On my birthday, I was … by my stepfather.’Photograph: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisThe centre is attached to the Paris university hospital service (AP-HP) and staffed by experts who can suggest to those who believe they may have been a victim of drugging and abuse what evidence there might be and how it can be obtained.Caroline Darian, daughter of Gisèle Pelicot, speaks: ‘How can you rebuild when your father is the worst sexual predator in decades?’Read moreDarian, the founder of the associationMendorspas(Don’t Put Me to Sleep), said: “When you launch a campaign of this scale, having my mother’s backing sends a really powerful message. It’s also a message of hope for victims, showing that it is possible to get back on your feet.”The trial of Dominique Pelicot two years ago shocked the world. For almost a decade he had drugged his wife, raped her and invited strangers into their home in the village of Mazan, 20 miles from Avignon, to rape her while she was in a state of near coma.Pelicot’s horrific ordeal might have gone unremarked had she not decided to waive her anonymity and insist the case be held in public. Dominique Pelicot and 50 other men were convicted.The trial sparked the reporting ofother casesof what UK police call drug-facilitated sexual abuse, or DFSA. Earlier this month, a man in his 60spleaded guiltyto drugging and raping his wife over two decades and inviting strangers to abuse her, in the latest in a string of similar crimes.After the publication of her bookA Hymn to Life: Shame Has to Change Sidesearlier this year, Pelicot said: “Shame sticks to you, it sticks to your skin. And that shame is a double sentence, it’s a suffering you inflict on yourself.”View image in fullscreenThis poster’s caption reads: ‘Last night, I was … by my brother.’Photograph: Alice Moitiê/Havas ParisDarian told Le Parisien: “It’s not because someone doesn’t remember that there aren’t traces or tests possible. Our aim is that these women can take back their own stories, so they no longer feel ashamed or afraid of not being heard by the police, not believed by the legal system and not supported by their family or those close to them.”She added: “Launching a campaign on this scale is quite unprecedented for an issue that was not recognised at all as a public health concern as recently as five years ago. When I started campaigning, nobody had heard of it [chemical submission] apart from a small circle of doctors. The Mazan trial was a major turning point with a global reach.“We’re getting somewhere but the fight is far from over. The message we want to send is that if you have a doubt, you need to look into it. Just because you cannot remember something, doesn’t mean there are no traces of it.”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsGisèle PelicotFranceEuropeRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Daytime Russian strike on Kyiv’s science academy kills at least one | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Three others wounded as jet-powered drones increasingly target Ukraine’s capital, with medical centre also hit
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Three others wounded as jet-powered drones increasingly target Ukraine’s capital, with medical centre also hit
Content: 1:14Russian drone hits academy of sciences in Kyiv, killing one – videoUkraineDaytime Russian strike on Kyiv’s science academy kills at least oneThree others wounded as jet-powered drones increasingly target Ukraine’s capital, with medical centre also hitPjotr Sauerin KyivMon 28 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Russian drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, killing at least one person, in the latest daytime attack on Ukraine’s capital.Flames tore through the historic building as people clambered out of first- and second-floor windows to escape, in dramatic scenes increasingly familiar in the heavily bombarded city.At least one person was killed and three others were wounded, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said the injured had been taken to hospital.The 19th-century building stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings.Anatoliy Zagorodny, the president of the national academy, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside. Standing outside the burning building, he said he did not know whyRussiahad targeted a leading centre of scientific research.“We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said. He feared some of his colleagues could still be trapped inside the academy.While the sciences building is a civilian scientific institution, it has longstanding ties to Ukraine’s defence sector. Among those injured in Monday’s strike was Volodymyr Horbulin, the academy’s first vice-president and a former high-ranking security official.Another Russian drone struck a nearby private medical centre, killing at least one person.View image in fullscreenThe building of a private medical clinic was also hit by a Russian drone in Kyiv.Photograph: Nikoletta Stoyanova/Getty ImagesRussian strikes over the past week involving missiles and increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones have hit apartment blocks, offices, warehouses and datacentres across the capital, killing and wounding civilians almost daily and giving Kyiv an increasingly frontline feel as it faces some of its most sustained bombardment since the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.The drone and missile campaign is designed to grind down public resilience and damage the economy. Monday’s double strike is likely to raise fresh concerns over Ukraine’s ability to protect even the most heavily guarded parts of the capital.The newer jet-powered drones fly faster and are harder to intercept than the older Shahed or Geran-2 models that were the backbone of Moscow’s air campaign. Ukraine is racing to develop and manufacture interceptors capable of bringing them down.Graphic showing the increasing speed of Russian drones and missilesMoscow has also changed its tactics, launching more attacks in daylight hours so that residents in major cities have to spend more of the day under air raid alerts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBuildings hit during daytime strikes are often occupied because many Ukrainians work through drone alerts rather than spend hours in shelters.The long-range drone war: Ukraine and Russia scramble for supremacy in the skiesRead moreMeanwhile, a Russian jet-powered drone struck western Ukraine near the border crossing with Poland, prompting Warsaw to issue an alert warning of a possible air attack and urging residents in the eastern Lublin region to seek shelter.Russian forces have increasingly targeted Ukrainian border crossings with Poland and Moldova, leading Kyiv to consider relocating joint customs checkpoints to the territory of neighbouring countries. “It’s again a threat very close to our border,” said Lt Col Jacek Goryszewski, speaking to Poland’s broadcaster TVN24.Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called on western countries to intensify their pressure on Russia. “Every Russian terrorist attack is a loss of life that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total,” he wrote on X on Monday. “The world must understand that terrorists will go further if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine. And we cannot turn a blind eye to such brutal strikes.”Russia has signalled that its attacks on Ukraine could intensify, and US-brokered efforts to end the war show little sign of progress.“Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters on Monday, referring to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory. “That is happening right now.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Heat pump sales soar across Europe after states cut electricity taxes, data shows | Heat pumps | The Guardian
description: EU to push member states to cut tax rate below duty on gas, with 11% surge in sales also put down to fallout from Iran war
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: EU to push member states to cut tax rate below duty on gas, with 11% surge in sales also put down to fallout from Iran war
Content: The Bosch Home Comfort group factory n Eschenburg, Germany. The EHPA said countries that tax electricity more than gas experience slower adoption of heat pumps and are more dependent on fossil fuels.Photograph: Sascha Schuermann/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Bosch Home Comfort group factory n Eschenburg, Germany. The EHPA said countries that tax electricity more than gas experience slower adoption of heat pumps and are more dependent on fossil fuels.Photograph: Sascha Schuermann/Getty ImagesHeat pumpsHeat pump sales soar across Europe after states cut electricity taxes, data showsEU to push member states to cut tax rate below duty on gas, with 11% surge in sales also put down to fallout from Iran warBusiness live – latest updatesEurope live – latest updatesJulia KolleweMon 28 Sep 2026 09.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSales of residential heat pumps increased 11% across Europe in the first six months of the year as theIran warsent oil and gas prices rocketing and some countries lowered electricity taxes.Homeowners bought 1.16m heat pumps across 12 European countries, up from 1.05m in the first half of 2025, according to the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA).Iran’s de facto closure of thestrait of Hormuz, an important shipping passage, severely disrupted the flow of oil and gas shipments and sent the price of crude oil as high as$126 a barrel in late April.Soon after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February that started the war, the European Commission published plans to encourage EU governments to lower electricity taxes and speed up the shift from fossil fuels oil and gas to renewable sources of energy.Air source heat pumps: how the costs and savings stack upRead moreSoaring energy prices and electricity tax changes have fuelled the growth in heat pump sales so far this year, said the EHPA, which has long argued that the popularity of the heating systems depends heavily on the price of electricity.Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, the pumps transfer heat energy from one place to another and can be used forwarmingandcoolinga home.In its electrification action plan, the commission said tax on electricity should be no higher than that on gas. Brussels hopes to amend the network charges that consumers pay on their utility bills to reward flexible options such as heat pumps.Heat pump sales have risen in European countries where electricity taxes have been cut, the EHPA said. In Germany, a subsidy scheme has led to heat pumps being the No 1 heating tech being installed, it added.The 12 countries covered in the data are Austria, Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal and Sweden.Paul Kenny, the EHPA director general, said: “Europe is ending its addiction to a toxic, costly drug from dodgy suppliers: gas. The sooner electricity becomes the most affordable solution, the quicker we’ll get clean.“The fix? Dropping taxes on electricity and shifting them over to fossil fuels. The European Commission has made this clear – but now all EU governments must enact it, following in the footsteps of the Netherlands and Belgium.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe industry bodyfoundthat taxes on electricity were often higher than on gas, which drives up the cost sharply. In the UK,electricity costs more than four times as muchas gas, similar to Belgium. The only country where the ratio is higher is Romania, where electricity prices are five times as high as those for gas.The EHPA said countries that taxed electricity more than gas saw slower adoption of heat pumps and were more dependent on fossil fuels. It pointed to Belgium, where heat pump uptake remains low, although the government announced tax changes for 2026 that will cut electricity costs by 3% and raise gas costs by 3%.Separately, a two-year study by the London-based Centre for Net Zero found that installing solar panels and a battery in a UK home saves £681 a year on average. Families’ annual bills fell by almost two-thirds (62%) after they received free solar panels and a battery, based on smart meter data used to calculate their electricity bills, in news first reported by the Times.Great Britain recordedmore new solar power installationsin the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, according to government figures published in July.Explore more on these topicsHeat pumpsEuropeEnergyOilGasCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Official says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 people
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Official says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 people
Content: People rescued from the dinghy were supported by emergency services in Calais.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople rescued from the dinghy were supported by emergency services in Calais.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumThree people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UKOfficial says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 peopleRajeev Syaland agenciesMon 28 Sep 2026 07.45 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 10-year-old child and two women died ⁠attempting ​to cross the Channel on Monday, French authorities have said.Their deaths and the injuries of dozens of others in a large dinghy were probably caused by crushing, according to a French official.France’s maritime ​police ‌said ‌they received a ‌distress call in the early hours from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people that had ‌run into trouble in calm seas.The three passengers were treated onboard but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter.François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, told a press conference: “Apparently there was no drowning, it was likely crushing – which is just as dreadful, especially if we think of the 10-year-old child.”The incident happened off the coast of Wissant, a village about 14 miles (23km) from Calais.A spokesperson for the local prefecture confirmed “a provisional total of three deaths and many more injured”, adding that “sea conditions were calm – the weather is good”. The prefecture described the boat as a “water taxi”, saying it had arrived relatively empty from an inland waterway before picking up passengers from the beach at Wissant.At 10.30am local time (9.30am UK time) six rescue boats were still at the scene searching for people in the water.At least 17 people, including women and children, have died in the Channel this year while attempting to reach the UK. Many have drowned, while others have died in incidents involving overcrowded boats.Three bodies were found last week after chaotic “water taxi” departures of this kind in northern France.So far this year, 18,609 people have made the Channel crossing – more than 40% fewer than at the same point last year. The number is also more than 25% lower than at this stage in 2024, when 25,165 people had crossed the Channel.Last week there were two uncontrolled landings in the UK, where dinghies arrived without being intercepted by authorities.It comes as more than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died while attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands by sea in August.On Monday, a rescue boat arrived at the port of Calais in the mid-morning, where it began disembarking people rescued from the accident. A coach, fire service and police vehicles were deployed at the scene.The northern beaches of France have become a key crossing point for people without visas hoping to cross the Channel. They pay people smugglers to board unstable rubber dinghies to make the journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.At least 29 people lost their lives last year trying to cross the Channel, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official French and British sources.Official figures cited by the UN refugee agency, the UNHCR, show irregular migration to the EU – notably via Mediterranean sea routes – has plummeted since its peak during the 2015 refugee crisis.Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary,will on Monday announce the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UKas she says “fairness” is at the heart of her vision for the Home Office. It will come as she focuses on safe and legal refugee routes to the UK in her Labour party conference speech.The UK resettlement scheme will reopen immediately, with about a quarter of those admitted to the UK under it expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan.UK government sources said officials were aware of the fatalities.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFranceMigrationRefugeesShabana MahmoodEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Questions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plot | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed
Content: A police checkpoint near RAF Fairford after a major incident was declared on Sunday.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenA police checkpoint near RAF Fairford after a major incident was declared on Sunday.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAUK security and counter-terrorismAnalysisQuestions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plotDan SabbaghDefence and security editorTehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixedMon 28 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.52 EDTShareInvestigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a village just outside RAF Fairford in the small hours of Sunday – but the fact they have all beenreleased on bail without immediate chargesuggests they are not deemed to pose a serious and violent threat.In a moment where wider geopolitical tensions mean external threats are perceived to be close, the question of whetherIranhad a hand in the alleged plot remains open. Nonetheless, the bailing of the men is a mercifully lower-key development in an investigation that appeared of the utmost gravity.Farmer who alerted police to RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot says there was ‘no follow-up’Read moreNigel Farage, the leader of Reform, had earlier insisted that the Fairford incident “proves my point on Iran” and argued that anybody arriving on small boats should not be allowed to move around in the UK. The latter point was an irrelevant argument, already weakened when police said at lunchtime that all five were UK nationals from London.Though the five were arrested on suspicion of carrying explosives and involvement in a terror plot, after more than 24 hours of searches, nothing had been discovered that would prompt further police action – perhaps explaining why MI5 had no idea that the men and their vans would turn up a mile from the base with unclear intent.View image in fullscreenA US bomber and armoured car at RAF Fairford.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianBritish officials admitted on Sunday the arrests were not led by intelligence, but rather last-minute warnings on the ground. Counter-terror police said they were first aware of three vehicles travelling to the base at 12.45am on Sunday, whilea local farmer phoned 999 at 1.36am after the vans blocked the entrance to her drive.The next day Trump made a characteristically inflated claim that the US and UK had been monitoring the men for “a long time” and that they had been trying to do “big damage”. Threat levels at Fairford have been at the highest level for several days, apparently backing this up – but UK sources say this was related to wider concerns about threats to US bases, not specific to the site.RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring.The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford,were “legitimate targets”.That would give Fairford an obvious value, though it is not clear why anyone from London would feel bold enough to attack a military base, given it would be expected to be protected by armed personnel.
