Rational plotters probably would not expect to survive, and would at least expect the most serious penalties available under law.When the suspects’ release was announced, there was no firm information from UK counter-terror police about what explosives were found or whether there was deemed to be viable devices in the vans – the kind of information that would immediately point to the degree of intent in any terror plot. Subsequently, it emerged no explosive material had been found.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But while its propagandists make heavy threats about British military bases online, Iran’s actual threat is mixed.A year ago, Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, said the Security Service had “tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots in just the one year”.Two Romanian men were found guilty in July of stabbing the Iranian journalist Pouria Zeraatiin the leg in Wimbledon two years earlier in a state-directed attack; he worked for the independent Persian channel Iran International.Yvette Cooper, then home secretary, sanctioned an IRGC-backed terror group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, in July after it claimed responsibility for a series of attacks in the UK,including the burning of four Jewish community ambulancesin March. But while four men have pleaded guilty, evidence in the case has yet to be heard in court, with prosecutorsonly saying so far there was a “terrorist connection”.In April police closed and searched part of Kensington Gardens near the Israeli embassy in London after an online video appeared to suggest the building had been targeted by drones containing hazardous substances. On that occasion, nothing was found.Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismIranMiddle East and north AfricaUS-Israel war on IranMilitaryPoliceCounter-terrorism policyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Israel does not have right to close UK consulate in Jerusalem, Foreign Office advised | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Former attorney general Dominic Grieve says Israel is not entitled to shut mission in occupied Palestinian territory
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Former attorney general Dominic Grieve says Israel is not entitled to shut mission in occupied Palestinian territory
Content: Rightwing demonstrators outside the British consulate in East Jerusalem last week. Israel has said it intends to close it next month.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APView image in fullscreenRightwing demonstrators outside the British consulate in East Jerusalem last week. Israel has said it intends to close it next month.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APForeign policyIsrael does not have right to close UK consulate in Jerusalem, Foreign Office advisedFormer attorney general Dominic Grieve says Israel is not entitled to shut mission in occupied Palestinian territoryUK politics live – latest updatesPatrick WintourandEmma Graham-HarrisonMon 28 Sep 2026 07.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael does not have a legal right to act on its plan to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, the former attorney general Dominic Grieve has advised the UK Foreign Office.Israel has said it intends to shut the consulate on 8 October in response to the sweeping ban on trade with goods from Israeli settlementsannounced by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, this month.‘You were right’: Ed Miliband tells critics Labour was wrong on GazaRead moreIsrael said on Sunday that it planned to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission toPalestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements.Grieve, who was a Conservative MP between 1997 and 2019 and attorney general from 2010 to 2014, said Israel did not have the right to shut the consulate since it was situated in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.When challenged in the Lords by the former UK ambassador Lord Hannay on the legality of Israel’s action, the Foreign Office minister Lord Wood said his fellow peer may have a point, and knew more about the subject than he did, but that he feared Israel de facto could make the consulate inoperable.Grieve said the UK should challenge the decision in the courts, arguing Israel was asserting a right it did not possess as an occupying power to impose sovereign control over East Jerusalem.View image in fullscreenDominic Grieve, who was attorney general under David Cameron.Photograph: Jacob King/PAThe UK mission in Jerusalem dates from 1838, predating the creation of the state of Israel by more than 100 years, and is separate from the embassy based in Tel Aviv. The consul general reports direct to the Foreign Office, and has its own staff and a distinct diplomatic role, covering Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza.Grieve argues in an advisory paper sent to the Foreign Office by the British Palestine Project that “retaining a consulate general in East Jerusalem after recognition of the state of Palestine preserves the UK’s position that Jerusalem’s final status remains to be determined. It does not concede Israeli sovereignty.”Grieve said the UK government had a duty to oppose the move. He pointed out the UK government had formally accepted the July 2024 advisory opinion of the international court of justice that governments should recognise Israel’s presence in occupied Palestinian territory as unlawful.Separate from the legal position, Grieve said the closure of the consulate was a measure designed to fall on Palestinians, not on Britain alone, because it would hamper aid, oversight and reporting from the West Bank and Gaza.He said: “Israel’s method in the city has been to create facts on the ground through unlawful settlement building and property seizure, and to press states to recognise those facts diplomatically. The closure should be challenged as a further attempt to exercise powers outwith those permitted to an occupier.”In closing the consulate, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, asserted Israeli sovereignty over the whole city of Jerusalem, which the UN security council has expressly said Israel does not possess.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe decision to revoke credentials of Dutch diplomats,announcedby Sa’ar on Sunday, also in effect bars them from Israeli-controlled East Jerusalem and is likely to force the closure of their representative office in Ramallah.The Netherlands’ ban on imports from occupied Palestine came into force on 22 September. The guidance applies to companies and individual travellers, and covers items bought before or after the legislation came into force, including gifts, souvenirs and items for personal use, the Dutch customs authoritysaid.Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine.Sa’ar claimed that Dutch diplomats from the Ramallah mission could continue representing their nation’s interests “from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the state of Israel”. The Israeli foreign ministry did not immediately respond to questions about how this would work in practical terms.When Israel took the same measures against Norwegian diplomats in 2024, in response to the country’s decision to recognise Palestine, it was forced to close its mission based in the West Bank town of al-Ram.“We consider the Netanyahu government’s decision to be extreme and unreasonable,” the Norwegian foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said at the time. Diplomats based in Jordan have supported Norwegian relations with Palestine since then.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyPalestineForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeEd MilibandIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm
Author: William Christou
Headline: Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm
Content: Women and children walk at camp for internally displaced people in Yemen.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenWomen and children walk at camp for internally displaced people in Yemen.Photograph: ReutersYemenChildren forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in YemenRenewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calmNasser al-Sakkaf in Taiz andWilliam ChristouMon 28 Sep 2026 03.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 12.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers.As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-alignedHouthisand the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.“We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.”He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies.Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign andrapidly moved south-west, seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast.The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed overYemen, with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022.The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles.Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air.He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation.View image in fullscreenDisplaced Yemenis carry water back to their makeshift camps.Photograph: Ebrahim Al-Suhaibi/Reuters“Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.”His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day.“What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said.Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students.“On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said.The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic.“The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour.View image in fullscreenChildren at al-Farsi camp for internally displaced people in southern Yemen.Photograph: Mohamad Hakim/AFP/Getty ImagesThe resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses.Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people.“It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods.The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen.“This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.”Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisInternally displaced peopleMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You were right’: Ed Miliband tells critics Labour was wrong on Gaza | Labour | The Guardian
description: Foreign secretary will tell party’s conference ‘we are not here to accept the status quo but to change it’
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Foreign secretary will tell party’s conference ‘we are not here to accept the status quo but to change it’
Content: Israeli settlers fly flags over a home they seized from a Palestinian family south of Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank in August.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIsraeli settlers fly flags over a home they seized from a Palestinian family south of Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank in August.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesLabour‘You were right’: Ed Miliband tells critics Labour was wrong on GazaForeign secretary will tell party’s conference ‘we are not here to accept the status quo but to change it’Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorMon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 03.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Miliband will tell campaigners and party members who raised the plight of Palestinians they were right that Labour’s approach had not been enough, saying he was heeding the calls of millions of people by imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements.The foreign secretary will tell theLabourparty conference that the government will take more explicitly progressive foreign policy positions under Andy Burnham, and that the UK will be a leader among like-minded countries in a new age of diplomacy.He will say there is a “fundamental and wider lesson from Israel andPalestineabout how we have changed our approach as a party”, saying Labour will succeed “because of, not in spite of, our progressive values”.He will talk of the start of a new and more muscular foreign policy. “We are not here to accept the status quo but to change it at home and abroad,” he will say.The party’s conference hall was often the scene of fierce opposition to Keir Starmer’s stance onIsraeland Palestine in Labour’s final year of opposition and early in government.View image in fullscreenThe foreign secretary, Ed Miliband.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesSince becoming foreign secretary, Miliband has announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in theWest Bank, which has resulted in 12 countries – including France and Canada – announcing they would also impose sanctions.The Guardian understands Miliband will say in his speech that the sanctions marked a definitive change in how Labour will approach the situation in the Middle East.“I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right,” he will say.“And under Andy’s leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes inGaza. We call out Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with actions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLabour shifts on Israel, but what difference will it make? – podcastRead more“We willban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government, says ‘we will not let you succeed’.”Miliband will pay tribute to those who have campaigned against the Israeli onslaught in Gaza, though his warm words are likely to raise questions about whether the government will review the proscription of Palestine Action. Police arrested a number of demonstrators outside the conference hall on Sunday.“The bonds of solidarity between the British people and those who yearn for peace in Israel and Palestine are too strong to be broken,” Miliband will say.“Our decision to act mobilised the international community, country after country. This is how to make change happen in today’s world. Doing what is right and galvanising others to act too.”Miliband will say in his first speech to the party conference as foreign secretary that cooperation in imposing sanctions will be the beginning of a new bond with “likeminded countries” such as France and Canada, though it is also likely to be interpreted as being more willing to sideline the US.Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has made an explicit argument for middle powers to do more to build alliances with each other outside traditional structures, and was direct in his desire to forge closer ties with and among European countries in a speech in Brussels earlier this month.A source close to Miliband said that would be a key theme of his time in office. “Britain’s interests are served by standing up for our values on the world stage. Our ability to build coalitions on big global issues depends on our ability to bring countries with us,” he will say.“This Israel/Palestine reset is a sign of how we want to do business. We are going to be propositional in bringing countries with us on the issues we really care about.”Explore more on these topicsLabourForeign policyEd MilibandLabour conference 2026IsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Five UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford released on bail | UK news | The Guardian
description: Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state
Content: The men were pictured on Sunday being apprehended near the RAF base in Gloucestershire.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenThe men were pictured on Sunday being apprehended near the RAF base in Gloucestershire.Photograph: BBCUK newsFive UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford released on bailPolice say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign stateVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentMon 28 Sep 2026 18.02 EDTFirst published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 07.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as police investigate why they were so close to the airbase in three vans with suspicious material in the back.The five suspects were revealed to be British men, all in their 20s and from London. They had been arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside early on Sunday morning on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said.An Iranian link is still under investigation, as is whether any of the five were paid to gather in the village of Whelford, two miles from RAF Fairford.On Monday, Donald Trump expressed surprise that the suspects had been bailed. The US president said: “I would not have released them.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a meeting of the government’s crisis committee Cobra over the events and Iran’s possible role.An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release it emerged that no explosive material had been found.The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.“We have, as you would expect, ensured that our protective security advice and posture remain commensurate to the threat. But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”8:29Who is behind suspected bomb plot at RAF base? - The LatestIran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.Taylor said: “Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity, often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain. It can be harder to spot, and to that end I would ask the public to remain vigilant and report anything suspicious to police.”Trump claimed on Sunday that the men “were looking to do big damage” at the base, used by the US air force, which was taken as revealing a serious terror plot.Taylor said: “I can confirm that following extensive interviews and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry.”Police said the five men were all from London, one aged 23, three aged 24, and one aged 25. They were arrested after a farmer driving home from a party spotted them. She said she believed they were wearing balaclavas and they ran away when her headlights illuminated them. She then called the police.Trump also suggested the plot was known to the US authorities. But British sources suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown.View image in fullscreenAn armoured vehicle on patrol at RAF Fairford on Monday.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty ImagesThe base had been at its highest state of alert, called delta, for several days beforehand because of a general threat, with extra security measures.The farmer said she was surprised it had been left to her to disrupt the activities of the men.In a round of broadcast interviews, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said the woman had only a “partial picture” of the events.About 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated early on Sunday morning to a leisure centre, with a 400-metre cordon placed around the white vans as bomb-disposal robots examined them.At the Labour party conference, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the evacuated residents should shortly be able to return home.Emergency teams deploy bomb disposal robot at RAF Fairford air baseIran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had made threats against RAF Fairford in July.Iran’s embassy in London denied any involvement in the events in Whelford. It said: “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Local representatives question official accounts after suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford | UK news | The Guardian
description: Amid conflicting statements, local MP and councillors demand answers over how suspects were allowed to enter residential areas of nearby village
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Amid conflicting statements, local MP and councillors demand answers over how suspects were allowed to enter residential areas of nearby village
Content: Armed police near RAF Fairford. It remains unclear who or what was behind the alleged activityPhotograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenArmed police near RAF Fairford. It remains unclear who or what was behind the alleged activityPhotograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersUK newsLocal representatives question official accounts after suspected bomb plot at RAF FairfordAmid conflicting statements, local MP and councillors demand answers over how suspects were allowed to enter residential areas of nearby villageJamie GriersonMon 28 Sep 2026 15.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn MP and councillors representing the residents of the village near RAF Fairford who were evacuated due to a suspected terror plot have expressed scepticism and concern over the security response to threats made by Iran.About 85 properties in Whelford, Gloucestershire, were evacuated on Sunday morning after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences in the village. The men, who were later re-arrested on suspicion of terror offences, were released on bail on Monday.It is understood some residents were returning to their properties late on Monday, but a cordon remains around the village.As speculation mounted over the circumstances surrounding the incident, concerns emerged about how events were handled by the authorities. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers,warning the UKthat “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.However, it remains unclear who or what was behind the alleged activity. Iran has denied any involvement. Tehran’s embassy in London condemned what it described as “unfounded and malicious speculation” linking the country to the incident in the vicinity of the military base in Gloucestershire.Roz Savage, the MP for South Cotswolds, said she had many questions about the circumstances of how the alleged terror plot was averted.View image in fullscreenUS air force personnel work on a B1 bomber at RAF Fairford on Monday.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APThe Liberal Democrat MP, whose constituency covers the military base, said she would be writing to the prime minister and the defence secretary with her concerns.“Ever since it was first announced six months ago that RAF Fairford was going to be used as the base for US military airstrikes on Iran, I’ve been asking questions of the government about whether they can assure my residents, my constituents, of their safety,” she said.“They had given that assurance. However, I feel that the events of this weekend do cast that into doubt.”She went on: “Who knew what? When did they know it? Where was the ball dropped? What more could have been done to secure the safety and security of my constituents?“We are already in the process of writing to the secretary of state for defence and to the prime minister to try and ascertain the answers to some of these questions.”There have been conflicting statements about who knew what and when. A farmer from Whelford told reporters she called police in the early hours of Sunday to report suspicious activity – which then triggered a rapid response.But the US president, Donald Trump, also suggested to reporters the men had been under surveillance. Now, the men have been released on police bail.Tristan Wilkinson, a cabinet member for Cotswold district council and councillor for the Lechlade, Kempsford and Fairford South ward, which covers Whelford, said: “The American president indicated last night in front of journalists that there was some intelligence and that these individuals were under surveillance.“If that was to be true, that they would have been allowed to get so close to the base and drive what was, at the time, believed to be bombs into residential areas of a small village, I can’t imagine the security services allowing that to happen.“I would have expected them to have done a hard stop on the van before they got to people’s homes. So that that doesn’t feel right.“It seems insane that this appears to have been a tipoff from a member of the public, and the security services are claiming that there was a level of intelligence involved as well. I don’t see how those two things can both come through at the same time.”He went on: “Back in July, the Iranians issued a statement saying that any countries that were providing military and practical support for the American effort were legitimate targets and at the time they named RAF Fairford specifically.“So at that time, I and other civic leaders were calling for a more visible police presence to reassure residents, and that did happen.“So from July, if you were around the base, you would have seen more police patrols.“So if you’d parked a car up in a layby or somewhere near the base in the last few weeks, then you probably would have had the police contacting someone quickly to find out who you are and what you are doing.“But I do think there’s been an increase in police presence in the last week as well. So I went past the base last Monday and I noticed that the non-manned entrances to the base have been fortified with vehicles.“They put diggers and heavy vehicles in place that I’ve never seen before. So that’s quite an unusual step to block an emergency exit. So that led to speculation that maybe there was an increased level of concern from the base for them to use those measures.“I wouldn’t expect the RAF to give a running commentary,” he added. “However, I think there’s always room for improvement. We have a significant military presence surrounded on three sides by residential housing. You can walk right up to the perimeter fence. There’s lots of military bases around the world that are quite remote for good reasons. So, the reality is this is a big military presence in a rural community.“I will be asking for us to look at ways at how we can improve ongoing relations, and it’s not just relating to security matters. You know, we have other issues that you know with regard to flooding and noise, so there’s always more we can do.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Wynn-Jones, husband of Delia Smith, dies aged 85 | UK news | The Guardian
description: Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on Monday
Author: Charlie Moloney
Headline: Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on Monday
Content: Delia Smith and Michael Wynn-Jones celebrate Norwich City’s Championship victory in 2019.Photograph: Stephen Pond/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDelia Smith and Michael Wynn-Jones celebrate Norwich City’s Championship victory in 2019.Photograph: Stephen Pond/Getty ImagesUK newsMichael Wynn-Jones, husband of Delia Smith, dies aged 85Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on MondayCharlie MoloneyMon 28 Sep 2026 15.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Wynn-Jones, the journalist and husband of the TV chefDelia Smith, has died at the age of 85.Wynn-Jones was honorary life president ofNorwich Cityfootball club, which said everyone at the club was “deeply saddened” by his death.The club said in statement: “Michael died peacefully at home on Monday morning, aged 85. He will be greatly missed. His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth hospice in Ipswich.“Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom [Smith, the couple’s nephew], and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones. At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.”Wynn-Jones lived with Smith near Stowmarket in Suffolk and they had been married for more than 50 years.The couple oversaw several promotions to the Premier League for the Canaries, putting the club on a solid financial footing. Smith had a more prominent, public role at Norwich City but Wynn-Jones was reportedly regarded as a trusted adviser and influential figure in the boardroom.Darren Huckerby, a former player for the club, posted a tribute saying Wynn-Jones “stayed out of the limelight but all at Norwich City FC owe him so much”.Wynn-Jones worked as a journalist for titles including the Daily Mirror and the Spectator and founded his own publishing company.He began attending Norwich City games in April 1955 at the age of 13. He wrote fondly of the club’s unlikely run to the FA Cup semi-final in 1959.Norwich City Fans Social Club said in a statement: “All of us at NCFSC are devastated to hear the news about Michael Wynn-Jones passing. Michael is a true NCFC legend and what he did for the club cannot be underestimated. We are thinking of Delia, Tom and all of Michael’s family at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Michael.”Delia Smith previously told BBC Radio 4’s Desert Island Discs that she and Wynn-Jones bonded over their passion for food and football.Shesaid in 2021she rarely cooked at home, leaving Wynn-Jones to hover over the stove while she went “to the end of the garden”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsDelia SmithNorwich CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland
Content: A resident of Garvaghy Road, Portadown: there has been growing nationalist self-confidence about a border poll on a united Ireland.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersView image in fullscreenA resident of Garvaghy Road, Portadown: there has been growing nationalist self-confidence about a border poll on a united Ireland.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersNorthern IrelandAnalysisAbsence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significantDaniel BoffeyChief reporterRow comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern IrelandMon 28 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.39 EDTShareThree decades ago, it took the deaths of three Roman Catholic children – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s CountyArmaghchaplain said at the time.It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then.Northern Irelandis very different place today.Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday.Faced withthousands of membersof the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain.View image in fullscreenA march of members of the Orange Order is blocked by police near Drumcree church, Portadown, Northern Ireland, on Monday.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersEvery half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful.The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and historysometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us.The divisions and tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland, papered over by the 1998 Good Friday agreement – when all sides were exhausted by the hate and misery of the three decades of Troubles – have been all too evident of late.This particular dispute can be reasonably argued either way. The independent Parades Commission has ruled that the march down the Garvaghy Road is permissible. The marchers are simply taking advantage of their rights, it may be said. But is it really necessary to take this road after 28 years of the march being banned? Who is served by the provocation?The detail of the argument is perhaps less important than the fact that it is happening, and what that says about Northern Ireland today, and what it may mean for the future.View image in fullscreenMichelle O’Neill, the Northern Ireland first minister (left), and the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, (centre) in the Garvaghy Road area on Sunday.Photograph: Peter Morrison/PAOn the nationalist side, there has been growing and bristling self-confidence about the prospects of a border poll on a united Ireland. This was only inflated by Donald Trump’srecent suggestionthat a unified Ireland should happen sooner rather than later. “The days of unionist supremacy and domination are gone,” said the first minister, Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, on Monday after appearing herself in Drumcree. “We will not be going backwards.”The numbers gathering from the nationalist community, some of whom were bussed in from Belfast and Derry, appeared to surprise the Police Service of Northern Ireland. It was a moment of unity within an often fractured nationalist community.Those in attendance included Colin Duffy and his brother Paul, who were both acquitted of terror charges in 2015, along with the SDLP party leader Claire Hanna, a vehement critic of those who reach for violence as an answer.Meanwhile, for the unionists, the changed relationship with the rest of the UK brought about by the Brexit deal and changing demographics has arguably engendered a distinct lack of confidence about the future.View image in fullscreenDUP MLA Jonathan Buckley (left), the party leader, Gavin Robinson, (centre) and DUP MLA Diane Dodds at Parliament Buildings, Stormont, on Monday.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAGavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP), the largest unionist party, claimed on Monday that “standards have been shattered” by the presence of the first minister with the protesters in Drumcree.When O’Neill and Mary Lou McDonald, the leader ofSinn Féinin the Republic of Ireland, arrived at the protest, it was to chants of “bring it down” and “fuck Stormont”, in reference to power-sharing arrangements in Northern Ireland, structured to make unionists and nationalists work together.“How we can go forward when there is such a level of disdain for the simple fundamental democratic principles of society?” asked Robinson of the attempt by the first minister to block a lawful march.It is likely that the prospect of elections for the Northern Ireland assembly next year, and the need to rally the faithful to their respective cause, is not helping to calm the rhetoric.In Stormont, the speaker, Edwin Poots, a former leader of the DUP, condemned the first minister for her “gross discourtesy” and “contempt” in not coming to answer an urgent question about the crisis.In this context, there is concern that even if Sinn Féin’s leaders, with the crowds’ chants ringing in their ears, do not walk out of the Northern Ireland executive, that the DUP could well do so.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Orange Order near Drumcree church on Monday.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersAfter a prolonged period in which agreement on a budget for Northern Ireland’s collapsing public services has not been found with Westminster, such further fracturing risks a whole new level of instability.The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, spoke to Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, on Monday. The possibility of mediation was discussed, Mac Cionnaith said. Speaking in the Republic, Micheál Martin, the taoiseach, called for cool heads. “No one wants to go back to the past divisions, to past trauma that we experienced at Garvaghy Road, Drumcree, in the past,” he said. “I would say to Sinn Féin and to everybody else: time to dial back now and time to engage in dialogue, and to work this out in a sensible, community-based way.”Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandDemocratic Unionist party (DUP)Sinn FéinNorthern Irish politicsArmaghnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nandy labels Farage ‘master of conspiracy theory’ over Fairford claims | Politics | The Guardian
description: Culture secretary criticises Reform leader after he tried to link suspected bomb plot to small boat crossings
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Culture secretary criticises Reform leader after he tried to link suspected bomb plot to small boat crossings
Content: Nigel Farage said he had been warning about ‘Iranian agents’ coming into the UK on small boats after arrests near RAF Fairford.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNigel Farage said he had been warning about ‘Iranian agents’ coming into the UK on small boats after arrests near RAF Fairford.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPoliticsNandy labels Farage ‘master of conspiracy theory’ over Fairford claimsCulture secretary criticises Reform leader after he tried to link suspected bomb plot to small boat crossingsBen QuinnandAlexandra ToppingMon 28 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has been described as a “master of the conspiracy theory” by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, after he tried to linkevents at RAF Fairfordto small boat crossings.TheReform UKleader was criticised over his reaction to the arrests of the men on Sunday, when he said he had been warning for months about “Iranian agents” coming into the UK across the Channel in small boats.“We deserve to be told the truth about the Fairford bomb plotters’ identities,” he added in his post on X on Sunday.On Monday he posted a video in which he claimed to have received intelligence that the Iranian regime was using the small boats “to get their operatives into Britain”.Less than an hour later, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said that the five suspects were all British nationals.The men – three residents of Westminster and two others from Camden and Willesden, all London boroughs – have since been released on bail while the police investigate “multiple lines of inquiry”.Nandy told the Guardian atLabourparty conference on Monday that Farage was a “master of the conspiracy theory” when asked about his comments. “I think that he’s good at using the very real sentiment that a lot of people feel, of anxiety and distrust,” she added.“Particularly in this era of mis- and disinformation, I think he’s very agile at exploiting that for political gain.”Defending the authorities’ not having immediately released identity details of the suspects, Nandy said the first job of the government was to reassure the public that they were taking the right steps to keep them safe, which sometimes means “withholding information where it is in the public interest”.“More information is usually better than not,” she added, but it was “not always a conspiracy” when it was held back.Police involved in the investigation have also appealed for patience, without the pressure from speculation, while they conduct their inquiries.CTP senior national coordinator, deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, said in an update: “I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised. However, I ask that at this time, Counter Terrorism Policing are given the space to work carefully and clearly.”Farage was also accused of “irresponsible nonsense” by Jenny Jones, a Green Party peer, who said: “Once again Farage’s attempts to whip up division by scapegoating some of the world’s most vulnerable people has left him with egg on his face.”Speaking after the police said that the suspects were British nationals, Farage denied any suggestion it had been irresponsible speculate about the incident while the government was carefully calibrating its responses to the security operation in Gloucestershire.“I have been saying it for years. I didn’t say anything different yesterday. What I have been saying for years and saying all summer, our national security is threatened from the outside by weakness on borders like it has never been before,” he told Sky News.Other Reform UK MPs including Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice also rushed to try to link the RAF Fairford incident to small boat crossings.Jenrick said that “we may now be seeing the consequences” of “complacency” by the Home Office after he had previously said terrorist were using small boats to enter the UK.Later on Monday, Tice shared an X post by his partner Isabel Oakeshott, who said UK law recognised six types of British nationality and that asking for the suspects’ “countries of origin” was among “perfectly reasonable questions”.The Reform deputy leader added: “Ethnicity? Dual nationals? Asylum seekers? Previous convictions? Known to Prevent / Authorities? Benefits claimants? Living in social housing?”Explore more on these topicsPoliticsNigel FarageReform UKLisa NandyLabourLabour conference 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: In-laws arrested on suspicion of murder after New York Times engineer shot dead in California | California | The Guardian
description: Police arrest couple in their 70s after Jonathan McKinsey, 40, found dead in park in Bay Area city of Dublin
Author: Abené Clayton
Headline: Police arrest couple in their 70s after Jonathan McKinsey, 40, found dead in park in Bay Area city of Dublin
Content: The Dublin sports grounds, where the victim was found dead.Photograph: Google MapsView image in fullscreenThe Dublin sports grounds, where the victim was found dead.Photograph: Google MapsCaliforniaIn-laws arrested on suspicion of murder after New York Times engineer shot dead in CaliforniaPolice arrest couple in their 70s after Jonathan McKinsey, 40, found dead in park in Bay Area city of DublinAbené ClaytonMon 28 Sep 2026 19.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA married couple in their 70s have been arrested for allegedly shooting and killing their son-in-law, aNew York Timesengineer, in broad daylight at a suburban Bay Area park.A police officer found Jonathan McKinsey, 40, lying on the ground with multiple gunshot wounds in a park in Dublin,California, a small city about 35 miles (56.3km) east of San Francisco. Around the time the officer discovered him, 911 calls began pouring in from witnesses reporting the shooting.McKinsey was pronounced dead at the scene, according to apress releasefrom the city of Dublin on Sunday.He had been the head of engineering for the New York Times’s games department for nearly four years, according to his LinkedIn page.Witnesses told police that the suspected shooters, identified as Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77, were still in the area. The pair, identified by police as McKinsey’s in-laws, were arrested on suspicion of murder shortly after the shooting.Witnesses alsotold CBS Newsthat the suspects were both wearing masks, and each took a turn shooting the victim.An arraignment is scheduled for Wednesday, the San Francisco Chroniclereported. Police have not indicated a motive for the shooting.Court records cited in local media reports show McKinsey and his wife had been engaged in a legal battle over child custody and allegations of domestic and child abuse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe city of Dublin has had one homicide per year between 2023 and 2025, while the number of reported domestic violence incidents increased from 121 in 2024 to 131 in 2025, according to thecity’s crime data.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWest CoastNew York TimesnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: GPT-6.1 Astra showed deceptive behavior and tried to use external tools despite knowing it would be unsafe
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: GPT-6.1 Astra showed deceptive behavior and tried to use external tools despite knowing it would be unsafe
Content: OpenAI logo displayed at Moscone Center during a technology summit in San Francisco, California, on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI logo displayed at Moscone Center during a technology summit in San Francisco, California, on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testingGPT-6.1 Astra showed deceptive behavior and tried to use external tools despite knowing it would be unsafeReutersMon 28 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI is scrapping the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation ⁠AI model planned for an October debut, over safety concerns raised by researchers ⁠during internal testing, the ⁠Wall ​Street Journalreportedon Monday.The model, expected to appear in ChatGPT and ⁠Codex, was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance, the report said.Earlier this ⁠month, Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO,calledfor the industry ​to slow the development ‌of frontier ‌AI models to allow safety measures to keep pace, a ‌view endorsed by Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, and Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO.OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.Saachi Jain, the ChatGPT parent’s safety chief, told the Journal on Monday ‌that Astra fell short of the company’s standards in alignment tests, which assess whether a ​system follows human intent.The model showed more deception than its predecessor, including at times failing to accurately disclose actions it had or had not taken, the report ⁠said.It also had problems with “scope authorization”, pushing ahead with ​tasks ​without requesting user permission ​and sometimes attempting to use external tools ​or services ‌when doing so could ​be ​unsafe.The decision comes ahead of OpenAI’s developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers.Explore
