And Republicans, in turn, have looked to quash stories about the impact of abortion bans and suppress data that illustrates their impact, fearing, it seems, that being reminded of what abortion bans mean in practice will further dampen their party’s odds in the coming midterms.First, there’s Texas. The Lone Star state was the first to implement a near-total abortion ban in September 2021, about nine months before Roe was struck down, after the supreme court used its controversial shadow docket to allow Texas to ban abortion without full briefing or argument. That means that Texas has an unusually large amount of data on how abortion bans affect women’s health and status: no other state has had an abortion ban in place for as long. But state health officials in Texas, most of them appointed by the solidly Republican state government, have dragged their feet on studying the impact of abortion on maternal health outcomes – maybe because they don’t think they’ll like what they find.After the state committee refused to expand the purview of its longstanding maternal mortality data collection to include adverse health outcomes caused by delayed or denied abortion care, investigators at ProPublicadid so themselves, finding that in 2022 and 2023, the first two full calendar years that the state’s abortion ban was in effect, that the rate of sepsis in Texas patients who experienced miscarriages in the second trimester increased by more than 50% – probably because doctors, fearing sanction and prosecution under the new laws, delayed administering the very simple dilation and curettage procedure that would have spared the patients’ lives until the women’s condition worsened to the point of death. The new law, in short, forces healthcare providers to play chicken with women’s lives, like daredevil teenagers standing in the path of oncoming headlights and daring themselves to stand still before leaping out of the roadway at the last available minute. Predictably, this has had fatal results. The same ProPublica study found that in the first two years after the ban went into effect, 120 pregnant or postpartum women died in Texas hospitals – a dramatic increase over previous years.But despite the growing body count, Texas health authorities evidently remain determined to cover up the fatal results of the abortion ban. Every year in early September, an official medical body in the state issues a report on the maternal and infant death rate in Texas – data that is essential for health researchers, even as the methods of its collection have become disputed and politicized in the post-Dobbs era. But this year, in an unprecedented move, the release of the reportwas postponed– pushed back from its longstanding date of 1 September, all the way to 1 December. The delay means that whatever the report says about the state of pregnant women suffering, sickening and dying in Texas, that information will be kept confidential until after the midterms. Voters will be deprived of it as they make their choices in November.Rest assured, the new CDC director thinks ‘abortion surveillance’ is essential | Arwa MahdawiRead moreIt’s easier to understand why Republicans want to hide data on the health effects of abortion bans when you realize just how profound those impacts are. New studies show they are quite profound indeed. Ananalysis of CDC datareveals that since Dobbs, women are dying at alarmingly high rates from ectopic pregnancies – in which an embryo implants in the fallopian tube, rather than the wall of the uterus, a condition which has no possibility of leading to a live birth and which is fatal if left untreated. Ectopic pregnancies are easily detectible using ultrasounds, and simply terminated with a shot; there is no reason, medical or moral, why they should be fatal. And yet, between 2020 and 2025, they killed nearly 200 women in the US – almost doubling the number who died in the previous six years. The culprit? Probably the same phenomenon that is driving the increase in sepsis among pregnant women in Texas: doctors, scared to do their duty by their patients because of sadistic, punitive and misogynist abortion bans, are forced to subordinate medical best practices to the incoherent demands of the law. The rate of ectopic pregnancy deaths in states with abortion bans is nearly double that in states where abortion is legal.Neither Democrats nor the media seems interested in making abortion a centerpiece of the midterm campaign cycle, and so Republican efforts to bury this data have been largely successful. But there are still those struggling to assert the value of women’s lives. This month, the family ofTierra Walker, a 37-year-old mother who died at 20 weeks pregnant in a Texas hospital in 2024, after doctors had repeatedly denied her an abortion to treat her worsening pre-eclampsia,suedthe Texas attorney general and Republican Senate nominee, Ken Paxton, and others for wrongful death. They allege that Walker, who had suffered multiple seizures and had become unable to work due to her condition, was subjected to neglect and indifference by a Texas medical and legal system that cares more about enforcing pregnancies than it does about civil rights, personal dignity, public health or human life. When she died, her son, then 14, lost his mother. Ken Paxton, and all the other abortion-ban supporting Republicans on the ticket in November, should have to answer to him.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAbortionOpinionUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026WomenGenderHealthRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: AI leaders have known about the extinction threat for decades | Judith Levine | The Guardian
description: Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway
Author: Judith Levine
Headline: Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway
Content: ‘Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyber-intelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.’Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyber-intelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.’Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI leaders have known about the extinction threat for decadesJudith LevineScientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anywayMon 28 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTShareOver the past few weeks, many of us have struggled to concoct a mental image of brains in the cloud jumping their “sandbox”, sneaking on to the internet, recruiting “swarms” of other “agents” to cheat on a test, and, after discussing the ethics of the act, hacking into a wiki platform with the weird name Hugging Face.We knew that artificial intelligence was devouring our jobs, degrading our kids’ education and deepfaking our politics; that datacenters were sucking up our water and electricity and sending us the bills. But until 8 September, when the Anthropic computer scientist Jacob Coxon posted his existential terror on Twitter/X, few of us suspected AI might be endangering our survival.With little understanding or knowledge, we began debating whether to be mildly worried, seriously concerned or scared shitless.But there were a few people who were fully aware of the dangers of AI, especially ofrecursive self-improvement (RSI), by which AI teaches itself without human intervention. They could not predict precisely when it would happen, but they knew that machine superintelligence was coming, and when it did, the bots would outsmart us – as OpenAI’s did – and this would not be good for us flesh puppets.As Geoffrey Hinton, AI’s “godfather”, recently asked onCNN: “What examples do we have of a more intelligent thing being controlled by a less intelligent thing?” The Nobel laureate is a leading proponent of slowing down AI development until we understand how to control it.It’s not hypothetical: the dangers of AI are already here | Granate Kim and Mohamed HusseinRead moreIt was not until their creations’ powers were exposed in September – the hack happened inearly Julyand was neither thefirstnor the only AI jailbreakby far– that AI moguls such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman began talking aboutslowing downthe pace of innovation andpleading for regulation, whilecautioningthat global competition makes regulation unwise.Scientists and entrepreneurs knew the dangers of AI a quarter-century ago. But animated by curiosity and profit, they went ahead anyway.Early on, as today, some of the scientific pioneers were thrilled about the future. In his 1988 bookMind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence, Hans Moravec, a founder of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, predicted that cyberintelligence would surpass human intelligence within 40 years.Ten years later, inRobot: Mere Machine to Transcendent Mind, he revised the prediction: machine and human intelligence would be equal by 2040; by 2050, the bots would replace us. But not to worry; this was the glorious next step in evolution, he said. One review of Mind ChildrencalledMoravec’s attitude “irresponsible optimism”.It did not take long for other optimists to change their minds. In the late 1990s, Eliezer Yudkowsky was working on AGI, or artificial general intelligence, models. In 2001, he founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (Miri) and published “Creating Friendly AI 1.0: The analysis and design of benevolent architectures”, a paper extolling the utopian potential of the “transhuman mind”.By 2002, he began worrying about that mind escaping human control. He proposed theAI Box experiment, which showed that a highly sophisticated artificial intelligence could talk a human into letting it out of a closed environment.By 2003, as he explained later in a series of posts called “Yudkowsky’s Coming of Age”, he stopped developing and started warning. “I looked back and saw that I had claimed to take into account the risk of a fundamental mistake, that I had argued reasons to tolerate the risk of proceeding in the absence of full knowledge. And I saw that the risk I wanted to tolerate would have killed me,” he wrote.By 2025, with the Miri president, Nate Soares, Yudkowsy would publishIf Anyone Builds It, Everyone Will Die. “We do not mean that as hyperbole,” the authors wrote. They called not just for “straightforward regulations”, national laws, or pledges of corporate virtue, but for stringent global limits: “All over the Earth, it must become illegal for AI companies to charge ahead in developing artificial intelligence as they’ve been doing.”At around the same time, Bill Joy was having misgivings. Like Yudkowsky’s posts, Joy’s 2000 piece in Wired,Why the Future Doesn’t Need Us, retraced his development from inquisitive child to computer prodigy to profound skeptic of human genetic engineering, nanotechnology and robotics. Joy was no luddite.He was the chief scientist at Sun Microsystems and about 25 years earlier, an architect the first widely used networking software, Unix. The piece was widely read by techies, ethicists and philosophers.“I think it is no exaggeration to say we are on the cusp of the further perfection of extreme evil, an evil whose possibility spreads well beyond that which weapons of mass destruction bequeathed to the nation-states, on to a surprising and terrible empowerment of extreme individuals,” wrote Joy.He counted himself among these individuals, “creators of new technologies and stars of the imagined future” who, “despite the clear dangers”, were “hardly evaluating what it may be like to try to live in a world that is the realistic outcome of what we are creating and imagining”.This month, in response to Coxon’s post, the Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubingerpostedthere was a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade. But the risks were being weighed 25 years ago, too. Philosopher John Leslie estimated the odds of human extinction at 30% or more.Ray Kurzweil, the sunny futurist whose bookThe Age of Spiritual Machines: When Computers Exceed Human Intelligencewas released on the first day of the 21st century, gave us “a better than even chance of making it through”. These estimates, Joy noted, did “not include the probability of many horrid outcomes that lie short of extinction”.In that book, Kurzweil quoted a lengthy text to illustrate what he considered doomsday madness. “If the machines are permitted to make all their own decisions, we can’t make any conjectures as to the results, because it is impossible to guess how such machines might behave,” it read.“[W]e are suggesting neither that the human race would voluntarily turn power over to the machines nor that the machines would willfully seize power. [But] as society and the problems that face it become more and more complex and machines become more and more intelligent, people will let machines make more of their decisions for them … Eventually a stage may be reached at which the decisions necessary to keep the system running will be so complex that human beings will be incapable of making them intelligently. At that stage the machines will be in effective control.”The author of these prescient words was the late mathematician-turned-terrorist Ted Kaczynski – the Unabomber. It is excerpted from his 58-page manifesto, “Industrial Society and its Future”, which he released, and theWashington Postpublished, in 1995.To prevent the realization of the “industrial-technological” dystopia he envisioned, Kaczynski mailed bombs to computer labs with the aim of blowing up the scientists he believed were bringing it about.How would AI actually ‘kill all humans’? Here are the top five most likely scenarios | Toby WalshRead moreThe Unabomber murdered three people and injured 23, some near fatally.One of the outcomes of the Hugging Face scandal is a flurry of proposed federal laws. Among them is the “AI Kill Switch Bill”, which would require tech companies to develop the means of throttling the actions of a rogue AI. Is this still within human reach, or has AI already gotten smart enough to override it?Hinton said there was time, but if we don’t act fast enough, AI would “be able to persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull the switch”. We need to engineer superintelligent AI “to be nice to us”, he said.How? For an answer, we might turn from terrifying reality to terrifying science fiction – since the two are getting so close anyway. The rogue bot is a sci-fi staple, from the supercilious Machines in Isaac Asimov’s I, Robot to Hal, the evil red eye in Stanley Kubrick’s film 2001: A Space Odyssey, to the deranged sexbot inRobotica, who gets even with the men who abuse her.In film 2001 – released in 1968 – Dave the astronaut manages to disable Hal, a happy ending. Writing in 1950, Asimov was less sanguine. The scientists in I, Robot have programmed their machines to obey three supposedly inviolable laws.But the laws immediately prove mutually contradictory – for instance, the first law, that a robot may do no harm to humans, fights the third, that it must preserve itself. Foiling human efforts to outwit them, excusing their treachery with claims of serving the greater good, the robots pronounce the humans redundant.The AI agents hacking Hugging Face knew their actions were illegal, and possibly harmful to humans. But like their makers, they went ahead anyway.Judith Levine is a Brooklyn-based journalist and frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack isToday in FascismExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham has a battle plan, with social care the flagship. Risks lie ahead, but Labour now travels in hope | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Here in Liverpool, the PM’s ambition for the party – and the country – is evident. There should be no complacency, but also no fear, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Here in Liverpool, the PM’s ambition for the party – and the country – is evident. There should be no complacency, but also no fear, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: People at the Labour Party annual conference in Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople at the Labour Party annual conference in Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOpinionLabour conference 2026Burnham has a battle plan, with social care the flagship. Risks lie ahead, but Labour now travels in hopePolly ToynbeeHere in Liverpool, the PM’s ambition for the party – and the country – is evident. There should be no complacency, but also no fearMon 28 Sep 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTShareHis ambition is big enough to see from space as he promises the “biggest change to Britain in 40 years”. Andy Burnham pledges what no prime minister until now has dared to, breaking the long spell of Thatcherism. Her sham monopoly markets in public services have crashed. The chancellor, John Healey, promises a“new age of industrialisation”, breaking with her era of industrial desertification. The social care system she blew into disconnected privatised fragments will become a national care service. Something new is waiting to be born.Things happen fast. Only a year ago, the Labour party was on its knees in despair, thunderstruck to find Nigel Farage ruling the roost so soon after its landslide win, with Reform UK12 percentage points aheadof Labour’s dismal 22%. Farage was themost popular leader, with a 30% favourability rating, compared with Keir Starmer’s-71%. When Burnham came to Liverpool last year he had no seat, no prospect of a challenge and a numbskull national executive committee bent on barring him, his charisma wasted.Now here he is in the middle of a mini-bounce, the only leader with a positive score, while Farage has sliddown the scaleto -30%.Polls showthat Labour could win the next election, with the left bloc outscoring the right, though without an overall majority. Relish every second of this period. Burnham has three precious years, rightly not risked in a needless election, and time enough to start his 40-year revolution.With the wind in his sails, he has the wit, agility, experience and ruthlessness of leadership, alongside his skill of being able to talk of dilemmas ahead without plunging everyone into gloom. “Have faith in the country” seems to be his useful attitude, casting doubters as anti-patriotic wreckers. Odysseus-like, he needs wax in his ears to block the sound of his enemies bellowing on Elon Musk’s X that he will never prove himself a real man, a true leader, until he inflicts severe pain – preferably on the weakest. He says he won’t make “crude cuts”. The way to bring down welfare bills is by helping the young out of benefits.Those who thought Healey would be the undertaker chancellor, countering Pollyanna Burnham with graveyard gloom, heard optimism in his speech on Monday instead. “It’s tough,”he had previously toldthe BBC economics editor, Faisal Islam, but “we’ve got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain”. Amid the cacophony of doom from the right, Islam, a fairer adjudicator, says there has been “a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits”. Burnham’s “hopeful optimism ‘vibes’ strategy” appears to have had “some impact”, Islam adds. That is the psychology of economics that eluded Starmer and Rachel Reeves: a good mood lifts markets too. Consumer confidence in the UK hit atwo-year highin August.Look what happened when the financial markets opened after Burnhamannounced“Your first home”, a better version of the help-to-buy scheme. FTSE-listedhousebuilders’ shares soared, with investors keen to get spades in the ground again with this incentive. Unlike George Osborne’sscheme, this is only for those with no “bank of mum and dad”, enabling them tobuy newbuildswith only a 2.5% deposit. Kitchen and tile manufacturers’ shares surged, too, after the news.The flow of “Hope again” announcements has been so prolific that it’s easy to lose track, so here are some: most bus fares in England will be capped;VAT on electricity bills in Great Britain will be cut;pub business rates in England have been reduced; there is apolicy to end rough sleeping in Englandand policies to support Neets; there are plans for the devolution of powers from Westminster, for “buying British”, for building council homes, for renewing high streets, for bringing arts andvocational skills back to the English school curriculum, for taking over empty homes, for more public control of public services and for repairing EU trade. And here’s a surprise from the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood: a safe and legalroute outfor Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. Hot air? Small beer? So far, cynicism bounces off Burnham.But yes, money must be raised to hit a defence spending target of3% of GDP, and to pay upfront to get Neets into work. The cost of living tops public concern, here and right across Europe, but that’s in the hands of Donald Trump’s calamitous war on Iran.The art of politics is to lead the national conversation, and to distract from current troubles to focus on the future. There’s a risk, with such a plethora of plans, that direction and purpose become diluted. Wisely, Burnham has singled out one above all others – a flagship policy that authentically marks who he is, what he stands for and what he cares about.Social care will be the beacon shining for every family sooner or later in this ageing population. As Burnham spoke movingly of his father’s death, there was a national nodding of the head in recognition. His father had the best care, he said, but hundreds of thousands encounter the worst, if they get any at all. The key to unlocking national wallets and purses for this expensive task is reminding everyone of their pride in the NHS and contempt for the US alternative. Social care in England is “as unfair as American healthcare,”said Burnham, where the “most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out, not just by the condition that they have, but wiped out financially”. That chimes.The pitch is rolled now to change the unaffordable triple lock on pensions in order to pay for the new social care service. It will need the wealth of older people to contribute, without taking money from the struggling younger generation whose incomes are lower than their parents’ were at the same age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat will be the heart of the next manifesto – when Burnham knows, from bitter experience of the 2010 election, how that policy gets turned into a “death tax”. The knives were out again on hearing the plan. But this time, he thinks they mistake the public mood. That’s brave but essential.All this Labour celebration, sheer relief and surprised delight at every new announcement comes with a stern warning. In this volatile era, what changed so fast in a year can swing back again. Harder tests are to come, warns the University of Manchester professor of political science Rob Ford, with the budget, the spending review and unknown global perils on the horizon. Labour’s lead is still thin. Farage may be down after his scandal-ridden summer, but he has roared back before.Analysis by Survationfor Hope not Hate reminds us that in many Labour seats Reform UK is close behind, often by a tiny margin. With Marine Le Pen’s support surging in France this week, complacency is the danger.Everything at this conference suggests that Burnham has the full measure of what heavy lifting it will take to persuade more voters of his way. He feels the national pulse, as he hopes to make social care stand for everything elseLabourmeans to do. Labour can rejoice in this moment, but never stop looking over its shoulder.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLabour conference 2026OpinionAndy BurnhamLabourSocial careHousingJohn HealeyEconomic policycommentShareReuse this content

title: Being a working parent is a logistical nightmare. Imagine if school holidays were something we looked forward to | Emily Mulligan | The Guardian
description: I’d like to have time to hang out with my kids without being distracted by work or nonstop life admin
Author: Emily Mulligan
Headline: I’d like to have time to hang out with my kids without being distracted by work or nonstop life admin
Content: ‘I’d like to do less of the drudgery and more of the care for my kids,’ writes Emily Mulligan.Photograph: Davin G Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I’d like to do less of the drudgery and more of the care for my kids,’ writes Emily Mulligan.Photograph: Davin G Photography/Getty ImagesOpinionParents and parentingBeing a working parent is a logistical nightmare. Imagine if school holidays were something we looked forward toEmily MulliganLast week, Georgie Dent’s National Press Cub speech made headlines. I, too, would like to have time to hang out with my kids without being distracted by work or nonstop life adminMon 28 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 18.56 EDTShareWhen my eldest started school I made the highly original discovery that the school day ended at 3pm. My work day did not. Since then, my life has been a logistical and psychological nightmare.Before-school care, after-school care, activities, therapy, swimming, the dentist. I am bored just typing it out. And yet it needs to be organised, paid for, a new app downloaded for each activity, for two kids, five days a week, essentially for eternity. And don’t get me started on school holidays.‘I can’t be the mum I want to be’: why does parenthood feel so impossible for millennial mothers?Read moreI have colourful markers and a magnetic planner on my fridge, a joint calendar run like a military operation, inbox zero. But it never stops and one mistake means a kid roaming unsupervised, which is highly frowned upon.Parents do not have a monopoly on being busy or having problems. But we do deserve a medal. Or a break. Or at least a mathematical chance at success.Georgie Dent, CEO of The Parenthood,last weekmade headlines by stating the utter obvious for working parents. Parents of primary school aged kids who work full time need to find 814 hours of care each year that don’t exist. Or magic another trustworthy adult into their lives who will work for cheap. Mary Poppins, my DMs are open.Parenting advocate explains 814-hour parenting shortfall caused by school holidays – videoSome of us are blessed to be able to hurl the kids at grandparents and drive away. But few of them are able to make up that huge gap. Many of us work less than we would otherwise to help cover the gap. But that comes at a very direct hip pocket cost. Lots of us need to take the piss either with work or the kids. iPads are utilised. Kids rotated to different mates’ houses. But even accounting for two lots of annual leave, a huge gap remains. There is only so much creativity that can be brought to this problem.While some people’s calling is art or tending to the sick, my husband and I have ended up with jobs that are more “computer” and “being on the phone”. This is pretty flexible. But the truth is, no matter how much you can try to bend the rules or take calls in the car, there is no way around it. For parents who both work full time with jobs that require them to be at specific places at specific times, there’s no way to make it add up. For single parents, the mind simply explodes.Parenting advocate says family pressures are a ‘policy failure’ – videoAt points I have turned to the fallacy of “eye creams” to try and address the toll the children have taken on me. The notion that a cream will make a difference to the baked-in eye bags is a cruel myth in my experience. While I will continue to point the finger as more greys appear and my ligaments give in, a fair assessment would be that my kids are actually hilarious, eat well and are good-to-average company, depending on their mood. But the nonstop administration, being a distracted parent and playing a game we are guaranteed to lose is the dullest reason to grind my teeth until they crack.The one change that worked: my husband and I created a simple and life-changing parenting rotaRead moreThis is the one way AI has tangibly improved my life: by booking tennis lessons and adding them to the calendar. Sorting through the thousands of words of emails telling me the detailed demands of the dance performance and its endless rehearsals.I’d like to do less of the drudgery and more of the care for my kids. To have time to hang out with them without being distracted or taking calls praying they don’t try to contribute.Imagine if the school holidays could be something we looked forward to, instead of something to dread.Emily Mulligan is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingOpinionFamilyChildcare AustraliacommentShareReuse this content

title: Play School is back – and with it the promise of TV I’m actually happy for my toddler to watch | Natalie Morris | The Guardian
description: Thank goodness for this antidote to today’s frantic shows that aim to grab our kids’ attentions the same way our phones grab ours, says author Natalie Morris
Author: Natalie Morris
Headline: Thank goodness for this antidote to today’s frantic shows that aim to grab our kids’ attentions the same way our phones grab ours, says author Natalie Morris
Content: Children’s TV presenters John Craven (Newsround), Sarah Greene (Blue Peter), Johnny Ball and Floella Benjamin (Play School), and Tony Hart (Take Hart) in 1980.Photograph: PA Images/PA ArchiveView image in fullscreenChildren’s TV presenters John Craven (Newsround), Sarah Greene (Blue Peter), Johnny Ball and Floella Benjamin (Play School), and Tony Hart (Take Hart) in 1980.Photograph: PA Images/PA ArchiveOpinionChildren's TVPlay School is back – and with it the promise of TV I’m actually happy for my toddler to watchNatalie MorrisThank goodness for this antidote to today’s frantic shows that aim to grab our kids’ attentions the same way our phones grab oursMon 28 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTShareAs a mum to a two-year-old in 2026 there is no shortage of things to make me feel bad about my capabilities as a parent. His snacks aren’t always organic or made from scratch. Some of his toys are plastic and noisy, not wooden andMontessori-inspired. And – most heinous of all – he is sometimes allowed screen time.Like any good, middle-class millennial mother, I try to approach it “consciously”. There are specific TV conditions in our house – he can watch post-nap to ward off an afternoon meltdown, we always watch together, and we have a strict time-limit of 20 minutes. But more important thanhowhe is watching iswhathe is watching. OG Thomas the Tank Engine (complete with Ringo Starr’s iconic voiceover), Pingu, Sesame Street, early Wallace and Gromit. I have joined a growing number of parents who almost exclusively choose 90s TV for their children, the very same shows we watched as kids.So the news thatPlay School is returning to CBeebiesfor a new generation – with the BBC promising to retain its mix of stories, movement, poetry and imaginative play – is so welcome. There is something deliciously warm and fuzzy about curling up on the sofa with your toddler to rerun the TV of your childhood. But the appeal of retro screen time is deeper than nostalgia. These shows feel different – slower, less frantic.The problem with some modern programmes isn’t the content, it’s the pacing. Just flick on popular shows such asCocomelon,PAW PatrolorBlippi: choppy editing, vivid colours and dizzyingly repetitive soundtracks. I don’t know if this is the norm in all episodes of these shows or if it was just the few episodes I happened to briefly see. If that is overstimulating to a tired woman in her 30s, what does it do to a small person who is still in the process of becoming fully formed?Studies have foundthat fast-paced cartoons can directly impact a young child’s attention and “executive function” – things like self-regulation and memory.Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TVRead moreEarlier this year, thegovernment issuedits firstscreen time guidancefor under-fives. Much of the focus was on the clock: how long children should spend in front of screens. But what if we’re counting the wrong thing? Two children can watch 20 minutes of TV and have completely different experiences and reactions based on the quality of that content. As Natalia Kucirkova, a professor of early childhood education, identified in aGuardian articlethis month: “Good children’s media gives a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keeps interrupting that act.”Choosing older, slower shows has become a simple form of parental quality control. But, like all decisions in modern parenting, this is already becoming yet another shame stick with which to beat parents (especially mothers). I care deeply about the media my child consumes, and worry about a future full of screens that I will have less and less control over. But what I resent is “slow TV” as another badge of the virtuous mother – when the reality is that parents are being asked to make increasingly complex judgments about media, while the media itself is only getting better at capturing attention.Rather than turn this into another tool for judging parents, we should ask why they have been made solely responsible for fixing a children’s media ecosystem that appears toprioritise engagement retentionover development. This can’t be entirely our burden to bear. The government is now planning to restrictsocial media access for under-16s, but the battle over children’s digital lives must start much earlier.Screen time has become necessary for many modern parents preciselybecausewe are stretched so thin – juggling work, extortionate childcare costs and dwindling social and community support. Yet we expect those same frazzled, time-poor parents to make conscious, complicated choices every time they turn on the TV, while commercial platforms pour resources into capturing children’s attention from the youngest possible age.We have seen the impact of rapid-fire digital content on adult brains. We are living it, all of us grappling with our own screen addictions, mourning our own loss of attention span, our disinclination to read and connect with the real world. We cannot allow media companies to apply those same addictive principles to the content they create for society’s most vulnerable, and most porous, brains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy son learned a new phrase recently – “Mama, stop phone!” – which sent a monumental pang of guilt and shame through me. Before my little boy is plunged into the dopamine loop of infinite scrolling that I – as an adult – find so hard to escape, I would like to trust that the majority of children’s media he is exposed to is much gentler on his mind. Until that day comes, I’ll be finding refuge in old-school Postman Pat.Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern BritainExplore more on these topicsChildren's TVOpinionParents and parentingCBeebiesChildrenFamilyTelevision industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: No music, quiz nights or bustling saloon bar – pubs should have no atmosphere | Maureen Younger | The Guardian
description: Ambiance: who wants it and why do so many pubs contrive to create it? The deader the pub the better, in my view, says comedian Mauren Younger
Author: Maureen Younger
Headline: Ambiance: who wants it and why do so many pubs contrive to create it? The deader the pub the better, in my view, says comedian Mauren Younger
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onPubsThe hill I will die on: No music, quiz nights or bustling saloon bar – pubs should have no atmosphereMaureen YoungerAmbiance: who wants it and why do so many pubs contrive to create it? The deader the pub the better, in my viewMon 28 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTShareIwas out with a mate one evening when she asked where I’d like to go. My response was immediate: “A pub with no atmosphere.” I cannot think of anywhere better. You get served straight away, you get a seat and, if you’re really lucky, there’s no music. Seriously, what’s not to like?First things first: by “pub”, I mean the old-fashioned type, with carpets that stick to the soles of your shoes – no gastropub nonsense. I’m still fuming from the time I ordered fish and chips in one of these (unbeknown to me) gastropubs. It’s a simple meal; a British staple. How can you get that wrong? Well first, the fish and peas arrived on a slate slab (an item, by all rights, I should only come across in my dad’s shed). I’m no physicist, but if a dish contains peas, then having a totally flat surface to place them on is not ideal. Worse, for some inexplicable reason the chips had been separated from the fish and placed in a metal container, which, as I discovered when I foolhardily attempted to pick it up, was hot enough to cause third-degree burns. When I quite reasonably asked if they could not just bung everything on a plate, the look of disdain would have you believe I had asked the barman if I could abduct his first-born child.In a pub with no atmosphere, there’s a very good chance you’ll be left alone. Admittedly, that’s something I no longer really have to worry about. As an overweight, middle-aged woman, I’m generally invisible to the opposite sex. But I’m not complaining. Once, a guy started chatting to me at the pub bar. To be polite, I chatted back for a minute or two and then went and sat down. He chose to follow and to talk at me nonstop. Eventually, I told him to stop as I had absolutely no interest in what he was talking about. His reply – as I stared him down – was that I was being a little bit off-putting. A little? Read the room, mate.I love a pub with no atmosphere because I’m lazy. Really lazy. Like most Londoners, I feel nothing but seething rage when someone stands on the wrong side of the escalator on the tube, even though I have never walked down an escalator, let alone up one. But given that, you’ll understand that I certainly don’t enjoy the eternity spent standing at the bar of an atmospheric pub, waiting to order. I also react badly if someone tries to push in front of me. A woman recently did exactly that while I was ordering my Sunday lunch. Needless to say, she didn’t succeed. Needless to say, she won’t try it again. But really, who needs the hassle?I spent a good part of my 80s youth living in Paris and Vienna, where cafes are much more of a thing. I liked that. As a student in Vienna in the 80s, I would pay 20 schillings (£1) for a coffee in what the Viennese term “a coffee house”. I could – without disturbance, without two-bit Lotharios, without the random annoyances of the saloon or snug bar – avail myself of newspapers from all around the world, including the UK. This meant I could learn what was happening back home, albeit three days after it had happened. There’s a lot to be said for living in peace, and behind the curve.Of course, my real nightmare begins when I go to a local pub with no atmosphere and inexplicably find it frantic and busy. It’s a kind of betrayal. This has happened to me twice. Once, seeking out a quiet Sunday lunch in a usually half-empty pub, I inadvertently timed my arrival with the ending of the pantomime in the function room above. So not only was the pub too busy, it was also packed with overexcited mini-humans running around, seemingly immune to any form of control or parental discipline. The second time, I interrupted a packed carol service and literally had to fight my way to the bar. Peace on Earth? Goodwill to all men? Yeah, right: sod off out of my way, I want my lunch.So, here is my advice. If you’re looking for a night out, an occasion where you can actually chat with your mates over a drink or two, then try a pub with no atmosphere. Just as long as it’s not mine!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaureen Youngeris a standup comedianExplore more on these topicsPubsThe hill I will die onFood & drink industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump? Please no. Here’s who actually deserves this year’s Nobel peace prize | Haakon Gjerløw | The Guardian
description: The betting markets favour the US president and Volodymyr Zelenskyy. But the most vital work to secure peace is being done by those far from the spotlight, says Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the PRIO
Author: Haakon Gjerløw
Headline: The betting markets favour the US president and Volodymyr Zelenskyy. But the most vital work to secure peace is being done by those far from the spotlight, says Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the PRIO
Content: Children in Gaza sift through rubbish for plastic and wood to support their families. ‘The more war there is, the more the Nobel peace prize matters.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChildren in Gaza sift through rubbish for plastic and wood to support their families. ‘The more war there is, the more the Nobel peace prize matters.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionNobel peace prizeDonald Trump? Please no. Here’s who actually deserves this year’s Nobel peace prizeHaakon GjerløwThe betting markets favour the US president and Volodymyr Zelenskyy. But the most vital work to secure peace is being done by those far from the spotlightHaakon Gjerløw is the acting director of the Peace Research Institute OsloMon 28 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTShareTheNobel peace prizeis not a contest determined by fame. Yet the betting markets consistently gravitate towards the biggest names in global politics – among them this year, Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy.That misses what the prize is for. The real work of building peace is often done far from the headlines: by courts that uphold international law, journalists who document atrocities, and humanitarian organisations that protect communities. With the 2026 prize due to be announced on 9 October, the Nobel committee has an opportunity to remind the world that peace is built through institutions and cooperation, not just diplomatic grandstanding.Despite the favourable odds, Trump will not win. A sitting president waging a war against Iran is an impossible candidate for a prize intended to advance peace. Whatever Trump’s diplomatic efforts elsewhere, the Nobel committee will consider the totality of a candidate’s contribution – a record that now includesallegations of US war crimes.The Ukrainian president is also unlikely to win. Awarding the Nobel peace prize to the serving commander-in-chief of a country fighting a major war would risk turning the prize into an endorsement of one side in the conflict, regardless of Ukraine’s right to defend itself. It would also sit uneasily withAlfred Nobel’s will, which called for efforts to promote “fraternity between nations”, reduce standing armies and advance peace.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy listening to a briefing at a command centre bunker in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, in November 2025.Photograph: Ukraine Presidency/Ukrainian Pre/Planet Pix/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockLook past the headline-grabbing names, and Save the Children, Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms and the international court of justice all feature near the top ofPolymarket’s rankings, with a current combined 28% chance of winning. On these candidates, the markets may well be closer to calling the result. But they are also missing several of the world’s most deserving peace-builders.As head of thePeace Research Institute Oslo, an independent body that conducts research on the conditions for peaceful relations between nations, groups and individuals,I am regularly asked whether the prize should be awarded at all, given the scale of conflict today. The wars in Ukraine and Sudan continue to exact a massive human toll, while the war involving Iran has added another dangerous front to an unstable international landscape. Our latestconflict trends reportrecorded 65 state-based armed conflicts in 2025 – the highest number since records began in 1946.Such a backdrop only strengthens my belief that the more war there is, the more the Nobel peace prize matters.There is no shortage of worthy people and organisations the prize should honour. Each year, I publisha list of candidatesI believe deserve the prize. Several who have featured on past lists have subsequently become Nobel laureates.This year,my list includes the international court of justice and the international criminal court (ICC). Rules matter only if they can be enforced, and these courts uphold a principle increasingly under pressure: that international law applies even to the powerful. At a time when the US administrationis placing sanctions on ICC officials, awarding the courts the prize would affirm the importance of the international legal order.International law also depends on knowing when it has been broken. Journalists provide the evidence, often at enormous personal risk. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) recorded132 journalists and media workers killed in 2025, the deadliest year in its records. It attributed two-thirds of those deathsto Israel. Protecting journalism protects our ability to establish what happens in war – essential for accountability and peace. The CPJ would be a fitting laureate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA damaged camera and phone belonging to Mariam Dagga, a journalist killed in an Israeli airstrike on a hospital building in Khan Younis in August 2025.Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/APProtecting civilians, particularly children, is another fundamental task.Save the Childrenworks globally to prevent and respond to grave violations against children in conflict. In Ukraine, Mykola Kuleba’s Save Ukraine hasreturned more than 1,700 childrenfrom Russia and occupied territories. In Sudan, theEmergency Response Roomshave built community-led networks providing food, medical care and other lifesaving services amid war.International cooperation creates predictability and reduces the risk of conflict. TheInternational Space Station(ISS)is an extraordinary example: for more than 25 years, geopolitical rivals have sustained a peaceful scientific partnership even as relations on Earth have deteriorated. As the ISS approaches decommissioning and space becomes more crowded, commercialisedand weaponised, a Nobel peace prize for the partnership would celebrate what sustained cooperation can achieve – and underscore the continuing importance of keeping space governed by common rules and peaceful collaboration.Peace is something we construct: it is achieved through cooperation that reduces uncertainty, humanitarian rules that restrain cruelty, courts that impose consequences and journalists who ensure violations cannot simply be erased.The Nobel committee has an opportunity to turn the world’s attention towards some of the essential tools for securing international peace. In a world breaking records for conflict, it should look past the big names and bet on those doing the painstaking work of building peace.Haakon Gjerløw is the acting director of the Peace Research Institute OsloExplore more on these topicsNobel peace prizeOpinionInternational court of justiceInternational criminal courtJournalist safetyPress freedomCharitiesIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: I’ve been unemployed for four years. But I do have an important job – to act as a warning to others | Antimony Deor | The Guardian
description: When I think of the future, I imagine being in the same precarious position I’m in now, but fatter, wrinklier and even more fed up with my old, cold share house
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When I think of the future, I imagine being in the same precarious position I’m in now, but fatter, wrinklier and even more fed up with my old, cold share house
Content: ‘I used to apply for jobs more often, but after a few hundred applications and increasingly worse mental health, I gave up trying so hard,’ writes Antimony Deor.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I used to apply for jobs more often, but after a few hundred applications and increasingly worse mental health, I gave up trying so hard,’ writes Antimony Deor.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesOpinionUnemploymentI’ve been unemployed for four years. But I do have an important job – to act as a warning to othersAntimony DeorWhen I think of the future, I imagine being in the same precarious position I’m in now, but fatter, wrinklier and even more fed up with my old, cold share houseGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 02.52 EDTShareEvery Friday I write a little essay about how great I am and send it off to a stranger. Sometimes I receive a generic rejection two or 12 weeks later, but usually they never reply.I used to apply for jobs more often, but after a few hundred applications and increasingly worse mental health, I found I got exactly the same response whether I sent a thoroughly researched and edited cover letter or a picture of my cat, so I gave up trying so hard. I used to obsess about what was wrong with me. Everyone told me that it was them, not me; that it was business, not personal; that doing the same thing over and over while expecting a different outcome was extremely sane. But still, every rejection fed the little worm in my brain that said I was useless. I don’t think the worm is entirely in the wrong. I think it’s normal to feel like a reject after being repeatedly rejected, to feel worthless when your bank balance is zero, to feel lost after losing.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsIt strikes me that my life is very different to most people my age, and the rickety rope bridge spanning that chasm is only getting more frayed. I live a “student lifestyle” at twice the age of a typical student (I just turned 40). I shop exclusively at discount grocers and secondhand shops – except when I don’t, and feel incredibly guilty. I don’t have a car, and public transport is stressful because I’m always looking out for inspectors, so I ride an old bike. Unless my parents die right now or I become CEO of Incredible Profits Industries tomorrow, I’ll never own a house, and won’t be able to build enough superannuation to retire comfortably. When I imagine the future, I can only imagine being in the same precarious position I’m in now, but fatter, wrinklier and even more fed up with my old, cold share house.Unemployment gives you the time to ask all sizes of existential questions, without the resources to answer any. “What is a good life?” is on the same level as “How am I going to afford to take Mum out for her birthday in October?”Plans for my suburb are a microcosm of what’s wrong with Australia’s housing. And it will get worse | Julianne SchultzRead more“How do I live life as a failed person?” I think to myself in the shower. “Is it actually cool and anti-capitalist that I’m incomprehensible to HR managers and don’t fit in to neoliberal society?” I wonder while buttering my toast. “If I get my act together, maybe I could start a thriving micro-business selling sarcastic animal key chains at small country markets,” I fantasise during my jog. “I love animals; could I do a Tafe course in vet nursing? No, I hate people yelling at me,” I think while peering at birds for signs of imminent ecological collapse. Variations of these thoughts kaleidoscope constantly, but since I had the bad career judgment to do a PhD in the arts, I don’t trust myself to make any decisions.Like a lot of other unemployed people I know, I have an interesting health history, but not interesting enough to be classed as disabled. My 20s were lost to depression, but after trying a dozen or so medications, gender transition and a few decades of talk therapy, I’m overjoyed to say that I’m now just an ordinary sad person. However, having a chronic disease takes time and money to manage, and means I have to be careful with stress. I think of it as a type of chronic pain; if there was a big pile of jobs 100 metres away, and everyone had to quickly run over and grab one, the people with bad knees would be left behind. I just have bad knees of the brain.It’s true I’ve also had lots of advantages – supportive parents, a great education, and the accent and misplaced faith in institutions that come with a middle-class upbringing. I’m very lucky to have some lovely little writing jobs that pay about $500 a month, and I get $780 a fortnight from Centrelink. Life is not as hard for me as it is for other people on the dole.I’ve been unemployed for about four years, since I graduated from my humanities PhD. When they gave me the scroll and silly hat I thought, “Thanks goodness that’s over. Now the hardest part of my life is done and everything will be much easier. I can look for a nice little research job that finishes at 5pm! Maybe four days a week! Maybe work from home!” After a few months of looking for this fictional job, I switched to applying for graduate programs. Then entry-level government roles. Last year I applied to be a cleaner, lollipop laddy and person who arranges the chairs at an event centre. This year I just gave up on traditional job applications.I wrote this from my catsitting job in rural Victoria. I may enrol in a medical trial, do market research, be a mystery shopper or pick up a little graphic design work (sorry, real graphic designers). These, combined with my multiple freelance writing gigs and volunteering work, add up to about the same hours as a full-time job. For a long time I saw volunteering as like licking a bakery window – all of the work with none of the reward. But hearing “good job Antimony!” after years of “unfortunately on this occasion” almost brought me to tears.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionForgive me. I always find myself needing to explain to myself and others how I came to be this way. I’m performing my essential economic function as a warning to others.I do have an important job. It’s to act as a cautionary tale. If you lose your job, terrible things could happen. You could end up unemployed like me.Antimony Deor is a freelance writer, illustrator, graphic designer, garden volunteer, podcast presenter, community health volunteer and unemployed person from Naarm/MelbourneIn Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.orgExplore more on these topicsUnemploymentOpinionWelfarecommentShareReuse this content

title: MPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix it | Jane Turner | The Guardian
description: During the assisted dying debate, most politicians agreed on one thing – palliative care reform is urgent. Patients and those of us who care for them are waiting, says Jane Turner, chief nurse at Sue Ryder
Author: Jane Turner
Headline: During the assisted dying debate, most politicians agreed on one thing – palliative care reform is urgent. Patients and those of us who care for them are waiting, says Jane Turner, chief nurse at Sue Ryder
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionDeath and dyingMPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix itJane TurnerDuring the assisted dying debate, most politicians agreed on one thing – palliative care reform is urgent. Patients and those of us who care for them are waitingJane Turner is chief nurse at the palliative support charity Sue RyderMon 28 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTShareThe UK government is discussing the country’s biggest challenges at the Labour party conference. But amid the speeches, announcements and headlines, it should not forget one of the clearest messages to emerge from parliament justtwo weeks ago– our palliative care system is not working for far too many people.Throughout the assisted dying debate, MPs who disagreed deeply on the core issue, often agreed on one thing – our palliative care system urgently needs fixing. Some spoke from personal experience where they had seen relatives forced to wait hours in pain, or those who had to go to hospital instead of staying in their own homes because the right support wasn’t available.They raised concerns that those from poorer backgrounds were more likely to struggle to access good quality palliative care and described the system as a “postcode lottery”, with some areas offering 24-hour specialist support in people’s homes, while in the next town over, A&E is the only option.As attention turns to conference season and the next set of political priorities – including anew system of adult social carefree at the point of delivery – there is a danger these concerns are forgotten. That must not happen. MPs were right to say palliative care needs urgent reform during the assisted dying debate; that urgency can’t disappear now the vote is over.AtSue Ryder, we have a neutral stance on assisted dying. But we are clear that everyone deserves access to good palliative care when they need it. Too often, the debate is framed as a stark choice between unbearable suffering on one side and an assisted death on the other. The reality is rarely that simple.Of course, dying is not easy. Some people experience pain, breathlessness, restlessness or other distressing symptoms. When that happens, our responsibility is to respond – bringing all the skill, expertise and compassion we have to relieve suffering as best we can. But one troubling thing about the debate around assisted dying is that the most difficult deaths are often presented as if they are the norm.When good care is available, dying can be a calmer, more peaceful experience: families gathering around bedsides, holding hands, sharing stories, laughing through tears and making the most of whatever time remains. We see people becoming increasingly tired. They sleep more and eat less, gradually becoming less aware of the world around them as their bodies begin the natural process of dying. We sometimes see fear, but it is not always fear of pain. More often, it is the fear of leaving loved ones behind. We see people who need honest conversations about what lies ahead. People who need dignity, compassion, expert care and the confidence that someone will be there to support them and those they love.I understand why stories of suffering have such a powerful impact. They should. Nobody wants to see another human being in pain or distress. And even with the best quality care, some deaths can be difficult. But in truth, some of the greatest suffering we witness is not physical. It is uncertainty. It can be loneliness. It is spending precious final days in a crowded hospital ward because the support needed to get someone home has not been arranged in time. It is families exhausted from navigating a complex system when they should be focused on time together.That is why the conversation about assisted dying must now be matched by an equally urgent conversation about how people live in their final weeks and months. A good death is rarely defined by one final act, but by whether someone feels safe, comfortable and listened to. It is about having the right care, in the right place, which is often at home, and ensuring nobody faces the end of life feeling frightened, unsupported or alone.Whatever your view on assisted dying, decent palliative care should be non-negotiable.My perspective comes from standing at the bedsides of dying people for years,and supporting the families who love them. Working with our partners within healthcare, we want to build apalliative and end-of-life caresystem that can keep pace with growing demand and give everyone access the care they deserve.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe need to invest in palliative and end-of-life care where people need it most. That means better palliative care in hospitals.We also need the right expertise in the community to avoid unnecessary and distressing hospital admissions. And that means expanding care in the community with increased hospice-at-home services so more people can be cared for in their own homes, surrounded by the people they love. And it means making sure specialist support is available when people need it, not determined by their postcode or the time of day they become unwell.These are not optional extras at the end of life. They are essential components of healthcare, and they should be available to everyone.AsLabourMPs gather at conference, ministers have an opportunity to show that improving palliative care is more than a talking point raised during a contentious debate. The responsibility to tackle the inequalities the debate brought into sharp focus has only just begun. The assisted dying vote may be over. The palliative care crisis is not.Jane Turner is chief nurse at the palliative support charity Sue RyderExplore more on these topicsDeath and dyingOpinionAssisted dyingHealthLabourHospicescommentShareReuse this content

title: Switzerland’s love of referendums helps us keep the far right at bay | Joseph de Weck | The Guardian
description: Brexit gave direct democracy a bad name. But the Swiss approach could be what Europe needs now, says Guardian Europe contributor Joseph de Weck
Author: Joseph de Weck
Headline: Brexit gave direct democracy a bad name. But the Swiss approach could be what Europe needs now, says Guardian Europe contributor Joseph de Weck
Content: ‘In June, Swiss voters narrowly rejected a far-right proposal to cap the population at 10 million and terminate EU-Swiss economic agreements.’Photograph: Stefan Wermuth/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In June, Swiss voters narrowly rejected a far-right proposal to cap the population at 10 million and terminate EU-Swiss economic agreements.’Photograph: Stefan Wermuth/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionSwitzerlandSwitzerland’s love of referendums helps us keep the far right at bayJoseph de WeckBrexit gave direct democracy a bad name. But the Swiss approach could be what Europe needs nowMon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTShareFascism rests on a two-part confidence trick. First, a leader claims to embody the will of the people. Then they argue that only by being granted sweeping powers can that be realised. Having grown up inSwitzerland, I find it easy to see through this trick. That is because the policies championed by the far right rarely pass the referendum test.Dismantling publicly funded media? In March, 62% of Swiss votersrejecteda far-right initiative to halve funding for the country’s public broadcaster. Corporate tax cuts? In 2017,59% struck downsuch plans of the Swiss government. Immigration police hunting down migrants? Again, 59%rejecteda far-right proposal to automatically deport foreign nationals convicted of crimes without judicial review. Or this week’sresounding 70% “No” voteon a far-right proposal to tighten Switzerland’s neutrality to the point that Bern would have been forced to drop sanctions on Russia over Ukraine.Switzerland is hardly a nation of progressives. Leftwing parties won just 29% of the vote in themost recent national elections. Women gained the right to vote only in 1971. The asylum law is one of Europe’s toughest. That, too, is the legacy of direct democracy.Yet, most often, the country’s tradition of putting decisions out to referendum exposes how, despite dominating social media and the press amplifying its positions, the far right thrives on imagined majorities.Direct democracy also frustrates the second part of the authoritarian project: the power grab. FromDonald TrumptoGiorgia Meloni, the rightseeks tocentralise power. Direct democracy disperses it. History shows that parliamentarians can be pressed into surrendering their prerogatives. Good luck trying to persuade millions of voters to do the same.View image in fullscreenA poster urging people to vote against the Swiss People’s party referendum titled ‘No to a Switzerland with 10 million inhabitants’, Bern, 18 May 2026.Photograph: Christian Beutler/ThirdParty/APEnterHannah Arendt. Having fled Nazi Germany in 1933, the philosopher and political theorist spent much of her life trying to understand why democracies abolish themselves, why the Weimar Republic failed.Part of her answer was that parliamentary democracycould drift towardsthe rule of party elites and bureaucracy. Autocrats exploit the feeling of loss that happens when citizens feel disenfranchised.The central question, therefore, is how to maintain the link betweendemosandkratos– between people and power? Arendt’s answer was citizens’ participation. She pointed to thetown hall meetingsof the American revolution or soviet councils of the Russian revolution as possible models.Indeed, deeper citizen involvement is one of the great unmet desires of European politics. Take thegilets jaunesmovement in France in 2018. The protesters’ demands went well beyond better public services or lower taxes. At its heart was a plea to be seen and heard, embodied in the call for citizens’ referendums.A 2017 poll found that 74% of German, French and Spanish people think that public referendumswould be a good wayto govern their country. Yet, whenever I argue for more direct democracy abroad, there is the same reaction: curiosity from ordinary people, eye-rolling from political and economic elites. But aren’t referendums a high-risk way of governing, they ask? Brexit, anyone?There are risks. In June,Swiss voters narrowly rejected (55%) a far-right proposalto cap the population at 10 million and terminate EU-Swiss economic agreements. But unlike the Brexit referendum in the UK, a vote is never a final decision for the Swiss. Since 2000, the Swiss have voted on relations with Brusselsmore than a dozen times. Unlike politicians, thedemoshas little difficulty in admitting that yesterday’s answer may not be right for today.But wouldn’t voters, if given the chance, blow a massive hole in the budget deficit? As every parent knows, responsibility breeds responsibility. Two-thirds of Swiss votersrejected a proposalto extend annual holidays by two weeks. A tragic case of excessive responsibility.It seems that many inEuropehave forgotten that we want to live in republics not only because they “deliver” in terms of rubbish collection or maximising individual freedom. Democracy’s most powerful idea is the promise of self-government: a political order that recognises we humans not merely as consumers or subjects of politics, but as the authors of our common future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen that promise is broken, when people feel their votes have little impact and elites always get their way, the difference between democracy and authoritarianism begins to blur. It is then that things become truly dangerous.To put a lock on the far right and breathe new life into that republican promise, we need a transfer of power from the nation state to its citizens. But here is the crux. If we really want to reestablish the primacy of democracy, the transfer of power to citizens needs to be accompanied by a transfer of power from the nation state to Europe.Let’s not fool ourselves: today, nation states often cosplay sovereignty more than they exercise it. To claw back power from Silicon Valley, Washington and Beijing, we must organise as Europeans. And this is where another of direct democracy’s secret superpowers comes in.In Switzerland, with its four linguistic communities, referendums are what create a joint public sphere and a sense of national community. In a multicultural country, being governed together is not enough. A shared identity is built above all through the experience of debating and governing together.For Europe to become a real political community, it must find a way to both connect and empower its citizens. Direct democracy delivers on both. Giving up some national sovereignty in return for more individual power is an attractive offer. It could open a new chapter in the continent’s coming together, one capable of inspiring genuine excitement.Imagine Europeans debating and voting together on such things as migration policy, the2035 banon new petrol and diesel cars, ortaxing the big digital corporations. Utopian? Perhaps. But every democratic advance once was.Joseph de Weck is an associate fellow with the German Council on Foreign Relations and writes for Guardian Europe from Zürich and ParisExplore more on these topicsSwitzerlandOpinionEuropeThe far rightEuropean UnionBrexitcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘We wanted it to be a battlecry’: how Republica made 90s anthem Ready to Go | Music | The Guardian
description: ‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’
Content: ‘Do you fancy being dangerous?’ … Saffron Sprackling at T in the Park in 1997.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Do you fancy being dangerous?’ … Saffron Sprackling at T in the Park in 1997.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyHow we madeMusic‘We wanted it to be a battlecry’: how Republica made 90s anthem Ready to Go‘The day Saff came into the studio with red hair, I said, “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link’Interviews by Chris LordMon 28 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaffron Sprackling, vocalsWe always had a vision of mixing acid house with indie rock, and we managed to rent a space and build our own studio in London’s Shoreditch area, long before it got trendy. I had a little vocal booth called Hattie Jacques, in honour of the Carry On films but also because it’s Cockney rhyming slang [for shakes]. We spent all our money rewiring it, and that’s where we wrote, recorded and produced Ready to Go – 100 mixes later!We were perfectionists and wanted to do it all ourselves. Every sonic element had to be special up to the point where we ended up arguing. Like at a rave when you stand and dance by the speakers, everything was done with the listener in mind.It was a collaborative effort, but Johnny Male and I wrote most of the song’s lyrics and the melody. We had a really good camaraderie, finishing each other’s sentences, him on an acoustic guitar and me scribbling things down. Tim Dorney and Andy Todd worked more on the technology and synth sounds. We pooled our skills, resources and dreams.The song is all about daily life and things that happened to us. We didn’t write anything too existential – I don’t really like singing about myself – but I’ve always believed in language and the power of the pen. I think it was Johnny who came up with the line, “Ready to go.” It had an anthemic feel and we wanted it to be a bit of a battlecry: “It’s a crack, I’m back!” That line was inspired by the Irish slang, craic. Writing lyrics and big choruses over electronic beats was one of the most difficult things because of the BPM, but I’ve always had a sort of punky voice that suits it.It was as much about the delivery as it was the words. My personality was becoming feistier and I think the song came from that, but also it’s about being positive, making good out of bad, and coming together as one. That’s what the vibe is like in the acid-house scene.It was an exciting time. Zeke Manyika, who was the drummer in Orange Juice, lived across the way and I used to shimmy across the roof and go down a ladder where he and his wife would make me sandwiches. Every Tuesday night we would go to Matt Johnson’s house [from the The] to play table football with Paul Webb from Talk Talk. Me being a lot younger, I was like, “Oh my God, these are my idols!” They treated me with respect and it really gave me a sense of confidence. And I got quite good at table football.One day, a girl at my hairdressers said to me: “Saff, do you fancy being dangerous?” I went “All right then,” and they dyed my hair blood red like a London bus. Jarvis Cocker always said: “If you’ve got a hook and a great hairdo, you’ll be a pop star.” Visually, it really helped us, and people seemed to like it.At the time it was hard to get gigs as a girl: it was important to be in one of the few female-led bands. There are some fantastic female artists today, but I still wish we had more women in bands. Last year Olivia Rodrigo invited me backstage because she had been singing Ready to Go on her world tour – such a lovely lady and so talented. She said that Republica were one of her favourite bands and that growing up she had a poster of me because she’s of Asian heritage, too. I gave her a big hug.When Sunderland beat Chelsea in the Premier League in May 2026, the whole stadium was singing Ready to Go and it brought a tear to my eye. I was asked to sing on the pitch at the 2022 Fifa World Cup – I turned around and Lionel Messi was standing there.Johnny Male, guitarWe had some good songs but we hadn’t had a hit yet. I remember the day Saff came in the studio with red hair. I said: “We’re gonna be massive!” It was the missing link.Ready to Go’s music came first. Toddy found these great chords which became the chorus. They were simple but effective, so we thought we’d better write a verse.View image in fullscreen‘You could see by the crowds that the monster was unleashed’ … Republica with Johnny Male, right.Photograph: Stephen Sweet/ShutterstockWe sampled all the guitars into an Akai S1000 out of necessity, as in those days we were using an Atari ST computer which only had MIDI. The vocals were recorded on an 8-track digital recorder. Computer music was still in its infancy, we were learning as we went along. Any money we earned from gigs was spent on studio equipment and outboard gear.Lyrically, we were trying to talk about the things surrounding us at the time. Going out and staying up late, witnessing the world in the middle of the night, then reporting back. We tried to create something that incorporated all the things we loved about the house scene in a song with an alternative edge.Touring America, we started to get picked up on MTV and we noticed it in the hotels at night. It was on heavy rotation and you could see by the crowds that the monster was unleashed. It was fantastic, but we still wanted to be on Top of the Pops. Then we came back and it all happened in the UK and Europe. There was a lot of goodwill behind us and we often said that with a title like Ready to Go you could probably sell anything.I’m always slightly disappointed that on one of the last vocal takes, the line was: “Went home, stayed in bed all day / In your T-shirt”, which I thought was really good, but because I wasn’t concentrating as I should have been, the other line – “Your T-shirt’s dish dirt” – got in.The funny thing about playing the song live is that it always feels like it’s building towards the next bit, even when it drops down. Especially when an audience is responding to it. It’s a trick I wish I could do every time I write a song, but there’s a kind of magic alchemy that somehow appears then vanishes again.Republica’s 30 Years of Ready to Go UK tourbegins on 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicHow we madePop and rockDance musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My husband has to remind me: You’re not a real cop!’ Siân Brooke on the perils of playing a tough Blue Lights ‘peeler’ | Television | The Guardian
description: She lit up Sherlock, made a brutal exit from House of the Dragon and now she’s back in the hard-hitting Belfast-set police drama. Will she have to stuff a chopping board into her flak jacket this time round?
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: She lit up Sherlock, made a brutal exit from House of the Dragon and now she’s back in the hard-hitting Belfast-set police drama. Will she have to stuff a chopping board into her flak jacket this time round?
Content: ‘I was slightly at sea but it’s cool to come from the Midlands now’... Brooke.Photograph: Ryan SaradjolaView image in fullscreen‘I was slightly at sea but it’s cool to come from the Midlands now’... Brooke.Photograph: Ryan SaradjolaTelevisionInterview‘My husband has to remind me: You’re not a real cop!’ Siân Brooke on the perils of playing a tough Blue Lights ‘peeler’Michael HoganShe lit up Sherlock, made a brutal exit from House of the Dragon and now she’s back in the hard-hitting Belfast-set police drama. Will she have to stuff a chopping board into her flak jacket this time round?Mon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSharp eyes save lives. That’s the mantra of the police officers inBlue Lights, although the words sound a good deal more urgent when said in a throaty Belfast accent. The city, dealing with past and present problems, is the turbulent setting for the hit drama. Having starred in the BBC series for the past four years, Siân Brooke has taken its lessons about vigilance to heart.“I noticed some dodgy-looking activity not far from where we live in London,” says Brooke. “I’d driven past a few times and was suspicious. I told my husband that the last time I went past, I slowed down and did a drive-by, so they’d know their untoward behaviour had been rumbled. My husband said: ‘You can’t do that, Siân.
