You’re not a real cop!’” She laughs. “I think Blue Lights has got to me. What was I going to do, make a citizen’s arrest?”double quotation markIt was a shame Queen Aemma Arryn died giving birth. I would have liked to ride a dragonBrooke was Bafta-nominated this year for her leading role as Constable Grace Ellis: a social worker and single mother who switches career in her 40s to join the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI). As the acclaimed drama returns – for a fourth series taglined “their toughest shift yet” – viewers are flung straight into the action as protests outside a migrant centre erupt into a full-blown riot.View image in fullscreen‘We had to have weapons training’ ... in Blue Lights.Photograph: BBC/Two Cities Television“There’s an intense energy to filming those high-octane sequences,” says Brooke. “Adrenaline pumps through you. I injured my elbow but didn’t notice until I had to pull my gun and couldn’t do it. I needed steroid injections.” Could such fearless dedication to stunt work make Brooke the new Tom Cruise? “I’m glad you noticed,” she grins. “The only difference is he jumps off cliffs, whereas I pulled a muscle picking up a wheelie bin.”The scenes proved eerily prescient. Weeks after filming them in spring, anti-immigration riots broke out on the streets of Belfast for real. “That was remarkable,” she says. “Our writers really do their research and have their fingers on the pulse. That’s partly why their scripts are so good. They’re urgent, authentic, almost documentary-style.” This could also be because Declan Lawn and Adam Patterson, the show’s writers and co-creators, are former Panorama journalists.Police advisers ensure that Blue Lights gets the finer details right. “They’re always on set. That day, we had people who worked in public order policing. They explained the protocols and how to manage disturbances. After four years, our experts have become a key part of the team. They’re very open about their experiences and how they affected them. That feeds into the show.”Such commitment to realism meant firearms courses for the cast. “We had weapons training before series one. We were rookie actors playing rookie police officers, so it made sense. Now the armourers give us regular refreshers: how to hold our guns, where to rest your trigger finger and the like.”Equally challenging is wearing the PSNI uniform, with its bulky stab vest and tactical belt. “My goodness, there’s so much paraphernalia,” says Brooke. “You’d think they might have streamlined it by now. I’ve asked real officers: ‘How do you run with all that stuff on?’ Apparently everything just flies off. When they’re chasing baddies down the street, their pepper spray is propelled one way and their notebook another.”It certainly isn’t a costume that screams glamour. “Not the most flattering,” she agrees. “During filming, my flak jacket wouldn’t behave. Every time I got into the squad car, it would ride up until I resembled a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle. The costume department ended up putting in a piece of wood to weigh it down. For two series, I was walking around with a chopping board down my jacket. Everyone would knock on it and make wisecracks about my acting being wooden.”Importantly, the show has the seal of approval from Brooke’s father. “He was in the force for many years and when I first got the role I sent him the scripts. I thought it captured the camaraderie and banter. He agreed and has been a big fan ever since. He’ll binge the new series. Being able to talk much more about his career has been an unexpected gift from this. Police officers often tell me they’re touched by how the show shines a light on the difficulties of the job.” Brooke is even inspiring the next generation: “A friend’s daughter has said she wants to join the police because of Blue Lights.”One theme in the upcoming series is social media’s ability to mobilise communities – something worryingly close to home for Brooke’s character. “Someone reveals Grace’s identity online and puts her safety at risk. Social media is scary. I worry about its addictive nature and its impact on society, especially as a mum to two teenagers. I recently did [cyber-thriller] The Undeclared War about how social media infiltrates politics. It’s frightening stuff.”On screen, her partner is Sergeant Stevie Neil, played by Martin McCann. As half of one of TV’s sweetest couples, is she ever asked for relationship advice by fans? “No, thankfully!” she laughs. “Maybe me and Martin should start a column in the Guardian. Would you have us as guest agony aunts? Grace and Stevie on middle-aged romances in the workplace.”After Brooke had a decade of success on stage, her TV breakthrough came in 2017. She’d played Ophelia opposite Benedict Cumberbatch in Hamlet at London’s Barbican then reunited with him in BBC blockbuster Sherlock. She auditioned for three roles before being told they were all the same character: the sleuth’s secret sister Eurus, a master of disguise.View image in fullscreen‘It was short and violent’... in House of the DragonPhotograph: Landmark Media/Alamy“Having been a genuine fan of Sherlock, I had to pinch myself,” she recalls. “My sole objective was: ‘Don’t mess it up.’ It was mad being in the midst of Sherlockmania. Oddly enough, my kids are now of an age where they’ve started watching Sherlock from the start. It’ll blow their minds when they get to series four. They might disown me.”Brooke shone briefly but brightly in HBO’s Game of Thrones prequel, House of the Dragon, playing Queen Aemma Arryn, first wife of King Viserys. Was she disappointed to die so graphically during childbirth in the first episode? “It was a shame because I would’ve loved to ride a dragon! I turned the page of the script and was like: ‘Oh well.’ She definitely made an impact though. It wasn’t short and sweet. It was short and violent.”Brooke has steadily worked her way to becoming one of TV’s top-tier performers. Her current hot streak includes scene-stealing turns in Netflix superhero drama Supacell as shadowy bureaucrat Victoria Kesh (“Her villainy definitely cranks up in the second series”) and Apple comedy Trying as the overopinionated Karen (“I love playing someone so deliciously forthright”). Next up is fact-based ITV drama Mavis Eccleston. Due early next year, it’s a poignant account of the 80-year-old woman who survived a 2018 suicide pact with her terminally ill husband before being accused and found not guilty of his murder.“It’s a sensitively told story about this loving family,” says Brooke. “A big pull for me was that it all happened 20 minutes from where I grew up in Lichfield. As a Staffordshire girl, you don’t get many stories that local.” Penelope Wilton plays Mavis, with Jonathan Pryce as her husband Dennis. Brooke is their daughter Joy, someone the actor has met several times. “She’s warm, kind and naturally very protective of her parents’ story. The care she shows her mum is inspiring. You feel a huge sense of responsibility playing real people.”View image in fullscreen‘Don’t mess it up’ … as master-of-disguise Eurus Holmes in Sherlock.Photograph: Hartswood Films/ShutterstockDid it change Brooke’s view of assisted dying? “For me, everybody should be able to give themselves the ending they wish. It’s their life and their right. It didn’t change my opinion but it did give me greater understanding of the complexities. I’m hoping it sparks conversations at home.”‘I’m fearless. I was in a boys’ rugby team’: Slow Horses’ Aimee-Ffion Edwards on playing a cocaine-snorting spyRead moreMention of Lichfield brings to mind her Instagram bio’s declaration of “Midlander”. Is she proud of her roots? “Very proud but it wasn’t always that way. When I came down to study at Rada, it seemed that being from Manchester, Glasgow or Dublin gave you a strong identity. Somehow it wasn’t the case with the Midlands. I was slightly at sea for the first chunk of my career. A bit lost and didn’t know what my voice was. With age, I’ve claimed my heritage. Maybe it’s the Peaky Blinders effect, but it feels cool now. I want to champion stories from the Midlands.”She’s an ambassador for two charities close to her heart. While researching a Blue Lights storyline, she forged a relationship with Belfast-based Macs, which helps young people with homelessness and leaving the care system. Climate change adaptation group the Glacier Trust is currently dealing with the aftermath of the flash floods in Nepal. “Both organisations are brilliant,” she says. “Working with them is just my tiny offering.”Having worked nonstop for 15 months, Brooke felt she’d earned her break this summer. “It’s been a glorious period of work but it was lovely to spend time with my kids. Although I suspect they got fed up with me by the end. Six weeks off school is maybe a week too long. I’d advocate for five weeks and adding an extra week to the October half-term.” The campaign for Siân Brooke as education secretary starts here. “Why not?” she laughs. “If Andy Burnham wants to talk, he knows where I am.”Blue Lights returns to BBC One and BBC iPlayer at 9pm on 29 September in the UK, with an Australian airdate on SBS yet to be announced.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV crime dramaDramaBlue LightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mighty Sparrow obituary | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Trinidadian singer and songwriter hailed as a living legend and the greatest calypsonian of all time
Author: Peter Mason
Headline: Trinidadian singer and songwriter hailed as a living legend and the greatest calypsonian of all time
Content: Mighty Sparrow performing at the Melkweg in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, in 1989.Photograph: Frans Schellekens/RedfernsView image in fullscreenMighty Sparrow performing at the Melkweg in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, in 1989.Photograph: Frans Schellekens/RedfernsPop and rockObituaryMighty Sparrow obituaryTrinidadian singer and songwriter hailed as a living legend and the greatest calypsonian of all timePeter MasonMon 28 Sep 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe singer and songwriter Mighty Sparrow, who has died aged 91, was quite simply the greatest calypsonian there has ever been. For at least five decades he was a monumental figure on theCaribbeanmusic scene, while also capturing the hearts and minds of millions of fans around the world with self-penned songs that were the quintessential calypso mix of political commentary, humour, sexual innuendo and melody.Loved and feted by Trinidadians more than any other public figure in the island’s history, he was to calypso what Bob Marley was to reggae – an inspirational living legend. In Britain, no less than elsewhere, the sheer wit and quality of classic songs such asJean and Dinah,Congo ManandMae Maebrought calypso to many who would never otherwise have encountered the music form, particularly in the 1950s, 60s and 70s, when he was in his prime.In 1956, aged 20, Sparrow made a breathtaking appearance in Trinidad’s annual calypso monarch competition, where he was mistakenly introduced on stage asLord Melody, who was his idol. Showing the presence of mind, sense of fun and self-confidence that characterised his stage appearances, he jokingly began to sing a Melody tune before launching into his own new composition – Jean and Dinah.A tongue-in-cheek celebration of the recent withdrawal of American military personnel from Trinidad – and the fact that local women would now have to turn their attentions to people such as Sparrow rather than their gum-chewing, nylon-toting guests – the song became an instant classic and gave its composer the title of Calypso Monarch, the ultimate achievement for a calypsonian.View image in fullscreenMighty Sparrow being presented with a crown.Photograph: Echoes/RedfernsFor good measure, its infectious melody also won Sparrow the 1956 Road March crown, awarded to the singer of the tune played most often on the streets at carnival each year. It was a hitherto unprecedented double and set him off on a period of dominance that would never seriously abate.He went on to win both titles seven more times in all, a feat that was all the more notable because he essentially retired from the calypso monarch competition in the mid-70s. His only real rival throughout his career was his friendLord Kitchener, who often beat him to the Road March title but failed to match his consistency.Although he was known throughout the world as a Trinidadian, Sparrow was born on the nearby island ofGrenada, in Grand Roy, a fishing community. When he was 18 months old his carpenter father, Rupert, who had moved to Trinidad seeking work, paid for his family to take the boat to join him in Port of Spain, where new oil wealth had tempted thousands of other “small islanders” to gather.Then known as Slinger Francisco, Sparrow spent his early life in the impoverished sectors of Port of Spain, which helped to shape the left-leaning political beliefs that later came out in songs such asCapitalism Gone MadandNeurosis of the Rich. He often liked to call himself the “mouthpiece of the underprivileged”.His mother, Clarissa, claimed her son’s musical bent derived from the fact that she was strutting her stuff at a dancehall at 4am when her labour pains began. His talent soon manifested itself at Port of Spain’s Newtown Catholic boys’ school, where he relished singing Gregorian chants and plainsong in Latin as head choir boy, as well as performing at the weekly Friday school concerts.At home he would reproduce some of the less risque local calypsos in front of his mother while playing on a comb and paper, and was influenced by the songs of Nat King Cole, Sarah Vaughan and Frank Sinatra on the radio.View image in fullscreenMighty Sparrow performing in the New Orleans jazz festival in 1998.Photograph: David Redfern/RedfernsAlthough straitened circumstances meant he did not finish his schooling, he was a bright boy who was well-behaved. He did, however, have a cheeky streak, and although his intelligence landed him a government job as a teenager, he was drawn to the exciting world of calypso. His mother was dismayed, for at the time calypso was viewed as beyond the pale by members of “respectable” society. As it turned out, her son did more than anyone to bring such music into global acceptance.In his early days at the calypso venues, older singers ribbed Francisco for his unusually hyperactive movements around the stage, which they said made him look “like a little sparrow”. The name stuck, with the epithet “mighty” later added by popular acclamation once his greatness could no longer be disputed. He was also affectionately known as “Birdie”.The key to Sparrow’s long-term success, aside from his versatile and honeyed voice, was his rare ability to deliver songs that were irresistible as good-time dance tunes but also worked on other levels, making political and social points with a subtlety that often elevated them to works of art.While this was evident in many of his more overtly political tunes, it was perhaps best epitomised by one of his most enduring hits, Congo Man (1965), about two white women who are captured and eaten by a cannibal in the Congo.Laced with sexual innuendo and underscored with unspoken racial hang-ups, the song draws in the listener with a cliched tale of the two unfortunates being boiled in a pot, accompanied by the memorable lines: “I envy the Congo man / I wish it was me, I would ’a shake he hand / He eat ’til he stomach upset / and I never eat a white meat yet’. Though superficially a frivolous party tune, there can scarcely have been a more succinct commentary on the sensitivities and myths surrounding inter-racial relationships.View image in fullscreenMighty Sparrow arriving at London airport in 1962.Photograph: George Stroud/Getty ImagesSparrow’s ability to wrap a serious message in a humorous, tuneful coating made him an important figure in the Caribbean, and it is no exaggeration to say that he was a significant educator and champion of the region’s masses. He put forward the cause of West Indian self-determination during the late 50s and 60s, and was a vocal supporter, in song, of Trinidad’s long-serving left-of-centre nationalist prime minister Eric Williams, although he admitted to becoming more centrist in later life.During his early career he wrote compositions that encouraged nation-building, Caribbean unity and self-improvement, including songs such asOur Model Nation(1962), celebrating Trinidadian independence,Pay As You Earn(1958), supporting Williams’s new tax system,Federation(1959), bemoaning the impending break-up of the short-lived West Indies Federation, andDan Is the Man in the Van(1963), an attack on the legacy of culturally insensitive British colonial education.Later on he branched out into commentary on myriad aspects of international affairs, addressing issues such as the Crown Heights racial riots inNew York, the divorce of Princess Anne, the Kerry Packer affair, Idi Amin’s brutal rule in Uganda, and the fall of the Shah.Although his output was prodigious – he was responsible for more than 500 calypsos and released more than 70 albums during an immensely hard-working career – Sparrow maintained high standards throughout. He rode changes in musical taste with ease, not least when calypso transmogrified into the more funky, electrified form of soca in the 70s.While much of his later material fared less well in sales terms, he was in huge demand as a live performer throughout his life and made a handsome living out of his trade – a rarity in the hand-to-mouth world of calypso. From the mid-80s he began to spend increasingly long periods in New York, where he bought a second home.He was presented with honours all around the world from various governments and cities, took Trinidad’s highest accolade, the Order of the Republic of Trinidad & Tobago, was given many degrees, and inNigeriawas made honorary chief of the Yorubas as Chief Omowale of Ikoyi. In 2015 he was appointed OBE. For good measure he also proclaimed himself “calypso king of the world”.Supremely self-assured yet down-to-earth and rarely egotistical, Sparrow was confident of his legacy in his later years. If ever asked whether anyone was likely to surpass his feats, he was often fond of replying, with some justification, that “he ain’t born yet and he mudder dead”.A father of nine, he is survived by his Barbadian wife, Margaret Skinner.Mighty Sparrow (Slinger Francisco), calypsonian, born 9 July 1935; died 27 September 2026Explore more on these topicsPop and rockCaribbeanGrenadaTrinidad and TobagoNew YorkNigeriaobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Painting the French Riviera review – about as erotic and glamorous as a wet day in Margate | Art and design | The Guardian
description: They’ve marginalised Matisse and given Picasso the cold shoulder – and what’s left seems more informed by pedantic geography than sensual art
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: They’ve marginalised Matisse and given Picasso the cold shoulder – and what’s left seems more informed by pedantic geography than sensual art
Content: Obscure eroticism: Paul Cézanne’s Bathers, oil on canvas.Photograph: Saint Louis Art Museum, Funds given by Mrs. Mark C. SteinbergView image in fullscreenObscure eroticism: Paul Cézanne’s Bathers, oil on canvas.Photograph: Saint Louis Art Museum, Funds given by Mrs. Mark C. SteinbergArt and designReviewPainting the French Riviera review – about as erotic and glamorous as a wet day in MargateRoyal Academy of Arts, LondonThey’ve marginalised Matisse and given Picasso the cold shoulder – and what’s left seems more informed by pedantic geography than sensual artJonathan JonesMon 28 Sep 2026 07.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French Riviera is not a place. It is a dream of paradise, one of those Arcadias we long for – timeless, perfect worlds saturated with light. In the modern age, artists found theirs in the south of France. Yet this exhibition misses the point entirely. Instead of the modern myth of the Med, what we get here is a pedantic obsession with the geography of France’s southern coast. Artists get rewarded for which bit of it they painted. This leads to some serious distortions.The neo-impressionists – the dot-fixated movement led by Paul Signac – and their paintings of the Côte d’Azur get a grand, spacious setting. That’s OK; though when you’ve seen one pixelated shoreline, you’ve seen them all. What’s baffling is that Henri Matisse and the Fauves have been squeezed into a smaller, less weighty adjoining display. The revolution that Matisse and his friends enacted at the seaside town of Collioure, replacing nature with the colours in their heads, was far more radical, exciting and visually brilliant than Signac and co. I couldn’t fathom it.View image in fullscreenMonet’s Morning at Antibes, 1888, oil on canvas.Photograph: Philadelphia Museum of Art: Bequest of Charlotte Dorrance WrightThen I looked at a map. Collioure is on the far west of Mediterranean France, close to the Pyrenees. The Côte d’Azur to the east is the Riviera proper, including all your favourites: Nice, Cannes, Antibes, Saint-Tropez. The Fauves are punished for straying from it.This is ridiculous. In fact there seems to be a grudge against poor Matisse. A mere handful of his 1920s paintings that linger adoringly on women in Nice hotel rooms have to share space with cosy Raoul Dufy who was at best a Matisse imitator. Then at the end a single late Matisse cut-out, a serpentine white line through aquatic blue called The Wave, is juxtaposed with a lot of blue imprints of bare-naked ladies by the showboating 1960s artist Yves Klein.Yet it is Matisse who defines with one captivating work what Painting the French Riviera should have been about. His 1904 Study for Luxe, calme et volupté, in the little Fauve room, depicts a seaside Eden with unfettered passion and hedonism. Gold, green and violet dots, much freer than the neo-impressionists’ pedantic fields, fleck this little canvas in which Matisse experiments with a group of female nudes, gracefully posing by the shore, that he would finalise in the completed version of Luxe, calme et volupté in the Musée d’Orsay. “Luxury, peace and pleasure” – the title comes from Baudelaire – is Matisse’s ideal. It’s 1904, the new century is full of nationalists, revolutionaries, discontent, but he dreams of a perfect day by the sea surrounded by beautiful beach bodies.View image in fullscreenPainting the French Riviera at the Royal Academy of Arts brings together over 120 paintings, sculptures and drawings.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockThe fascination of this study is its rawness: these might just be actual women on a beach. They haven’t yet become the mythic beings of the final version. Matisse stares at real life bathers until they become goddesses – it’s the essence of the Riviera in French modern art, both a mythological Arcadia and a place you can get to on the Blue Train.Picasso’s backcloth for the Ballets Russes production The Blue Train hangs here. It is not actually by him but an enlarged copy by a scene painter of his small intense 1922 original Two Women Running on the Beach. Exciting, if you didn’t recently see it at V&A Storehouse East. Yet the show’s choice of Picasso is even more dispiriting than its meanness with Matisse.Much stress is placed on how Picasso saw the Riviera through a classical lens, from sculpture-like women to flute-playing fauns. But that’s a children’s book. For Picasso, as for Matisse, the Riviera meant sex. This show leaves out Picasso’s outrageous multi-orificed beach volleyball players, his prints of voluptuous women laid out for the eyes of artists and fauns, his erotic reveries over Marie-Thérèse Walter. Only one work captures his equation of sun, sea and lust: a witty woman-shaped vase from 1961 with a bikini painted on its pink terracotta form.Why am I banging on about Picasso and Matisse? It’s because any exhibition about the Riviera worth its salad niçoise would put them at its heart: it would be Matisse-Picasso, the Rematch. So many of their dazzling creations feast on this paradise – and reveal its dark side.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHenri Matisse’s Interior at Nice (Room at Beau-Rivage), 1917-1918, oil on canvasPhotograph: Joseph Hu/Philadelphia Museum of Art; AE Gallatin CollectionInstead of a dive in that sea, this is a collection of dry little diversions. It gives more space to Monet than Cézanne, which is tomfoolery. Monet’s views of Antibes are lovely but this Normandy-born artist is not southern in the same way as Cézanne, who sees his native Provence with painful intensity, burning his eyes at midday. In his painting Bathers, a group of near-nude young men pose against sky and water that seem to be baked rock hard by the sun. You instantly recognise the dream of the Med, the reverie, the obscure eroticism: pink flesh, dark blue sea, light blue sky.Then more detours. You linger with Bonnard and wonder what Picabia is doing here. Meanwhile, you have to ask why they didn’t include van Gogh, who did paint southern beaches, and owned the sun.The Riviera is left looking about as sublimely erotic and glamorous as a wet day in Margate. Tender Is the Night this is not. I don’t know whether the problem is pretension or, more depressingly, pandering to visitors the RA thinks want nice sunsets without the disturbing desires. If you go to this beach, leave your brain behind.At Royal Academy, London, from 2 October to 31 January 2027Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtRoyal Academy of ArtsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sex, drugs and floral fabrics: Celia Birtwell relives her wild times – and wilder outfits – with Ossie Clark | Textile art | The Guardian
description: They dressed – and partied with – the innermost in-crowd. As a swirling new show celebrates their fashion creations, Birtwell recalls her happy days with Clark and her sorrow at the loss of David Hockney
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: They dressed – and partied with – the innermost in-crowd. As a swirling new show celebrates their fashion creations, Birtwell recalls her happy days with Clark and her sorrow at the loss of David Hockney
Content: ‘He was spectacular – at the beginning’ ... the pair in 1971.Photograph: Evening Standard/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He was spectacular – at the beginning’ ... the pair in 1971.Photograph: Evening Standard/Getty ImagesTextile artSex, drugs and floral fabrics: Celia Birtwell relives her wild times – and wilder outfits – with Ossie ClarkThey dressed – and partied with – the innermost in-crowd. As a swirling new show celebrates their fashion creations, Birtwell recalls her happy days with Clark and her sorrow at the loss of David HockneyJess Cartner-MorleyMon 28 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the mythical age of bohemia, the psychedelic decade between Mary Quant’s cheerful miniskirts and the first snarls of punk, Celia Birtwell and Ossie Clark were London’s most fashionable couple. Birtwell created the fabrics: daydreamy, botanical doodles that captured the idealism and looseness of the times in wisps of chiffon. Clark magicked these into sensual bias-cut dresses with a freewheeling grandeur that was part Hollywood glamour, part rock’n’roll anarchy.More than just designers, they were a whole vibe. They dressed – and partied with – the innermost of the in-crowd. Talitha Getty, Marianne Faithfull and Anita Pallenberg hung out at Quorum, their Chelsea boutique. At a catwalk show in 1970, there were two Beatles, Cecil Beaton and Brigitte Bardot in the audience – and, after Clark began making stage clothes for Mick Jagger, he accompanied the Rolling Stones on tour. David Hockney’s portrait of the couple in their pomp – Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy, painted two years into their marriage, when Birtwell was pregnant with their second child – sealed their place in the mythology of the period.View image in fullscreenFreewheeling grandeur … actor Gala Mitchell in one of their dresses.Photograph: Celia BirtwellSpoiler alert: stories of sex, drugs and rock’n’roll tend not to have happy endings. The couple split in 1974 after five years of marriage, and Clark descended into addiction and bankruptcy long before his death at 54, brutally murdered in his west London flat by an ex-boyfriend. But their partnership, and the sumptuous clothes they made together, is enjoying another moment in the sun with a new exhibition, Ossie Clark + Celia Birtwell, about to open at London’s Fashion and Textile Museum.These days Celia Birtwell does a terrific impression of being just a sweet old lady. In fact she is so convincing that although she mentions, chatting to me on the phone from her kitchen in Shepherd’s Bush, that she has been doing a few bits and pieces in fashion lately, she is so low-key that I don’t think much of it. It is only a few weeks later, when I am at Burberry’s London fashion week show and she is sitting opposite me, that it turns out “a few bits and pieces” involved co-designing the entire catwalk collection with Daniel Lee, the creative director of Britain’s biggest luxury brand. Do not be fooled by the mild-mannered image: Birtwell is, and always has been, a player.The 85-year-old chats amiably about her grandchildren, the garden of her Shropshire cottage, and the struggles of having fine hair. “The last interviewer caught me in my curlers. I have little plastic ones now because Carmen rollers, which I had for years, bloody burn my poor hair.” She was always the calm, blue-eyed yin to Clark’s rakish, hedonistic yang. They met as art students when she was 19, introduced in a Manchester coffee bar by a mutual friend who wanted to show her a “really mad boy”.Being married to Ossie sounds like a lot. He was fabulously handsome and openly bisexual, prodigiously talented but chaotic and easily distracted. The day after their wedding in the summer of 1969, he left his pregnant wife at home to honeymoon in Barbados on his own. “Oh, but he was spectacular, at the beginning,” says Birtwell. “Just wonderful. The first two or three years were very nice. He would come back from Portobello with lovely vases or pieces of fabric he thought I’d like. Every week he came home with a new disc, we had fabulous music.” She didn’t go in for the all-night parties, but did enjoy hanging out with the beautiful people at Quorum. “I always thought Pattie Boyd was adorable, a little slim body with rather round bosoms. She looked so lovely in Ossie’s clothes. He really was so talented, but he wanted to party more than he wanted anything else. And once he got famous, the partying got a bit too much.”View image in fullscreen‘Oh, I miss him’ … Birtwell and Hockney in front of Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APHer wedding dress – a diaphanous daisy daydream with a contrast graphic print defining the yoked bodice – is her favourite piece in the new show. “I always liked putting prints together, not being boring with just one print. I didn’t make it as a wedding dress, but I was pregnant and it fitted me beautifully.” They had just two guests at their wedding: Clark’s sister Kay and Hockney, who had been friends, perhaps lovers, with Clark and had recently begun to draw Birtwell. In the wedding photo, Hockney – unmistakable platinum mop and dark owlish specs – is wearing a crumpled suit with a green carnation at a rakish angle on the lapel. “I made him wear the buttonhole, because he looked a bit scruffy,” Birtwell recalls, with a tranquil chuckle.double quotation markMost textile designers sit behind a designer and never get a mention. I was luckyBirtwell went on to become one of Hockney’s favourite subjects, sitting for him around 100 times over six decades, those long hours deepening into friendship. It is easy to see what drew him to her. Angelically pretty – she still is – she has a stillness that seems suited to the patient intimacy of the portrait studio. “We just always found it easy to talk to each other. I don’t know why, really. I was from Lancashire and he was from Yorkshire, and maybe there was something about both being northern.” Heartbreak bonded them too. Hockney’s love affair with Peter Schlesinger ended around the same time as Birtwell’s marriage was falling apart, and they supported each other.Hockney loved Clark but hated to watch him wasting his talent. “He used to tell him, ‘You’ve got to work harder, you’ve got to improve, you should be working all the time!’ But of course Ossie didn’t listen.” When the Clarks split, it was Birtwell with whom Hockney remained close. “I adored him. He was so clever. I think he found me a bit ridiculous sometimes. He would tease me, but I knew it was always fondly said.” Becoming part of his artistic circle, she says, “opened my life up”. In recent years, she spent time with him in Normandy, where “he had a huge garden and a pretty little house, with two barns on either side, one of which was converted into the most beautiful studio I’ve ever seen. Oh, it was lovely there.”His death in June was a huge blow. “I never thought he’d die before I did,” she says. “Because he was obsessed with his work, always had new ideas and plans. Whenever he heard someone had died, he’d always ask, ‘How old was he?’ Or, ‘How old was she?’ He was obsessed with keeping going, which I suppose is just as well, because it means he’s left us with this huge volume of marvellous work. He wanted to carry on, but he had that many damn things wrong with him by the end. Oh, I miss him.”View image in fullscreenSumptuous clothes … models wearing Birtwell’s designs in 1973.Photograph: Duffy ArchiveThere was a time when Birtwell could have been content to be Hockney’s muse – “It was a bit like another career” – but she kept working. She has always been “a homebody”, she says. “Ossie wanted to go out all the time, but I just wanted to make a nest and be in it. I’m mad for homes, for moving a room around.” She channelled this passion into designing fabrics for interiors. But she never truly left fashion. In 2006, she designed a limited edition collection for Topshop: there were queues around the block when it went on sale, which she got a kick out of.She designed for Uniqlo, too: “I would have done more, if they’d asked.” In 2015, she was commissioned by then Valentino designers Maria Grazia Chiuri and Pierpaolo Piccioli, now at Fendi and Balenciaga respectively, to make botanical prints for a catwalk collection. “They printed them marvellously,” she notes. “Top drawer stuff.” In 2011, she was awarded a CBE.Print designers seldom get the visibility they deserve, I say. “I agree. Most textile designers sit behind a designer and never get a mention. I was one of the lucky ones. If I hadn’t met Ossie, I think it’s highly unlikely another designer would have let me show off like he did.” Ossie was happy to share billing because he loved her and trusted her, and perhaps because he was too busy having fun to bother hogging the limelight. “Ossie just said, ‘Do what you feel.’ I had complete control. I’d work at home and print up 10 metre lengths of fabric and take them to his studio and throw the rolls on the table.”Avant-garments: the wild world of wearable art – in picturesRead moreThe show makes clear that Birtwell was Clark’s equal as a talent and an innovator. Her inspiration came from trips to the V&A, and to Vita Sackville-West’s gardens. Her study of Matisse informed her famous Candyflower print, with its cut-out swirls and stark negative space; Sonia Delaunay’s avant-garde art deco costumes for the Ballet Russes inspired the kinetic energy that made her designs a natural fit for fashion.You’ve had quite a life, I say. “Hmm, I suppose so,” she agrees in a placid, low-key tone that probably comes naturally when you have been a Swinging London icon and have a famous portrait of you hanging in the Tate. She is still working: she has been “rather let down” recently by a British textile design company for whom she designed home furnishing fabrics. “The thing is, you don’t win every game.” Anyway, she has another project on the go that she can’t tell me about because she’s signed an NDA. “But I don’t want to work quite as much any more. I’m not bothered about travelling far these days, but I do like to spend time in the countryside.” She has a longtime partner, Andrew, and is devoted to her six twentysomething grandkids – “four beautiful girls and two boys”, the children of her and Clark’s sons George and Albert.Birtwell never expected a retrospective like this to happen, not least because she sold most of her own Ossie Clark archive to a vintage dealer in California some years ago. “Half of me cries about that,” she says, “but the thing is that if you are going to keep clothes for a long time, you have to store them properly. There is refrigeration and all sorts to think about, so the other half of me thinks the moths would have got them. All in all, it probably worked out for the best.”Ossie Clark + Celia Birtwell is at the Fashion and Textile Museum, London, 2 October to 11 AprilExplore more on these topicsTextile artfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Richly rewarding’: why Netflix’s A Different World is the only TV reboot worth watching this year | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: With zany twists and lovable new faces, reboot of the Black sitcom is a worthy sequel to the trailblazing 1980s original
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: With zany twists and lovable new faces, reboot of the Black sitcom is a worthy sequel to the trailblazing 1980s original
Content: Maleah Joi Moon and Vincent Jamal Hooper in A Different World.Photograph: Eli Ade/NetflixView image in fullscreenMaleah Joi Moon and Vincent Jamal Hooper in A Different World.Photograph: Eli Ade/NetflixTV comedy‘Richly rewarding’: why Netflix’s A Different World is the only TV reboot worth watching this yearWith zany twists and lovable new faces, reboot of the Black sitcom is a worthy sequel to the trailblazing 1980s originalAndrew LawrenceMon 28 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s often the case that nothing disappoints like a sitcomreboot. The Malcolm in the Middle revival ismissing Dewey. The updatedSaved By the Bellfelt like detention punishment. And Just Like That … had Sex and the City diehardssharpening their stilettos.WhenNetflixannounced plans to rebootA Different Worldtwo years ago, fans of the Cosby Show spinoff mostly saw reasons not to. Too much time had passed since the show’s 1992 sign-off. Too much cultural currency had been invested in the show and in Hillman College – the series backdrop that was like Wakanda before Wakanda, a grand bastion of fictional yet somehow tangible Black excellence that drove attendance at historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) and acrowd-sourced CRT education boomonline. And too much cynicism had set in among American TV viewers to bother replicating the show’s classic multi-cam setup – too dusty and fusty, they might sneer.A Different World review – it was only a matter of time before they remade this trailblazing black sitcomRead moreDespite all this, the born-again A Different World landed on the streamer this week, and I am relieved – and, really, quite stunned to report that we finally have a sitcom reboot that actually meets the brief.The sitcom reboot would seem to have a tougher assignment thanits filmand TV drama counterparts. It’s not enough to simply advance the story, update the premise or facilitate a clean handoff from the beloved foundational cast to the new. It has to feel fresh and like old times, bring back the long-lost ritual of gathering around the TV as a country to escape into a world where laughter helps navigate us past our differences and disagreements on the way to genuine community.A Different World wasn’t justa Black thing. It was spun off from themostinfluential sitcomof its time, mainstream America’s introduction to an upwardly mobile Black family that reveled in African American culture, history and arts. A Different World followed Lisa Bonet’s Denise Huxtable, the bohemian in the family, as she studied at her parents’ alma mater, Hillman – already well established as part of The Cosby Show’s general commitment to promoting real HBCUs such as Howard, Tuskegee and Wilberforce. But when Bonet became pregnant with her first child,Zoë Kravitz, in the middle of A Different World’s first season, it made Bill Cosby wary of the optics of portraying an expectant mother in college. Bonet exited A Different World after its debut season and returned to The Cosby Show.Debbie Allen, the prodigious actor, dancer and Howard alumna, took over as the showrunner for A Different World in season two and effectively saved the series from cancellation. Her masterstroke was retooling what had been a Bonet-focused cast into a true ensemble and reorganizing the show around the will-they/won’t-they tension between the southern belle Whitley Gilbert and slick math nerd Dwayne Wayne, played by the estimable Jasmine Guy and Kadeem Hardison. Not only did their clashes become a cultural flashpoint – their marriage kicked off with Whitley jilting another man at the altar when Dwayne registeredone of the most notable objections in TV history– but so did all the hairstyles, clothes and music on the show. It became a showcase for Black Hollywood mainstays (Loretta Devine, Diahann Carroll) and then up-and-comers (Halle Berry, Jada Pinkett), while providing a platform to raise awareness of Aids, domestic violence and other pressing issues of the day.View image in fullscreenThe original cast of A Different World.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesFelicia Pride, the showrunner of the reboot (the original appears as A Different World 1987 in the Netflix carousel now), gives this tradition a modern spin. Her single-cam production uses the same visual grammar of Grown-ish andDear White Peopleto establish a tone that’s more underplayed and nuance-driven, stopping just short of making the full Bel-Air pivot into drama. A zany scene about a freshman bootlegging scheme at a football game, broken up by a campus cop on a Segway, ends with one of the bootleggers confessing he’s already on probation for another case – a pointed reminder of the wildly different lives students can bring with them to an HBCU. When another character, Glynn Turman’suptight Col Bradford Taylor, punctuates a matter-of-fact cancer survival story with an instruction to “check that prostate”, there was no mistaking the fleeting moment for what it was: a vintage network TV PSA.Price hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience?Read morePride broke the franchise out of its Hollywood sound stage and shot the reboot at the Atlanta University Center – the interconnected campuses of Morehouse College, Spelman College and Clark Atlanta University. Her reboot doesn’t embellish modest campus accommodations or shy from bringing controversies ripped from the headlines into the story:institutional graft,chronicunderfunding,enrollmentchaos,campus bomb threats. Hillman’s star quarterbackchooses the school overthe bright lights and big money of a predominantly white institution, while the storyline about a queer male student who competes with his super-Christian girl bestie for guys taps into evergreen discussions around Black religiosity and tolerance for relationships that don’t fit the mold. Meanwhile, the obligatory efforts to connect with younger viewers – through on-screen text message bubbles, narrative-driven social media screeds and cameos from modern influencers (from the NFL’s Cam Jordan to the Howard-bornPartners in Prime) – read more like tiny textures than outright pandering.But Pride had another advantage: college was a natural mesh point between the old and new. She got all the main players in the original cast who are still around to return for the reboot and gave them meaningful connections to the new kids. And it isn’t just Maleah Joi Moon’s Deborah (pronounced deb-BOR-ah), Dwayne and Whitley’s problem third child, who has a legacy at Hillman – where her mother sits on the board and her father is interim provost. When her roommate, Rashida, phones home, the woman on the other end is actor Alijah Kai’s actual mother –sitcom queen Tichina Arnold, a second layer of nepotism that makes Easter egg-loving audiences melt.View image in fullscreenChibuikem Uche, Cornell Young IV and Jordan Aaron Hall in A Different World.Photograph: Quantrell Colbert/Netflix/APThen, for a third layer of irony, Alijah wears a Coogi-inspired crop dress in one episode – a clear nod to the sweater-loving creator who was canceled and divorced from this TV universeduring #MeToooversexualassaultallegations. (Cosby is not credited in the new series.) In another episode, Deborah and Rashida team up in hopes of convincing Summer Walker to headline a homecoming concert, ambushing the Girls Need Love singer in her hotel room. Walker doesn’t just come through and perform; she evokes a TV heyday when the hottest rap and R&B artists crashed Black sitcoms on the regular. Incorporating Method Man into the new ensemble as Hillman’s football coach just speaks to how much those artists have evolved.But the thing that really makes the A Different World reboot stand out is how richly it rewards fans for sticking with the franchise. When Dwayne and his buddies reminisce about their college days, it isn’t just immediately a recognizable “uncstorytime”. It’s a callback to moments, exchanges and references that fans have come to know by heart. When Dwayne later reveals, quite sheepishly, that he and Whitley are separated, it suddenly hit me:of course they’re separated! We were all witnesses to the doomed wedding, after all!When Deborah vents to Cree Summer’s Freddie, a free-spirited Hillman professor now, about her “warden” mother and Freddie rolls her eyes in agreement, that moment resonates too – not just because Whitley is a lot, but because we remember the hell she put Freddie through when they were Hillman kids. We’re inside the inside jokes.View image in fullscreenDebbie Allen in A Different World.Photograph: Netflix/APAnd if that’s simplytoo much nostalgiato bear, I wonder: what other shows really imagineBlack charactersin the future? As adults who realized their dreams? Sustained decades-long friendships? Have kids to carry on their legacies? How many other TV shows have really explored how healthy relationships in the Black community grow over time? With so much of Black cultural memory organized around trauma and separation, death and destruction, it’s high time someone seized the occasion to celebrate achievement, admire continuity and wallow in joy. If A Different World wants to take a stroll down memory lane, no one can say it didn’t earn the trip.That sense of familiarity, of comfort, isn’t merely a sitcom device. It’s what makes HBCUs an attractive proposition for Black students who are often marginalized or neglected in the academic settings leading up to college. It’s why A Different World was created: to shine a light on these safe spaces – and I suspect another enrollment boom is in the offing. The new series, though, does more than continue the tradition while bridging the generational viewership divide with aplomb. It’s wholly satisfying, a different world for sitcom reboots indeed.Explore more on these topicsTV comedyBlack US cultureUS televisionComedyTelevisionNetflixBill CosbyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve never watched a whole episode of Peep Show’: Matt King on surviving a stroke and reviving Super Hans | Peep Show | The Guardian
description: The actor is returning to his character in the cult Channel 4 sitcom with a new autobiography – despite barely watching the series. He talks about his ‘terrifying’ hospital stay and why strangers still shout at him about crack being ‘moreish’
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The actor is returning to his character in the cult Channel 4 sitcom with a new autobiography – despite barely watching the series. He talks about his ‘terrifying’ hospital stay and why strangers still shout at him about crack being ‘moreish’
Content: You need Hans … Matt King as Peep Show’s king of chaos.Photograph: Kenny McCrackenView image in fullscreenYou need Hans … Matt King as Peep Show’s king of chaos.Photograph: Kenny McCrackenPeep Show‘I’ve never watched a whole episode of Peep Show’: Matt King on surviving a stroke and reviving Super HansThe actor is returning to his character in the cult Channel 4 sitcom with a new autobiography – despite barely watching the series. He talks about his ‘terrifying’ hospital stay and why strangers still shout at him about crack being ‘moreish’Rich PelleyMon 28 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuper Hans is back! What’s he been up to since we last saw him?Splitting up withMolly, the twins, themoped-rental business inMacedonia…Well, Super Hans finds a legal loophole in the marriage certificate, which means it’s null and void and … hang on … I’m basically telling you the whole plot of the book!Is the book just you, Matt King, writing on behalf of Super Hans? Or does your inner Super Hans just come out and write it for you?It’s neither. He comes around my house every morning. I put the kettle on, he borrows my computer and off he goes. I don’t know what he gets up to. I usually try to get out of the way, go for a nice walk.Is Super Hans your golden goose – or the albatrossround your neck?Well,Peep Showended in 2015. It started 23 years ago as an acting job, for want of a better term. A lot has happened since then, including having a stroke in April this year, which often means I totally lose the thread of what I’m saying, as you may have noticed.double quotation markI’ve seen Bake Off now I’ve been on it, but never watched a whole episode of Peep ShowHaving a stroke must have been awful. Even so, you seemed to be very good-humoured about it on social media from the get-go.I mean, initially it was absolutely terrifying because I was paralysed for 36 hours. I don’t remember the ambulance ride, or the first day and a half. I woke up on the stroke ward at Royal Sussex County hospital. But yes, I think I was quite good-natured about it. I had a very rare type of stroke, quite low down on the spinal cord. The doctors told me that I could have ended up in a wheelchair, or worse. I was very lucky, so I spent most of my time in hospital feeling very grateful. Cognitively, I’m quite a bit different from how I was before the stroke, although I am improving. I still had around a quarter of the book to write when it happened. In a weird way, my brain jumping all over the place helped on the home stretch.Could we see a Super Hans spin-off TV show?I would be more interested in a film based on this – the first of many books. I’m not going to be able to get away with playing him for much longer. I was talking to David Mitchell when we did The Great Peep Show Christmas Bake Off last year. We both remember [Peep Show creators] Jesse [Armstrong] and Sam [Bain] saying to us on the last day of filming: “See you in 10 years.” Ten years came and went, and none of us got the call. Maybe it’s because Jesse had some show called Succession going on.View image in fullscreenLift off … Matt King in the season nine Peep Show episode The William Morris Years.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyPerhaps the most surprising thing you revealed while appearing onThe Great Peep Show Christmas Bake Offwas that you’d never seen Bake Off – or, indeed, Peep Show.I have seen Bake Off – now that I’ve been on it. But it’s true that I have never watched a whole episode of Peep Show.Does that make it more difficult dealing with obsessive fans – and needy journalists – who can quote every episode word for word?For example,how many of the bands you and Jez were in can you name?The Hair Blair Bunch, Curse These Metal Hands, Coming Up for Blair, Various Artists …Have you heard about the now-annualAccidentally Run to Windsor, where people actually run from Croydon to Windsor, inspired by Super Hans giving up all his vices but becoming addicted to endorphins?Yes. I was meant to be at the finish line last year, but I was unwell. This year, I think I’m going to be firing the starter’s pistol.Why are you not the pacemaker for the first, say, 13 miles?I think the answer to that would be evident from looking at me. But that’s not to say that I’m not going to run across the finish line first. I’ll just be getting in the van the other 25 and a half miles.double quotation markTwo years ago, my daughter came home from school and went: 'It’s happened. Everyone is watching Peep Show, and they all know you’re my dad'What do people shout the most at you when they see you?“That crack is really moreish”, from the other end of a tube compartment. If they go too niche, I’ve no idea what they’re talking about. Often, I’ll have no recollection of saying it, so I get a disappointed response when they have to explain that it was in season seven, episode four, or whatever.Peep Show seems to be bigger now than when you finished making it.Why do you think it keeps finding new generations of fans?Obviously, it’s brilliant. Obviously, it’s endlessly quotable. Obviously, it’s funny. But there aren’t any other shows from that era that are still watched by ever-changing generations. My daughter is 17. About two years ago, she came home from school and went: “It’s happened. Everyone at school is watching fucking Peep Show, and they all know that you’re my dad.” My son, who’s 22 now, had gone through the same thing. The wave just keeps going.Has Super Hans somehow become timeless, then?More people come up to me now than they did 10 years ago. I was in an underground swimming pool in Morocco and there was another geezer doing lengths next to me. When I got out of the pool, he said: “Do you mind if I just interrupt you?” Turns out, he had gone to Sandhurst. He said they all used to watch it and that the box set belonged to Will. I said: “Who’s Will?” “Prince William.” There’s footage of David Bowie being interviewed in his house, and he’s got the box set of all nine series of Peep Show on DVD behind him. Between that and builders shouting it from scaffolding, it’s got every colour of the rainbow, every type of humanity.Is it hard to know where Matt ends and Super Hans begins? What are your views on Coldplay, for example?Let’s just say, my views on Coldplay are even more extreme than his!Moreish: My Mad Autobiographyby Super Hans is out now published by Mudlark.Explore more on these topicsPeep ShowTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatre | Stage | The Guardian
description: The actors are working together for the first time ever, in Noël Coward’s comedy Hay Fever. Backstage, there’s no stopping their tales of skinny-dipping, fat-shaming and warring co-stars
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: The actors are working together for the first time ever, in Noël Coward’s comedy Hay Fever. Backstage, there’s no stopping their tales of skinny-dipping, fat-shaming and warring co-stars
Content: ‘It’s camp that’s elegant’ … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski star in Hay Fever.Photograph: Oliver RosserView image in fullscreen‘It’s camp that’s elegant’ … Richard E Grant and Christine Baranski star in Hay Fever.Photograph: Oliver RosserDouble actsStage‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatreThe actors are working together for the first time ever, in Noël Coward’s comedy Hay Fever. Backstage, there’s no stopping their tales of skinny-dipping, fat-shaming and warring co-starsRyan GilbeyMon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard EGrant: Despite our vast combined vintage, our paths have never crossed before, have they?Christine Baranski: Regrettably not. We could have had some good fun a few decades ago. A girl could have got into some real trouble. But here we are, and now we’re the veterans. You’re among the great character actors, popping up delightfully in so many things and always being spot-on.REG: My late wife said I’m in the condiment years, where you’re added to the meal in these cameo roles like vinegar or ketchup or mustard, spice or pickle or whatever. I think that’s absolutely accurate.CB: It makes for an interesting and varied career. You have a shelf life certainly if you’re a leading lady. It’s a harder perch to descend from, which is sort of what Hay Fever is about. My character, Judith Bliss, can’t quite accept that she’s not up there doing it any more. I’ve had a long career because I was comfortable being the supporting actress. I did The Real Thing by Tom Stoppard on Broadway in 1984 [for which she won the first of two Tony awards]. My character in that, Charlotte, is so bitingly witty and she has this marvellous repartee with Henry, played by Jeremy Irons. I’d do my scenes, then go up to my dressing room, and people would say: “Oh, we wanted you to come back!” They’ll have their fill of me with Hay Fever. It’ll be more like: “When is she going to leave the stage?”View image in fullscreenGrant and Baranski in rehearsals for Hay Fever.Photograph: Marc BrennerRyan Gilbey: Judith in Hay Fever has been played by everyone fromEdith EvansandCelia JohnsontoJudi Dench,Penelope KeithandLindsay Duncan. Why is the part such a magnet for great performers?CB: Well, she’s an ageing actress, and how delicious to play that in your later years. It’s all about the vanity and vulnerability of ageing. There’s a poignancy to it; I really find her rather dear. You don’t have to be an ageing actress to feel that way as a woman, particularly in our culture. We cling to youth for dear life. You could say it all borders on the camp, but because it’s Coward and he’s writing affectionately as well as cynically about theatre people, it has a sweetness to it – it’s camp that’s elegant. He wrote it at 24, so even as a young man he had that sense of something behind all the fame and glamour.Christine, this is your first time in the West End but your fourth Coward play. What’s the secret to mastering him?CB: If you find out, will you please tell us? Speed, facility, lightness of tone. He uses words as weapons. I really want people to sit up and listen because we don’t use language like that any more, do we?Judith and her husband,David, played byRichard, are decidedly poor hosts. What makes a good host and a decent party?REG: My late wife said that everyone there should know a minimum of two people. It’s foolproof, and it means that you as the host can let people get on with it. If nobody knows anybody, you’re buggered. I’ve found that whenever a party has been awkward, it’s because there’s not enough social glue to begin with.CB: We had the most wonderful party at Richard’s house on the first weekend I was here in London. It’s the most enchanting, magical house. You can describe it for me, Richard.REG: Maximalist.CB: Sitting around, having drinks and laughing were Steve Martin and Martin Short, Helena Bonham Carter, Gary Oldman, various spouses and Richard’s daughter and son-in-law. It was so relaxing despite the extraordinary pedigrees of all these talented people with big egos.REG: There were 12 of us, so you could still hear someone at the other end of the table and you didn’t feel cut off. Christine already knew Steve, Marty and Helena but not Gary. Gary knew Helena but not Steve and Marty. There was enough glue.View image in fullscreenGrant (left) and Paul McGann in Withnail and I.Photograph: Handmade Films/Kobal/ShutterstockYou and Gary Oldman have worked together a few times, haven’t you, Richard? Including on one of your first credits,Les Blair’s BBC film Honest, Decent and True.REG: Yes, that was 1985. The day I landed here when I emigrated from Swaziland in 1982, I went to see Gary in the play Summit Conference with Glenda Jackson as Eva Braun and Georgina Hale as Clara Petacci, the mistresses of Hitler and Mussolini. That was where I first met him. We each got married at the same time – well, Gary’s been married five times – and my daughter was born around the same time as his first child. When I had to lose weight for Withnail and I, I asked Gary how he’d done it for Sid and Nancy. I had just spent almost a year when I was unemployed trying to gain weight because I’d read in a magazine that if you’re six foot, you should weigh 12 stone. Now, I’d never weighed 12 stone in my life, so I was doing all the weight-gain powder and the gym and all that. Then Bruce Robinson, the director of Withnail, said, “Could you lose a stone?” So I called Gary, who I think had eaten nothing but tuna and melon; he even ended up hospitalised at one point. I went to Boots instead and got weight-gain-off powder, and my year’s work disappeared within a week.Before that, didn’t Bruce say you looked like “a fat Dirk Bogarde”?REG: He did. He still calls me Fatty.As you were going in to audition for Withnail, you passedBill Nighycoming out.REG: Bill Nighy. Kenneth Branagh. A whole bunch of people went up for it. I had to read the kitchen scene at the start of the film. Bruce told me: “Drop the Noël Coward. The character is not as affected as you’re thinking. Read it with more rage.” I’d been unemployed for nine months so that rage was very easy to tap into.Christine, do you host?CB: I have a marvellous house on a lake in Connecticut and I’ve hosted some very famous actors there. It has a very long dock that has been “grandfathered” in, as in they don’t allow a dock that long to be built any more, but this is about 100 years old. You sit in the living room in summer and watch the sun set, and then go out into the evening and skinny dip in the lake. When I did Boeing-Boeing for nine months on Broadway with Mark Rylance, he became a great pal – he’s a godfather to my third grandson – and we’d be out there howling at the moon at four in the morning. So much fun.REG: Have you ever had anybody who won’t take their clothes off?CB: Oh, it’s not a prerequisite. I encourage people only if they’re comfortable and if it’s pitch dark. Although one actress I adore insisted on sunbathing stark naked in the middle of the afternoon. In fact, she would spend all night on the dock, fall asleep on there and then wake up at dawn and there she was!You won anEmmyin1995for the sitcomCybill, where you playedCybill Shepherd’s divorced best friend. But you’d been reluctant to do TV, hadn’t you?CB: Absolutely. Mainly because I didn’t want to live in Los Angeles. I also had a very active theatre career, going from play to play; I loved it. It just became a question of raising two kids and having tuition bills to pay. So at 41 or 42, I began my television career with the caveat that I would commute. I never bought real estate in LA. I lived in a hotel and was on the first red-eye back to the kids. Winning the Emmy gave me this visibility. I’d worked with Mike Nichols on The Real Thing, but it was because of the Emmy that he cast me in The Birdcage. Most of my film and television stuff happened after the age of 40.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve had a long career because I was comfortable being the supporting actress’ … Baranski in Cybill.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/Getty ImagesREG: I read yesterday that there was an unprecedented number of Emmys going to female actors over 50 this year.CB: It’s about time.Christine and one of this year’s winners,Jean Smart from Hacks, playedbiker chicksinThe Odd Couple II.CB: Well done! Yes, Jean danced with Jack Lemmon and I got to dance with Walter Matthau. It was not a good movie, but to work with those guys at the end of their careers … oh, I adored them. Lemmon was the consummate professional, always the first one on set, and Matthau was this curmudgeonly, lovable old woolly bear.REG: Talking of Mike Nichols, I had dinner with Mike 22 years ago, the night before I went to Africa to make the only film I’ve directed, Wah-Wah. I asked him for advice and he said – apart from getting good caterers – that actors can always act faster than they think they can. He said: “Do the takes that you’re happy with. Give the actors the takes they’re happy with. And then tell them: ‘Let’s do one for Mike.’” It’s amazing, the speed and effectiveness when people aren’t pausing and breaking … up … lines … all … the … time. Because we don’t do that in life, do we? It was great advice.CB: It was. He couldn’t tolerate indulgence. He was so fiercely intelligent and he loved clarity. Richard, did you have a wonderful time working with Robert Altman?REG: I did. I worked with him on The Player and Gosford Park and a terrible film called Pret-a-Porter. Whereas the other two had scripts, Pret-a-Porter was like this: “Ryan, Christine and Richard meet in a small room. She spills the water. They argue. Improvise.” It had no structure and it was a car crash as a result. If you’ve got a good script, you can embellish and add stuff, but this was a free-for-all. There was one insane day when Danny Aiello completely lost the plot. Sophia Loren was supposed to have fainted, and he infiltrated the scene and started taking it over: “I’ll give her mouth-to-mouth resuscitation!” He called Lauren Bacall “a left-wing Commie bitch”. Then he insulted Rupert Everett for being English and for being …View image in fullscreenGrant in rehearsals for Hay Fever.Photograph: Marc BrennerCB: Oh dear. Did Lauren eat him up and spit him out?REG: She took no prisoners. She ripped him five new ones. It was more dramatic than anything that happened in the actual film. None of the cast would talk to Danny after that; they sent him to Coventry.CB: We all have our stories.Christine, have you ever worked the way Altman did, with multiple cameras and the actors not always knowing for sure if they are in shot?CB: A little bit on television. I think it’s a great way of keeping actors on their toes. Sitcoms can be harrowing, though. If the studio audience doesn’t laugh, the writers go away and come up with a different joke there and then. They’re always adjusting and you’ve got to nail those one-liners. You know you’ve got to get that laugh because it’s your job. It’s a wonderful discipline. After all that comedy, I told my manager: “It’s time for me to do a dramatic role.” Be careful what you wish for, because if The Gilded Age goes for a fifth year, that’ll be 18 straight years of television work, after The Good Wife and The Good Fight.With you inThe Gilded Age, and Richard inGosford ParkandDownton Abbey, you’re both part of theJulian FellowesDramatic Universe.REG: Yes, but we’re not as rich as Julian Fellowes. Well, Christine probably is, but I’m not.I noticed a few other similarities on your CVs. You both appeared in great Steve Martin comedies: Richard in LA Story, Christine inBowfinger.CB: Underrated, I think. It’s certainly got some of Eddie Murphy’s greatest work. He was huge then. His first day on set, I had to walk across the street and assault him. He’s a really intelligent actor. And God, does he have comedic instincts! He’s also a very private person.View image in fullscreenBaranski with Walter Matthau and Jean Smart in The Odd Couple II.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyREG: So he won’t be skinny-dipping in Connecticut?CB: No skinny-dipping with Eddie Murphy.Early in your careers, you also each appeared in a scandalous erotic movie. Richard was inHenry & June, the film for which the controversialNC-17rating (the highest age rating)was created in the US.REG: That’s right. It has a lot of bonking and brothel scenes.CB: We’re notknownfor the erotic works, I should say. But yes, mine was 9½ Weeks. I played Kim Basinger’s friend. I have a dinner scene where I balance a teaspoon on the end of my nose. And I can drink while it’s sort of hanging there.REG: You should do that during the breakfast scene in Hay Fever.CB: And upstage you, my darling?Hay Fever is atWyndham’s theatre, London, until 12DecemberExplore more on these topicsStageDouble actsTheatreRichard E GrantTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: MTV VMAs 2026: Taylor Swift and Madonna win at awards dominated by female artists | MTV Video Music Awards | The Guardian
description: Madonna and Swift take home four of six prizes given out during ceremony telecast, alongside K-pop star Lisa and British newcomer Sienna Spiro
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Madonna and Swift take home four of six prizes given out during ceremony telecast, alongside K-pop star Lisa and British newcomer Sienna Spiro
Content: Taylor Swift and Madonna at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards (VMAs). The two artists won four of the six awards given out during the telecast.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTaylor Swift and Madonna at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards (VMAs). The two artists won four of the six awards given out during the telecast.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesMTV Video Music AwardsMTV VMAs 2026: Taylor Swift and Madonna win at awards dominated by female artistsMadonna and Swift take home four of six prizes given out during ceremony telecast, alongside K-pop star Lisa and British newcomer Sienna SpiroMTV VMAs 2026 red carpet: Taylor Swift, Charli xcx, Troye Sivan and more – in picturesMTV VMAs: full list of winnersAdrian HortonSun 27 Sep 2026 23.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMadonnaandTaylor Swifttriumphed at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards, with the former winning three trophies and the latter winning the night’s top honor, extending her run as the most-awarded artist in VMAs history.In a ceremony that largely awarded female artists,Madonnaentered the evening as the most nominated artist of the year with 13 nods and won seven, including three during the telecast: for best collaboration (with Sabrina Carpenter), best dance, and artist of the year.MTV VMAs 2026 red carpet: Taylor Swift, Charli xcx, Troye Sivan and more – in picturesRead more“Most of you were probably not born when I performed at the very first VMAs 43 years ago,” the 68-year-old said while accepting the award for artist of the year, which she won over Swift, Carpenter, Ariana Grande,Bruno Marsand Morgan Wallen.After recalling how she fell and accidentally exposed her rear, threatening her nascent career in a very different media landscape, Madonna ended on a more serious note. “I spent the last year and a half finding myself, believing in myself and really making the music that I wanted to make,” she said. “My hope for all of you here tonight is that you … do the same. Find yourself and believe in yourself.”View image in fullscreenSienna Spiro accepts the best new artist award.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesMadonna, whose provocative performances in the 1980s helped cement the VMAs as a can’t-miss cultural event, opened the show at the Peacock theater in Los Angeles with her first VMAs performance in 23 years, the first since her infamous onstage kiss with Britney Spears in 2003.She performed two songs from this summer’sConfessions II: Bring Your Love with Carpenter, and a intricate, lively rendition of Danceteria, her tribute to New York’s 1980s club scene, with Charli xcx and a who’s who of background dancers including Julia Garner, the actor who was cast to play Madonna in a long-gestating biopic that wascancelledafter a “falling out” with Universal Studios.Taylor Swift: The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore review – flashes of humanity and bafflingly vindictive love songsRead moreSwift won three categories, including the night’s top honor – video of the year – for The Fate of Ophelia, and the inaugural artist director honors. The new award, to celebrate “groundbreaking music artists whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video”, honored Swift’s status as the most-decorated music video director in the show’s history, as well as itsmost-awarded solo artist.Swift dedicated her win to “the ultimate showgirl” Dolly Parton,who died last month at 80 after being diagnosed with cancer.“Listening to her songs, it’s like watching the best music video you have ever seen in your life, every single time you hear what she’s written,” she said. “And she handled this thing with such grace and joy and love and gratitude for the fact that she got to do this, and everything that happened in her life or her career, she channelled back into love and gratitude and appreciation for her fans.“I’m lucky I got to be one of them, and I’ll always be one of them. I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time.”View image in fullscreenKacey Musgraves pays tribute to Dolly Parton at the VMAs.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesAfter reflecting on her 20 years of making nearly 60 music videos, 18 of which she wrote and directed, Swift premiered her new video for Patient Zero, the lead single fromThe Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, her four-track addition to last year’scritically maligned album. The new video sees her twinning with actor Dakota Johnson in a showdown with a mutual ex played by Colin Farrell.Country singerKacey Musgravespaid tribute to Parton by harmonizing with archival video of the late singer performing her hit I Will Always Love You, to a visibly moved crowd. Later on, Sombr, Raye, Teddy Swims and Adam Lambert performed hits from George Michael’s Faith tour, 10 years after the English singer’s death aged 53.Madonna and Swift’s dominance – the duo won four of the six awards handed out during the two-and-a-half-hour telecast, which was delayed by more than 20 minutes by an NFL game – injected some much-needed star power in a show that has struggled to find its identity in the streaming era.Presided over by a largely absent, if reliably chill first-time host, Snoop Dogg, the 2026 VMA telecast was once again dominated by female artists. K-pop star Lisa won best pop for her song Dream, while British newcomer Sienna Spiro was named best new artist after fans voted throughout the show.View image in fullscreen(L-R) Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear of Nirvana accept the video vanguard award.Photograph: Rich Polk/Billboard/Getty Images‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the yearRead moreThe Michael Jackson video vanguard award, a honorary lifetime achievement prize, went toNirvana, for the influence of the era-defining grunge band’s music videos. The visual concepts for Smells Like Teen Spirit, Come As You Are, In Bloom, Heart-shaped Box and All Apologies “came out of the vision of one of the greatest artists of all time, Kurt Cobain,” said Krist Novoselic, the band’s bassist, speaking on behalf of drummer Dave Grohl and guitarist Pat Smear, who joined the band on tour beginning in 1993.Cobain, who took his own life in 1994, was “one of one” he added, noting that the band’s music still resonates because “people are still hungry for authenticity, for something real, something uncompromising … Kurt would have loved that legacy.”In categories not included in the telecast, K-pop group BTS won best group and best K-pop and song of the year for their hit Swim, Bruno Mars won best R&B for I Just Might, Cardi B and Kehlani won best hip-hop for Safe, Bad Bunny won best Latin for NUEVAYoL, Olivia Rodrigo won best alternative for The Cure, and Ella Langley won best country forher record-breaking hitChoosin’ Texas.Explore more on these topicsMTV Video Music AwardsMTVMadonnaAwards and prizesTaylor SwiftKacey MusgravesNirvananewsShareReuse this content

title: Rediscovered chalk drawing of child attributed to Édouard Manet | Édouard Manet | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Work, whose subject resembles street urchin in masterpiece by artist, discovered in private collection
Author: Dalya Alberge
Headline: Exclusive: Work, whose subject resembles street urchin in masterpiece by artist, discovered in private collection
Content: The study of a crouching child, which has been attributed to Manet.Illustration: Private CollectionView image in fullscreenThe study of a crouching child, which has been attributed to Manet.Illustration: Private CollectionÉdouard ManetRediscovered chalk drawing of child attributed to Édouard ManetExclusive: Work, whose subject resembles street urchin in masterpiece by artist, chanced upon in private collectionDalya AlbergeMon 28 Sep 2026 05.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA red chalk drawing of a crouching child, spotted in a private Italian collection, has been attributed by an art historian to the French modernist painterÉdouard Manet.The child, whose identity has yet to be established, resembles a street urchin in the Manet masterpieceThe Old Musician, in which he sought to show the humanity of homeless and marginalised people.The art historian Emily Beeny, a specialist in French paintings and drawings of the 17th to 19th centuries, said she sensed the drawing’s potential as soon as she received a photograph from a colleague, Francesco Baccanelli, who had noticed the drawing in the Italian collection.“It just felt like: ‘Oh gosh, that’s exciting,’” she said. “Lots of people send me things they imagine might be by Manet, but this is the only one so far that has given me an immediate sense of recognition. I’m not sure when the last unpublished drawing by Manet was discovered, but it has definitely been many years.”It is characteristic of red chalk life studies that Manet made in the 1850s and 1860s, influenced by his close study of Renaissance draughtsmanship in Florence. Similar sketches relate to masterpieces such asLe Déjeuner sur l’herbe, as well as The Old Musician.View image in fullscreenLe Déjeuner sur l’herbeby Édouard Manet, 1863.Photograph: Fine Art/Corbis/Getty ImagesBeeny is chief curator of theLegion of Honor at the Fine Arts Museums of San Franciscoand her exhibitions have included Manet and Modern Beauty, staged by the Getty Museum in Los Angeles and the Art Institute of Chicago.Art historians often disagreed on attributions, but this drawing was also correct stylistically, she said, pointing to “the abrupt transitions between light and shadow, and the peculiar plump, tapered fingers – little figural tics that are very characteristic of Manet”.Crucially, UV analysis has revealed Manet’s faded studio stamp in the lower right-hand corner.The drawing measures 20.5cm by 17.5cm and although it is squared for transfer to a canvas, no such composition by the artist is known.Baccanelli specialises in 17th- and 18th-century paintings and prints, mostly from Lombardy and Veneto.
