On a visit to “a small and little-known collection” in northern Italy, he said, the owner pointed out an inscription on the reverse of the mount identifying the drawing as a work by Manet, but that no art historian had ever studied it.View image in fullscreenArt historian Emily Beeny said it’s possible the chalk drawing is of the same person who posed for a little girl, with a very similar hairstyle, who stands at left in the finished version of The Old Musician (pictured).Illustration: Manet, Edouard/Chester Dale collectionHe said: “I was completely captivated by it … The more I studied it, the more convinced I became that it was indeed a work by Manet … I contacted Emily Beeny, one of the world’s leading experts on Manet.”Beeny and Baccanelli will publish their findings in the October issue of the scholarly journalthe Burlington Magazine.Speculating on the figure’s identity, they refer to Alexandre, a youth hired by Manet in the late 1850s to clean his brushes and palettes, who occasionally posed for him. Although this drawing may depict him, they say, it seems to show a little girl, perhaps aged around six.Beeny said: “It’s quite possible that she’s the same person who posed for a little girl, with a very similar hairstyle, who stands at left in the finished version of The Old Musician. It’s clearly a drawing with which he took some time and effort, and with which he was pleased, considering that he squared it for transfer.”She said she hoped it would be included in the next edition of the definitive Manet catalogue raisonné, produced by theWildenstein Plattner Institute, which has yet to study the drawing.Research has revealed that the drawing was sold twice in the 1930s, in Germany and then in Switzerland, although it did not make it into any scholarly publications on the artist. The academics write in the Burlington: “For now, the drawing’s original purpose remains as mysterious as its early history.”Explore more on these topicsÉdouard ManetPaintingArtDrawingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rod Stewart announces final tour for 2027: ‘Most definitely my last’ | Rod Stewart | The Guardian
description: The 81-year-old singer will wrap up a touring career that stretches back to his mid-teens in the early 1960s, with dates planned for UK and Europe
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: The 81-year-old singer will wrap up a touring career that stretches back to his mid-teens in the early 1960s, with dates planned for UK and Europe
Content: Rod Stewart performing at Glastonbury festival, June 2025.Photograph: Harry Durrant/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRod Stewart performing at Glastonbury festival, June 2025.Photograph: Harry Durrant/Getty ImagesRod StewartRod Stewart announces final tour for 2027: ‘Most definitely my last’The 81-year-old singer will wrap up a touring career that stretches back to his mid-teens in the early 1960s, with dates planned for UK and EuropeBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 28 Sep 2026 04.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRod Stewart has announced that his next tour will be his last.The 81-year-old singer has been touring since the early 1960s, when he set out across Europe with a harmonica – and ended up getting deported from Spain for vagrancy – in a duo with folk singer Wizz Jones.But while he hasn’t ruled out one-off gigs in the future, the touring element of his career is coming to an end with Rod Stewart: The Final Encore, a tour of the UK and Europe beginning April 2027.The arena run includes UK dates in Belfast, Glasgow, Birmingham, Manchester and London, and after an extensive European run, finishes up in Hanover, Germany, in July.Promising “one hell of a show”, Stewart said: “The time has come to say farewell to life on the road. After more than six decades, The Final Encore will most definitely be my last. I’ve been singing the music I love since I was 19 years old, and I’ve had the privilege of taking it around the world to all of you. It has given me a life beyond anything I could ever have imagined, and I hope I’ve given you some fond memories in return. So, may I take this opportunity to thank you for making this extraordinary life possible.”Stewart still has a couple of live dates currently scheduled for after the end of the tour, in Red Rocks, Colorado, in September 2027. Those are dates he was forced to reschedule from June this year, due to inflamed vocal cords.The June dates were part of One Last Time, his farewell tour of the US. He later paused a concert in Utah to use an oxygen mask after nearly fainting during the performance, then cancelled the remainder of the tour after undergoing a heart procedure.Earlier on the One Last Time tour, in 2025, he had to cancel concerts due to flu, Covid and strep throat, and for needing vocal rest. It looked like his Glastonbury “legends slot” performance was at risk of cancellation due to flu, but he went through with the gig.A Guardian review described him as being “in good voice, especially given he cancelled gigs … It helps that he’s never had a clear or stereotypically youthful voice to begin with; the years show, mostly, in his struggle to sustain long notes.” It also heralded him as “a physical performer, writhing and launching around like one of the leggier Muppets”.Stewart has been touring since his teens. After his duo with Jones, he spent time shuttling between groups such as Jimmy Powell & the Five Dimensions, Steampacket and Shotgun Express before joining the Jeff Beck Group, and then Faces. His solo career began in earnest at the close of the 1960s, and Stewart became a huge commercial success: after 1971’s chart-topping Every Picture Tells a Story, all but one of his 29 studio albums since have reached the UK Top 10. The most recent, 2024’s Swing Fever – a collaboration with Jools Holland – reached No 1.Though Stewart may be retiring from touring, he could well release more studio projects. He told Desert Island Discs that he and former Faces bandmate Ronnie Wood had “songs that we’re working on from back in the day, but it’s hard to make our times tally. When we do get a chance to get in the studio again, we will finish off these songs. We’ve got a good body of songs going.”Rod Stewart: The Final Tour dates in fullApril 233Arena, Dublin, IrelandApril 27SSE Arena, Belfast, UKApril 29OVO Hydro, Glasgow, UKMay 4Utilita Arena, Birmingham, UKMay 6Co-op Live, Manchester, UKMay 11The O2, London, UKMay 28Ziggo Dome, Amsterdam, NetherlandsMay 29AFAS Dome, Antwerp, BelgiumJune 1Uber Arena, Berlin, GermanyJune 3PSD Bank Dome, Düsseldorf, GermanyJune 6Royal Arena, Copenhagen, DenmarkJune 9Veikkaus Arena, Helsinki, FinlandJune 11Dalhalla, Rättvik, SwedenJune 13Sverresboro, Trondheim, NorwayJune 15Plenen, Bergen, NorwayJune 18Sportsarena, Budapest, HungaryJune 20Olympiahalle, Munich, GermanyJune 22Pula Arena, Pula, CroatiaJune 24O2 Arena, Prague, Czech RepublicJuly 20Tauron Arena, Kraków, PolandJuly 24ZAG Arena, Hanover, GermanyExplore more on these topicsRod StewartPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: The endangered native ponies of Eriskay in the Outer Hebrides – a photo essay | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Fewer than 400 Eriskay ponies remain. One of the rarest native breeds in the world, their plight is unique because the community living on their tiny Hebridean island are fighting for them. The ponies wander the village and townsfolk care for them together
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fewer than 400 Eriskay ponies remain. One of the rarest native breeds in the world, their plight is unique because the community living on their tiny Hebridean island are fighting for them. The ponies wander the village and townsfolk care for them together
Content: An Eriskay pony snoozes in the sunshine on a warm spring afternoonFewer than 400 Eriskay ponies remain. One of the rarest native breeds in the world, their plight is unique because the community living on their tiny Hebridean island are fighting for them. The ponies wander the village and townsfolk care for them togetherByEmily WhitneyMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 04.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the slopes of Beinn Sciathan, a rocky outcrop in the Outer Hebrides, white and grey ponies roam freely. Eriskay ponies, one of the rarest native breeds in the world, are critically endangered.EriskayThey have often been mixed with the Highland pony and other breeds, giving the false impression of higher population numbers. Only about 300 to 400 Eriskay ponies are thought to remain.View image in fullscreenPonies grazing at dawn on EriskayView image in fullscreenEfforts have been made to boost their numbers since the 1970s, both on their small homeland, Eriskay Island, and on the mainland. The island’s ponies have a lifestyle fascinating enough to draw tourists. They are neither wild nor kept enclosed. For half of the year, including winter, they are free to roam the island and its village. Each pony has an owner who can easily identify their own despite them looking nearly identical to the average observer.View image in fullscreenSandra MacInnes, the chair of Comann Each nan Eilean, the island’s pony society, married into the community caring for the ponies and her affection for them has only grown over timeAbout 150 people live on Eriskay, many of whom speak Gaelic. It is a close-knit community, but over time the island has become a tourist destination known for stunning beaches with clear blue water, the grounding of the SS Politician, and even a Fifa-recognised football pitch. But its history of fishing, croftingand Catholicism, and of course its ponies, are integral to its culture.“It all makes Eriskay what it is today,” says Sandra MacInnes, the chair ofComann Each nan Eilean, the island’s pony society, who owns several of the animals.View image in fullscreenEriskay ponies grazing outside the community hallIn the 1850s, thousands of families in the Outer Hebrides were forced from Barra and South Uist during the Highland clearances. For many, Eriskay became a crowded refuge. MacInnes says: “[The landlords] thought it’s rubbish for grazing so they sent them here thinking they’ll never survive. They came here and made their houses … They were cleared from crofting communities and had to learn fishing, but then they thrived.”View image in fullscreenTwo Eriskay ponies grooming each otherOnce the Eriskay community was established, the ponies thrived because of their role in the region’s social fabric. Originally used for crofting, they would be fitted with creels to bring peat up the hill and move seaweed as fertiliser for crops.In the 1970s, however, their population shrank to a low of about 20 purebreds. Mechanisation was one of the main reasons for their decline, and Comann Each nan Eilean was founded in 1972 to restore the breed.View image in fullscreenA mare recently brought to the island works out her place in the herdView image in fullscreenEriskay ponies grazing on a rocky outcropCommunity members also note that the climate crisis has begun to affect their island. Recent winters have hit hard, and the beaches are starting to erode. But the ponies adapt well to harsh and fluctuating winters with their hardy coats and their ability to navigate the island to stay out of the wind.Triona MacKinnon owns two ponies on Eriskay and a few others on South Uist.“Winters are getting longer and wetter,” she says, noting that the community is having to help more in feeding the ponies – but at the same time that milder weather encourages ticks, which affect the animals.View image in fullscreenTriona MacKinnon and her childrenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenChildren play at their family’s croft“This winter’s been particularly long,” she says. “You can get loads of rain. Some ponies can get rain scald, and you’re not used to seeing that.”The ponies have shaped the town’s culture over time. Local people quote the former parish priest Father Calum MacLellan, who once said: “Without the people of Eriskay there would be no pony, but without the pony there would have been no people on Eriskay.”Or as MacInnes says: “They both needed each other.”View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe ponies’ population has increased in the last 60 years, but there is still work to do. Comann Each nan Eilean is developing a breeding programme, and it manages the herd numbers to ensure the the grazing land can sustain the animals without them overrunning the community.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenFiona Misselbrook pets her Eriskay foal at her farm in Haddington near EdinburghOne foal was born on the island this year, and the community hopes for a few more next year. When first born, the ponies are almost black and then become lighter as they age. Most turn white, but some actually develop a brown coat.In the winter months, the ponies need extra food and their owners feed them with support from the island’s pony society. In the summer, the ponies are kept up on Beinn Sciathan to allow the soil on lower slopes to recover so it can be used for farming.View image in fullscreenEriskay ponies grazing on a hillsideOwners hike up and down whenever they can to check on their ponies. Some tend to their own ponies’ hooves, but many need to pay for a farrier, as well as veterinary care when needed. The work is financially demanding and time-consuming, but many islanders see a life alongside the ponies as something beautiful and part of their heritage.View image in fullscreenThe crystal clear waters of EriskayAlthough MacInnes married into the community caring for ponies, she has since become attached to them.View image in fullscreenAn Eriskay pony roams the town“You get to know how docile they are. They all have their own personalities, they all have names, they all have little characters,” she says. “It’s nice to see herd dynamics as families. They are families.”To donate toComann Each nan Eilean’s work and theconservation of the Eriskayponies,click hereExplore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayScotlandHorsesWildlifeConservationEndangered speciesAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Michael Palin encounters ‘recycled chicken’ in the Philippines | Television | The Guardian
description: The adventurous Python visits a country of contrasts. Plus: get ready to shed some tears with Pete Wicks and his dogs. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The adventurous Python visits a country of contrasts. Plus: get ready to shed some tears with Pete Wicks and his dogs. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Michael Palin in the Philippines.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/ITN Productions/Neil Ferguson & Jaimie GramstonView image in fullscreenMichael Palin in the Philippines.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/ITN Productions/Neil Ferguson & Jaimie GramstonTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Michael Palin encounters ‘recycled chicken’ in the PhilippinesThe adventurous Python visits a country of contrasts. Plus: get ready to shed some tears with Pete Wicks and his dogs. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hannah Verdier,Ali Catterall,Alexi DugginsandSimon WardellMon 28 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Palin in the Philippines9pm, Channel 5Michael Palin remains an adventurous traveller in the Philippines, a complex and challenging country. He explores the chaotic soap opera generated by the Marcos family, now back in government thanks to the rise of Bongbong, the president – who turns out to be a Monty Python fan. Elsewhere, Palin sees the country’s poverty, meeting a woman selling “recycled chicken”.Phil HarrisonJamie’s 20 Minute Meals8pm, Channel 4Jamie Oliver is back with a new gimmick: he’s cooking his recipes in one single shot to offer proof of concept. It’s not really necessary – as ever, while the man himself may be an acquired taste, his food (camembert and onion rice and a crispy chicken dish) looks both achievable and delicious.PHClickbait Clinic With Stacey Dooley8.30pm, BBC OneIs munching on a diet of only meat good for you? It sounds like a question that’s too stupid to answer, but Dooley is determined to give it a fair crack. A lovable bodybuilder states his case for the carnivore diet, then doctors Nighat Arif and Alex George give their perspectives.Hannah VerdierFinding Britain’s Slave Traders With David Olusoga9pm, BBC TwoThe expansion of the slave trade in the 18th century spread wealth and commerce across Britain. In Bristol alone, social-climbing merchants and investors funded charities, built grand homes – and what ultimately became the Bristol Old Vic. “Institutions they knew would outlive them,” as David Olusoga points out, in the second part of this furious two-part exposé.Ali CatterallPete Wicks: For Dogs’ Sake9pm, U&WView image in fullscreenHeartstring-tugging business.Photograph: James Rudland/James Rudland / U&WThe reality star begins his fourth series profiling the work of canine charity the Dogs Trust. It’s heartstring-tugging business as usual, as Wicks meets a traumatised jack russell cross undergoing rehab for past trauma and a labrador hoping for a new life as an assistance dog. Hankies at the ready.Alexi DugginsColin from Accounts10pm, BBC TwoWe all know where this sublime romcom is going – but the journey is as much fun as the arrival. This penultimate episode once again proves that much of the show’s hilarity is mined from real emotional heft. Ash attends her grandmother’s funeral and, with feelings running high, decides it’s time for her and Gordon to face facts.PHFilm choiceNickel Boys(RaMell Ross, 2024),11.05pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenEthan Herisse, left, and Brandon Wilson in Nickel Boys.Photograph: Orion Pictures/APBased on the Pulitzer prize-winning novel by Colson Whitehead, RaMell Ross’s sublime drama is, unusually, shot from the first-person point of view. It’s a bold move that pays off, as we’re immersed in the life of Elwood (Ethan Herisse), a Black student raised by his grandma (a standout Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor) in early 60s Florida. A miscarriage of justice sends him to a brutal, segregated reform school called the Nickel Academy. His only respite is a friendship with another inmate, Turner (Brandon Wilson), as he tries to work out how to live in a world intent on beating him down.Simon WardellImmaculate(Michael Mohan, 2024),midnight, BBC ThreeThis ripe piece of nunsploitation from Michael Mohan owes a lot to Rosemary’s Baby – but the evil forces at play here are entirely Christian. Controversy magnet Sydney Sweeney plays a young American who arrives at a rural Italian convent to take her vows. Soon, however, she falls mysteriously pregnant. “It’s a miracle,” proclaim the mother superior, doctor and priests (including Money Heist’s Álvaro Morte) – but how did this virgin birth occur? With creaky doors and creepy sisters, it’s classic, bloodily accomplished horror.SWLive sportUefa Nations Leaguefootball: Northern Ireland v Hungary7.30pm, BBC Three. Ukraine v Northern Ireland is on Friday at 7.30pm on BBC Two.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Deep into the Sixties: Britain 1965-66 by David Kynaston review – a tour de force of popular history | History books | The Guardian
description: From the Beatles and the World Cup to racism and homophobia, the latest instalment in Kynaston’s series captures a society in the throes of change
Author: Blake Morrison
Headline: From the Beatles and the World Cup to racism and homophobia, the latest instalment in Kynaston’s series captures a society in the throes of change
Content: Beatles Fans.R0JEMN Police try to hold back Beatles Fans.Photograph: Album/AlamyView image in fullscreenBeatles Fans.R0JEMN Police try to hold back Beatles Fans.Photograph: Album/AlamyBook of the dayHistory booksReviewDeep into the Sixties: Britain 1965-66 by David Kynaston review – a tour de force of popular historyFrom the Beatles and the World Cup to racism and homophobia, the latest instalment in Kynaston’s series captures a society in the throes of changeBlake MorrisonMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 02.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February 1965, the civil rights activist Malcolm X visited Smethwick, in the Midlands, where the Conservative-run council was planning to buy up houses to stop the area becoming a “coloured ghetto”. He wanted to see how bad the racism was and he experienced it first-hand when refused service in a pub. White residents thought his visit a “disgusting” intrusion. Nine days later, back in the US, he was shot dead.Britain in the mid-60s is associated with Carnaby Street, the Beatles and miniskirts, not racism. But what Black people endured, from a colour bar on property to the abuse of Leeds United winger Albert Johanneson as a “golliwog”, is no less a period marker than Harold Wilson’s pipe, Twiggy’s haircut, Mary Whitehouse’s clean-up TV campaign and Bob Dylan’s use of an electric guitar. David Kynaston doesn’t underplay the excitements of the period. But he rightly emphasises that the rotten old 50s – patriarchal, homophobic, class-divided and bigoted – wouldn’t just fade away.His mammoth project, a history of Britain from 1945‑79, is now past halfway. He originally expected this volume to continue to 1967. In the event it covers just 18 months, from February 1965 to July 1966, and (with notes) runs to nearly 700 pages. The challenge is to balance an in-depth account of politics, economics, industry, education and culture with personal stories of what it was like to be there: the food you ate, the clothes you wore, the films you saw. The sources he draws on range from statistical surveys and sociological reports to political biographies, personal diaries and the grouchy letters of Philip Larkin. No living historian is as comprehensive.With much to accommodate, he relies on the semicolon for day-by-day narration: “At a Monday morning cabinet session…;” “later that afternoon …;” “on the box the same evening …;” “next morning in Manchester … ;”and so on. The sentences are long but full of humour and never dull. The high point comes with a “freewheelin’, mid-60s play list” (duly abbreviated here) that takes up five pages:Multi-flavoured Golden Wonder crisps displacing Smith’s plain; one-third of new marriages now civil marriages; pubs reluctantly installing fruit machines; Jimmy Hill’s Sky-Blue revolution at Coventry City; AA patrols no longer required to salute; picture rails, seen as dust traps, removed en masse from Victorian and Edwardian houses; Boots from 1965 at last consenting to sell condoms; arrival of open-plan offices; arrival, too, of the hot drinks vending machine; no car more iconic of modernity than the Mini Cooper …As well as giving us snippets from daily life and reminding us how nasty the 60s could be (Ian Brady, Myra Hindley and the Kray brothers), Kynaston devotes chapters to larger-scale cultural shifts, chief among them in education. Harold Wilson dreamed of “a Britain in which anyone can get to the top on merit and ability, not on social or family connections”, and the shift to comprehensive schools was integral to that. Grammar schools resisted, public schools clung on to their independence, and refusenik local authorities caricatured the change as a Nazi-like conspiracy designed to “tyrannise the minds of the young” and create “animal farms” run by state commissars. But Anthony Crosland pushed hard for the reform and it did Labour no harm in the March 1966 general election, which kept them in power with a majority of 97 seats.Polytechnics arrived too – 30 of them over the following eight years, along with the Open University. This wasn’t quite the age of social mobility it’s cracked up to be. Most children still left school at 15. Whereas 50% of high-school graduates in the US went on to university, it was still less than 6% in the UK. But expansion was under way. And many of the era’s famous names – David Bailey, Albert Finney, Michael Caine, Jean Shrimpton, Harold Evans, Terence Stamp, Cilla Black and Lulu – had working-class roots.Kynaston also explores the rebuilding of cities: slum clearances, tower blocks and (in the words of the song by pop band Unit 4 Plus 2), concrete and clay. It was a peak time for high rises, with whole streets destroyed (as if wartime bombing had resumed) and millions of people displaced to new estates. Some were grateful to escape the damp and squalor of the houses they’d been in; many were not: “I’d rather have a tent on the moors.” Kynaston detects “a certain residual arrogance” in the architects and planners. The pendulum would gradually swing against a “dim-witted adulation of Le Corbusier”, but until then the vogue was for streets in the sky.Happily, there was also a vogue for liberalisation: of birth control, abortion law, consensual sex between men, and greater opportunities for women. All were much needed: homosexuality was widely vilified; the Factories Act forbade women to do night shifts and only 80 of 1,707 candidates at the election were female; family planning clinics wouldn’t see young, unmarried women, one of whom asked agony aunt Marjorie Proops: “If a girl has intercourse, and then has nothing to do with boys for a year, can she have become a virgin again?” More surprising is to find that half the workforce in 1966 was already in the service industry and that the City of London was a hub of global power long before the 1980s.The book’s likeliest readers will be those alive at the time, whose memories will be triggered by what was new (the Post Office Tower, microwaves, Laker Airways), what needed phasing out (bottom-pinching, outdoor loos, “the brain-damaging heaviness” of leather footballs) and what songs, plays, films and television programmes had to say about contemporary life. Kynaston quotes generously from reviews, many of them more robust than you find today (“pretentious bunkum”, “inane, asinine, witless”); the BBC’s brilliant Wednesday Play series infuriated audiences and even the Beatles were denounced when awarded MBEs: “All they do is exploit a basic jungle rhythm for money.” A younger audience may be struck by the parallels between then and now: a Labour prime minister from the north, economic strife, the US in a pointless war, hostility to immigrants. We’re not facing devaluation of the pound, as Harold Wilson was. Still, the continuities stretch forward as well as back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe last section of the book is a tour de force, interspersing Kenneth Wolstenholme’s commentary on the World Cup final (“Four minutes now left to play and the crowd biting fingernails down to the knuckles”) with the reactions of those watching on television, among them young Laurence Marks, the finest of the diarists quoted in the book, who stood to lose £2/12 shillings on a bet if England won, and Kynaston himself, on his 15th birthday: “I retreat upstairs to my bedroom and play a side of a Nancy Sinatra album, reckoning it will see both me and England through.” It did. The match was a triumph and so is the book. But spare a thought for the 6,000-strong crowd in Devon who’d paid to see the Kinks perform that night. The band stayed in London till the match was over and, arriving two hours late at 11.45pm, were allowed to play for just 10 minutes.Deep into the Sixties: Britain 1965-66 by David Kynaston is published by Bloomsbury (£35). title: Range by Dorthe Nors review – an astrophysicist at odds with reality | Fiction | The Guardian
description: In the Danish writer’s latest novel, an eminent scientist withdraws to the countryside
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In the Danish writer’s latest novel, an eminent scientist withdraws to the countryside
Content: Dorthe Nors.Photograph: Lea MeilandtDorthe Nors.Photograph: Lea MeilandtFictionReviewRange by Dorthe Nors review – an astrophysicist at odds with realityIn the Danish writer’s latest novel, an eminent scientist withdraws to the countrysideCaleb KlacesMon 28 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Gunn Haven, an eminent professor of astrophysics at an urban university, moves to rural Denmark, she tells a local newspaper: “It’s to do with the sky.” From the outset of Range, Danish author Dorthe Nors’s fifth full-length novel, it is apparent this is not the whole truth. Soon after arriving, Gunn is compelled to trespass along a nearby track to look at a farmhouse with collapsed gable walls, her curiosity driven by personal interest rather than scientific inquiry. A woman pulls up in a dark blue BMW. She is dressed in “hunter’s camouflage, fleshy-faced. And ponytailed. Weapon raised: a phone, filming Gunn.” Gunn reluctantly retreats.Gunn is distracted by this woman, Krista, who works at the local potato flour factory. Gunn should be working ona general introduction to astrophysics, “the Work”. Instead, the Professor finds herself wondering what “Gable Woman” would do if she came to “the Institute”, where Gunn researches “light from the oldest galaxies”. She would draw a dick on a blackboard, Gunn imagines, “with a small titillated smile”. Gunn is more generous to promising young scientists. She pays for a former student to travel to America. Closer to home, she begins to help Jenny, the teenage daughter of her hairdresser, with a school project on black holes. Jenny is an “uneducated creature” who smells “faintly of iron”, with a “faint red to the cheeks, from shyness or cold. Oddly sexless, and she had been here before, but with her mother.”The construction of that sentence – from fragments and obtrusive conjunctions – is typical of Caroline Waight’s English translation of Range. The novel’s imagery is equally difficult to understand. During a lecture, Gunn thinks: “I’m coated in saliva.” Speculating on how a colony on Mars might develop, she says: “second generation: identical glasses and spit”.double quotation markThe scenes of awkward intimacy between Gunn and Jenny are the tender heart of Range, but they are wrapped in a predictable plotNors’s previous novel translated into English,Mirror, Shoulder, Signal, is also about a woman whose interior world is at odds with external reality. The novel, shortlisted for the 2017 International Booker prize, follows Sonja, a middle-aged translator of Swedish crime novels, as she embarks on driving lessons. Sonja makes a living finding just the right words for acts of graphic violence. The novel’s subtle humour comes in the juxtaposition between the details of this violence and the mundane challenges of Sonja’s life, such as learning to use a gated stick shift. In Range, the incongruity between Gunn and those around her feels darker and more cryptic. Gunn receives a dead bird in her post box and a “For Sale” sign is moved close to her house. These hostile acts trigger memories of Gunn’s early life, which filter through her studies of the universe’s earliest light. Gunn’s mother died in a traffic accident. Her childhood with her father was poor but loving, with “moments of equations so long they went beyond any greasy cooker hood”. This might explain why, in adult life, Gunn is so concerned with the celestial that she fails to understand more local phenomena, such as other people.Gunn’s thinking, however, is improbably imprecise. “The Work” is jumbled and vague. Gunn imagines evolution will soon mean “we’ll be born with Vaseline glands”. If this construction is distracting, the following description is dismaying: “But she didn’t get that far: she heard the car before she saw it. Rather like with thunder, and she turned back to the living room, crouched.” Gunn, an astrophysicist so renowned that her moving house is reported in the local newspaper, seems to believe that thunder is heard before lightning is seen.Gunn is interested in Jane Austen’s novel Persuasion because “the word was nice”. She buys a copy of a Danish translation and is disappointed to find a glaring mistake on page one (“1810” had become “1801”). “Such sloppiness was unforgivable, and the sentences trickled on and on, riddled with mistakes no doubt.” She impatiently flips to the end of the book and decides that the story’s moral is “to listen to Lady Russell”, a “seemingly childless” widow who is “like a mother” to the central character, Anne. There is an obvious parallel between Lady Russell and Gunn, who we learn is both mentor and mentee, taken in by the woman from whom she inherited the house. The scenes of awkward intimacy between Gunn and Jenny are the tender heart of Range, but they are wrapped in a predictable plot, leading to an unconvincing altercation with “brutish” Krista that confirms Gunn’s prejudices about rural life. I kept thinking of a line from Mirror, Shoulder, Signal, in which Sonja comments on the many people who feel forced to move from the countryside to Copenhagen: “Shaming the provinces is just a covert form of deportation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Pandora’s Legacy review – fascinating profile of silent film legend GW Pabst | Movies | The Guardian
description: Through intimate letters and family interviews, this probing documentary about the Austrian film-maker reveals a complicated figure
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Through intimate letters and family interviews, this probing documentary about the Austrian film-maker reveals a complicated figure
Content: Wealth of archive material … Pandora’s Legacy.Photograph: Max BernerView image in fullscreenWealth of archive material … Pandora’s Legacy.Photograph: Max BernerMoviesReviewPandora’s Legacy review – fascinating profile of silent film legend GW PabstThrough intimate letters and family interviews, this probing documentary about the Austrian film-maker reveals a complicated figurePhuong LeMon 28 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtitan of silent cinema, Austrian director GW Pabst left behind a treasure trove of classics. Working in WeimarGermany, Pabst gave Greta Garbo her second ever lead role in The Joyless Street (1925), and propelled Louise Brooks to international stardom with Pandora’s Box (1929) and Diary of a Lost Girl (1929). Attentive to the marginalised elements of society, these early triumphs exemplified the kind of free-spirited film-making that flourished before the rise of the Nazi regime. Faced with this colossal legacy, Angela Christlieb’s probing documentary takes a more winding path through Pabst’s personal archive. Through intimate letters, family albums, and interviews with his descendants, the film foregrounds the man behind the images, while bringing another figure into the spotlight: Gertrude Pabst, the director’s wife of more than 40 years.Far from a hagiographic portrait, Christlieb’s film reveals Pabst to be a complicated and patriarchal figure. His grandchildren – Marion, Daniel and Ben – describe the great film-maker as a distant figure, who instilled fear rather than love in his two sons. Pabst’s films have been praised for their modern and strong-willed female characters, yet in private he forbade Gertrude from pursuing her own acting aspirations. She also reluctantly underwent numerous abortions – seven in total – so as not to derail her husband’s career.Christlieb often uses scenes from Pabst’s films to illustrate these family frictions, an approach that feels strained and contrived; these sequences showcase the brilliance of the director’s filmography, but risk drawing a simplistic biographical link between his work and his life, undermining both the richness of his creative visions and the difficulties endured by those in his orbit. Meanwhile the detours into Marion, Daniel and Ben’s careers are interesting, but they distract from Gertrude’s story, which could have merited more screen time. These structural missteps aside, the wealth of archive material is fascinating to behold, revealing a hidden side to a much-discussed film legend.Pandora’s Legacy is on True Story from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsSilent filmGermanyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Should have garnered the actor an Oscar’: why Liar Liar is my feelgood movie | Jim Carrey | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers paying tribute to the films they watch when they need a lift is an appreciation of Jim Carrey’s manic 90s comedy
Author: Rob LeDonne
Headline: The latest in our series of writers paying tribute to the films they watch when they need a lift is an appreciation of Jim Carrey’s manic 90s comedy
Content: Jim Carrey and Jennifer Tilly in Liar Liar.Photograph: Moviestore Collection/REXView image in fullscreenJim Carrey and Jennifer Tilly in Liar Liar.Photograph: Moviestore Collection/REXMy feelgood movieJim Carrey‘Should have garnered the actor an Oscar’: why Liar Liar is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers paying tribute to the films they watch when they need a lift is an appreciation of Jim Carrey’s manic 90s comedyRob LeDonneMon 28 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo be completely honest, whenever anybody asks what my favorite movies are, my list has some typical standbys: Goodfellas and It’s a Wonderful Life among them. The holiday classic National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation is another. But there’s one feelgood fave on my list that always surprises people: Jim Carrey’s 1997 blockbuster Liar Liar.‘Still feel a jolt of joy’: why Dirty Dancing is my feelgood movieRead moreThe movie (for the lack of a better word) lies on the bedrock of a simple premise: a lawyer and doting father is physically unable to tell an untruth due to a birthday wish. In the hands of a less competent creative team and cast,Liar Liarwould have been yet another forgettable piece of 90s comedy junk; destined for the bottom of a discount VHS bin, forgotten as the years trudged on. But largely thanks to an unbelievable performance courtesy of Carrey, who was working with a smart and peppy script, the film ascends into rarefied air.The bellylaugh-o-meter breaks its springs on a regular basis throughout its brisk 86-minute runtime. In fact, it’s on par, or even surpassing, fellow comedy powerhouses such as Airplane! and The Naked Gun when it comes to the sheer volume of gags, set pieces and jokes. Tom Shadyac, the director, who previously directed Carrey in his 1993 breakout Ace Ventura: Pet Detective, wisely unleashes Carrey, who spins out and around the scenery like the Tasmanian Devil, remarkably combining such a manic and energetic performance with one grounded in pure emotion.At the center of Carrey’s character, Fletcher Reede, is love for his son; with themes of fatherhood and parenthood the beating heart of the film. There’s inherent likability inside the hamminess, a trick Carrey delivers as if that combination is almost totally impossible. What Carrey pulls off is a performance that, in a fair world, should have garnered the actor an Oscar. Comedic turns, and comedy films in general, are arguably much more difficult to pull off as opposed to the understated and moody dramas the Academy likes to honor.However, it was quickly proven that even when Carrey transformed himself into a formidable dramatic actor with 1999’s Man on the Moon, the Academy snubbed that too. (Thankfully, he was indeed nominated for a Golden Globe for Liar Liar).What defines a feelgood movie, along with being a comfy joy to experience, is its bevy of rewatchable scenes: the kind that make you stop in your tracks when flicking through TV channels. (The Ringer’s Bill Simmons devised a whole delicious podcast about this). Liar Liar serves up can’t-miss-’em scenes in spades. In one of them, Carrey, realizing he’s cursed to tell the truth, tries to say that a blue pen is red but can’t bring himself to, later revealing he put himself through a physical wringer. (He latersaidthe entire self-tussle had one simple direction: Fletcher “beats himself up”). Who can also forget Carrey’s epic meltdown after he’s baited into joining a stuffy meeting at the law firm and roasts everybody in sight? “You’ve got your head so far up Mr Alan’s ass, I can’t tell where you end and he begins!” The final courtroom showdown is another gem, rivaling any scene in A Few Good Men.I vividly remember watching its epic LAX-set grand finale where Carrey’s Reede hijacks a mobile airplane stairway as his son Max is about to fly out of California and wowed by the hilarious spectacle of the stunt in a movie that, up until that point, consisted of scenes in courtrooms, offices and homes. But by the time we wrap things up with Carrey battered and bruised, albeit with his son back, the bloopers inserted at the end of the film demonstrating the insanity Carrey unleashed on set, were the cherry on top of the whole shebang, and stand as one of the rare cases of a gag reel being actually funny as opposed to a series of awkward flubs.A cozy rewatch also reminds one of how a film with as many pure chuckles as Liar Liar is a nonexistent entity at theaters in the modern era. It’s almost as if recent studio comedies such as One Night Only and Anyone But You forgot they were supposed to elicit laughs, instead of subtle smirks at best. It’s also the type of movie one can take away lessons from at any point in one’s life. When I was 10 and watched Liar Liar, I obviously gravitated towards the kid’s perspective. But as the decades roll on, you can glean something from it at every stage of life.It’s an underdog of a feelgood movie, and one that gets lost in the hubbub of fellow Carrey classics such as Dumb and Dumber. But whether the headlines got you down, it’s a rainy night or the family’s simply getting together, one can’t go wrong with popping on Carrey’s unreal tour de force in Liar Liar. And that’s the truth, so help me God.Liar Liar is available on Netflix in the US, NOW TV in the UK and Paramount+ and Binge in AustraliaThis article was amended on 28 September 2026. An earlier version said that in Liar Liar Jim Carrey tries to say that a blue pen is black; in fact, he says it is red.Explore more on these topicsJim CarreyMy feelgood movieLiar LiarComedy filmsComedyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Just Play Dead review – Samuel L Jackson and Eva Green punch up switchback crime caper  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Jackson and Green just about manage to distract viewers from the sub-par Tarantinoesque flourishes, confusing plot points and tired stereotypes
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Jackson and Green just about manage to distract viewers from the sub-par Tarantinoesque flourishes, confusing plot points and tired stereotypes
Content: ‘Faintly engaging’ … Samuel L Jackson and Eva Green in Just Play Dead.Photograph: Rico Torres/Safe Place Films Ltd.View image in fullscreen‘Faintly engaging’ … Samuel L Jackson and Eva Green in Just Play Dead.Photograph: Rico Torres/Safe Place Films Ltd.MoviesReviewJust Play Dead review – Samuel L Jackson and Eva Green punch up switchback crime caperJackson and Green just about manage to distract viewers from the sub-par Tarantinoesque flourishes, confusing plot points and tired stereotypesPhil HoadMon 28 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaving shot five films since 2020, 82-year-old Martin Campbell is a certified member of the post-retirement director’s club that includes Ridley Scott, Martin Scorsese, Woody Allen et al.Samuel L Jackson(a mere 77) sports his worst hairdo since Jackie Brown – a grey, crimped ponytail with an undercut – in this overworked crime caper, though he is on positively cuddly form by his standards.Interrupting his retirement on a Spanish-speaking Caribbean island with the odd poisoning (seen in the intro), kingpin Jack Wolfe (Jackson) is getting antsy. Afraid the law is close behind him, he hatches a scheme with his philandering wife Nora (Eva Green): help him frame her surfer lover Chad (Jason Fernández) for his supposed murder, and they will split the big-bucks insurance payout. He covers his back for the possibility she might do him in for real by recording her saying as much. But she ropes Chad anyway into her murder conspiracy, plotting to let him take the fall – or perhaps her detective bit on the side Dani (Eoin Macken) will get there first.Trying to follow the particulars will probably age you by a couple of decades – especially once Jack turns the tables on Nora by approaching Chad with his own proposition. Not that following it is really the point: this throwback Elmore Leonard-esque business is the backdrop as the married couple tear strips out of each other. But lacking much mordant snap in the dialogue, and dependent on a trio of over-familiar stereotypes – droll gangster mastermind, uber-MILF gold-digger and airhead surfer – it’s never quite as funny or sharp as it thinks it is.It has its moments, though; mostly when the seasoned players really get their claws into the hapless Chad. First Green, her natural bearing making Nora a proper piece of work, hammers it home that her scheme is an offer he can’t refuse; then Jackson chivvies him into signing up as his improbable adopted son. But by kicking off with some Tarantinoesque ring-a-ding non-linearity, before chucking in a few imagined homicide scenarios for the climax, then gratuitously retconning the ending, Just Play Dead strains a lot only to wind up faintly engaging. Reclining on his wicker lounge furniture, pulling the strings over a cocktail, Jackson is like the Jackanory narrator of this self-satisfied enterprise.Just Play Dead is on digital platforms from 5 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersSamuel L JacksonEva GreenCrime filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kikuyu Land review – the colonial-era misery behind our morning cup of tea | Movies | The Guardian
description: The impact of colonial then corporate agricultural development is unravelled in a sobering documentary that takes a dramatic turn when a family secret is discovered
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: The impact of colonial then corporate agricultural development is unravelled in a sobering documentary that takes a dramatic turn when a family secret is discovered
Content: Traditions that span centuries … Kikuyu Land.Photograph: Andrew H BrownView image in fullscreenTraditions that span centuries … Kikuyu Land.Photograph: Andrew H BrownMoviesReviewKikuyu Land review – the colonial-era misery behind our morning cup of teaThe impact of colonial then corporate agricultural development is unravelled in a sobering documentary that takes a dramatic turn when a family secret is discoveredPhuong LeMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe central highlands of Kenya are renowned for their lush tea plantations, which stretch as far as the eye can see. Most of the field workers come from the Kikuyu community, whose farming traditions span centuries. In Andrew Harrison Brown and Bea Wangondu’s sobering documentary, these resplendent vistas are also enshrouded in misery. Opening with a televised speech byEvelyn Baring, the colonial governor of Kenya during the 1950s, the film lays out the imperialist impetus behind Britain’s agricultural development of the country. The Kikuyu people were stripped of their ancestral lands, their labour extracted to enrich their colonisers. This system of inequality continues until now, with multinational corporations taking up the playbook of exploitation left by colonial control.An investigative journalist, Wangondu also appears on screen weaving together a multitude of narratives. There’s the decades-long struggle for justice undertaken by Mr Mungai, a pastor and activist who has fought numerous court cases to reclaim his family land. Wangondu talks to plantation workers of past and present, whose harrowing ordeals of physical and sexual violence have been swept under the carpet by both corporate indifference and government corruption. We also hear from an officer in the national intelligence service, who reveals the gruesome methods used by the state to dispose of its critics. These interviews conjure a menacing atmosphere of intimidation and retaliation, from which there seems no way out.The film then takes a dramatic turn when Wangondu discovers an uncomfortable family secret: her beloved grandfather, a well-respected landowner, was also a perpetrator of colonial abuse. The shattering revelation not only collapses the distance between Wangondu and her subjects, but also points to other forms of complicity. For lovers of tea worldwide, Kikuyu Land suggests that ordinary consumers take a cold hard look at where their product comes from.Kikuyu Land is in UK cinemas from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsKenyaColonialismTeareviewsShareReuse this content

title: The First Year (of the Gaza Genocide in the Media) review – bold but uneven focus on Palestinian voices | Stage | The Guardian
description: Passionate production based on testimonies from Gaza poses many questions regarding Israel’s actions but gets overwhelmed by fact-delivery and form-switches
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Passionate production based on testimonies from Gaza poses many questions regarding Israel’s actions but gets overwhelmed by fact-delivery and form-switches
Content: ‘Should be admired for its ambition’ … The First Year.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreen‘Should be admired for its ambition’ … The First Year.Photograph: Alex BrennerStageReviewThe First Year (of the Gaza Genocide in the Media) review – bold but uneven focus on Palestinian voicesNew Diorama theatre, LondonPassionate production based on testimonies from Gaza poses many questions regarding Israel’s actions but gets overwhelmed by fact-delivery and form-switchesArifa AkbarMon 28 Sep 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do news outlets cover war in a region where independent foreign journalists are blocked entry? What to make of the reports of theIsrael-Gaza warby the western press in relation to the livestreamed footage on our phones?These are some of the questions that come to mind when thinking about Israel’s actions in Gaza, triggered by Hamas’s attack on 7 October 2023, and bringing apocalyptic brutality and death tolls. This 90-minute production by British-Romanian collectiveBÉZNĂ theatreasks many more in its polyphony of satire, song, graphics, snatches of history, absurdism and sincerity. The four-strong cast – comprising Maryam Abu Khaled, Sara Masry, Luca Kamleh Chapman and Sofia – juggle it all in a series of mini lectures, dramatised dialogue, poetic monologues and meta theatre.Written and directed by Sînziana Cojocărescu, it is a production of utmost integrity, centring Palestinian voices, including short excerpts from works by playwrights Ahmed Masoud and Hannah Khalil, and anonymous writings. They hint at the difficulty in bringing this show to a stage, mentioning two PR companies that shied away.For a play that questions the framing of facts and stories, there is formal innovation around the presentation of these here. But the drama is beached by its own welter of facts and its experimental switches in form. The latter leave you stranded, some scenes so elliptical you are unsure of who is talking and what is happening, with the tone wobbling between plaintive laments, comedy and justified outrage.The trigger warnings, spoken into a microphone, go on for quite a while, and the dramatised material, when it comes, is horrific, such as the report of an Israeli strike first from the point of view of a western marine rescuing a hostage who relays a narrative of squeaky-clean heroism, followed by a report of the same event from the point of view of Palestinian civilians who witness a massacre around them, air-bushed out of the first report. An actor climbs into a glass box beneath the stage, in Jida Akil’s set design (immensely atmospheric, if underused, with mounds of earth) as if hiding from war terror. “I woke up this morning to nothing and fled to nothing,” says one character. We hear thestory of a Palestinian man with Down’s syndrome, mauled by an Israeli army dog and locked in a room by IDF soldiers, whose body was found decomposing by his family.These moments are powerful, bringing the play to life, but it is a shame that there is not enough of them and it seems less a drama than a static narration, despite the (sometimes abstruse) movement. A blizzard of facts and figures including the daily death tolls of journalists and of Palestinians are projected on the walls, as well as context that conveys the actions of the Israeli military. But these come and go in flashes, too fast to absorb or even read. Performers bring verve but are sometimes halting. The overall effect is disjointed and convoluted, with so much hard-hitting material but not enough clear-sighted focus.So its power is drowned out, yet still this is a production that should be admired for its ambition to say something profound in a fresh and radical way. It feels like a show still finding its centre, playing out prematurely. It is one I would like to see, in due course, containing just as much dimension and depth but with greater clarity and rigour alongside it.AtNew Diorama theatre, London, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatrePolitical theatreIsrael-Gaza warreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Happy Days review – Beckett’s bewitching heroine buries her existential fears | Stage | The Guardian
description: In what feels now like a premonition of the climate crisis, Siobhán Redmond is compelling as the everywoman putting on a brave face in an unforgiving landscape
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: In what feels now like a premonition of the climate crisis, Siobhán Redmond is compelling as the everywoman putting on a brave face in an unforgiving landscape
Content: A twinkle in her eyes … Siobhán Redmond (Winnie), with Forbes Masson (Willie) in the background, in Happy Days at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanView image in fullscreenA twinkle in her eyes … Siobhán Redmond (Winnie), with Forbes Masson (Willie) in the background, in Happy Days at Pitlochry Festival theatre.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanStageReviewHappy Days review – Beckett’s bewitching heroine buries her existential fearsPitlochry Festival theatreIn what feels now like a premonition of the climate crisis, Siobhán Redmond is compelling as the everywoman putting on a brave face in an unforgiving landscapeMark FisherMon 28 Sep 2026 08.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSamuel Beckett’s play is always staged with a radiant brightness. It is hot enough to set a parasol alight. If, on its premiere in 1961, that resonated with audience anxieties about nuclear Armageddon, in 2026, it feels like a premonition of the climate crisis. Is this how it ends?Emma Bailey’s set is a dune of bleached-white sand, clumps of sea grass forcing their way through into a scorched environment, baked by Colin Grenfell’s lighting. When Forbes Masson crawls out of his hole as Willie, keeping his back to us, he reveals nothing more than his neck and shoulders, raw and sunburnt, his scarred head protected by a handkerchief (used).View image in fullscreenTremendous vocal range … Siobhán Redmond.Photograph: Tommy Ga-Ken WanNot that Siobhán Redmond would admit to such discomfort. As Winnie, she is irrepressibly cheery, a woman incapable of entertaining a negative thought without batting it back with a positive spin. Even when she talks about a “black night without end” in a second half of even greater bleakness, she maintains a genteel smile and a twinkle in her eyes.By that point, twinkle is pretty much all her eyes can do. Buried deep and then deeper still in this unforgiving landscape, she is deprived of movement and not totally unwillingly: Willie’s carnal grunts are uncouth, humanity at its most base and fundamental, where she is all bodiless elegance. She needs him as an audience – an actor is nothing if she is not seen and heard – but is faintly alarmed by his physical presence.With eyeshadow to match her turquoise ballgown, her crystal earrings and black fascinator in check, even if her blonde bob is dishevelled, she is a figure in denial of her circumstances. She would never mention the arrival of a migraine, but celebrates its passing with elan, an everywoman putting on a brave face in preference to existential despair.Showing tremendous vocal range, from girlish singsong to notes of dark resonance, Redmond is compelling in Roxana Silbert’s carefully controlled production. In a play that lands somewhere between the time-watching of Waiting for Godot and the mutual dependency ofEndgame, she is a bewitching metaphor for the futility of existence and the urgency to carry on regardless.At Pitlochry Festival theatre until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatrePitlochry Festival theatreSamuel BeckettreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Paraorchestra; Sinfonietta/Jonny Greenwood review – Reich’s kaleidoscopic music bursts into life | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Paraorchestra’s immersive performance of Music for 18 Musicians was immaculate and exhilarating; London Sinfonietta and the Radiohead guitarist’s vibrant tribute to the almost 90-year-old composer followed
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Paraorchestra’s immersive performance of Music for 18 Musicians was immaculate and exhilarating; London Sinfonietta and the Radiohead guitarist’s vibrant tribute to the almost 90-year-old composer followed
Content: ‘Grins on faces’ … Paraorchestra get the Steve Reich party started.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorView image in fullscreen‘Grins on faces’ … Paraorchestra get the Steve Reich party started.Photograph: Siân O’ConnorClassical musicReviewParaorchestra; Sinfonietta/Jonny Greenwood review – Reich’s kaleidoscopic music bursts into lifeSouthbank Centre, LondonParaorchestra’s immersive performance of Music for 18 Musicians was immaculate and exhilarating; London Sinfonietta and the Radiohead guitarist’s vibrant tribute to the almost 90-year-old composer followedClive PagetMon 28 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo birthdays were celebrated at Southbank Centre’s Steve Reich-fest. First,the composer himself, a supremely influential artist who has shifted the classical music dial over decades with his evolving yet instantly recognisable soundworld. He turns 90 on 3 October. And then there was Music for 18 Musicians, one of his signature works, which notches up a half-century this year. An immersive performance of the latter invited the audience to mingle with an ensemble dotted around the Clore Ballroom, the collective grins on faces proof positive of the work’s enduring power to raise the spirits.View image in fullscreen‘Clean-as-a-whistle technique’ … Jonny Greenwood alongside the London Sinfonietta.Photograph: seb.gardner/seb gardnerDoing the honours wasParaorchestra, Charles Hazlewood’s enterprising collective of disabled and non-disabled musicians, who brought Reich’s kaleidoscopic music to life with ironclad discipline. Freed from fixed seats, the itinerant audience peered at musicians on podiums as if they were objects in an exhibition, marvelling at the precision of polyrhythmic marimba players, or grooving in a central mosh pit with a flexuous quintet of dancers who persuaded children and grandparents alike to go with the flow. Line dancing, disco lights – this exhilarating performance had it all.Twenty minutes to catch the breath and it was upstairs to the Festival Hall for the London Sinfonietta and guitaristJonny Greenwood. If the formal atmosphere was more subdued and the hall less intimate, the playing, under conductor Chloe Rooke, was crisp and controlled. Pulse, written in 2015, saw canonic wind and string melodies spun out over piano-led ostinatos in one of the composer’s more relaxed works. Greenwood played electric bass, providing a neat link with Radio Rewrite, a Sinfonietta commission from 2013, in which Reich partly absorbs and partly riffs on a pair of songs by Radiohead.Opening the second half, Greenwood brought clean-as-a-whistle technique and a distinctive personality (not always associated with this composer’s music) to Electric Counterpoint. A tenacious performance pitted live electric guitar against his own pre-recorded version of Reich’s original backing track. To finish, the Sinfonietta gave a gritty account of City Life. Sampling keyboards introduced urban sounds, from car horns and door slams to heartbeats and police sirens, into the orchestral mix in a kinetic tribute to Reich’s native New York.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicSteve ReichThe London SinfoniettareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Obama and Tom Hanks have an inspirational chat: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Daring to defy the norms of political lobbying, the ex-US president is becoming a podcast mainstay – and is opening up about the books that inspired him. Plus, is the Richard Gere gerbil rumour true?
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Daring to defy the norms of political lobbying, the ex-US president is becoming a podcast mainstay – and is opening up about the books that inspired him. Plus, is the Richard Gere gerbil rumour true?
Content: Lit chit-chat … Barack Obama.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty Images for NetflixView image in fullscreenLit chit-chat … Barack Obama.Photograph: Arturo Holmes/Getty Images for NetflixBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioObama and Tom Hanks have an inspirational chat: best podcasts of the weekDaring to defy the norms of political lobbying, the ex-US president is becoming a podcast mainstay – and is opening up about the books that inspired him. Plus, is the Richard Gere gerbil rumour true?Hannah J Davies,Alexi DugginsandPhil HarrisonMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 06.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekA Great Book With Barack ObamaBarack Obama is now a podcast mainstay (good on him for not just defaulting to questionable lobbying). His latest Audibleshow– via his and Michelle’s company, Higher Ground – is a six-parter about the books that have inspired him, from James Baldwin to John le Carré. The first guest is Tom Hanks, who joins him for a frank chat on parenting and family, prompted by Marilynne Robinson’s Pulitzer-winning novel Gilead.Hannah J DaviesAudible, out nowPublic ApologyMilo Edwards hosts this livelynew series(with Sophie Garrad and Ed Campbell) which explores public scandals. The range of subject matters is illustrated by the first two: the Profumo affair and the boyband Blue. Why do some scandals ruin lives while others seem to be forgotten almost instantly?Phil HarrisonWidely available, episodes weeklyGerbilView image in fullscreenRumour has it … Richard Gere.Photograph: Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesDid Richard Gere really arrive at hospital asking for the removal of a gerbil he’d somehow fired up his own bum?Thisattempt to apply some rigorous journalism to the infamous rumour meets Gere superfans, tries to track down ex-doctors and meets a gay rights activist – who explains the way very similar rumours have a track record of being used as homophobic slurs.Alexi DugginsWidely available, episodes weeklyReaching OutThis Futuropodcastwas called “the best new show I’ve heard in years” by This American Life’s Ira Glass. It’s high praise, but understandable: Sayre Quevedo’s very personal story of his search for his absent dad is poetic, profound and witty, spiked with pandemic loneliness, sibling love and queer yearning.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDeath of an ArtistThis grippingshowopens with unanswered voicemail messages that get increasingly frantic – until someone picks up the phone and confirms that its owners are dead. Slow Burn host Leon Neyfakh and his journalist wife Alice Gregory tell the tale of Petra and Michael Mathers, a celebrated kids’ book creator and photographer whose double suicide in their 70s shocked the world.ADWidely available, episodes weeklyWhat are you listening to this week?
