title: ‘The champagne of pale ales’: my search for the perfect kölsch beer in Cologne | Travel | The Guardian
description: ‘Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion’ in Cologne, and it’s only brewed in and around the German city. But which of the many beautiful, storied beer halls serves up the best?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion’ in Cologne, and it’s only brewed in and around the German city. But which of the many beautiful, storied beer halls serves up the best?
Content: Two beer stangen – the narrow glasses designed to be drained quickly, then swiftly replaced.Photograph: Jotily/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenTwo beer stangen – the narrow glasses designed to be drained quickly, then swiftly replaced.Photograph: Jotily/Getty Images/iStockphotoTravel‘The champagne of pale ales’: my search for the perfect kölsch beer in Cologne‘Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion’ in Cologne, and it’s only brewed in and around the German city. But which of the many beautiful, storied beer halls serves up the best?Scott AntcliffeMon 28 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a saying in Cologne, repeated with the mild smugness of people who know they’re right: kölsch is the only culture you can drink. It sounds like a line lifted straight from the tourist board’s brochure. Then you spend a day working your way around the city’s traditional brewhouses and realise it’s a statement of fact.Since 1997, kölsch has held a protected geographical indication within the EU, guaranteeing that any beer bearing the name is brewed within 50km of the city and made strictly to the Kölsch-Konvention. That agreement, signed in 1986, defined the style as “a light, highly attenuated, hop-accentuated, clear, top-fermenting ‘vollbier’ [full-beer]”, restricting production exclusively to the local area. It is, in effect, the champagne of pale ales: locally adored and tied to a city that has always insisted on doing things its own way.double quotation markYou never order a second; you never need to. They only stop when you place your beer mat on top of your glassThe delivery is as ritualised as the brewing itself. You sit. Aköbes– the traditionally deadpan, blue-aproned brewhouse waiter – arrives carrying akranz(a circular tray) holding a ring ofstangen, narrow 200ml glasses designed to keep the beer cold and effervescent long enough for you to drain one before the next takes its place. You drink. He marks a tally on your beer mat with a stub of pencil. You never order a second; you never need to. The conveyor belt only stops when you place your beer mat on top of your glass.Ten hours, seven brewhouses and an inadvisable number of tally marks later, I had formed some very firm opinions about Cologne’s legendary liquid culture.Brauhaus Früh am DomView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeThe twin spires of Cologne cathedral are visible from the doorway of this brewhouse. So, unfortunately, is the gift shop and a tour group from Ohio. Früh am Dom, arguably the most internationally recognisable kölsch brand, is housed in a sprawling warren of vaulted dining rooms, cellars and long oak bars. It is enormous and boisterous, yet the kölsch, poured at speed to a rotating cast of daytrippers, lacks the crisp clarity found elsewhere. Being on the cathedral’s doorstep makes this prime real estate, but the footfall turns the room into something closer to a transit lounge, where most visitors drop in for a quick photo with theirstangebefore rushing off.4.5/10,€2.50Brauhaus SionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeFounded in 1912 and heavily renovated since, Sion merges a contemporary interior with old-world charm. The result is the slickest room on this list: warm mood lighting, clean lines and a menu that reaches beyond the usual brewhouse staples of fried pork and potatoes. The kölsch itself is technically flawless and refreshing, though it lacks the rustic bite of the city’s smaller producers. It’s a fine spot for a proper sit-down dinner rather than a session – and even the köbes here shows genuine warmth, a demeanour that feels either refreshing or faintly suspicious depending on how strictly you hold to Rhenish brusqueness.6/10,€2.60Brauhaus PäffgenView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mauritius Images /AlamyBeyond the tourist centre, in the lively and historic Friesenviertel district, is the hallowed Päffgen. Operating on Friesenstraße since 1883, this is one of the lasthausbrauereien(brew pubs) that refuses to bottle for supermarket shelves; if you want Päffgen, you come here or haul a wooden keg home yourself. The beer is tapped straight from wooden barrels on the counter, giving a pour with a floral, grassy hop aroma, a hint of stone fruit and a crisp bitter finish. The room feels untouched by time – look out for the old woodenbeichtstuhl(“confessional”), the elevated booth where the innkeeper once oversaw the floor and counted the day’s takings. One of the köbesse, sliding a freshstangeacross the counter without breaking stride, put it more bluntly than any brochure could: “Kölsch is not a drink, it is a religion. And this is the church.” With its gruff, lightning-fast staff and a leafy beer garden out the back, Päffgen is the gold standard of kölsch culture.9.5/10,€2.60Peters BrauhausView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Kolnik/AlamyTucked into the historic old town, Peters is what the cathedral-adjacent halls wish they were. It strikes the finest balance in central Cologne, fiercely popular with local people while remaining welcoming to passing travellers. The interior is gorgeous – stained-glass skylights throwing amber light across scrubbed, decades-old wooden tables, dark wainscoting framing the chatter of the room. The kölsch is beautifully balanced: smooth, clean and poured properly cold. We might have come at a bad time, though, as it wasn’t particularly busy and lacked atmosphere.7/10,€2.50skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrauerei zur MalzmühleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeSitting on the edge of the historic Heumarkt, Malzmühle is the second-oldest brewery in Cologne, operating on this spot since 1858. Destroyed almost entirely in the second world war, only the stone portal survived; you now pass through that same archway into a sprawling hall of rustic brickwork and heavy oak benches. Malzmühle brews Mühlen Kölsch, a pour favoured by the former US president Bill Clinton, who declared “Ich bin ein Kölsch” on a visit in 1999. It is slightly darker and maltier than its peers, with a gentle honey note against a solid bitter backbone. The atmosphere is unapologetically noisy and authentic – a meeting ground where workers in hi-vis vests share benches with executives in suits. We spoke to one of theköbesse, Carl, who told us he’d worked here for 38 years: “This is the place to be. These walls have seen so much and heard so many conversations. I wouldn’t work anywhere else.”8.5/10,€2.50Gaffel am DomView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeGaffel is a heavy hitter among local people, distributed widely across the city’s bars and football stadiums. Its flagship hall, opposite the central station, is handsome and impeccably run, with high ceilings and sweeping arches giving it real metropolitan energy. The kölsch is consistently good – bright, sharply carbonated and noticeably hop-forward, exactly as the Konvention prescribes. Knowing this same beer is sold at the gate in Cologne Bonn airport slightly undercuts the local romance, though; it’s reliable in a high-volume, commercial way. The kitchen redeems it somewhat with a stellarhimmel unääd– crispy black pudding with smooth mash and stewed apples – comfort food good enough to justify the visit alone.6.5/10,€2.50Brauhaus Sünner im WalfischView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Scott AntcliffeDown a cobbled alley in the old town, Sünner im Walfisch is pure historical theatre. Housed in a striking 17th-century step-gabled building, dismantled and rebuilt brick by brick on its current site, it serves as the old town outpost for Sünner, Cologne’s oldest operating kölsch brewery. Inside, narrow timber-framed rooms and low ceilings transport you back to medieval Rhineland. The beer is fantastic – crisp and dry with a peppery hop finish that makes it dangerously easy to drink – and it’s quieter and more intimate than the echoing halls near the station, its köbesse still delivering drinks with a wink of humour. A favourite for decor and character, if not quite for atmosphere.8/10,€2.50Scott Antcliffe’stravel to Cologne wasprovided byVikingas part ofits8-dayRhine Getaway,from £1,695Explore more on these topicsTravelCologne holidaysGerman food and drinkFood and drinkGermany holidaysEurope holidaysCity breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sanjana Modha’s quick and easy recipe for baked beans butter masala  | Food | The Guardian
description: Transform two tins of baked beans into this creamy curry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Transform two tins of baked beans into this creamy curry
Content: Sanjana Modha’s baked beans butter masala.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenSanjana Modha’s baked beans butter masala.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.Quick and easyFoodSanjana Modha’s quick and easy recipe for baked beans butter masalaTransform two tins of baked beans into this creamy currySanjana ModhaMon 28 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMasala baked beans, tadka baked beans, curried baked beans, spicy baked beans; all avatars of spice-laced baked beans are a mainstay of British Asian kitchens. We were raised on this stuff – use as a toastie filler, to smother jacket potatoes, or scoop them up with roti. Enter baked beans butter masala. With a sharp sweetness, a versatile tin of baked beans already has all the foundations required to build a brilliant butter masala, so all we’re doing is dressing them up. I like to think of it as though the beans are donning a frock made of all the good stuff: butter, cream and spices.Baked beans butter masalaThis creamy, dreamy baked bean curry is delicious with naan or served as any of the suggestions mentioned above. To make this vegan, use your favourite plant-based butter and an oat- or soya-based cream. Coconut milk also works in place of cream.Prep15 minCook20 minServes42tbsp salted butter, plus a little extra to garnish (optional)1 small brown onion, peeled and finely chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped1tsp minced ginger1tbsp tomato puree2410gtins baked beans½tsp ground turmeric1tsp kashmiri chilli powder4 greencardamom pods, smashed open and seeds finely ground3tsp garam masala1 small pinch salt150mlsinglecream2tsp dried fenugreek leaves2tbsp chopped coriander, including stalks, to garnishMelt the butter in a medium saucepan, then add the onion and saute for three to five minutes, until soft and translucent. Add the garlic, ginger and tomato puree, and cook for another minute, until aromatic.Add all the baked beans, along with all the sauce from the cans, stir in the turmeric, chilli powder, ground cardamom, garam masala and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.Stir in the cream (reserve a few tablespoons to serve), cover the pan with a lid and leave the curry to come to a simmer over a low heat for 10 minutes, stirring often to stop the beans sticking to the base of the pan.Take off the lid and add the dried fenugreek leaves, rubbing them between your palms to break them into a fine powder. Swirl in the reserved cream and, if using, the extra butter, garnish with the coriander and serve.This recipe is an edited extract from Modern Masala, by Sanjana Modha, published by Quadrille at £25. To order a copy for £22.50, go toguardianbookshop.com.Explore more on these topicsFoodQuick and easyBeans, pulses and legumesIndian food and drinkVegetablesHerbs and spicesCurryrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Rice ‘polenta’ with sausage sauce and rice with pork, lemon and saffron: Pasta Grannies’ Italian rice recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Spoons at the ready for 83-year-old Maria’s rustic risotto with pork and saffron, and Rita’s polenta-style rice with a punchy sauce
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Spoons at the ready for 83-year-old Maria’s rustic risotto with pork and saffron, and Rita’s polenta-style rice with a punchy sauce
Content: Pasta Grannies’ Sardinian rice with pork and saffron.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenPasta Grannies’ Sardinian rice with pork and saffron.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodRice ‘polenta’ with sausage sauce and rice with pork, lemon and saffron: Pasta Grannies’ Italian rice recipesSpoons at the ready for 83-year-old Maria’s rustic risotto with pork and saffron, and Rita’s polenta-style rice with a punchy sauceVicky BennisonMon 28 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf I were to say “Italian rice”, you might well think “risotto” and “the Po Valley”. However, these two recipes come from Sardinia and the Marche, mainly because I wanted to share a few easy, not-laden-with-rules Italian rice dishes.Maria’s riso con maiale e zafferano (rice with pork and saffron)Eighty-three-year-old Maria was widowed young and, to make ends meet, set up an agriturismo dining space in her home near Oristano in Sardinia’s rice-growing heartland. This rustic risotto with a wonderful combination of flavours was one of her customers’ favourites, and it’s a great recipe if you are nervous about making a classic risotto with all its rules.Prep20 minStock2 hr+(optional)Cook1 hr 20 minServes4For the stock (optional)1kg pork bones1 sun-dried tomato, or ½ tsp tomato puree1 onion, peeled2 celery sticks1 carrotFor the riceExtra-virgin olive oil1 carrot, dicedSea salt andblack pepper500gpork shoulder steak, or other stewing pork, cut into 1cm chunks1 onion, peeled and chopped1 sprig fresh rosemary1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed1 sun-dried tomato, minced (optional; see method)3½ tbsp white wine(vernaccia, if you can find it, otherwise any dry white wine)100gpassata750ml hot meat stock, homemade (see above and method) or bought in250garborio riceZest of 1 lemon, ½ finely grated, the rest pared off in strips and julienned20.1g sachets saffron powder, or 1 pinch saffron threads soaked in hot water or stock50gpecorino, grated, plus extra to serveIf you’re making your own stock, simmer the pork bones in plenty of water with the tomato, onion, celery and carrot for several hours, until deeply flavoured. Strain and keep hot if you are going to use it immediately.Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pan, then fry the diced carrot with a pinch of salt until it starts to soften. Add the diced pork, fry, stirring, until browned all over, then add the onion, rosemary and garlic, season well and cook for five or so minutes, until the onion is translucent.If you didn’t use a sun-dried tomato in your stock, add the minced one now – it’s Maria’s secret for boosting umami. Pour in the wine, let the liquid evaporate, then stir in the passata. Add a ladle of hot stock and simmer gently for anything between 20 and 40 minutes, depending on your cut of pork: you want the stew to have cooked properly before making a risotto with it. Indeed, you can make it the day before to improve its flavour; just reheat first.When the stew is ready and bubbling and the stock is keeping hot in another pot next door, add the rice to the stew, stirring to coat it in the sauce. Add more hot stock a ladleful at a time, stirring frequently until absorbed. Tasteand add salt if necessary. When the rice is about halfway cooked, stir in the grated lemon zest and julienned peel.Dissolve the saffron in a little hot stock, then stir it through the rice. Keep cooking, stirring and adding stock as needed, until the rice is tender but still has some bite; the finished dish should be more like a pilaf than a creamy northern Italian risotto, and the whole process will take about 20 minutes.To finish, stir through the grated pecorino and serve with extra cheese at the table.Rita’sfrascarelli con sugo di finocchietto e salsiccia(rice “polenta” with wild fennel and sausage sauce)View image in fullscreenPasta Grannies’ rice polenta with fennel and sausage sauce.Rita, Adriana and Brunhilde are the bustling heart of my home town, Cingoli inLe Marche,where they organise asagra, or food festival, at which they serve this rice “polenta” that has sustained families in the region for centuries. Frascarelli was traditionally served plain to invalids and new mothers, because it was considered nourishing and easy to digest, but when dressed with a spicy, robust sauce, it becomes a hearty meal for the whole family. It was originally served on a communal polenta board, because in the old days people didn’t have individual crockery, andour Instagram post of the three friends demonstrating thiswent viral (some viewers were horrified); of course, these days, everyone uses plates or bowls.Prep10 minCook45 minServes6For the sauce1 bunchwild fennel fronds, or 1 tsp freshly ground fennel seedsExtra-virgin olive oil½ tspdried chilli flakes, or to taste1 splash white wine3 large, meaty Italian sausages1 garlic clove, peeled and crushed (optional; see method)400ml passata1tspcastersugarSalt, to tasteFor the frascarelli400garborio rice50gplainflour1 generous pinchsaltBegin by making the sauce. Pick through the fennel fronds for the tenderest pieces and wash thoroughly; otherwise, use freshly ground fennel seeds, or substitute with chervil or parsley. Heat a generous amount of oil in a large pan on a medium heat. Add the fennel, chilli flakes and white wine, and cook gently for a few minutes, to release the aromatics. (Adriana says the older the herb, the longer it will need to simmer, and that you should cook it for at least 10 minutes.)Skin the sausages, crumble the meat into the pan and cook, stirring frequently, until it begins to brown and release its fat (if your sausages aren’t Italian, add the crushed garlic clove at this point and fry for an extra minute). Add the passata, rinse out the jar with a little water to capture every drop, and add that, too. Stir in the sugar to balance the acidity of the tomatoes, then simmer gently for at least 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Check the seasoning and keep warm.For the frascarelli, bring two litres of water to a gentle simmer in a large, heavy-based saucepan. Add the rice, stir well and season with a good pinch of salt. Keep the heat moderate, to prevent the rice boiling over – Rita is vigilant about this – and cook, stirring regularly to prevent the rice sticking to the bottom of the pan. After about 10 minutes, when the rice is nearly tender, the mix will still be liquid. Gradually whisk in the flour to thicken it to a soft, polenta-like consistency; the texture should be creamy but not too thick.Spoon the frascarelli into warmed bowls, top generously with the fennel and sausage sauce and serve immediately.These recipes are edited extracts from Pasta Grannies: Eat Everything – Pasta and Beyond for the Good Life, by Vicky Bennison, published by Rizzoli at £29.95. To order a copy for £26.95, go toguardianbookshop.comThis article was amended on 28 September 2026. The headline of an earlier version said these were both Sardinian recipes, but the second one hails from the Marche.Explore more on these topicsFoodRiceItalian food and drinkMain coursePorkMeatVegetablesrecipesShareReuse this content
